Unlimited PTO.title: What Is Unlimited PTO? How It Works and What to Ask
sections: What unlimited PTO means

Unlimited PTO is a paid time off policy with no set number of vacation days. Instead of earning hours each pay period, you ask for time off when you need it, and your manager approves it if your work is covered.

“Unlimited” does not mean you can take as much as you want. Approval, workload, team coverage and performance expectations still limit how much time you actually get. Some companies call it flexible PTO, open PTO or discretionary time off.
No federal law in the US requires employers to give paid vacation, so the policy is the employer’s choice. It is more common in salaried office and tech jobs than in hourly roles.
How it works in practice

You usually submit a request in an HR tool or tell your manager ahead of time. Many policies ask for more notice for longer trips and may block time off during busy periods, such as a product launch or the end of a quarter.

Paid holidays, parental leave and sick leave are often handled separately. Some states and cities require paid sick leave, and an employer may use its unlimited PTO policy to meet that rule if the policy meets the law’s terms.
Unpaid leave protected by law, such as leave under the Family and Medical Leave Act (FMLA) for eligible workers, still applies. Unlimited PTO does not replace those rights.
Benefits and drawbacks
The upside is flexibility. You do not have to save up days, wait to accrue time as a new hire or lose days at the end of the year.

The downside is that nothing accrues, so there is usually no balance to pay out when you leave. Some states require payout of earned, unused vacation under a traditional policy, but how they treat unlimited plans can differ, so check with your state labor department if this matters to you.

Without a set number, some people take less time off than they would under a fixed policy, because they are unsure what is normal or worry about how it looks. Team culture and your manager’s habits shape the real policy.
What to ask before you accept a job
Ask how many days people on the team typically took last year, whether there is a minimum the company encourages and whether managers take real vacations themselves.

Ask whether holidays, sick days and parental leave are separate, how much notice is expected and whether there are blackout periods. If you are comparing offers, remember that a fixed policy with a payout may be worth more when you leave.
qa: Is unlimited PTO really unlimited?

No. You can request as much time as you want, but each request needs approval, and your manager weighs workload, coverage and performance. In practice there is an unwritten limit set by team culture and expectations.
Do you get paid for unused unlimited PTO when you quit?

Usually not. Because unlimited PTO does not build up a balance, there is normally nothing to pay out. State payout laws apply to earned vacation, and rules differ by state, so ask your state labor department if you think you are owed money.
Is unlimited PTO better than a fixed number of days?

It depends on the employer. Unlimited PTO can mean more flexibility and no waiting to accrue days. A fixed policy gives you a clear number and often a payout when you leave. Ask how much time people on the team actually take before deciding.
Can my employer deny unlimited PTO requests?

Yes. Under most unlimited PTO policies, time off still needs approval, and an employer can say no for business reasons such as staffing or deadlines. It cannot deny leave in a way that breaks laws on protected leave, discrimination or required paid sick time.
How many days do people usually take with unlimited PTO?

There is no standard number. It varies by company, team and manager. The best way to find out is to ask the hiring manager or future teammates how many days they took last year and whether taking a full week off is normal.

Shortlist.title: What Is a Shortlist? What Being Shortlisted for a Job Means
sections: What a shortlist is in hiring

A shortlist is the small group of candidates an employer picks to move forward after a first review of all the applications. Being shortlisted usually means you have been chosen for an interview or another next step, such as a phone screen or a skills test.

The word is used in the US, the UK and elsewhere. American recruiters may also say a candidate “made the cut” or “advanced to the next round.” As a verb, to shortlist someone means to put them on that list.
Some employers build a longlist first. That is a larger group that meets the basic requirements, which is then narrowed down to the shortlist.
How employers build a shortlist

A recruiter or hiring manager reviews applications, often inside an applicant tracking system. They check must-have requirements first, such as work authorization, location, a required license or a certain number of years of experience.
Next they look for the strongest matches on skills, job titles and results. Many reviewers spend only a short time on each resume at this stage, so the top of the page carries the most weight.
Screening questions, a short phone call or a work sample can also decide who makes the list. The size of a shortlist varies by employer, role and the number of applicants.
How to get on the shortlist
Make the first lines of your resume match the posting. A summary that names the job title and two or three must-have skills you really have helps a busy reviewer see the fit quickly.
Use the same words the posting uses for skills, tools and titles where they are true for you. Put measurable results under each job, such as money saved, time cut or customers served.
Answer every screening question accurately and completely. A wrong answer to a knock-out question can remove you before anyone reads your resume.
Apply early when you can. Some employers start reviewing and shortlisting while the posting is still open, and a few close it once they have enough strong candidates.
What happens after you are shortlisted
You will usually get an email or call inviting you to an interview or assessment. Reply promptly, confirm the time and time zone, and ask who you will meet and what format to expect.
Being shortlisted is not a job offer. Prepare as you would for any interview by researching the employer, rereading the posting and preparing examples that show the skills it asks for.
qa: What does it mean to be shortlisted for a job?

It means the employer reviewed the applications and picked you as one of a small group to move to the next stage. That next stage is usually an interview, but it can also be a phone screen, a test or a work sample.
Does being shortlisted mean I got the job?

No. It means you passed the first review and are now competing with the other shortlisted candidates. The employer will compare everyone through interviews or assessments before making an offer, and it may also decide not to hire anyone.
How many people are usually on a shortlist?

There is no fixed number. It depends on the employer, the role, how many people applied and how many interview rounds are planned. Many employers keep it small enough that the hiring team can interview everyone on it.
What is the difference between a shortlist and a longlist?

A longlist is a wider group of applicants who meet the basic requirements. A shortlist is the smaller group chosen from the longlist, or straight from all applicants, to be interviewed. Not every employer uses a longlist.
How long does it take to hear back after being shortlisted?

It varies widely by employer and by how many rounds of interviews there are. If you were not given a timeline, ask the recruiter when you can expect an update, and follow up politely if that date passes with no news.

Employee handbook.title: What Is an Employee Handbook? What It Covers and Why It Matters
sections: What an employee handbook is

An employee handbook is a document, often a PDF or a page on the company intranet, that explains how the company works and what it expects from staff. It is sometimes called a staff handbook, employee manual or policy manual.

It usually covers working hours, pay days, overtime, paid time off, sick leave, holidays, remote work, expenses, dress code, conduct, use of company equipment, anti-harassment rules and how to raise a complaint.
Most employers hand it out on the first day or during onboarding and ask you to sign a form saying you received and read it. Many update it every year or two.
Is an employee handbook a contract

In the US, most handbooks say clearly that they are not a contract and that employment is at-will, meaning either side can end the job at any time for any legal reason. Courts usually respect that wording.

Rules differ by state. In some states, courts have found that promises in a handbook, such as a fixed discipline process, created an implied contract when there was no clear disclaimer. If a dispute turns on handbook wording, ask an employment lawyer.

Federal law does not require private employers to have a handbook. Some laws affect what goes in one: an employer covered by the Family and Medical Leave Act that has a handbook must describe FMLA leave in it, and states such as New York and California require written anti-harassment policies.
Why it matters to you

The handbook often decides things your offer letter leaves out, such as how much paid time off you earn, whether unused vacation carries over, and whether it is paid out when you leave. Some states, such as California, require payout of earned vacation; in many others, the written policy decides.
It also sets the steps for discipline, the notice the company asks you to give when you resign, rules on side jobs, and the process for reporting harassment or pay problems.

For most private-sector workers who are not supervisors, federal labor law protects the right to discuss pay and working conditions with coworkers. A handbook rule that seems to ban this may not be enforceable, and the National Labor Relations Board handles such complaints.
What to do with your handbook
If your offer letter refers to the handbook, ask for a copy before you accept. Read the sections on leave, remote work, notice, non-compete or outside work, and expenses.
Keep your own copy of the version you signed, and save later updates. Rules can change, and you may need to show what applied at a certain date.
If a section is unclear or seems to conflict with your offer letter, ask HR in writing and keep the reply. For questions about whether a policy is legal, contact your state labor department.
qa: Do I have to sign the employee handbook?

Employers usually ask you to sign an acknowledgment that you received and read it, and refusing can cause problems with your hire. Signing normally confirms receipt, not that you agree to every rule. Read it first and ask HR about anything unclear before you sign.
Is an employee handbook legally binding?

Usually not as a contract in the US, because most handbooks include an at-will disclaimer. You can still be disciplined for breaking its rules. In some states, clear promises without a disclaimer have been treated as an implied contract, so the answer depends on the wording and the state.
Can an employer change the handbook without telling employees?

Employers can generally update handbook policies, and most handbooks say so. Good practice, and sometimes state law, means telling staff about changes, especially those affecting pay or leave. Changes usually cannot take away pay or leave you have already earned.
Is an employee handbook required by law?

No federal law requires a private employer to have one. But if a covered employer has a handbook, it must include FMLA information, and some states require certain written policies, such as anti-harassment policies, which many employers place in the handbook.
What is the difference between an employee handbook and an employment contract?

An employment contract is an agreement with you personally, setting terms such as pay, length of employment or notice. A handbook sets general rules for all staff and usually says it is not a contract. Where the two conflict, the signed contract normally controls.

Hourly rate.title: What Is an Hourly Rate? How Hourly Pay Works and Compares
sections: What an hourly rate means
An hourly rate is the amount you are paid for each hour you work. If your rate is $18 and you work 30 hours in a week, you earn $540 before taxes and deductions.
Hourly pay is common in retail, food service, warehouses, health care support, trades and part-time or shift work. Contractors and freelancers also often bill clients by the hour.
The key difference from a salary is that your pay goes up and down with your hours. More hours mean more pay, and fewer shifts mean a smaller paycheck.
Hourly pay, overtime and the law

Under the federal Fair Labor Standards Act, most hourly employees are non-exempt. That means they must get overtime pay of at least one and a half times their regular rate for hours over 40 in a workweek.
Some states add more rules. California, for example, also requires overtime after 8 hours in a workday in most cases. Check your state labor department for the rules where you work.
Your hourly rate cannot be below the federal minimum wage or your state or city minimum, whichever is highest. Tipped workers may be paid a lower cash wage in some states, but not in all of them.

Independent contractors paid by the hour are not employees, so overtime and minimum wage laws usually do not apply. They also pay both the employee and employer shares of Social Security and Medicare tax as self-employment tax.
How to compare an hourly rate with a salary
A full-time year is often counted as 2,080 hours, which is 40 hours times 52 weeks. A quick estimate is to double the hourly rate and add three zeros, so $20 an hour is roughly $40,000 a year.
That estimate only holds if you really get 40 hours every week. Multiply by the hours the employer schedules in practice, and ask whether hours are guaranteed or change week to week.

Also count what the rate does not show: paid time off, paid holidays, health insurance, retirement contributions and shift differentials. An hourly job with no benefits may be worth less than a lower salary with good benefits.
Freelancers should set a higher rate than an employee doing similar work, because they pay their own taxes, benefits and equipment and are not paid for time spent finding clients.
qa: How do I convert an hourly rate to a yearly salary?

Multiply the hourly rate by the hours you work each week, then by 52. For a full-time job at 40 hours a week, that is the rate times 2,080. Add expected overtime separately, and subtract any unpaid weeks off.
Do hourly employees get paid overtime?

Most do. Federal law requires at least one and a half times the regular rate for hours over 40 in a workweek for non-exempt employees, and most hourly employees are non-exempt. Some states also require daily overtime. Independent contractors are not covered.
Do hourly workers get paid holidays?

Federal law does not require paid holidays or vacation for private-sector workers, hourly or salaried. Many employers offer them anyway, and some offer extra pay for working on holidays. Some states and cities require paid sick leave. Ask the employer what its policy is before you accept.
Is an hourly rate better than a salary?

It depends on the job. Hourly pay usually means you are paid for every hour, including overtime, which helps if you work long weeks. A salary gives a steady paycheck even when work is slow and is more often paired with benefits. Compare total yearly pay and benefits, not just the headline number.
How do freelancers set an hourly rate?

Start with the yearly income you need, add the cost of taxes, health insurance, retirement savings and equipment, then divide by the hours you can realistically bill, not all hours you work. Check what others with similar skills charge in your field and area.

Non-disclosure agreement (NDA).title: What Is an NDA (Non-Disclosure Agreement)? What You Agree To
sections: What a non-disclosure agreement is

A non-disclosure agreement, or NDA, is a contract in which you promise not to share or misuse information the employer treats as confidential. It is also called a confidentiality agreement, and it may be a separate form or part of an offer letter or employment contract.

Confidential information usually includes customer lists, prices, product plans, source code, financial results, internal processes and trade secrets. Most NDAs exclude information that is already public, that you knew before, or that you learn from someone else who had no duty to keep it secret.
Most employment NDAs are one-way, so only you promise secrecy. Mutual NDAs, where both sides make the same promise, are more common between businesses, contractors and partners.
When employers ask you to sign one

Many employers ask new hires to sign an NDA on the first day, along with tax and payroll forms. Some ask candidates to sign before a late-stage interview, an office visit or a take-home task that shows internal information.

Contractors and freelancers often sign one before they see a client’s systems or data. Employers may also add confidentiality terms to a severance agreement when you leave, sometimes in exchange for extra pay.
The duty usually lasts while you work there and for a set period afterward, often a number of years. Trade secrets are often protected for as long as they stay secret.
What an NDA cannot stop you from doing

Under the federal Defend Trade Secrets Act, you are immune from trade secret liability when you share a secret in confidence with a government official or a lawyer only to report or investigate a suspected violation of law, or in a court filing made under seal.

An NDA cannot stop you from filing a charge with, or taking part in an investigation by, agencies such as the EEOC, the NLRB, OSHA or the SEC. Most non-supervisory private-sector employees also have a right under the National Labor Relations Act to discuss pay and working conditions.

The federal Speak Out Act makes NDAs signed before a dispute arises unenforceable for later claims of sexual assault or sexual harassment. Several states, including California, New York and Washington, go further and limit NDAs about discrimination, harassment or other unlawful conduct.
What to check before you sign

Read how the agreement defines confidential information and how long the duty lasts. A very broad definition, such as everything you learn on the job, is hard to follow; your general skills and know-how usually stay yours, but the wording matters.

Check whether the document also includes an invention assignment clause, a non-compete or a non-solicitation clause. These are separate promises with their own rules, and they can affect your next job more than the secrecy terms do.

If the form lets you, list prior inventions, side projects or open-source work you want to keep. Keep a copy of what you sign, and talk to an employment lawyer before signing anything you do not understand.
When you leave, return or delete company files and do not take documents, customer contacts or code with you, even to a personal email account.
qa: Can I refuse to sign an NDA for a job?

You can, but because most US jobs are at will, the employer can usually withdraw the offer if you refuse. You can instead ask to narrow terms that seem too broad, such as the definition of confidential information or how long the duty lasts. Some employers accept reasonable edits.
What happens if you break an NDA?

The employer can sue for money damages, ask a court to order you to stop sharing the information, and may fire you if you still work there. If the information is a trade secret, federal and state trade secret laws can also apply. The outcome depends on the contract and the facts, so talk to a lawyer.
Is an NDA the same as a non-compete?

No. An NDA limits what information you share or use. A non-compete limits where you can work after you leave, such as for a competitor in a certain area for a certain time. Non-competes are banned or restricted in some states, including California, while reasonable NDAs are generally enforceable across the US.
Can an NDA stop me from talking about my salary?

For most non-supervisory private-sector employees, no. The National Labor Relations Act protects discussing your pay with coworkers, and many states have their own pay transparency or pay discussion laws. Supervisors and some other workers are not covered by the federal law, so check your state’s rules with the state labor department.
Can I tell a new employer about my old job if I signed an NDA?

Yes, you can describe your role, skills and results in general terms. What you cannot do is reveal protected details such as customer names, unreleased plans, prices or code. If an interviewer asks for that kind of detail, say politely that it is confidential.

Perk.title: What Is a Job Perk? Perks vs Benefits and How to Weigh Them
sections: What a perk means in a job

A perk is something an employer offers on top of your pay. It is meant to make the job more attractive or easier to do. The word is short for “perquisite,” an old word for an extra that comes with a position.

Common perks include remote or hybrid work, flexible hours, a learning budget for courses or conferences, a home office stipend, free meals or snacks, gym or wellness allowances, commuter help, extra paid days off and visa sponsorship.
Perks vary a lot between employers and even between roles at the same company. A posting may list a few, many or none, and the list is not always complete.
Perks vs benefits

People often use the two words as if they mean the same thing, but there is a usual difference. Benefits are the core package most full-time workers expect, such as health insurance, a retirement plan, paid time off and life or disability insurance.
Perks are the extras beyond that core. Some benefits are required by law in certain places, such as paid sick leave in some states and cities, while perks are almost always optional for the employer.
Because there is no legal definition of “perk,” one company may call something a benefit that another calls a perk. What matters is what you actually get, not the label.
Are perks taxed
Many perks count as taxable income in the US. Cash stipends, such as a monthly wellness or phone allowance, are usually taxed like wages and show up on your W-2.

Some perks are tax-free under IRS rules. Examples include small items of low value, tools you need for the job, and employer help with tuition or commuting costs up to a yearly or monthly limit set by the IRS.
State tax rules can differ from federal rules. If a perk is large, such as housing or relocation money, ask the employer how it is reported, and talk to an accountant about your own situation.
How to weigh perks when comparing offers
Start with base pay, bonus, equity and core benefits, since these usually make up most of what a job is worth. Then look at perks as a way to break a tie between offers that are close.
Put a rough dollar value on each perk you would really use. A commuter benefit is worth nothing if you work from home, and a gym allowance only helps if you go to the gym.
Some perks matter more than money for certain people. Visa sponsorship can decide whether you can take the job at all, and remote work can save hours of commuting each week.
Ask for details in writing before you accept. Find out the amount, who qualifies, when it starts and whether the company can change or end it.
qa: What is the difference between a perk and a benefit?

Benefits are the standard parts of a compensation package, such as health insurance, a retirement plan and paid time off. Perks are extras on top of that, such as free meals, a learning budget or a home office stipend. The line is not fixed by law, so employers use the words loosely.
What are examples of job perks?

Common job perks include remote or hybrid work, flexible hours, a budget for courses or conferences, a home office or phone stipend, free meals, wellness or gym allowances, commuter help, extra days off, employee discounts and visa sponsorship for workers who need it.
Can you negotiate perks?

Often yes. When an employer cannot raise base pay, it may agree to a signing bonus, more remote days, a larger learning budget, relocation help or an earlier review. Ask politely, explain why it matters to you and get any agreed change in writing.
Are job perks taxable?

Many are. Cash allowances are usually taxed like wages. Some perks are tax-free under IRS rules, such as low-value items, tools needed for the job and some tuition or commuting help up to limits the IRS sets. Check your pay stub or W-2, and ask an accountant about large perks.
Should I take a lower salary for better perks?

Usually not. Salary affects future raises, retirement savings and your next offer, while perks can be changed or removed. Take perks into account only for what they are really worth to you, and treat them as a tie-breaker between similar offers.

Home office stipend.title: What Is a Home Office Stipend? How It Works and How It’s Taxed
sections: What a home office stipend is
A home office stipend is money an employer gives remote or hybrid workers to set up and run a workspace at home. It often pays for a desk, a chair, a monitor, a headset or part of the internet bill.

Some employers pay it once when you start, often called a setup or onboarding stipend. Others pay a smaller amount every month or every year to cover ongoing costs such as internet, phone or supplies.
It is a benefit, not a legal right everywhere. Whether you get one, and how much, depends on the employer’s policy and, in some states, on expense reimbursement laws.
Stipend, reimbursement or company equipment
A true stipend is a fixed amount paid with your wages, and you usually do not have to show receipts. You can spend it as you see fit within the employer’s rules.
A reimbursement works differently. You buy approved items, send receipts and get paid back for what you spent, often up to a set limit.
Some employers skip the money and ship equipment directly, such as a laptop, monitor or chair. That equipment usually stays company property and may have to be returned when you leave.
How a home office stipend is taxed

Under federal rules, a flat stipend paid without receipts is generally treated as taxable wages. It is subject to income tax and Social Security and Medicare taxes, so you take home less than the stated amount.
Payments made under what the IRS calls an accountable plan are usually not taxable. Such a plan requires a business purpose, proof of the expense such as receipts, and return of any unspent money.
W-2 employees generally cannot deduct unreimbursed work expenses on their federal return. Some states treat this differently, so ask an accountant if you are unsure how your own payments are handled.
What to ask before you accept
Ask how much the stipend is, whether it is paid once or every year, and whether it comes as a flat payment or a reimbursement with receipts.
Ask whether the items you buy stay yours if you leave, or whether you must return them or repay part of the money if you quit within a set time.
Check the list of allowed items and keep your receipts either way. If your state requires employers to cover necessary work expenses, your state labor department can explain what applies to you.
qa: Is a home office stipend taxable?

Usually yes, if it is a flat amount paid without receipts. It is then treated as wages and taxed like your salary. Reimbursements paid under an accountable plan, where you prove the expense and return unused money, are generally not taxable. Check your pay stub to see how your employer reports it.
How much is a typical home office stipend?

There is no standard amount. It depends on the employer, the role and whether the payment is a one-time setup amount or a recurring monthly or yearly allowance. Compare it with what you would actually need to spend on furniture, equipment and internet.
Do employers have to pay for my home office?

Not under federal law in most cases. Some states, including California and Illinois, require employers to reimburse necessary business expenses, which can include part of the costs of working from home. Rules and details differ by state, so ask your state labor department or an employment lawyer about your situation.
Do I have to return equipment bought with a stipend?

It depends on the policy. Items you bought with a flat stipend are often yours to keep, while equipment the company bought or shipped usually stays company property. Some employers ask you to repay the stipend if you leave early, so get the rule in writing.
Can I negotiate a home office stipend?
Often yes, especially for remote roles. Ask during the offer stage, explain what you need to work well, and ask for the amount, timing and return rules to be written into the offer letter.

Burnout.title: What Is Burnout? Signs, Causes and What to Do About It at Work
sections: What burnout means
Burnout is a state of long-lasting exhaustion caused by work stress that has gone on too long without relief. It builds over months, not days, and a weekend off usually does not fix it.

The World Health Organization lists burnout in its disease classification (ICD-11) as an occupational phenomenon, not as a medical condition. It describes three signs: feeling drained of energy, growing distance or cynicism toward the job, and feeling less effective at work.
Burnout is about the job, not about personal weakness. It tends to come from how the work is set up, such as too much work, too little control or long hours, rather than from a lack of toughness.
Common signs and causes

Typical signs include constant tiredness, dreading the start of the workweek, irritability, trouble concentrating, poor sleep and caring less about work you used to like. Some people also notice headaches, stomach problems or getting sick more often.

Common causes include a workload that stays too heavy, unclear expectations, little say over how you work, being always reachable, unfair treatment, lack of support from a manager and work that clashes with your values.
Burnout can look like depression or anxiety, and the two can overlap. Only a doctor or mental health professional can tell them apart, which matters because the right help may differ.
What to do if you feel burned out
See a doctor or mental health professional about your symptoms. They can check for other conditions and suggest treatment, rest or time off work.

Talk to your manager about specific changes: which tasks can be dropped or moved, realistic deadlines, fewer after-hours messages or a change in schedule. Bring examples rather than general complaints, so the conversation stays practical.

If you need time off, ask HR what leave you have. The federal Family and Medical Leave Act gives eligible employees up to 12 weeks of unpaid, job-protected leave for a serious health condition, and some states add paid leave or disability programs. Whether you qualify depends on your employer, your hours and your diagnosis.
If you have thoughts of harming yourself, call or text 988, the Suicide and Crisis Lifeline in the US, at any time.
Using a job search to avoid burnout next time
If nothing changes at work, a new job may be the answer. Compare offers on hours, workload, on-call duties and flexibility, not only on pay.

In interviews, ask what a normal week looks like, how many people are on the team, how often people work evenings or weekends and why the role is open. Answers about frequent turnover or constant urgency are worth noting.
When asked why you are leaving, you do not need to mention burnout. A short, positive answer about wanting a better fit or a sustainable pace is enough.
qa: Is burnout a medical diagnosis?

Not on its own. The World Health Organization describes burnout as an occupational phenomenon linked to chronic work stress, not a medical condition. A doctor may still diagnose related conditions, such as depression, anxiety or a sleep disorder, and treat those.
Can I take time off work for burnout?

Possibly. Under the federal Family and Medical Leave Act, eligible employees can take up to 12 weeks of unpaid, job-protected leave for a serious health condition certified by a doctor. Some states offer paid medical leave or disability benefits. Ask HR about your options and check with your state labor department or a lawyer if you are unsure.
How long does it take to recover from burnout?

There is no fixed timeline. Recovery depends on how severe it is and whether the causes at work change. Some people feel better within weeks of real rest and a lighter workload, while others need months and professional help.
What is the difference between stress and burnout?

Stress usually feels like too much: too many demands and a sense of urgency, often with hope that things will improve. Burnout feels like not enough: exhaustion, detachment and a sense that effort no longer makes a difference. Long-term stress without relief can lead to burnout.
Should I tell my employer I am burned out?

You do not have to share health details, but describing the problem in work terms, such as too much workload or too many hours, can lead to practical changes. If you need leave or accommodations, HR may ask for a doctor’s note.

Job description.title: What Is a Job Description? What It Includes and How to Read It
sections: What a job description is

A job description is the written account of a job. It covers what the person does, what skills and experience the employer wants, and what the job offers in pay, benefits and working conditions. On job boards it usually makes up most of the posting.
Employers also keep internal job descriptions for HR purposes. These set out the duties and level of a role, help place it in a pay grade and guide performance reviews. Some are never published.

People often use job description and job posting to mean the same thing. Strictly, a posting is the advertisement for an open position, while the description is the text about the role itself. A posting usually contains a description plus instructions on how to apply.
What a job description usually includes

Most include a job title, the location or remote status, a short summary of the role, a list of duties or responsibilities, required qualifications, preferred qualifications, and details about pay, benefits and the company.

Required qualifications are what the employer says a candidate must have, such as a license, a degree or a set number of years of experience. Preferred or nice-to-have qualifications are extras, and many people are hired without all of them.

Several US states and cities have pay transparency laws that require many employers to show a pay range in job postings. Colorado, California, Washington and New York are among them. Who is covered differs by place, so a posting without a range is still legal in many areas.

Under the Americans with Disabilities Act, a written job description prepared before a job is advertised can be used as evidence of the job’s essential functions. This matters when a worker or applicant asks for a reasonable accommodation.
How to use a job description in your search
Read it once for the work itself. Ask whether the duties match what you want to do and can do. Then read it again for the exact words the employer uses for skills, tools and job titles.

Reuse those words in your resume and cover letter where they are true for you. Recruiters and applicant tracking systems often search for them, and matching language shows that you read the posting carefully.

Use it to prepare for interviews. Each main duty is a likely topic, so have a short example ready for each one. Note anything unclear, such as who you would report to or how much travel is involved, and ask about it.
Save a copy when you apply. Postings are often taken down, and you will want the text when a recruiter calls or when you compare an offer with what was advertised.
qa: What is the difference between a job description and a job specification?

A job description explains the job: its duties, purpose and working conditions. A job specification, called a person specification in the UK, describes the ideal candidate: skills, qualifications, experience and personal qualities. In most US postings the two are combined into one text, with the specification appearing as the requirements or qualifications list.
Should I apply if I don’t meet every requirement in a job description?

Often yes. Requirement lists frequently describe an ideal candidate, and preferred qualifications are not strict cut-offs. If you meet the true must-haves, such as a required license or work authorization, and most of the other points, applying is reasonable. Explain in your resume or cover letter how your experience covers the gaps.
Can an employer ask me to do tasks not in my job description?

Usually yes. Most US jobs are at-will, a job description is generally not a contract, and many end with a phrase such as “other duties as assigned.” Limits come from the law, for example on safety or discrimination, and from any union or individual employment contract. If you think a change breaks the law, ask your state labor department or a lawyer.
What does JD mean in a job posting?

JD is a common short form of job description, used by recruiters and hiring managers, as in “please see the attached JD.” In legal job postings, JD can also mean Juris Doctor, the US law degree, so read the context to tell which one is meant.

Fair chance hiring.title: What Is Fair Chance Hiring? Ban the Box Laws and Your Rights
sections: What fair chance hiring means

Fair chance hiring is a way of hiring people that does not screen out applicants with a criminal record at the first step. The employer looks at skills and experience first and asks about conviction history later, usually after a conditional job offer.

When the record does come up, the employer is expected to judge it against the actual job. A decades-old conviction unrelated to the work should not count the same as a recent one that bears directly on the duties.

Some employers adopt fair chance hiring because a law requires it. Others choose it on their own and say so in their job postings, often with phrases such as “fair chance employer” or “we welcome applicants with records.”
The laws behind it in the US

Many fair chance rules are called “ban the box” laws, after the checkbox on application forms that asked whether you had ever been convicted of a crime. These laws remove that question from the first stage of hiring.

The rules differ a lot by place. Many states and cities have ban the box rules for public jobs, and some, such as California, New York City and Illinois, also cover many private employers. Your state or city labor department can tell you what applies where you live.

At the federal level, the Fair Chance to Compete for Jobs Act generally stops federal agencies and federal contractors from asking about criminal history before a conditional offer. It does not cover most private employers.

Separately, the EEOC, the federal agency that enforces job discrimination laws, has guidance warning that blanket bans on anyone with a record can be unlawful discrimination. It asks employers to weigh the nature of the offense, the time that has passed and the nature of the job.
How the background check step works
Fair chance hiring delays the background check; it does not remove it. Most employers still run one, usually after making a conditional offer that depends on the results.

If the employer uses a background check company, the federal Fair Credit Reporting Act applies. You must give written permission first, and if the employer plans to reject you because of the report, it must first send you a copy and a summary of your rights.

Some states and cities add more steps, such as a written explanation of why the record matters for the job and a set number of days for you to respond. Jobs where a law requires a check, such as some roles in childcare, schools, security or finance, often have exceptions.
What job seekers with a record should do

Look for fair chance language in postings and in employer pages, and check whether your state or city has a ban the box law that covers the employer. Answer only what the form lawfully asks at each stage.

Get a copy of your own record before you apply, so nothing in a report surprises you. Check whether any convictions can be sealed or expunged under your state’s law; a legal aid office or reentry program can help.
Prepare a short, honest explanation for when the record comes up. Focus on what has changed, such as training, steady work, references or completed programs, and how you fit the job.
If you think an employer broke a fair chance law or skipped the required notices, contact your state or city labor or human rights agency, or a lawyer, for advice about your situation.
qa: What is the difference between fair chance hiring and ban the box?

Ban the box usually means removing the criminal history question from job applications, often because a law requires it. Fair chance hiring is broader. It covers the whole process: delaying questions about records, judging any record against the job, and giving the applicant a chance to explain before a final decision.
Can a fair chance employer still run a background check?

Yes. Fair chance hiring changes when and how a record is considered, not whether it can be checked. Most fair chance employers run a background check after a conditional offer. If a background check company is used, federal law requires your written consent and a copy of the report before the employer rejects you because of it.
Do I have to tell an employer about my criminal record?

You generally do not have to volunteer it, but if an employer lawfully asks, answer honestly, because a false answer can cost you the offer later. Rules on sealed, expunged or juvenile records and on arrests without a conviction vary by state, so check with a legal aid office or your state labor department.
Can an employer refuse to hire me because of a conviction?

Sometimes. Many employers may still decide not to hire based on a record that relates to the job, and some jobs legally bar certain convictions. But fair chance laws in many places require the employer to consider the offense, how long ago it was and the job’s duties, and to give you a chance to respond first.
Do fair chance laws apply to every employer?

No. There is no single US law covering all employers. The federal law covers federal agencies and contractors, and state and city laws vary in which public and private employers they cover, often based on size or location. Outside the US, rules differ again by country.

LinkedIn Easy Apply.title: What Is LinkedIn Easy Apply? How It Works and When to Use It
sections: What LinkedIn Easy Apply means

LinkedIn Easy Apply is a button on some LinkedIn job postings that lets you apply without leaving LinkedIn. Instead of going to the employer’s careers page, you send your LinkedIn profile, contact details and a resume in a short form.

The employer chooses whether a posting uses Easy Apply. Other postings show an Apply button that sends you to the company’s own site or applicant tracking system, where you fill in its full application.
The form often includes screening questions the employer added, such as years of experience with a skill, work authorization or willingness to work on site. Some postings also ask for a cover letter.
How Easy Apply works for you and the employer

LinkedIn fills in your name, email and phone from your profile, lets you pick a resume you uploaded before or add a new one, and can remember answers to common questions. The whole process can take a minute or two.

The employer receives your application in LinkedIn’s hiring tools or, in some cases, in its own applicant tracking system. The recruiter usually sees your resume, your answers and a link to your full profile.

Because applying is so quick, popular Easy Apply postings can collect a very large number of applications. Recruiters then rely heavily on screening answers and quick resume scans to narrow the list, so weak or rushed applications are easy to pass over.
You can see jobs you applied to under My Jobs on LinkedIn. Status updates, such as whether the employer viewed your application, depend on what the employer does in its tools.
How to use Easy Apply well
Before you apply, update your LinkedIn profile, because it travels with the application. Make your headline, recent job titles and skills match the kind of role you want.

Upload a resume tailored to the posting rather than one generic file. Use the posting’s own words for skills and titles where they are true for you, and keep the format simple so software can read it.
Answer screening questions honestly and carefully. A wrong answer to a required question, such as work authorization or a license, can end the application before anyone reads your resume.

For jobs you really want, consider also applying on the company’s site or messaging the recruiter or hiring manager briefly. A tailored application and a personal note tend to stand out more than one of many quick clicks.
qa: Is it better to use Easy Apply or apply on the company website?

It depends on how much you want the job. Easy Apply is fast and fine for casting a wider net. For roles you care about, applying on the company site with a tailored resume and cover letter, or contacting the recruiter, usually shows more effort and can help you stand out from the many quick applications.
Do recruiters actually look at Easy Apply applications?

Yes, Easy Apply applications go to the employer like any other application. But a popular posting can receive so many that recruiters may filter by screening answers or skim quickly, so a clear, relevant resume and accurate answers matter a lot.
Can employers see my whole LinkedIn profile when I use Easy Apply?

Usually yes. The application normally includes your contact details, the resume you chose, your answers to any questions and a link to your LinkedIn profile, so keep the profile current and consistent with your resume.
Can I withdraw a LinkedIn Easy Apply application?

In many cases you can withdraw it from the list of jobs you applied to on LinkedIn. Withdrawing removes it from the employer’s view in LinkedIn’s tools, but it cannot undo anything the employer already copied into its own system.
Are Easy Apply jobs ever scams?

Most are real, but fake postings appear on every job site. Be careful if a poster asks for money, bank details or your Social Security number early, or moves you to a chat app for an instant offer. Check the company’s own website before sharing personal information.

Level.title: What Is a Job Level? Junior, Senior, Staff and Principal Explained
sections: What a job level means

A job level, also called a seniority level or career level, shows how much experience and responsibility a role carries. It tells you whether the employer wants someone just starting out, someone who works on their own, or someone who leads others and shapes how the team works.

Common labels, from least to most experienced, are intern, entry-level or junior, mid-level, senior, and then lead, staff, principal or distinguished. Management roles usually run on a separate track: manager, senior manager, director, vice president and above.
Many companies also use internal codes such as L3, L4 and L5, or IC1 to IC6, where IC means individual contributor. These codes link each title to written expectations and to a pay band.
How levels differ between companies
There is no standard definition of each level. A senior title at a small startup may match a mid-level role at a large company, and some firms give senior titles early instead of higher pay.

Years of experience are only a rough guide. As a loose pattern, entry-level roles ask for little or no experience, mid-level roles a few years, and senior roles more, but the real test is scope: how big a problem you own and how much guidance you need.

Staff and principal roles are usually senior individual contributor jobs, not management jobs. People at these levels set technical or professional direction across several teams, mentor others and often have influence similar to a manager’s without having direct reports.
Why the level matters for pay and your search

Level usually decides the pay band, the bonus target and, where offered, the size of an equity grant. Two people with the same job title can earn very different amounts if they are placed at different levels.
Some US states and cities require employers to show a pay range in job postings. Where a range is shown, it often gives a better clue to the real level than the title does.
What a job seeker should do
Read the duties and requirements, not only the title. If the posting talks about leading projects, mentoring others or setting direction, it is likely a senior role even if the title is plain.
Apply one level up or down when the duties fit you. Job postings often list more requirements than the person hired actually has, so meeting most of them can be enough to apply.

During interviews, ask which level the role is and what the next level looks like. Before you accept an offer, confirm the level in writing, because changing it after you start is usually harder than negotiating it at the offer stage.
qa: What is the difference between junior, mid-level and senior?

A junior employee is still learning the job and needs regular guidance. A mid-level employee handles most tasks independently. A senior employee owns larger problems, makes decisions with little oversight and often helps train others. The years of experience for each level vary by company and field.
Is staff higher than senior?

At companies that use the term, yes. Staff usually comes after senior on the individual contributor track, followed by principal. A staff employee typically works across several teams rather than within one. Other companies use lead or senior II for a similar step, so check the duties.
How many years of experience is entry-level?

Entry-level roles are meant for people with little or no professional experience, such as recent graduates or career changers. Some postings labeled entry-level still ask for a year or two of experience, which often includes internships, projects or related work, so it is worth applying if you are close.
Can I negotiate my job level?

Often yes, especially before you accept an offer. If your experience matches the duties of a higher level, explain that with clear examples and ask whether the employer will consider it. A higher level can raise both your pay band and your future promotions.
Does a lead role mean managing people?

Not always. In some companies a lead manages a small team, while in others a lead guides the work of a project or group without being anyone’s formal manager. The posting or the recruiter can tell you whether the role includes direct reports.

Health savings account (HSA).title: What Is an HSA? How a Health Savings Account Works
sections: What a health savings account is

A health savings account (HSA) is a personal savings account for medical costs, available in the US. You can open and pay into one only while you are covered by an HSA-eligible health plan, usually called a high-deductible health plan (HDHP).
The account belongs to you, not your employer. The money rolls over every year, and it stays yours when you change jobs, lose your job or retire.
Many employers offer an HSA alongside their high-deductible plan and some add money to it. You can also open one yourself at a bank or HSA provider if you buy a qualifying plan on your own.
How the tax benefits work
Under federal tax rules an HSA has three tax breaks. Money goes in before income tax, it grows without tax, and withdrawals for qualified medical expenses are tax-free.
When you contribute through payroll at work, the money also usually skips Social Security and Medicare taxes. If you contribute on your own, you deduct it on your federal tax return.
Most states follow the federal rules, but a few, including California and New Jersey, tax HSA contributions and earnings. Check your state’s rules or ask an accountant.

If you take money out for something that is not a qualified medical expense, you pay income tax on it plus a 20% penalty before age 65. From 65, the penalty no longer applies, but non-medical withdrawals are still taxed as income.
Who can contribute and how much

To contribute, you must be covered by an HSA-eligible plan and generally have no other health coverage that pays before the deductible. You also cannot be enrolled in Medicare or be claimed as a dependent on someone else’s tax return.
The IRS sets a yearly limit, with a higher limit for family coverage than for self-only coverage. People 55 or older can add an extra catch-up amount.
Money your employer puts in counts toward the same yearly limit. Once you stop being eligible, you can no longer add money, but you can still spend what is already in the account.
What a job seeker should do

When comparing job offers, add any employer HSA contribution to the value of the pay package. Also compare the plan’s deductible and out-of-pocket maximum, since a high-deductible plan can cost more in a year with heavy medical bills.

If you can afford it, contribute enough to cover your deductible. Many providers let you invest the balance once it passes a set amount, which can turn the account into long-term savings for health costs in retirement.
Keep receipts for medical expenses. You can reimburse yourself later for qualified costs you paid after the account was opened, even years later, as long as you can prove them.
qa: What is the difference between an HSA and an FSA?

An HSA is yours, requires an HSA-eligible high-deductible plan, rolls over every year and moves with you when you leave a job. A flexible spending account (FSA) is tied to your employer, does not need a high-deductible plan, and money left at year-end is usually lost unless the plan allows a limited carryover or grace period.
What happens to my HSA if I quit my job?

The money stays yours, including what your employer put in. You can keep the account with the same provider, possibly paying a monthly fee, or move it to another HSA provider. You can keep using it for medical costs, but you can only add new money while covered by an HSA-eligible plan.
What can I use HSA money for?

You can use it tax-free for qualified medical expenses as defined by the IRS, such as doctor visits, prescriptions, dental care, glasses and many medical supplies. It can also pay those costs for your spouse and tax dependents. IRS Publication 502 lists what counts.
Can I have an HSA if I am on Medicare?

You can keep and spend an existing HSA, but you cannot add new money once you are enrolled in any part of Medicare. Medicare Part A coverage can start up to six months back when you sign up late, so check timing with your HSA provider or an accountant before enrolling.
Is an HSA worth it?

It depends on your health costs and finances. An HSA tends to suit people who can afford the higher deductible and want tax-free savings for medical bills. If you expect large or frequent medical costs, compare the total yearly cost of the high-deductible plan with other plans on offer.

Mock interview.title: What Is a Mock Interview? How It Works and How to Prepare
sections: What a mock interview is
A mock interview is a practice run of a job interview. Someone plays the interviewer, asks the kinds of questions a real employer would ask, and then tells you what went well and what to improve.

The interviewer can be a friend, a mentor, a career coach, a college career center adviser or someone who works in the field you are targeting. Some people also practice alone with recording software or AI-based interview tools.
Nothing is at stake, so you can make mistakes, stop, and try an answer again. That is the main difference from a real interview.
Why mock interviews help

Many people know their experience well but struggle to explain it clearly under pressure. Saying answers out loud shows you where you ramble, freeze, use filler words or leave out the result of a story.
Practice also lowers nerves. Once you have answered common questions such as “Tell me about yourself” or “Why do you want this job?” a few times, the real interview feels more familiar.
Feedback from another person catches things you cannot see yourself, such as weak eye contact, a flat tone, answers that run too long or missing examples of your impact.
Types of mock interviews

A general mock interview covers common and behavioral questions, the ones that start with “Tell me about a time when.” Many people use the STAR method (situation, task, action, result) to structure these answers.
Technical mock interviews focus on skills tests, such as coding problems, case studies for consulting, or role-specific scenarios. They are usually run by someone with experience in that field.
Mock interviews can be done in person, by phone or by video. If your real interview will be on video, practice on video too, so you can check your camera, lighting, sound and background.
How to get the most out of one
Give your practice interviewer the job posting and your resume ahead of time, so the questions match the role. Ask them to act like a real interviewer and not to go easy on you.
Treat it like the real thing: dress as you would, arrive or log in on time, and do not pause to chat between questions. Save the discussion for the end.
Record the session or ask for written notes. Then practice again the questions you found hardest, and do a second mock interview if you can.
Free help is often available. College career centers usually offer mock interviews to students and often to alumni, and local American Job Centers can help job seekers prepare for interviews.
qa: What happens in a mock interview?

You answer interview questions from someone acting as the interviewer, usually for 30 to 60 minutes, in the same format as a real interview. At the end, the interviewer gives feedback on your answers, your body language and how clearly you explained your experience, and suggests what to improve.
Who can do a mock interview with me?

A friend, family member, mentor, former coworker, career coach or college career center adviser can all play the interviewer. Someone who works in your target field or has hired people before will usually give the most useful feedback, especially for technical or industry-specific questions.
How many mock interviews should I do?

There is no set number. One or two sessions before an important interview is common, with practice on your weak questions in between. Keep going until you can answer the most likely questions clearly without reading notes, but stop before your answers start to sound memorized.
Are mock interviews worth it?

For most job seekers, yes. Speaking answers out loud and getting honest feedback shows problems you cannot spot by reading your notes, such as rambling, vague examples or nervous habits. Practice also tends to make the real interview feel less stressful.
Can I do a mock interview by myself?

Yes. Write down likely questions, answer them out loud and record yourself on video, then watch it back for clarity, length and body language. AI interview practice tools can also ask questions and give feedback. A real person is still useful for honest, human reactions.

W-2 employee.title: What Is a W-2 Employee? Taxes, Benefits and W-2 vs 1099
sections: What a W-2 employee is

A W-2 employee is a worker the employer treats as a regular employee for tax purposes in the US. The name comes from Form W-2, the Wage and Tax Statement the employer sends each year showing what you earned and what was withheld.
When you start the job, you fill out Form W-4 so the employer knows how much federal income tax to take from each paycheck. Many states have their own withholding form as well.
Full-time, part-time, seasonal and temporary workers can all be W-2 employees. What matters is how the work is controlled, not the number of hours.
How taxes work for a W-2 employee
The employer withholds federal income tax, your share of Social Security and Medicare taxes, and state or local income tax where they apply. It sends that money to the government for you.
The employer also pays its own matching share of Social Security and Medicare, plus federal and state unemployment taxes. You do not pay those employer amounts.
Employers must send your W-2 by January 31 for the previous year. You use it to file your tax return, where you either get a refund or owe more depending on how much was withheld.
W-2 employee vs 1099 contractor

An independent contractor, often called a 1099 worker, gets paid without withholding. The contractor pays income tax and the full self-employment tax, which covers both halves of Social Security and Medicare, usually through quarterly estimated payments.

Employees get protections that contractors usually do not: federal minimum wage and overtime rules for non-exempt jobs, unemployment insurance, and workers’ compensation in nearly every state. Employers often add health insurance, retirement plans and paid time off, though most benefits are not required by federal law.

Classification depends on the real relationship, not the job title or contract wording. The IRS looks at behavioral control, financial control and the type of relationship, and some states, such as California, use a stricter ABC test for certain laws.
What a job seeker should check
Read the offer to see whether it says W-2 or 1099. If the pay is the same, a W-2 job usually leaves more in your pocket because the employer pays part of the payroll taxes.

If a company sets your hours, gives you tools and supervises your work but calls you a contractor, ask why. You can request a ruling from the IRS with Form SS-8 or contact your state labor department.
For questions about your own taxes or a possible misclassification claim, talk to an accountant or an employment lawyer.
qa: What is the difference between a W-2 and a 1099 employee?

A W-2 employee has taxes withheld from each paycheck, and the employer pays part of Social Security and Medicare. A 1099 worker is an independent contractor who gets paid in full and must pay income tax and self-employment tax on their own. W-2 employees also get protections such as unemployment insurance and workers’ compensation.
Is it better to be W-2 or 1099?

It depends on the pay and your situation. W-2 jobs usually offer more security, employer-paid payroll taxes and access to benefits. 1099 work can pay a higher rate and give more freedom, but you cover your own taxes, insurance and retirement savings. Compare the full value, not just the hourly rate.
Do W-2 employees get benefits?

Often, but not always. Federal law does not require most benefits, though larger employers can face penalties under the Affordable Care Act if they do not offer health coverage to full-time staff. Some states and cities require paid sick leave. Check the offer letter for what the employer actually provides.
Can a part-time worker be a W-2 employee?

Yes. Part-time, seasonal and temporary workers are W-2 employees if the employer controls how, when and where they work. The number of hours does not decide the classification, although some employer benefits may only go to full-time staff.
What should I do if I think I was misclassified as a contractor?

Keep records of your schedule, tools, supervision and pay. You can file Form SS-8 to ask the IRS for a determination and contact your state labor department about wage or unemployment issues. An employment lawyer can explain your options for your specific case.

Rolling basis.title: Rolling Basis Meaning: How Rolling Applications Work
sections: What rolling basis means
When a job posting says applications are accepted on a rolling basis, the employer reads them as they come in. It does not wait for a deadline to review everyone together.
Interviews and offers can start as soon as a strong candidate applies. The opening stays up until the employer fills it, then it closes, often without warning.
The phrase also appears in school admissions, internships, grants and fellowships. In each case it means the same thing: decisions are made continuously, not all at once after a closing date.
Rolling basis, rolling admission and rolling deadline
Rolling admission is the same idea in college and graduate school admissions: the school reviews each application once it is complete and sends a decision within a few weeks, until the class is full.

A rolling deadline usually means there is no single closing date. Schools and grant programs often add a priority deadline: applications that arrive before it get first consideration for places, scholarships or funding, and later ones are read only while places remain.

In a job posting, rolling basis often comes with the words "until the position is filled". Both mean the same thing: interviews can start before any stated deadline, and the posting can close the day someone accepts an offer.
Example sentences and what they mean
"Applications will be reviewed on a rolling basis until the position is filled." Reading has already started and there is no closing date. Apply now.
"Applications are accepted on a rolling basis; the final deadline is March 1." Applications are read as they arrive. March 1 is the last day you can apply, but the job may be filled before then.
"Interviews will be conducted on a rolling basis." The employer invites people to interview as soon as a suitable application arrives, instead of waiting for a full shortlist.
"Admission is rolling, with a priority deadline of November 15." Apply before November 15 for the best chance of a place and of any scholarship; later applications are still read while seats remain.
How rolling hiring differs from a fixed deadline
With a fixed deadline, everyone who applies before the date is usually reviewed together, so applying on the first day or the last day makes little difference.

With rolling review, timing matters. Early applicants may be interviewed while later ones are still sending documents, and if the employer finds the right person, later applications may never be read.
Some postings say rolling basis but also list a final date. That date is the latest you can apply, but the job may be filled well before it.
What job seekers should do
Apply as soon as you can after you see the posting, ideally within the first few days. A complete, tailored application sent early usually beats a polished one sent weeks later.
Keep a basic resume and cover letter ready so you can adapt them quickly. Check that every required document is attached, since a missing item can delay review.
If the posting is still up after a few weeks, you can still apply. Roles stay open for many reasons, such as a large number of openings or a slow search.
What employers should keep in mind
Rolling review lets you fill urgent or hard-to-fill roles faster and keep strong candidates from accepting other offers while they wait.
Take the posting down or mark it closed once the role is filled, so people do not spend time on applications no one will read. Telling applicants when the search has ended is also good practice.
Other meanings of rolling basis
Grants and fellowships: a rolling submission date means proposals are accepted at any time and reviewed in batches as they come in, instead of in one funding round.
Contracts and subscriptions: a rolling monthly contract renews by itself each month until one side cancels, and rolling billing charges you on the same day each period from the date you started.
Finance and reporting: a rolling 12-month figure always covers the latest twelve months and moves forward each month; a rolling budget adds a new period each time one ends.
Payments: a rolling reserve holds back part of each day's card payments for a set time and releases the oldest amounts as new ones are held.
The idea is the same everywhere: the process keeps moving forward as new items arrive, rather than happening once at a fixed point.
qa: Is it better to apply early on a rolling basis?

Yes. Because the employer reviews applications as they arrive, early applicants have a chance to be interviewed before the role is filled. Applying late does not hurt you by itself, but the spot may already be taken.
Does rolling basis mean first come, first served?

Not exactly. Applications are read in the order they arrive, but the employer or school still chooses the best fit, not simply the first person. Applying early matters because places can be filled before later applications are read.
Is rolling basis the same as rolling admission?

Yes, it is the same idea. Rolling basis is the general phrase used in job postings, internships and grants; rolling admission is the name colleges and graduate schools use for reviewing applications as they are completed.
What is a priority deadline with rolling admission?
A date before which applications get first consideration, often for scholarships, funding or housing as well as a place. You can usually apply after it, but fewer places and less money may be left.
Is there a deadline for rolling applications?
Often there is no deadline at all, and the posting closes when the employer hires someone. Some postings give a final date as well, but the role can still be filled earlier than that.
How long does it take to hear back on a rolling basis?

It varies by employer. Some reply within days of an application, others take several weeks. Rolling review means your application can be read soon after you send it, but it does not promise a quick answer.
What does rolling basis mean for internships?
It means the company reviews internship applications as they come in and makes offers until all places are filled. Popular programs can fill early, so apply as soon as applications open.
Can I still apply if a rolling posting has been up for a long time?

Yes, if the posting is still open. The employer may not have found the right person yet or may be hiring for several openings. Apply, and if you can, contact the recruiter to ask whether the role is still active.

Flextime.title: What Is Flextime? Core Hours, Rules and How to Ask for It
sections: What flextime means

Flextime is a work schedule where you choose when your day starts and ends, within limits set by the employer. You still work the same total hours, such as 8 a day or 40 a week, but not at fixed times.

Most flextime plans have core hours, a block in the middle of the day when everyone must be working or reachable, for example 10 a.m. to 3 p.m. Around that block are flexible bands, such as 7 to 10 a.m. and 3 to 7 p.m., when you decide when to come and go.
Flextime is different from a compressed workweek, where you work longer days to get a day off, and from remote work, which is about where you work, not when. A job can have any mix of the three.
How flextime works in practice
Some employers write flextime into a formal policy with set bands and rules. Others leave it to each manager, so it can change when you get a new boss or when the team gets busy.

Some plans only let you pick a fixed daily schedule, such as 7 to 3 every day. Others let you change your hours day by day, as long as you cover core hours and reach your total for the week or pay period.

Shift jobs, customer-facing roles and jobs that depend on a set opening time often cannot offer flextime. It is more common in office, professional and remote roles where work does not need someone present at a fixed time.
Flextime and the law in the US

No federal law requires private employers to offer flextime. A few places give some workers a right to ask for flexible schedules, such as San Francisco for caregivers and Vermont, but the employer can usually refuse for business reasons.

If you are paid hourly and not exempt from overtime, federal law still requires overtime pay for hours over 40 in a workweek, even under flextime. Some states, such as California, also have daily overtime rules, so moving hours between days can affect your pay.

Many federal government workers can use flexible schedules under federal rules. In the UK, where the term flexitime is common, employees have a legal right to request flexible working. Ask your state labor department or a lawyer if you are unsure what applies to you.
What to ask before you accept a job with flextime
Ask what the core hours are, how early you can start and how late you can finish, and whether you can change your hours from day to day.
Ask whether flextime is a written company policy or an informal arrangement with your manager. A written policy is harder to take away than a favor.

Ask how hours are tracked and how the team handles meetings and coverage. If you get flextime, keep your calendar updated and answer messages during core hours, so the arrangement is easy for your manager to keep.
qa: What is an example of flextime?

A company sets core hours from 10 a.m. to 3 p.m. One employee works 7 a.m. to 3:30 p.m. to pick up children after school, and another works 10 a.m. to 6:30 p.m. Both work the same total hours and are both available during the core block.
Is flextime the same as flexible working?

Not quite. Flextime is one type of flexible working that changes when you work. Flexible working is a wider term that can also cover remote work, part-time hours, job sharing and compressed workweeks.
Do hourly workers get overtime under flextime?

Yes, if they are non-exempt. Federal law requires overtime for hours over 40 in a workweek, whatever the schedule. Some states, such as California, also require overtime for long single days, so check your state’s rules with the state labor department.
Can my employer take away flextime?

Usually yes, in the US. Unless a contract, union agreement or local law says otherwise, flextime is a benefit the employer can change or end. A written company policy is more stable than an informal agreement with one manager.
How do I ask for flextime?

Put your request in writing. Say what hours you want, how you will cover core hours and meetings, and how your work will not suffer. Offering a trial period of a few weeks can make it easier for a manager to agree.

Sourcer.title: What Is a Sourcer? What They Do and How They Find Candidates
sections: What a sourcer does
A sourcer is a member of a recruiting team whose job is to find people who have not applied for a job and get them interested in it. The work happens before any application exists.

Sourcers search professional networking sites, resume databases, portfolios, code repositories, published work and the company’s own list of past applicants. When they find a good match, they send a first message to start a conversation.
Common titles include talent sourcer, sourcing specialist and sourcing recruiter. At small companies one recruiter often does both the sourcing and the rest of the hiring process.
How a sourcer works with recruiters and hiring managers
A sourcer usually meets with the recruiter and hiring manager to learn what the role needs. They then build a list of possible candidates and reach out to them.
When someone replies with interest, the sourcer may hold a short first call and then hand the candidate to a recruiter. The recruiter runs the screening, interviews and offer.

Companies lean on sourcers for hard-to-fill roles, senior positions and specialist skills. In those fields the strongest people are often already employed and not reading job ads, so they are called passive candidates.
How sourcers find people

Most sourcing starts with a keyword search filtered by job title, skills, employer, location and experience. Sourcers often use Boolean search, which combines words with AND, OR and NOT to narrow the results.

They also look at personal websites, conference talks, open-source projects, articles and professional association lists. Some tools gather public information about a person into one profile, sometimes including a likely email address.
After finding a match, the sourcer sends a short message by email or through a networking site, often followed by one or two reminders. The goal is a first call, not a job offer.
What a job seeker should do

Keep your public profile current. Use a plain, standard job title, list your real skills and tools, and show your location and whether you are open to new roles, because these are the fields sourcers search.
When a sourcer contacts you, check that the message is real. Look for a company email address, a matching profile and a real job posting on the company’s careers page.
Never pay a fee, buy equipment or share your bank details or Social Security number at first contact. A real sourcer will not ask for these.
Ask about the role, the pay range, the location or remote policy and the next steps. If you are not interested, a short polite reply keeps the door open for later.
qa: What is the difference between a sourcer and a recruiter?

A sourcer finds and contacts people who have not applied. A recruiter manages candidates through screening, interviews and the offer. Many sourcers hand interested people to a recruiter after a first conversation, while at smaller companies one person does both jobs.
Is a sourcer the same as a headhunter?

Not quite. A headhunter usually works for an outside agency and is paid by the employer when a candidate is hired. A sourcer is often in-house, working for one company, though agencies also employ sourcers. In either case the candidate should never pay a fee.
Should I reply to a sourcer if I am not looking for a job?
A short reply is a good idea. You can say you are not looking now and ask to stay in touch. It costs little, and that contact may be useful when you do want to move or when a better role opens up.
How did a sourcer find my email address?

Sourcers often use public information such as your profiles, personal website or published work. Some use tools that guess an email address from common formats or buy contact data from data providers. If you do not want to be contacted, you can ask them to remove you from their list.
What skills does a sourcer need?

Sourcers need strong search skills, including Boolean search, curiosity, enough knowledge of the field to judge a profile, and clear, friendly writing for outreach messages. Many people start their recruiting careers as sourcers, and some move on to recruiter or recruiting manager roles.

Night shift.title: What Is a Night Shift? Hours, Pay and What to Ask Before You Start
sections: What a night shift is
A night shift is a work schedule that falls mostly between evening and morning. Common examples are 11 p.m. to 7 a.m. or 7 p.m. to 7 a.m., but the exact hours depend on the employer and the industry.
In the US it is often called the third shift or the graveyard shift. The first shift is usually the day shift and the second shift runs from afternoon into late evening.

Night shifts are common wherever work cannot stop: hospitals, nursing homes, police and fire services, factories, warehouses, hotels, security, transportation and customer support for other time zones.
How night shift pay works in the US
Many employers pay extra for night work, usually called a shift differential. It may be a set amount per hour or a percentage on top of the base rate.
