Federal law does not require private employers to pay more for night work. The Fair Labor Standards Act sets minimum wage and overtime rules but treats a night hour like any other hour, so the differential comes from company policy, an offer letter or a union contract.
Federal government employees are a separate case. Many of them receive a night pay differential set by federal law for regularly scheduled work at night.

If you do get a differential and you are paid hourly, the Department of Labor generally requires it to be included in your regular rate when overtime is calculated. If you think your pay is wrong, contact your state labor department or the federal Wage and Hour Division.
Health, sleep and daily life on nights

Working at night goes against the body’s natural sleep cycle. Some people adapt well, while others struggle with poor sleep, tiredness and trouble focusing. Doctors call ongoing problems of this kind shift work disorder.
A dark, quiet bedroom, a regular sleep time even on days off, and careful timing of caffeine can help. If tiredness affects your safety, for example when driving home, talk to a doctor.
Night work also changes family and social life. Think about childcare, commuting when public transit runs less often, and how you will spend time with people who work days.
What to ask before taking a night shift job
Ask whether the extra pay is written into your offer letter or contract, how much it is, and which hours count as night hours for the differential.
Ask whether the schedule is fixed nights or rotating between days and nights, how far ahead schedules are posted, and how often they change from week to week.

Ask about breaks, overtime, weekend and holiday rates, and whether you can move to a day shift later. Under federal rules, minors aged 14 and 15 cannot work late at night, and many states add their own limits for teenagers.
qa: What hours are considered night shift?

There is no single legal definition in the US. Most employers treat shifts that run mostly between about 11 p.m. and 7 a.m. as night shifts, while some count any work after 6 p.m. or 7 p.m. Check how your employer defines night hours, especially if extra pay depends on it.
Do employers have to pay more for night shifts?

No. Federal law does not require private employers to pay extra for night work, and state laws generally do not either. Many employers still offer a shift differential to attract workers, and union contracts often include one. Federal government employees are an exception, since many receive a night pay differential set by law.
Is working night shift bad for your health?

Night work disrupts the body’s natural sleep cycle, and many people sleep less or worse as a result. Effects vary from person to person. Keeping a steady sleep schedule, sleeping in a dark room and watching caffeine can help. If you have ongoing sleep problems or exhaustion, speak to a doctor.
What is the difference between night shift and graveyard shift?

In everyday US usage they mean the same thing: a shift that covers the overnight hours, often called the third shift. Some people use graveyard shift only for the latest hours, such as midnight to 8 a.m., but employers usually treat the terms as equal.
Does shift differential count toward overtime?

For hourly workers covered by the Fair Labor Standards Act, a shift differential is generally part of the regular rate of pay. That means overtime should be calculated on base pay plus the differential, not on base pay alone. Ask your state labor department if you think your overtime is figured incorrectly.

Raise.title: What Is a Raise? Types of Pay Raises and How to Ask for One
sections: What a raise is
A raise is an increase in your pay for the job you already do. It can be a higher hourly rate or a higher yearly salary, and it usually takes effect from a set date and stays in place going forward.
A raise is different from a one-time payment such as a bonus. A bonus is paid once, while a raise changes your base pay and so affects every paycheck after it.
Many employers review pay once a year, often around performance reviews or the start of a new budget year. Others give raises when a manager asks for one or when someone threatens to leave.
Common types of raises
A merit raise rewards strong performance. Its size often depends on your review rating and the budget your manager has for the team.
A cost-of-living adjustment, or COLA, is a raise meant to help pay keep up with rising prices. Some employers, unions and public pay systems give it to everyone in a group, not based on performance.
A market adjustment brings your pay closer to what other employers pay for the same role. A step increase is a set raise built into a pay scale, common in government, schools and union jobs.
A promotion usually comes with a pay increase too, but it involves a new title or more responsibility. Strictly speaking, a raise is for the same job.
How to ask for a raise

Start by finding out what the market pays for your role, level and location. Use salary surveys, pay ranges in job postings and conversations with people in your field. Some states and cities require employers to post pay ranges, which helps.
List your results with numbers where you can, such as money saved, sales closed, projects delivered or new duties you took on. Show how your work helps the team or the business.

Ask for a meeting with your manager and give a specific figure or range. Timing matters: asking before budgets are set or soon after a clear win often works better than asking after decisions are made.
What to do if the answer is no
Ask what you would need to do to earn a raise and when pay could be reviewed again. Get the answer in writing, or send a short email afterward that sums up what was agreed.

If money is tight, you can ask for other things, such as extra paid time off, remote work days, training or a new title. If your pay stays well below the market for a long time, looking at other jobs may be the way to a higher salary.
qa: How much of a raise should I ask for?

There is no single right figure. Base your request on what the market pays for your role and location, on your results and on any new duties you have taken on. Ask for a specific number or a narrow range, and be ready to explain how you reached it.
Are employers required to give raises every year?

No. In most US jobs, raises are up to the employer. They can be required by an employment contract, a union agreement or a public pay scale, and minimum wage increases can force raises for workers paid at or near the minimum.
What is the difference between a raise and a bonus?

A raise increases your base pay for the future, so every paycheck after it goes up. A bonus is a one-time payment, often tied to performance or company results, and it does not change your regular pay.
When is the best time to ask for a raise?

Good times include a few months before your employer sets its budget, during your performance review, and soon after you deliver a clear result. Asking right after the company announces layoffs or poor results is usually harder.
Can I talk about my raise with coworkers?

For most private-sector employees who are not supervisors, the National Labor Relations Act protects the right to discuss pay with coworkers. Some states add their own protections. If you think you were punished for discussing pay, contact the National Labor Relations Board or a lawyer.

Hiring system.title: What Is a Hiring System? How Employers Manage Job Applications
sections: What a hiring system is

A hiring system is the software an employer uses to run its recruiting. It is another name for an applicant tracking system, or ATS. You may also see it called recruiting software or a hiring platform.

It publishes job openings on the company’s careers page and often sends them to job boards. It collects every application in one place and tracks each candidate from first application to offer or rejection.
Common names include Greenhouse, Lever, Ashby, Workday, iCIMS, SmartRecruiters and Taleo. Many smaller employers use the hiring tools built into their HR or payroll software instead.
What happens to your application inside one

When you apply, the system saves your details, your resume and your answers to any screening questions. It usually tries to read your resume and fill in fields such as job titles, employers, dates and skills.
Recruiters then search, filter and sort applicants. They may filter on screening answers, such as work authorization, location or a required license, and search for keywords that match the job.

The system also moves you through stages such as screen, interview and offer. It schedules interviews, stores interviewer feedback and sends the automatic emails you receive, including confirmations and rejections.
Because the job is posted from the hiring system, a listing that comes straight from it shows whether the opening is still live. When the employer closes the job, it disappears from the careers page.
How to apply well through a hiring system
Use a simple resume layout: one column, standard headings and a common font. Save it as a .docx file or a text-based PDF, not a scan or an image, so the software can read it.
Use the posting’s own words for skills and job titles where they are true for you. Spell out an acronym once, such as “customer relationship management (CRM)”.
Answer every screening question carefully and honestly. A wrong answer to a required question can end the application before a person reads your resume.
Apply on the employer’s own careers page when you can, and keep a note of the jobs you applied to. Many systems let you create an account to check your application status later.
qa: Is a hiring system the same as an ATS?

Yes. A hiring system and an applicant tracking system (ATS) mean the same thing: software that posts jobs, collects applications and tracks candidates through the hiring process. Some vendors use other names, such as recruiting software or talent acquisition platform, but the basic job is the same.
Does a hiring system reject applicants automatically?

Usually not on its own judgment. Automatic rejections mostly come from screening questions the employer set as requirements, such as work authorization or a license. Otherwise, recruiters decide, often after searching or filtering applicants inside the system.
How can I tell which hiring system an employer uses?

Look at the web address of the application page. Addresses containing greenhouse.io, lever.co, ashbyhq.com, myworkdayjobs.com or icims.com show which system handles the application. The confirmation email often names it too.
Why do I have to create an account to apply for some jobs?

Some hiring systems, especially those used by large employers, require an account for each company. It stores your profile and lets you check your application status. Use a password manager, because each employer’s site often needs its own login.
Can I update my application after I submit it?

It depends on the system and the employer’s settings. Some let you edit your profile or upload a new resume while the job is open; others lock the application once submitted. If you need to fix something important, contact the recruiter directly.

Hiring manager.title: What Is a Hiring Manager? Their Role and How They Differ From Recruiters
sections: What a hiring manager is

A hiring manager is the person who needs a new employee on their team and who usually becomes that employee’s boss. They own the opening, define what the job requires and make or strongly shape the final hiring decision.

The title is a role in the hiring process, not a job title on an org chart. Depending on the company, the hiring manager might be a team lead, a department head, a store manager or, at a small business, the owner.
Hiring manager vs. recruiter

A recruiter runs the process: posting the job, screening applications, scheduling interviews and handling offers. The recruiter may work in-house in human resources or for an outside agency. The hiring manager decides who fits the work and the team.

Recruiters often screen against a list of requirements the hiring manager gave them, so their questions tend to be about experience, salary expectations and availability. Hiring managers ask deeper questions about how you do the work, solve problems and work with others.
At small companies there may be no recruiter at all, and the hiring manager handles every step themselves.
What the hiring manager does during hiring

Before the job is posted, the hiring manager usually writes or approves the job description and decides which skills are must-haves. They often review the shortlist the recruiter sends and pick who to interview.

They typically lead one or more interview rounds, gather feedback from other interviewers and recommend or choose the final candidate. Pay and the offer may still need approval from HR, finance or a more senior manager.
How to approach the hiring manager as a job seeker

Write your cover letter and prepare your answers for someone who knows the work. Show results, examples and how you would handle the problems the team faces, rather than repeating keywords from the posting.

Research the team before the interview, and ask the hiring manager about priorities for the first few months, how success is measured and how the team works. These questions also help you judge whether you want them as your boss.
If you can find the hiring manager’s name, a short, polite note or a referral through a mutual contact can help. Keep it brief and do not send repeated follow-ups.
qa: Is the hiring manager the same as HR?

No. HR staff and recruiters manage the hiring process and company policies, while the hiring manager is the person who leads the team with the opening. HR often makes sure the process follows the law and company rules, but the hiring manager usually decides who gets the job.
Does the hiring manager make the final decision?

Usually yes, or they make the main recommendation. At some companies a hiring committee, a senior leader or HR must approve the choice, the salary or the offer details. The final say varies by employer, so it is fine to ask the recruiter how decisions are made.
How do I find out who the hiring manager is?

Check the job posting, which sometimes names the team or the role you would report to. You can also look at the company’s team pages or professional networking profiles, or simply ask the recruiter who the position reports to.
Should I address my cover letter to the hiring manager?
Yes, if you know their name, address it to them directly. If you cannot find it, a greeting such as “Dear Hiring Manager” is widely accepted and will not count against you.
Should I contact the hiring manager directly?

A short, professional message can help, especially at smaller companies or through a referral. Mention the role, one or two relevant strengths and that you have applied. Respect any instruction in the posting to apply only through the official process, and do not pressure them for an answer.

Blind hiring.title: What Is Blind Hiring? How Anonymous Screening Works
sections: What blind hiring means

Blind hiring is a way of screening job applicants with details that identify them removed or hidden. Reviewers first judge skills, experience and work samples, not who the person is or where they come from.

What gets hidden varies by employer. It is usually the name, photo and contact details, and sometimes the schools attended, graduation years, addresses, hobbies or anything else that could hint at age, gender, race or background.
It is also called blind recruitment or anonymous hiring. In the UK, “name-blind recruitment” is a common term, especially in public sector hiring.
How blind hiring works in practice

Some employers use software that strips identifying details from resumes before a recruiter sees them. Others skip the resume at first and ask everyone the same written questions or give the same short task.

Work samples and skills tests are central. You might write a short piece, solve a coding problem, analyze a spreadsheet or answer a realistic scenario, and reviewers score answers against the same criteria.
The blind part usually ends at the interview stage, when the employer meets you. Many employers then use structured interviews, with set questions and a scoring guide, to keep the process consistent.
Why employers use it and its limits
The aim is to reduce bias, including unconscious bias, in the first screen. Well-known examples include orchestras that hold auditions behind a screen so judges hear the playing, not the player.

It also helps career changers, self-taught workers and people from less known schools, since the first decision rests on what they can do. Employers often say it widens the pool of people they consider.

Blind hiring is not required by federal law in the US. It does not remove bias from later stages, and any skills test must still be job related, because tests that screen out protected groups without a clear job reason can raise discrimination issues.
What job seekers should do
Treat the work sample as the most important part of the application. Follow the instructions exactly, keep to any word or time limit, and put your strongest relevant example first.
If the employer asks you to leave out your name or school, do it. Leaving identifying details in a sample or file name can work against you or get the application set aside.
Describe results and skills in concrete terms, since reviewers cannot rely on a familiar company or college name. Say what you did, how you did it and what changed because of it.
qa: What is an example of blind hiring?

A common example is a company that removes names, photos and schools from resumes before recruiters read them. Another is an employer that asks every applicant to complete the same short task, such as writing a sample email or fixing a piece of code, and scores the answers without knowing who wrote them.
Is blind hiring legal in the US?

Yes. Employers may choose to hide identifying details during screening, and no federal law requires or bans the practice. Employers must still follow anti-discrimination laws throughout hiring, and skills tests should measure abilities the job really needs. Some states and cities have related rules, such as limits on asking about criminal history or pay history early on.
Does blind hiring actually reduce bias?

It can reduce bias in the first screen, because reviewers cannot react to names, photos or schools. It does not remove bias at the interview and offer stages, where the person is known. Employers usually pair it with structured interviews and clear scoring to keep the whole process fair.
What is the difference between blind hiring and ban the box?

Blind hiring hides identifying details such as name, photo and school during early screening. Ban the box refers to laws or policies that stop employers from asking about criminal records on the first application. Ban-the-box rules differ by state and city, while blind hiring is usually a voluntary employer choice.
How do I stand out in a blind hiring process?

Focus on the parts reviewers can see: your work sample, test answers and written responses. Follow every instruction, answer the exact question asked, and show clear results. Avoid adding personal details the employer asked you to leave out.

Employment verification.title: What Is Employment Verification? How It Works and What Is Shared
sections: What employment verification means

Employment verification is a check that confirms you worked where you say you did. A new employer, a mortgage lender, a landlord or a government agency contacts your current or former employer, or a service that holds its records, and asks for facts about your job.
The basic facts are your start and end dates and your job title. Some checks also confirm whether you still work there, your pay or income, and whether you are eligible for rehire.
Do not confuse it with Form I-9 or E-Verify. Those confirm that you are allowed to work in the US, not that you held a past job, although people sometimes call them employment verification too.
How the check works

The verifier may call or email the HR or payroll department, send a form to fill in, or ask for a verification of employment (VOE) letter. Many large employers send all requests to an automated service, such as The Work Number, so HR staff do not answer them one by one.

When a hiring employer uses a background check company, the federal Fair Credit Reporting Act applies. The employer must tell you in writing and get your written permission first. If it plans to reject you because of the report, it must give you a copy and a summary of your rights before deciding.

Lenders and landlords usually ask for your signed permission to verify your job and income. Hiring employers often run the check only after a conditional job offer, so a mismatch can end an offer you already have.
What a former employer can share

No federal law requires an employer to answer a verification request, and none limits it to dates and title. Many employers choose by policy to confirm only dates and title, because sharing more can lead to legal claims if the information is wrong.

Rules differ by state. Some states protect employers who share truthful references in good faith, and a few have service letter laws that require a written statement of your job on request. Many states and cities also ban hiring employers from asking about your past pay.
If you think a former employer shared false and damaging information, ask an employment lawyer or your state labor department about your options.
How to prepare for a verification

Check that the job titles and dates on your resume and application match your employer’s records. If your official title differed from what you did, list the official title and explain your real work in the description.

Keep your own records: offer letters, pay stubs, W-2 forms and any separation letter. If a company has closed or will not respond, these papers, or an IRS wage and income transcript, can prove your employment.

You can request your file from a verification service that is a consumer reporting agency and dispute errors. Tell your references and former managers that a check is coming so they can answer quickly.
qa: What does employment verification usually show?

At minimum it shows your employer’s name, your start and end dates and your job title. Depending on who asks and the employer’s policy, it can also show whether you still work there, your pay, and whether you are eligible to be rehired. Income details are usually shared only with your consent, for example for a loan.
Can an employer refuse to verify employment?

Yes, in most cases. No federal law requires an employer to answer a verification request, though a few states have service letter laws that require a written record of your job if you ask. If an employer will not respond, offer pay stubs, W-2 forms or an offer letter instead.
Can a former employer say I was fired?

In most states, an employer may share truthful information, including that you were fired, but many choose not to by policy. Stating something false that harms you can be defamation. State laws differ, so ask an employment lawyer if you believe false information cost you a job.
How long does employment verification take?

Automated services can return results within minutes or hours. Manual checks by phone or email often take a few business days, and longer if the employer is slow to respond or has closed. Giving accurate contact details for HR or payroll helps speed it up.
How do I verify employment if the company closed?

Use your own records, such as W-2 forms, pay stubs, offer letters or tax returns. You can also request a wage and income transcript from the IRS, which lists the W-2 forms reported for you. A former manager may be able to confirm your role as a reference.

Case interview.title: What Is a Case Interview? How It Works and How to Prepare
sections: What a case interview is

A case interview is a job interview where you are given a business problem and asked to solve it out loud while the interviewer watches. The case usually takes part of an interview slot, often around half an hour, followed by regular questions about you.

Case interviews are the standard format in management consulting. They are also common for strategy, business operations, product management, finance and analyst roles, where the job itself is solving open problems with incomplete data.
There is rarely one right answer. The interviewer is judging how you break down a problem, how you handle numbers, how clearly you speak and whether you reach a sensible conclusion.
How a case interview works

It starts with a short prompt, such as a client whose profits have fallen, a company deciding whether to enter a new market, or a request to estimate how many of a product sell each year. Estimation questions like the last one are called market sizing or guesstimates.

You ask clarifying questions, then take a minute to lay out a structure, often drawn as an issue tree that splits the problem into parts. Next you work through the parts, read charts or tables the interviewer hands you and do the math, usually by hand.

In a candidate-led case you decide what to look at next. In an interviewer-led case the interviewer asks a series of set questions. Some employers also use written cases, group cases or product cases, such as improving a feature or explaining why a metric dropped.
Every case should end with a clear recommendation, the main reasons behind it, the risks and the next steps you would take.
How to prepare for a case interview

Practice out loud with a partner, ideally someone who can play the interviewer and give feedback. Reading cases alone helps you learn the formats, but speaking while you think is the skill being tested.
Sharpen your mental math: percentages, growth rates, break-even and multiplying large numbers with zeros. Round numbers to make the math easier and say that you are rounding.
Learn common frameworks such as profit equals revenue minus costs, but do not force a memorized template onto every case. Interviewers notice when a structure does not fit the question.
During the case, say your assumptions, check your math out loud, connect each number back to the question, and lead with your answer when you sum up.
qa: How long does a case interview last?

The case part often runs around 20 to 40 minutes, and it is usually one piece of a longer interview that also includes questions about your background. Consulting hiring processes often have several rounds, each with one or more cases. Ask the recruiter what to expect for your specific interview.
Can you use a calculator in a case interview?

In most live consulting case interviews you cannot, and you do the math on paper or in your head. Online assessments and written cases sometimes allow a calculator or spreadsheet. If you are not sure, ask the recruiter beforehand, and practice mental math either way.
What is a market sizing question?

A market sizing question asks you to estimate a number you cannot look up, such as how many coffee cups are sold in a city each day. You break it into steps, state an assumption for each, multiply through and sanity-check the result. The logic matters more than the final figure.
What is the difference between candidate-led and interviewer-led cases?

In a candidate-led case you drive the analysis: you choose which areas to explore and ask for the data you need. In an interviewer-led case the interviewer guides you through set questions, one after another. Both test structure, math and communication, so practice both styles.
Can I pass a case interview without a business background?

Yes. Employers that use cases often hire people from science, engineering, law and other fields, and the case tests reasoning more than business knowledge. Learn basic terms such as revenue, margin, fixed and variable costs and market share, then practice many cases out loud with a partner.

Stipend.title: What Is a Stipend? How It Works, How It’s Taxed and What to Ask
sections: What a stipend is
A stipend is a fixed amount of money paid for a set purpose, such as covering living costs during an internship or paying for a home office. It is not tied to an hourly rate or a yearly salary.

Stipends show up in two main places. Some people, such as interns, fellows or trainees, are paid a stipend instead of a wage. Regular employees may get a stipend on top of their salary for something specific, like internet, a phone or learning.
A stipend can be paid once, monthly, each semester or each pay period. The offer or program letter should say the amount, the schedule and what it is meant to cover.
Common types of stipends
Internship and fellowship stipends help cover rent, food and travel while you train or study. Graduate students, research fellows and some nonprofit programs often receive them.

Work perk stipends are given to employees for a purpose. Examples are remote work or home office stipends, phone and internet stipends, wellness or gym stipends, commuter stipends and learning or education stipends.
Some programs give a one-time stipend, such as a relocation or equipment stipend. Others pay a set amount each month for as long as the program or benefit lasts.
How stipends are taxed in the US
In the US, most stipends count as taxable income. A stipend paid to an employee is usually added to wages on the W-2, with income tax and payroll taxes withheld like regular pay.

A stipend paid to someone who is not an employee, such as some fellows, may come with no withholding at all. It may be reported on a Form 1099 or on no form, but it is generally still taxable, and you may need to pay estimated taxes during the year.

There are exceptions. A scholarship or fellowship used for tuition, required fees, books and supplies at a qualifying school can be tax-free, while amounts for room and board are taxable. Reimbursements paid against receipts under an employer’s accountable plan are also not taxed.
Because the rules depend on how the payment is set up, ask an accountant or a tax preparer if you are unsure how to report a stipend.
What to ask before you accept

Ask whether the stipend is taxed and withheld, how often it is paid, and whether you must show receipts or spend it on certain things. Also ask whether it continues if you change roles or leave early.

For an internship at a for-profit company, federal law usually requires interns who count as employees to earn at least the minimum wage for hours worked. A flat stipend must still meet that, and some states set higher wages or stricter rules. Your state labor department can explain what applies.
When comparing offers, treat a work perk stipend as part of your total pay, but remember that taxes often reduce what you actually keep.
qa: Is a stipend taxable income?

In the US, usually yes. Stipends paid to employees are taxed like wages. Stipends paid to fellows or other non-employees are generally taxable too, even if no tax is withheld. Scholarship money used for tuition, required fees, books and supplies, and receipt-based reimbursements under an accountable plan, are common exceptions.
What is the difference between a stipend and a salary?

A salary is pay for the work you do, set as a yearly amount and paid on a regular schedule. A stipend is a fixed sum for a purpose, such as living costs during training or a home office. A stipend may replace pay, as for some interns and fellows, or come on top of a salary as a perk.
Can an internship pay only a stipend?

Yes, as long as the stipend meets the law. At a for-profit employer, an intern who counts as an employee under federal law must earn at least the minimum wage for hours worked, so the stipend must cover that. Some states have stricter rules. Nonprofits and government programs have more room to use volunteers.
Do I have to report a stipend if I did not get a tax form?

Generally yes. Taxable income must be reported on your return even when no W-2 or 1099 arrives, which is common for fellowship stipends. Keep your award letter and payment records, and ask a tax preparer if you are unsure which part, if any, is tax-free.
What is a remote work stipend?

It is a set amount an employer pays remote or hybrid employees to cover costs such as internet, a desk, a chair or utilities. It may be paid monthly or once. If it is paid as a flat amount without receipts, it is usually taxed as part of your wages.

Cold outreach.title: What Is Cold Outreach? How to Message People for a Job
sections: What cold outreach means in a job search

Cold outreach is a first message to someone who does not know you. In a job search it is usually an email or a LinkedIn message to a hiring manager, a recruiter or an employee at a company you want to join.
The goal is not always a job offer. Common asks are a short call to learn about the team, advice on an opening, or a referral after you have talked.
It is called cold because there is no prior contact. A warm message, by contrast, goes to someone you have met or someone a mutual contact has introduced you to.
Why it matters and when it works

Many openings draw a large number of applications, and a resume can sit unread in an applicant tracking system. A short, relevant message to a real person can get your name noticed or lead to a referral.
Some roles are filled before they are posted, or never posted at all. Talking to people inside a company can tell you about these openings and about what the team really needs.
Cold outreach works best when the message is specific and the ask is small. Many people will not reply, often because they are busy, so treat silence as normal rather than as rejection.
How to write a cold outreach message
Keep it to about four sentences. Say who you are in one line, explain why you chose this person, make one clear ask, and give them an easy way to say no.
Make the reason personal and true. Mention their team’s work, a talk they gave, a post they wrote or a shared school or past employer, rather than a line that could go to anyone.
Ask for something small, such as a 15-minute call or a pointer to the right person. Asking a stranger directly for a job or a referral in the first message usually gets fewer replies.
Use a clear subject line, such as the role or team name, and include a link to your LinkedIn profile or portfolio. Check names and spelling before you send.
Following up and what to avoid
If you get no answer, one polite follow-up after about a week is reasonable. Keep it shorter than the first message, and stop after that if there is still no reply.
Avoid sending the same template to many people at one company, attaching a resume nobody asked for, or writing long paragraphs about yourself. Respect a no and thank people who reply, even briefly.
If someone helps you, tell them what happened, for example that you applied or got an interview. That keeps the contact warm for later.
qa: Is cold outreach effective for getting a job?

It can be, especially when the message is short, personal and asks for something small like a quick call. Many messages get no reply, so it works best as one part of a search alongside applications, referrals and networking, not as the only method.
How do I cold email a hiring manager?

Find the person who leads the team you want to join, then write a short email with a clear subject line. Say who you are, why you are writing to them specifically, ask one small question or for a brief call, and link to your profile or work.
How long should I wait before following up on a cold message?
About a week is a common gap. Send one short, friendly follow-up that repeats your ask in a sentence. If there is still no answer, move on, since repeated messages can hurt the impression you make.
What is the difference between cold outreach and networking?

Networking is the broader habit of building professional relationships. Cold outreach is one way to start them, by contacting someone who does not know you. Warm outreach, through a mutual contact or an earlier meeting, is also networking and usually gets more replies.
Should I send a cold message on LinkedIn or by email?

Either can work. LinkedIn is easy when you do not have an email address, and it shows your profile at once. Email can stand out more in a busy inbox. Use whichever the person seems most active on, and keep the message short in both.

Cost-of-living adjustment (COLA).title: What Is a Cost-of-Living Adjustment (COLA)? How COLA Raises Work
sections: What a cost-of-living adjustment means
A cost-of-living adjustment, or COLA, is an increase in pay or benefits meant to keep up with rising prices. Its goal is to protect what your money can buy, not to reward good work.
If prices rise and your pay stays the same, you can afford less each year. A COLA tries to close that gap so your real pay, meaning pay after inflation, stays about level.

The size of a COLA is often tied to an inflation measure such as the Consumer Price Index (CPI), which the Bureau of Labor Statistics publishes every month. Some employers simply pick a percentage they think is fair.
Where COLAs are used in the US
Social Security benefits get an automatic COLA each year. It is based on the CPI-W, a price index for urban wage earners and clerical workers, is announced in October and takes effect in January.

Federal and military retirement plans also give COLAs under their own rules, and some state and local pensions do too. Many union contracts include a COLA clause that raises wages when the CPI goes up.
Private employers are not required by any federal or state law to give a COLA. Some give a yearly cost-of-living raise to all staff, some fold it into merit raises and some give nothing.
How a COLA differs from other raises
A merit raise rewards your performance and can differ from person to person. A COLA usually goes to everyone in a group at the same rate, whatever their reviews say.
A promotion raise comes with a bigger job. A COLA keeps you in the same job and only tries to keep your pay from losing value.
Some employers also use the term for location pay, an extra amount for working in a high-cost city or abroad. This is a geographic differential and is separate from a yearly inflation raise.
What to do as an employee or job seeker
Compare any raise with recent inflation where you live. If prices rose more than your raise, your pay bought less than the year before, even though the number went up.
When you get an offer, ask how the company handles yearly raises and whether it gives cost-of-living increases separate from merit raises. Get the answer in writing if it matters to you.
If you are in a union, read the COLA clause in your contract to see which index it uses, how often it adjusts and whether there is a cap.
qa: Is a cost-of-living raise required by law?

No. In the US, private employers do not have to give cost-of-living raises. COLAs are required only where a law, pension plan or contract sets them, such as Social Security, federal retirement plans or a union agreement that includes a COLA clause.
How is the Social Security COLA calculated?

It compares the average CPI-W for July, August and September with the same months of the year before. The percentage increase becomes the COLA, which the Social Security Administration announces in October and applies to benefits starting in January. If the index does not rise, there is no increase.
What is the difference between a COLA and a merit raise?

A COLA is meant to offset rising prices and usually goes to everyone in a group at the same rate. A merit raise rewards individual performance, so the amount depends on your review. Some employers give both, while others combine them into one yearly raise.
What is a good COLA percentage?

There is no standard figure. A COLA that matches or beats the rise in prices where you live keeps your buying power level. One that is smaller than local inflation means your pay buys less than before, even though the number on your paycheck went up.
Is a COLA taxable?

A cost-of-living raise in wages is taxed like the rest of your pay. Social Security benefits, including the COLA part, may be partly taxable depending on your total income. Ask an accountant or check IRS guidance for your own situation.

Portfolio.title: What Is a Portfolio? What to Put in One for a Job Search
sections: What a portfolio is in a job search

A portfolio is a collection of your real work that shows an employer what you can do. Where a resume lists your skills, a portfolio proves them with examples such as designs, code, articles, campaigns or case studies.
Most portfolios today are online: a personal website, a profile on a design or writing platform, or a code repository. Some fields still use a PDF or a printed book that you bring to an interview.
A good portfolio is selective. It shows a few strong pieces chosen for the kind of job you want, not everything you have ever made.
Who needs a portfolio and what goes in it

Designers, writers, photographers, architects, developers, marketers and content creators are often expected to have one. Many postings for these roles ask for a portfolio link next to the resume, and some will not consider an application without it.
Other fields can use one too. A data analyst can show a dashboard or analysis, a teacher can share lesson plans, and a project manager can write up a project’s goals, steps and results.
Each piece should explain the problem or goal, what you did yourself, the tools or methods you used and the result. If you worked in a team, say clearly which part was yours.
How to build a strong portfolio
Start with three to six of your best pieces that match the jobs you are applying for. Put the strongest one first, because reviewers often look at only the first item or two.

Write a short case study for your main pieces. Describe the starting situation, your process, any changes you made along the way and what happened afterward, using measured results only when they are real and you can back them up.
If you are new to a field, use school projects, volunteer work, freelance jobs or personal projects you made to practice. Label them honestly as what they are.
Keep it easy to use. Make sure links work, pages load quickly on a phone, and your name, contact details and a link to your resume are easy to find.
Sharing your portfolio and handling confidential work
Put the portfolio link near the top of your resume, in your cover letter and on your professional profiles. When a posting asks for specific samples, send those instead of making the reviewer search.

Work you did for an employer or client may be covered by a confidentiality or nondisclosure agreement. Ask for permission before you show it, remove names and private data, or describe the work without showing the actual files.
Update your portfolio when you finish a project you are proud of, and remove older pieces that no longer reflect your skill or the work you want next.
qa: What should a portfolio include?

A short introduction about you, three to six of your best work samples that fit the job you want, a brief explanation of the goal, your role and the result for each piece, and your contact details with a link to your resume.
Do I need a portfolio if I am not in a creative field?

Not always, but it can help. Analysts, project managers, teachers, engineers and marketers can show reports, dashboards, plans or case studies. A few clear examples give an employer proof of your skills that a resume alone cannot.
How many projects should be in a portfolio?
Three to six strong pieces is a common range. Reviewers often spend only a few minutes on a portfolio, so a small set of well-explained, relevant projects works better than a long list of mixed work.
Can I put work from a previous job in my portfolio?

Only if you are allowed to. Check any confidentiality or nondisclosure agreement you signed and ask the employer or client if you are unsure. You can often remove names and private details, or describe the project in words without showing the files.
What is the difference between a portfolio and a resume?

A resume is a short summary of your experience, skills and education. A portfolio shows actual examples of your work. Employers in many fields read the resume to see your background and the portfolio to judge the quality of what you produce.

Non-solicitation clause.title: What Is a Non-Solicitation Clause? What It Covers and How Long
sections: What a non-solicitation clause means

A non-solicitation clause is a promise in an employment contract, offer letter or separate agreement. It says that after you leave, you will not try to take the employer’s clients, customers or staff with you for a set period.

“Solicit” means actively reaching out to ask someone to move their business or their job. The clause does not usually stop you from working for a competitor. That is what a non-compete does, which is why a non-solicit is called the narrower of the two.

Many contracts include both kinds. A customer non-solicit protects client relationships. An employee non-solicit, sometimes called a no-raid or no-poach clause, stops you from recruiting former coworkers to your new company.
How these clauses work and when they hold up

The clause usually names a time limit, such as one or two years after your last day, and a group of people it covers. That group might be every client of the company, only clients you served or learned about, or only staff you managed.

In the US, enforceability depends on state law, because there is no general federal rule on these clauses. Courts in many states enforce a non-solicit if it protects a real business interest and is reasonable in length and scope.

California treats most restrictions on former employees as void, and its courts have refused to enforce many customer and employee non-solicits, though rules protecting trade secrets still apply. Some other states also limit these clauses, so the same wording can be valid in one state and unenforceable in another.

If an employer believes you broke the clause, it may send a warning letter, ask a court for an order to stop you, or sue for money it says it lost. Some agreements also let the employer take back a bonus or severance.
What to check before you sign or leave

Read how long the restriction lasts and exactly who it covers. A clause limited to clients you personally worked with in the last year is much easier to live with than one covering every customer of the company.
Look for wording that goes beyond soliciting. A “no-service” or “no-acceptance” clause can stop you from working with former clients even when they come to you on their own, which is much broader.
You can ask to narrow the clause before you sign, for example a shorter period or only clients you served. Get any change in writing.

When you leave, do not take client lists or contact files, and be careful with messages to former clients and coworkers. If the stakes are high or the wording is unclear, ask an employment lawyer in your state before you act.
qa: What is the difference between a non-compete and a non-solicitation clause?

A non-compete stops you from working for a competitor or starting a competing business for a time. A non-solicitation clause lets you take that job but stops you from actively pulling away your old employer’s clients or employees. Because it restricts less, courts in many states enforce non-solicits more readily than non-competes.
Are non-solicitation clauses enforceable?

Often yes, but it depends on the state. Many courts enforce them when they protect a real business interest and are reasonable in time and scope. California and a few other states limit them sharply. An employment lawyer in your state can tell you how a specific clause is likely to be treated.
Can I work with a client who contacts me first?

Under a plain non-solicitation clause, accepting business from a client who reaches out on their own is often allowed, because you did not solicit them. Some contracts add a no-service or no-acceptance clause that forbids this too. Read the exact wording, and keep a record showing the client approached you.
Does announcing my new job on LinkedIn count as soliciting?

A general announcement to your network is usually not treated as solicitation, but courts have not all agreed, and messages sent directly to former clients or coworkers carry more risk. Avoid posts or messages that invite clients to move their business or ask colleagues to join you while the clause applies.
How long does a non-solicitation clause last?

The contract sets the length, and it commonly runs a year or two after your employment ends. Courts look harder at longer periods and may refuse to enforce, or in some states shorten, a period they find unreasonable for the job and the business.

Employee referral bonus.title: What Is an Employee Referral Bonus? How It Works and Who Gets Paid
sections: What an employee referral bonus is

An employee referral bonus is money a company pays a current employee who recommends a candidate that the company then hires. It is part of an employee referral program, which sets the rules for who can refer, which jobs count and how much is paid.

Employers offer these bonuses because referred candidates often come with a trusted introduction, can be hired faster and cost less than paying an outside recruiter. The bonus gives staff a reason to share openings with people they know.
The amount is set by each company and often varies by role. Hard-to-fill or senior positions usually carry a larger bonus than entry-level ones.
How referral bonuses usually work

The employee submits the candidate through an internal referral tool or the company’s applicant tracking system, so the referral is recorded. The candidate then goes through the normal hiring process.
Most programs pay only after the new hire starts and stays a set time, such as a few months. Some split the bonus into two payments, one at the start date and one later.
Common rules exclude recruiters, HR staff and the hiring manager for the role. Many programs also pay nothing if the candidate already applied on their own or was already in the company’s system.
In the US, a referral bonus is treated as taxable wages. It is usually paid through payroll as supplemental pay, with income tax, Social Security and Medicare withheld like other bonuses.
What job seekers should know

The bonus goes to the person who refers you, not to you, and it does not come out of your salary or offer. A referral can help your application get a closer look, but you still have to pass the interviews.

Ask the referral before you apply, since many programs will not pay if you are already in the system. Send a short summary of your experience, your resume and the job link so the referral takes little effort.
Only ask people who know your work or can speak honestly about you. A referral that comes with a few words about why you fit carries more weight than a bare name.
What employers should consider
Write down clear rules: eligible roles, the amount, the waiting period, who is excluded and what happens if two employees refer the same person. Apply them the same way to everyone.

Referrals tend to bring in people similar to your current staff. Keep other sourcing channels open and judge referred candidates by the same criteria as others to support fair hiring under equal employment opportunity laws.
Pay bonuses through payroll so taxes are withheld correctly. Ask an accountant or employment lawyer if you plan to pay people who are not employees, or to offer non-cash rewards.
qa: Is an employee referral bonus taxable?

Yes. In the US a referral bonus paid to an employee counts as wages. It is usually paid through payroll as supplemental pay, with federal income tax, Social Security and Medicare withheld, plus state income tax where the state has one. It appears on your W-2.
How long does a referred employee have to stay for the bonus to be paid?

It depends on the company’s program. Many require the new hire to stay a set period, often a few months, before the referring employee is paid. If the new hire leaves earlier, the bonus may be reduced or not paid. Check the written program rules.
Does a referral bonus lower the salary offered to the person referred?
No. The bonus is paid by the employer to the referring employee from a separate budget. It does not come out of the candidate’s pay, and the candidate negotiates salary the same way as anyone else.
Can I get a referral bonus if I don’t work at the company?

Usually not, because most programs are only for current employees. Some companies run separate programs that pay outsiders, such as former staff or contractors, but these are less common and have their own rules.
Is it OK to ask someone to refer me for a job?
Yes, and many employees are glad to, since they may earn a bonus. Ask people who know your work, ask before you apply, and send your resume, the job link and a short summary of why you fit.

Parental leave.title: What Is Parental Leave? How It Works and What US Law Requires
sections: What parental leave means
Parental leave is time off work to care for a new child after a birth, an adoption or a foster placement. Depending on the employer and the state, it can be fully paid, partly paid or unpaid.

It is usually open to any parent, including fathers, partners and adoptive parents. Maternity leave often refers to time for the birth parent to recover, while paternity leave refers to time for the other parent.
Some employers split their policy into primary caregiver and secondary caregiver leave, with more paid weeks for the parent who does most of the care.
What US law requires

No federal law requires private employers to pay for parental leave. The Family and Medical Leave Act (FMLA) gives eligible workers up to 12 weeks of unpaid, job-protected leave in a 12-month period for a birth, adoption or foster placement.

You are eligible for FMLA if your employer has at least 50 employees within 75 miles of your worksite, you have worked there at least 12 months, and you worked at least 1,250 hours in the past 12 months. Your group health coverage must continue on the same terms during the leave.

A growing number of states, including California, New York, New Jersey and Washington, plus the District of Columbia, run paid family leave programs. They pay part of your wages from a state fund, and the rules, amounts and job protection differ by state.

Most federal civilian employees get 12 weeks of paid parental leave under a separate federal law. Outside the US the term can mean something else; in the UK, parental leave is a separate unpaid right on top of maternity and paternity leave.
How employer policies work
Many employers offer paid leave beyond what the law requires. A policy may pay full salary for a set number of weeks, pay part of it, or top up a state benefit so you receive your full pay.

Birth parents may also get pay from short-term disability insurance for the recovery period, and some employers combine this with parental leave. Check whether the weeks run one after the other or overlap.
Some policies require you to have worked a minimum time before you qualify, and some ask you to repay part of the benefit if you do not return to work afterward.
What a job seeker should ask
Ask how many weeks are paid at full salary, how many at partial pay, and whether the leave applies from your first day or after a waiting period.
Ask whether the leave must be taken all at once or can be split, how it works with your state program, and whether your job and benefits are protected while you are away.
For questions about your own eligibility or a dispute with an employer, contact your state labor department, the US Department of Labor’s Wage and Hour Division or an employment lawyer.
qa: Is parental leave paid in the US?

Not by federal law for private employers. FMLA leave is unpaid, though it protects your job. Pay comes from your employer’s own policy, from a state paid family leave program where your state has one, or from short-term disability insurance for a birth parent’s recovery.
How long is parental leave in the US?

FMLA allows up to 12 weeks of unpaid, job-protected leave for eligible workers. Employer policies and state programs set their own lengths, so the paid weeks you get depend on where you work and who employs you.
Can fathers take parental leave?

Yes. FMLA covers any eligible parent, regardless of gender, for bonding with a new child within 12 months of the birth or placement. State programs and most employer policies also cover fathers, partners and adoptive parents.
What is the difference between parental leave and maternity leave?

Maternity leave usually means leave for the birth mother, often including recovery from childbirth. Parental leave is a broader term for leave any parent can take to care for a new child, including after adoption or foster placement.
Do I qualify for parental leave at a new job?

Often not right away under FMLA, which requires 12 months of employment and 1,250 hours worked. Some employer policies and some state programs have shorter or no waiting periods, so ask before you accept an offer.

Boolean search.title: What Is Boolean Search? Using AND, OR and NOT to Find Jobs
sections: What Boolean search means

Boolean search is a way of typing a search so that the search box follows exact rules instead of guessing. You join words with the operators AND, OR and NOT, put phrases in quotation marks and group terms with parentheses.

The name comes from George Boole, a 19th-century mathematician whose logic works with true and false. A Boolean search asks a simple yes or no question of every result: does it match all the rules you set?

Job seekers use it on job boards to cut a long list down to the openings they want. Recruiters use it to find candidates in resume databases, on professional networks and through general search engines.
How the operators work
AND means both words must appear, so nurse AND pediatric shows only results that contain both. OR means either word may appear, which is useful for job titles and skills that have several names.
NOT leaves out results that contain a word, such as NOT senior or NOT intern. Some sites use a minus sign instead, written with no space before the word, as in -senior.

Quotation marks keep a phrase together, so “project manager” will not match a page that says manager of a project. Parentheses group terms, as in (RN OR “registered nurse”), so the search reads them as one unit.
Some sites also accept an asterisk as a wildcard. On those sites, manag* matches manager, managers and management. Check the site’s help page, because many search boxes ignore it.
How to build a Boolean search for jobs

Start with the job title in quotes, add other titles for the same work with OR inside parentheses, then add one must-have skill with AND. For example: (“project manager” OR “program manager”) AND Agile NOT senior.

Type the operators in capital letters, because many sites read lowercase and, or and not as ordinary words. Each site has its own rules, and some job boards support only part of Boolean logic or none of it.

If you get no results, remove one condition at a time until jobs appear. If you get too many, add one more AND or NOT. Once the search works, save it and turn on job alerts so new matches come to you.
How recruiters use Boolean search

Recruiters write Boolean strings to find people with a certain title, skill and location, for example (“data analyst” OR “business analyst”) AND SQL AND Chicago. They run these strings in applicant tracking systems, resume databases and professional networks.
Some use a search engine with the site: operator to look inside one website, which is called X-ray search. This lets them find public profiles or resumes that match their string.

For job seekers, this means the exact words in your resume and online profile matter. Use the common names for your job title and skills, and spell out abbreviations once, so you match more of the strings recruiters type.
qa: What are the three main Boolean operators?

The three main operators are AND, OR and NOT. AND requires every word to appear, OR accepts any of the words, and NOT leaves out results with a word. Most Boolean searches also use quotation marks for exact phrases and parentheses to group terms.
Do Boolean operators have to be in capital letters?

On many sites, yes. Search boxes often treat lowercase and, or and not as ordinary words to look for. Typing AND, OR and NOT in capitals is the safe habit, and the site’s help page will say whether it matters there.
Does Google support Boolean search?

Partly. Google treats a space between words much like AND, accepts OR in capital letters, matches exact phrases in quotation marks and leaves out a word when you put a minus sign directly before it. It does not reliably follow NOT, so use the minus sign instead.
What is a Boolean string?

A Boolean string is a complete search written with operators, such as (“software engineer” OR developer) AND Python NOT intern. Recruiters save and reuse strings to find candidates, and job seekers can save them on job boards to get alerts for matching openings.
Why does my Boolean search return no results?

Usually the search has too many conditions, a typo, a missing quotation mark or an unclosed parenthesis. Some sites also do not support every operator. Remove one condition at a time, check the punctuation, and read the site’s search help to see which operators it accepts.

Technical interview.title: What Is a Technical Interview? Formats and How to Prepare
sections: What a technical interview is

A technical interview tests whether you can do the actual work of the job, not just talk about it. You solve a problem, design something or complete a task while an interviewer watches, asks questions or reviews your result afterward.

It is most common in software engineering, data science and IT, but analysts, engineers, designers and other skilled roles often face a version of it. A data analyst may write SQL queries, and a designer may walk through the decisions behind a portfolio piece.
It usually comes after a recruiter or hiring manager screen and before a final round. Some companies hold several technical rounds, each focused on a different skill.
Common technical interview formats

Live coding: you write code in a shared editor or on a whiteboard while talking through your approach. Problems often cover data structures and algorithms, such as arrays, hash maps, trees and graphs.

System design: you sketch how you would build a larger system, such as a messaging app or a link shortener. It is common for mid-level and senior roles and tests how you weigh trade-offs more than exact answers.

Take-home assignment or online assessment: you complete a small project on your own time and often discuss it in a follow-up call, or you take a timed test on a coding platform that may be scored automatically.

Technical questions and pair programming: some interviews are a conversation about tools and concepts you have used, or a session where you work alongside an engineer on a realistic task, such as fixing a bug.
What interviewers look for
A correct answer helps, but most interviewers also judge how you get there. They want to see you clarify the problem, break it into steps, choose a reasonable approach and explain why.
Communication counts. Thinking out loud lets the interviewer follow your reasoning and offer hints, while long silence makes it hard for them to give you credit for good ideas.
They also watch how you test your work, handle mistakes and respond to feedback. Spotting your own bug and fixing it calmly can leave a better impression than a perfect solution you cannot explain.
How to prepare for a technical interview
Ask the recruiter what format to expect, which language or tools you may use and how long each round lasts. Many companies share a preparation guide if you ask.

Practice under realistic conditions: solve problems out loud, on a timer, in a plain editor or on paper. Mock interviews with a friend or a practice site help you get used to explaining while you work.
In the interview, restate the problem, ask about inputs, limits and edge cases, and outline your plan before writing anything. Start with a simple working solution, then improve it if time allows.
For a take-home, follow the instructions closely, keep to the suggested time and add a short note on your choices and what you would change with more time.
qa: How long does a technical interview take?

A single live round often lasts 45 to 60 minutes. Online assessments are commonly 60 to 90 minutes, and take-home assignments are usually meant to take a few hours. A full onsite or virtual loop can include several rounds across most of a day.
Can I use Google during a technical interview?

It depends on the company. Some let you look up syntax or documentation, while many forbid outside help in timed assessments. Ask the interviewer at the start. Searching for answers or using AI tools without permission can end your candidacy.
What should I do if I get stuck in a technical interview?

Say what you are thinking and where you are stuck. Try a simpler version of the problem, work through a small example by hand or ask a clarifying question. Interviewers often give hints, and using one well counts in your favor.
Do you have to finish the problem to pass a technical interview?

Not always. Many interviewers score your reasoning, communication and code quality, not just whether the code runs. A clear, partly finished solution with a sound plan can beat a rushed one that works but that you cannot explain.
What is the difference between a technical and a behavioral interview?

A technical interview tests job skills directly through problems or tasks. A behavioral interview asks about past situations, such as how you handled a conflict or a tight deadline, to judge how you work with others. Most hiring processes for technical roles include both.

Apprenticeship.title: What Is an Apprenticeship? How It Works, Pay and How to Apply
sections: What an apprenticeship is

An apprenticeship is a real, paid job that comes with a structured training plan. You learn a skilled trade or profession by working alongside experienced people and by taking related classes, and you finish with a recognized credential.

Apprenticeships are best known in the building trades, such as electrician, plumber and carpenter. They also exist in manufacturing, health care, IT, cybersecurity, trucking, hospitality and many other fields.
Unlike an internship, an apprenticeship is usually longer, always paid, and built to lead to a full-time job in the occupation you trained for.
How Registered Apprenticeship works in the US

In the US, the main formal system is called Registered Apprenticeship. Programs are registered with the U.S. Department of Labor or, in some states, with a State Apprenticeship Agency, and must meet set standards for training, pay and safety.

Each program combines on-the-job learning under a mentor with related technical instruction. The instruction may happen at a community college, a union training center, an online course or the employer’s own classroom.
Pay usually follows a written wage schedule. You start at a set share of a fully trained worker’s wage, and your pay rises in steps as you gain skills and hours.

Programs often last from one to several years, depending on the occupation. When you finish, you receive a nationally recognized certificate of completion, and in some trades you can then sit for a state license exam.
Who can apply and what it costs

Most programs accept applicants from age 16, and many require age 18, especially in hazardous trades. Common requirements include a high school diploma or GED, a basic math test, a driver’s license, a drug test and an interview.
Many programs pay for the classroom training, but some charge for tuition, books or tools. Ask what you will pay before you sign, and whether any costs must be repaid if you leave early.
Veterans may be able to use GI Bill benefits during an approved apprenticeship. Check the details with the VA, because eligibility depends on your service and the program.
How to find and choose an apprenticeship

Search Apprenticeship.gov, your state’s apprenticeship office, local union training centers, community colleges and American Job Centers. Some employers also post apprenticeships directly on job boards.
If you are not ready yet, a pre-apprenticeship program can teach basic skills, safety and math and help you get accepted into a registered program.
Before you accept, check whether the program is registered, what credential you finish with, how the wage steps work, and whether the employer usually keeps apprentices after they complete.
The term means something a little different outside the US. In the UK, for example, apprenticeships have set levels, a minimum length and a separate apprentice minimum wage rate.
qa: Do apprentices get paid?

Yes. An apprenticeship is a job, so apprentices are paid for the hours they work and must get at least the applicable minimum wage. In a US Registered Apprenticeship, pay rises on a written schedule as you complete hours and show new skills.
How long does an apprenticeship take?

It depends on the occupation and the program. Some last about a year, while many skilled trades, such as electrician, take four or five years. The program’s written standards state the required hours of on-the-job learning and classroom instruction.
What is the difference between an apprenticeship and an internship?

An internship is usually short, may be unpaid in some cases, and gives work experience. An apprenticeship is a paid job that lasts longer, follows a structured training plan with classes, and ends with a recognized credential in a specific occupation.
What is a registered apprenticeship?

It is a program approved by the U.S. Department of Labor or a State Apprenticeship Agency. It must meet standards for paid work, mentoring, related classes, rising wages and safety, and graduates receive a nationally recognized certificate of completion.
Can adults start an apprenticeship?

Yes. There is generally a minimum age but no maximum, and many apprentices are adults changing careers. Requirements vary by program, so check each one’s entry rules, such as education, tests and physical demands.

Profit sharing.title: What Is Profit Sharing? How Payouts and Plans Work
sections: What profit sharing means
Profit sharing is when a company gives part of its profit to employees, usually once a year. The amount changes with how the business did, so it is variable pay, not part of your fixed salary.
In a good year the payout can be large. In a weak year it can be small or nothing at all, and the company usually decides each year whether to pay.
Cash payouts and retirement plan contributions

In the US, profit sharing comes in two main forms. A cash plan pays you money directly, much like a bonus. A deferred profit-sharing plan puts the money into a retirement account in your name instead.

A deferred plan is a qualified retirement plan under IRS rules. The money grows tax-deferred until you withdraw it, and total contributions to your account are capped by a yearly limit set by the IRS. Many employers add profit-sharing contributions to a 401(k) plan.
Despite the name, a company does not need a profit to contribute to a profit-sharing retirement plan. The employer can usually choose each year whether to contribute and how much.
How the amount is decided and split
The company first sets the total pool, sometimes by a formula tied to profit and sometimes at its own discretion. Then it splits the pool among eligible employees.

A common split is in proportion to pay, so everyone gets the same percentage of salary. Other formulas give equal amounts per person or weigh in age or job level. Retirement plans must follow IRS rules that stop them from unfairly favoring highly paid employees.
Plans often have eligibility rules, such as working a minimum time or being employed on the payout date. Employer contributions to a retirement account may also vest over several years.
What a job seeker should ask
Ask what was paid out in each of the last few years, as a percentage of salary or in dollars. Ask whether it comes as cash or goes into a retirement account, and how the pool is split.
Ask about eligibility and vesting: when you start to qualify, whether you must be on staff on the payout date, and how long until retirement contributions are fully yours.
When you compare offers, treat profit sharing like a bonus, not like salary. Base your budget on fixed pay and count past payouts only as a possible extra.
qa: How is profit sharing taxed?

Cash profit sharing is taxed as ordinary wages, with income tax, Social Security and Medicare withheld, often at a flat federal rate for supplemental pay. Contributions to a qualified retirement plan are generally not taxed when made; you pay income tax when you withdraw the money. For your own situation, ask a tax professional.
Is profit sharing the same as a 401(k)?

Not exactly. A 401(k) lets you put part of your own pay into a retirement account. A profit-sharing plan is funded by the employer. Many companies combine them, so profit-sharing contributions land in the same 401(k) account as your own savings.
Is profit sharing guaranteed?

Usually not. Most plans let the company decide each year whether to pay and how much, and payouts often fall or stop in a bad year. Check the plan document or offer letter, and treat any figure from past years as an example, not a promise.
What happens to my profit sharing if I quit?

For cash plans, many require you to be employed on the payout date, so leaving before then can mean no payment. For retirement plans, the vested part of your account stays yours and can often be rolled over, while unvested employer contributions are usually forfeited.
What is a good profit sharing percentage?

There is no standard figure. Payouts vary widely by company, industry and year. Compare the actual amounts paid over several years to your salary, and weigh them against the base pay and other benefits in each offer.

Promotion.title: What Is a Promotion? How It Works and How to Get One
sections: What a promotion means

A promotion is a move to a higher level in your organization. It usually comes with a new or higher title, more pay and more responsibility, such as leading a project, managing people or owning a bigger budget.

Promotions can happen inside the same team, such as going from analyst to senior analyst, or by moving to a higher role in another department. Both count as internal moves because you stay with the same employer.

Some promotions change the title without changing pay. This is often called a dry promotion. Others raise the level and pay but keep the title, which is common in companies that use numbered job levels.
How promotions are decided

Many employers decide promotions during yearly or twice-yearly review cycles. Managers put forward candidates, and a group of leaders compares them against written expectations for each level, often called a career ladder or leveling guide.

Other employers promote when a higher role opens up. They may post it internally, and the current team competes with outside applicants. Some states, such as Colorado, require employers to tell employees about promotion opportunities.

Federal law bars employers from basing promotion decisions on race, color, religion, sex, national origin, age if you are 40 or older, disability or genetic information, and many states add more protected traits. If you think you were passed over unfairly, ask a lawyer or contact the EEOC or your state’s civil rights agency.
What to do if you want a promotion
Ask your manager what the next level requires and get the answer in writing. Ask for specific skills, results or scope you need to show, not just general advice.

Keep a running list of your results, with numbers where you can, such as money saved, projects shipped or people trained. Share progress in regular check-ins so your manager has evidence when review time comes.

When a promotion is offered, ask for the new title, pay, start date and any changes to duties or schedule in writing. A move from an hourly role to a salaried manager role may change whether you earn overtime, so check that too.
qa: How much of a raise should a promotion come with?

There is no legal rule or fixed amount. The raise depends on the employer’s pay ranges for each level, your current pay and the market. Look up typical pay for the new title in your area, and if a pay range is listed for the role, use it to ask for an amount near what the new work is worth.
What is a dry promotion?

A dry promotion is a higher title or more responsibility without a pay increase. Employers sometimes offer one when budgets are tight. If you accept, ask when your pay will be reviewed and get that timing in writing.
Can I turn down a promotion?

Yes, in most cases you can decline a promotion, for example if the new role does not fit your goals or family needs. Explain your reasons politely and say what you would like instead. In an at-will job, an employer can still change your role, so talk it through with your manager.
How do I list a promotion on my resume?

Put the employer name once, then list each title underneath with its own dates, newest first. Add a few results under each title. This shows growth at one company more clearly than listing only your latest title.
How long should I wait before asking for a promotion?

There is no set time. Many employers expect at least one full review cycle in a role before a promotion. It is better to ask early what the next level requires, then raise the promotion once you can show you already do much of that work.

Entry-level.title: What Is an Entry-Level Job? Meaning, Experience and How to Apply
sections: What entry-level means

An entry-level job is designed for people with little or no professional experience in a field. The employer expects to train you, and the role is usually the first step on a career ladder in that line of work.

The label covers many kinds of work: internships for students, graduate or new-grad programs for recent college graduates, apprenticeships, and junior or associate roles. It also covers hourly jobs in retail, food service, warehouses and similar settings that need no prior experience.

Entry-level describes the experience needed, not the education. Some entry-level roles require a bachelor’s degree or a license, while others ask only for a high school diploma or have no education requirement at all.
Why entry-level postings often ask for experience

Many postings labeled entry-level still ask for one or two years of experience. That line is often a wish list copied from a template, and hiring managers regularly interview people who meet most, but not all, of the requirements.

Experience does not have to come from a full-time job. Internships, part-time and campus jobs, volunteer work, class projects, freelance work and military service all count when they show you have done tasks like the ones in the posting.

Job titles help you spot real entry-level roles. Words such as junior, associate, assistant, trainee, coordinator, new grad or a level number like Analyst I usually signal an early-career job, while senior, lead, manager or principal usually do not.
