How to apply for entry-level jobs
If you are a recent graduate, put your education near the top of your resume, then list internships, projects and relevant work with concrete results. One page is usually enough at this stage.
Use the posting’s own words for skills where they are true for you. When a cover letter is allowed, keep it short and explain why the field interests you and what you have already done in it.

In some fields, such as finance, consulting and parts of tech, large employers recruit new graduates months before the start date, often in the fall for jobs starting the next summer. Check timelines early so you do not miss them.

Check pay and terms before you accept. Overtime rights depend on your duties and pay, not on the entry-level label, and unpaid internships at for-profit companies are legal only in limited cases. Ask your state labor department if you are unsure.
qa: How many years of experience is entry-level?

Entry-level usually means zero to two years of experience in the field. Many true entry-level jobs require none at all. When a posting asks for one or two years, internships, part-time work, volunteer roles and substantial class projects can often fill that gap, so it is usually worth applying.
Is an internship the same as an entry-level job?

Not exactly. An internship is usually a short, often temporary role for students or recent graduates, meant for learning. An entry-level job is usually a regular, ongoing position. Both are early-career roles, and an internship often helps you get an entry-level job afterward, sometimes at the same employer.
Do entry-level jobs require a college degree?

Some do and many do not. Office roles in fields like finance, engineering or marketing often ask for a bachelor’s degree, while jobs in retail, hospitality, logistics and many skilled trades through apprenticeships do not. A growing number of employers also accept equivalent experience or certifications instead of a degree, so read each posting carefully.
How much do entry-level jobs pay?

Pay varies widely by field, location and employer, from minimum-wage hourly work to salaried professional roles. Several states and cities require employers to include a pay range in job postings, which helps you compare offers. You can also check salary data for the job title in your area before you apply or negotiate.
Can I apply for entry-level jobs if I already have work experience?

Yes. Career changers often start at entry level in a new field, and that is common and accepted. In your resume and cover letter, explain why you are switching and point out skills from past jobs that transfer, such as customer service, project management or working with data.

Posting.title: What Is a Job Posting? What It Includes and How to Read One
sections: What a job posting is

A job posting is a single advertisement for an open position. It tells you what the job is, what the employer wants from candidates and how to apply. People also call it a job listing, a job ad or a job opening.

Employers publish postings on their own careers page, on job boards and sometimes on social media. The same posting often appears on several sites at once, because many job boards copy listings from company careers pages.

A posting is not the same as a job description. The job description is the employer’s internal document about the role, while the posting is the public ad, which often includes parts of the description plus pay, benefits and application steps.
What a posting usually includes
Most postings list the job title, the company, the location or whether the work is remote or hybrid, and the type of job, such as full-time, part-time, contract or temporary.

The main body usually covers duties, required qualifications and preferred qualifications. Required items are what the employer says it needs. Preferred items, often marked “nice to have” or “a plus,” are extras that help but are not always deal breakers.

Many postings also show a pay range, benefits, the work schedule and an equal opportunity statement. Some states and cities, such as Colorado, California, Washington and New York, require employers covered by their laws to include a pay range in postings. Rules differ by place, and many areas have no such requirement.
How to read a posting before you apply

Read the whole posting twice. First check the basics: location, schedule, pay and any must-haves like a license, a degree or work authorization. If you clearly cannot meet one, the application may be screened out early.

Then mark the skills and job titles the posting repeats. Use the same words in your resume and cover letter where they are true for you, because recruiters and applicant tracking systems often search for those terms.

Save a copy of every posting you apply to, as a PDF or a screenshot. Employers often take postings down once they stop accepting applications, and you will want the exact text to prepare for the interview.
Why postings disappear or stay up
A posting may close because the job was filled, enough applicants applied, the budget changed or the role was put on hold. Closed postings are usually removed without notice to applicants.
Some postings stay up for a long time. The employer may hire for the same role often, collect resumes for future openings or simply forget to take the ad down. These are sometimes called ghost jobs.
Check the posting date, look for the same job on the company’s own careers page and apply soon after a posting goes up when you can.
qa: What is the difference between a job posting and a job description?

A job description is the employer’s internal document listing a role’s duties, reporting line and requirements. A job posting is the public advertisement used to attract applicants. A posting often borrows from the description but adds things like pay, benefits, location and how to apply.
How long do job postings usually stay up?

There is no fixed rule. Some postings come down within days once enough people apply, while others stay up for weeks or months, especially for roles the employer fills often. If a posting looks old, check the company’s careers page to see if it is still open.
Should I apply if I do not meet every requirement in a job posting?

Often yes. Postings frequently describe an ideal candidate, and employers hire people who meet most but not all points. Focus on the hard must-haves, such as a required license or work authorization. If you meet those and most of the rest, applying is usually worth it.
Do job postings have to include the salary?

It depends on where the job is. Several states and some cities, including Colorado, California, Washington and New York, require covered employers to list a pay range in postings. There is no federal rule requiring it, so in many places employers can leave pay out.
What is a ghost job posting?

A ghost job is a posting for a role the employer is not actively trying to fill, or a listing that stays up after the job is filled. Signs include a very old posting date, a vague description and no reply after applying. Checking the company’s own careers page can help.

Geographic pay.title: What Is Geographic Pay? How Location-Based Pay Works
sections: What geographic pay means

Geographic pay, also called location-based pay or geo pay, means an employer pays different amounts for the same job depending on where the employee lives or works. A software engineer in one city may earn more than an engineer with the same title and level in another city.
It is most common at large companies that hire remote workers across many states or countries. Instead of one salary range for a role, the employer keeps several ranges, one for each location group.

The federal government uses a similar idea called locality pay. Many federal employees on the General Schedule get a percentage added to base pay that depends on the area where their official worksite is.
How employers set location-based pay

Most employers sort locations into zones or tiers. A top tier might include a few high-cost metro areas, and lower tiers cover other cities, smaller towns and rural areas. Each tier has its own pay range for every job level.

Employers usually base the tiers on salary survey data about what other employers pay in each area, often called cost of labor. Cost of living, meaning rent, food and other prices, often moves in the same direction but is a separate measure.
Some companies use a single national range for all US workers instead. Others pay one range for remote staff and higher ranges only for people who work in certain offices.
In states and cities with pay transparency laws, job postings often must show a pay range. Companies with geographic pay sometimes list several ranges in one posting, one per location tier.
What happens if you move

If you move to an area in a different tier, your employer may change your pay to match the new location. Some companies cut pay when you move to a lower-cost area and raise it when you move to a higher-cost one.
Other employers freeze your current pay, adjust it only at the next review or leave it unchanged. The answer depends on the company’s written policy, so read it before you sign a lease or buy a home.

Moving to another state can also change which state’s tax, wage and leave laws apply to you. Your employer needs to know, because it must withhold the right state income tax and may need to register in that state.
What a job seeker should do
Ask the recruiter which city or tier your offer is based on and what the range is for that tier. Check that the location on file is correct, because a wrong zip code can put you in a lower range.
Ask what happens to your pay if you move, and get the answer in writing if a move is likely. Also ask whether bonuses, equity grants and raises follow the same location rules.

When you compare offers, look at total pay after taxes and living costs, not only the base salary. If you think a pay change broke your contract or state law, contact your state labor department or an employment lawyer.
qa: Is it legal to pay remote workers differently based on location?

In the US, it is generally legal to set pay by location, as long as the employer applies the rule fairly and does not use it to pay people differently because of sex, race or another protected trait. Some states have stricter equal pay laws, so the details can differ by state.
Will my salary go down if I move to a cheaper city?

It might. Some employers lower pay when you move to a lower-cost area, some freeze it until pay catches up, and some do not change it at all. Check your company’s written policy and ask HR before you move, since the answer differs from one employer to the next.
What is the difference between cost of living and cost of labor?

Cost of living is how much it costs to live in a place, such as rent, food and transport. Cost of labor is what employers in that place typically pay for a given job. Most geographic pay systems are based on cost of labor, although the two often move together.
What is locality pay?

Locality pay is the federal government’s version of geographic pay. Many federal employees on the General Schedule receive an extra percentage on top of base pay that depends on the locality pay area of their official worksite. The rates are updated from time to time and are published by the Office of Personnel Management.
Do I have to tell my employer if I move?

Usually yes. Most employers require it, and your employer needs your correct address to withhold the right state and local taxes and follow the labor laws of your new state. Not reporting a move can cause tax problems and may break company policy.

Salary history ban.title: What Is a Salary History Ban? What It Covers and How It Works
sections: What a salary history ban is

A salary history ban is a state or local law that stops employers from asking job applicants what they were paid in past jobs. Many laws also stop employers from looking up your past pay or using it to decide whether to hire you or what to offer.

The idea is that pay should be set by the job and your skills, not by what a past employer chose to pay you. Supporters say it keeps old pay gaps, including gaps tied to gender and race, from following people from job to job.
Where salary history bans apply

There is no federal law that bans private employers from asking about salary history. The bans come from states, cities and counties, and the list has grown over time, so check the current law where the job is located.

Some state laws cover all employers, while others cover only public employers such as state agencies. Some cities have their own bans, and a few states have laws that stop cities from passing them, so the rules can differ even within one state.

The details vary a lot. Some laws let employers use pay history you share on your own, some let them confirm it after an offer, and many have exceptions for internal promotions or pay that is already public. Your state labor department’s website usually explains the local rules.
What employers usually can and cannot do

Where a ban applies, an employer generally cannot ask about your past pay on an application form, in an interview or through a recruiter. It usually cannot ask your past employers either, and cannot refuse to hire you because you decline to answer.
Most bans still let employers ask what pay you expect or want for the new job. That question is about the future, not the past, so it is usually allowed.
Employers that hire in many places often drop salary history questions everywhere to keep one process. Hiring managers and recruiters should be trained on which questions are off limits.
What to do as a job seeker
Before interviews, look up whether the place where the job is based has a ban. Research the market pay for the role so you can give a clear expected range with a short reason.

If someone asks about past pay, you can politely steer back to your expectations, for example by saying you would rather focus on the pay range for this role. Where no ban applies, you can still choose not to share it, though the employer may weigh that.
If you think an employer broke the law, keep notes of what was asked and when. You can contact your state or city labor or human rights agency, or an employment lawyer, about your options.
qa: Is it illegal for employers to ask about your salary history?

It depends on where the job is. A number of US states and cities make it illegal for some or all employers to ask, but there is no federal ban for private employers. In places without a ban, an employer may legally ask, and you can decide whether to answer.
Can an employer ask about my salary expectations instead?

Usually yes. Most salary history bans cover only what you were paid before, not what you want to be paid now. Asking about your expected salary or pay range is generally allowed, so prepare a researched range you can explain.
What if I share my old salary voluntarily?

The rules differ by state and city. Some laws let an employer consider pay history that you offer on your own, without being asked, while others limit how it can be used. Check the local law before deciding to share it.
Does a salary history ban apply to remote jobs?

It often depends on where the job or the worker is located, and laws define this differently. A remote applicant living in a state with a ban may be covered even if the employer is elsewhere. Your state labor department can explain how its law applies.
What can I do if an employer asks about my salary history where it is banned?

You can decline to answer and give your expected range instead. Keep a record of the question, who asked and when. You may be able to file a complaint with your state or city labor agency, or ask an employment lawyer about your options.

Diversity statement.title: What Is a Diversity Statement? Meaning and How to Write One
sections: What a diversity statement means
The term has two meanings in a job search. It can be a short paragraph in a job posting where the employer says it offers equal opportunity and welcomes applicants from all backgrounds.

It can also be a document some employers ask candidates to write, usually one or two pages, describing how they have supported people from different backgrounds in their work. This kind is most common in academic hiring at colleges and universities.
The two are easy to tell apart. If it sits at the bottom of a posting, it is the employer’s statement. If the application asks you to upload one, it is yours to write.
The diversity statement in a job posting

Many postings end with an equal employment opportunity (EEO) statement. It usually says the employer does not discriminate based on traits protected by law, such as race, color, religion, sex, national origin, age, disability or veteran status.

Federal law, mainly Title VII of the Civil Rights Act, the Age Discrimination in Employment Act and the Americans with Disabilities Act, bans this discrimination whether or not a posting says so. Many state and city laws protect more traits, so the list can differ by location.

Some employers add a longer paragraph about the kind of workplace they want to build. Read it as a description of stated policy, then check what you can learn about the actual workplace during interviews.
Diversity statements candidates write

In academic hiring, a diversity statement often sits next to the research and teaching statements. It asks how you have helped students or colleagues from different backgrounds succeed in teaching, mentoring, research or service.

Their use is changing. Several states have passed laws that stop public colleges and universities from requiring them, some private universities have dropped them, and federal policy on diversity programs has shifted. Check each application’s instructions rather than assuming.
Outside academia they are less common, but some nonprofits, public agencies and other employers ask a similar question in an essay prompt or interview.
How to write a strong one

Focus on things you did, not values you hold. Describe specific actions, such as mentoring first-generation students, changing a course to make it more accessible or running an outreach program, and say what happened as a result.
Organize it around past work, current work and plans for the new job. Connect your plans to programs or needs at that employer, which shows you read about them.
Keep to the length asked for, often one to two pages. You do not need to share personal details about your own identity unless you choose to.
qa: What should a diversity statement include?

It should include concrete examples of what you have done to support people from different backgrounds, the results of that work, and what you plan to do in the new role. Tie your plans to the employer’s own programs or student population where you can. Avoid long passages about general beliefs.
How long should a diversity statement be?

Follow the length in the application instructions. When none is given, one to two pages is typical for academic jobs. Shorter prompts in other applications may ask for a few hundred words, so check for a word or character limit before you start.
Is a diversity statement the same as an EEO statement?

Not quite. An EEO statement is the employer’s short note in a posting saying it does not discriminate based on legally protected traits. A diversity statement can mean that note or a longer paragraph about workplace culture, and it can also mean an essay a candidate writes.
Do I need to belong to an underrepresented group to write a diversity statement?

No. The statement is about what you have done to support others and make your work open to more people. Anyone can write one well with clear examples. Sharing details about your own background is optional.
Are diversity statements still required for jobs?

It depends on the employer and the state. Several states bar public colleges from requiring them, and some private institutions have stopped asking. Others still request them. Read each application’s instructions to see whether one is required, optional or not requested.

Overtime.title: What Is Overtime? How Overtime Pay Works and Who Gets It
sections: What overtime means
Overtime is time you work beyond your normal hours. In everyday speech it can mean any extra hours, but in US employment law it has a precise meaning: hours worked over 40 in a single workweek.

Under the federal Fair Labor Standards Act (FLSA), employers must pay covered workers at least one and a half times their regular rate of pay for those extra hours. People often call this “time and a half.”
A workweek is a fixed, repeating period of seven days in a row that the employer sets. Each week stands alone, so a short week cannot be averaged with a long one to avoid overtime.
Who gets overtime pay
Federal overtime rules cover non-exempt employees. Most hourly workers are non-exempt, and some salaried workers are too. Being paid a salary does not on its own remove the right to overtime.

Exempt employees are not owed overtime. To be exempt, a worker usually must be paid a set salary of at least a threshold set by federal rules and do duties that fit a category such as executive, administrative or professional work. The job title alone does not decide it.

States can add more protection. California requires overtime for work over eight hours in a day and double time in some cases, and a few other states, such as Alaska, Nevada and Colorado, have daily overtime rules. Some states also set a higher salary threshold for exemption.

Independent contractors are not covered by overtime law, because they are not employees. If you are treated as a contractor but work like an employee, ask your state labor department or the US Department of Labor.
How overtime pay is worked out
Overtime is based on your regular rate, not just your base hourly wage. Many bonuses, shift differentials and commissions must be included in the regular rate, which can raise the overtime rate.
Federal law does not require extra pay for weekends, holidays or nights unless those hours push you over 40 in the week. Some employers pay a premium anyway by policy or under a union contract.

If your employer knew or should have known you were working extra hours, it generally must pay for them, even if it did not approve them in advance. It can discipline you for breaking a rule, but it cannot withhold the pay.
What a job seeker should ask
Ask whether the role is exempt or non-exempt, how many hours a typical week runs and how often overtime happens. A busy season or on-call duty can change real weekly hours a lot.

Ask how overtime is handled: paid at a higher rate, given as time off, or expected without extra pay. Private-sector employers generally cannot give comp time instead of required overtime pay, though public employers can under set rules.
Keep your own record of hours worked. If you think you are owed overtime, contact your state labor department, the US Department of Labor’s Wage and Hour Division or an employment lawyer.
qa: Is overtime mandatory?

Under federal law, an employer can generally require adult employees to work overtime and can discipline those who refuse, as long as the hours are paid correctly. Some states limit mandatory overtime for certain jobs, such as nurses in health care. Union contracts may also set limits.
Do salaried employees get overtime?

Some do. A salaried employee is owed overtime unless the job meets the tests for an exemption, which include a minimum salary and specific duties. Salaried workers paid below the threshold, or whose duties do not fit an exempt category, must get overtime for hours over 40 in a workweek.
Is overtime taxed more than regular pay?

No. Overtime is taxed at the same rates as other wages, though withholding on a larger paycheck can look higher. A 2025 federal law added a temporary income tax deduction for part of required overtime pay, with a yearly cap and income limits. Ask a tax professional how it applies to you.
Can my employer give me time off instead of overtime pay?

Private employers generally must pay required overtime in money, not comp time. They may adjust your schedule within the same workweek so you stay at or under 40 hours. State and local government employers may offer comp time at one and a half hours per overtime hour under federal rules.
How is overtime calculated?

Multiply your regular rate by one and a half, then by the hours over 40 in the workweek. The regular rate includes most bonuses, commissions and shift pay, not just base wages. In states with daily overtime, hours over a daily limit may also count.

Resignation letter.title: What Is a Resignation Letter? What to Include and How to Send It
sections: What a resignation letter is

A resignation letter is a short letter or email that tells your employer you are quitting and gives your last day of work. It turns a conversation into a written record that both sides can point to later.

In the US most jobs are at-will, so no federal law requires a resignation letter or a set amount of notice. Two weeks is the common custom, but your employment contract, a union agreement or the company handbook may ask for more or require notice in writing.
Many people tell their manager in person or on a call first, then send the letter the same day. The letter usually goes to the manager, with a copy to human resources (HR).
What to include and what to leave out
State clearly that you are resigning, the job title you hold and your last working day as a full date, such as Friday, June 14. A date avoids any argument about how notice is counted.
Add a short thank-you, an offer to help with the handover of your work and a personal email or phone number for later questions. Sign it with your full name and the date.

Leave out complaints, criticism of coworkers and long explanations. You do not have to give a reason for leaving. The letter may sit in your personnel file and be read by people you may need for a reference later.
How and when to send it
Wait until you have a written job offer and any conditions, such as a background check, are cleared. Resigning before then risks leaving you with no job if the offer falls through.
Email is accepted by most employers. If your company uses an HR system or a form for resignations, follow that process too, and keep a copy of what you sent and when.
Count your notice from the day you give it. If your contract asks for a set notice period, make sure your last day falls on or after its end.
What happens after you resign

Your employer may ask you to work until your last day, or it may end your job sooner. In an at-will job it generally does not have to pay you for the notice days you do not work, unless a contract or company policy says otherwise.
When your final paycheck is due and whether unused vacation is paid out depend on the state where you work. Your state labor department can tell you the rules that apply.

Quitting usually makes you ineligible for unemployment benefits unless your state finds you had good cause, and each state defines that differently. Ask your state unemployment agency before resigning if you may need benefits.
qa: Do I have to write a resignation letter?

In most US jobs, no law requires one. Your contract, a union agreement or company policy may require written notice, though. Even when it is optional, a short letter gives you a dated record of when you resigned and what last day you gave.
Can I resign by email?

Yes. Most employers accept an email resignation, and it creates a clear record with a timestamp. It is polite to tell your manager in person or by phone first, then send the email the same day. Follow any HR form or system your company uses as well.
How much notice should a resignation letter give?

Two weeks is the usual custom in the US, though at-will jobs generally do not legally require any notice. Check your contract and the employee handbook, since some roles, especially senior ones, ask for longer. State your last day as a specific date.
Should I give a reason in my resignation letter?

You do not have to. Many people simply say they have accepted another opportunity or are leaving for personal reasons. Keep any explanation short and neutral, and save detailed feedback for an exit interview if you choose to give it.
Can my employer refuse my resignation?

Not in an at-will job; you are free to leave. Your employer can, however, decide to end your job before the last day you gave. If that happens, ask HR about your final pay and check with your state about any effect on unemployment eligibility.

Vesting cliff.title: What Is a Vesting Cliff? How the One-Year Cliff Works
sections: What a vesting cliff means

A vesting cliff is a waiting period at the start of a vesting schedule. During it, nothing vests, so none of the stock options, restricted stock units (RSUs) or other grant is yours yet. When the cliff ends, the portion that would have vested over that time vests all at once.
The name comes from the shape of the schedule on a chart: a flat line at zero, then a sudden jump on the cliff date. After that, vesting usually continues in small steps.

The most common setup for startup and tech equity is a four-year schedule with a one-year cliff. Cliffs can also apply to an employer’s contributions to a retirement plan, where the rules are different.
How a one-year cliff works in practice

Say you get 4,800 options vesting over four years with a one-year cliff. For your first 12 months, nothing vests. On your first anniversary, 1,200 options, a quarter of the grant, vest at once. The rest then usually vests monthly or quarterly until the end of year four.
If you leave before the cliff date, whether you quit or are let go, you usually keep nothing from that grant. Leaving one day after the cliff means you keep the first quarter.

Companies use cliffs so that people who leave quickly do not walk away with equity. Some employers use shorter cliffs, such as six months, and some RSU grants have no cliff at all and vest quarterly from the start.
Cliff vesting in retirement plans
In a 401(k) or similar plan, the money you put in from your own pay is always 100% yours. A vesting schedule can only apply to the employer’s contributions, such as a match.

Federal law sets maximums. Under cliff vesting, employer contributions to a 401(k) must be fully vested after no more than three years of service. Under graded vesting, they must be fully vested after no more than six years.
Your plan’s summary plan description states the exact schedule and how a year of service is counted. Check it before you leave a job close to a vesting date.
What to check and negotiate

Ask for the vesting start date, the cliff length and how often vesting happens after it, all in writing. The start date is sometimes your first day and sometimes the date the board approves the grant, which can be later.
Ask what happens to the cliff if you are laid off, if the company is sold or if you take a leave of absence. Some plans pause vesting during certain leaves.

Some candidates negotiate a shorter cliff, credit for time already worked, or a sign-on bonus to make up for equity they lose by leaving a job before their own cliff. For large or complex grants, an accountant or employment lawyer can review the terms.
qa: What happens if I get fired before my vesting cliff?

In most equity plans, you lose the whole grant, because nothing has vested yet. This is true whether you quit or are let go, unless your offer letter or grant agreement says otherwise. Some people negotiate partial vesting or a cliff waiver if they are laid off, so read the agreement and ask before you sign.
How much vests at a one-year cliff?

On a four-year schedule with a one-year cliff, a quarter of the grant vests on your first anniversary. That is the amount that would have vested over the first year if vesting had been spread out. The remaining three quarters then usually vest in monthly or quarterly steps.
Is a vesting cliff the same as a vesting schedule?

No. The vesting schedule is the full plan for when every part of a grant becomes yours. The cliff is only the first piece of it: the waiting period before anything vests. A schedule can have a cliff, or it can start vesting right away.
Can you negotiate a vesting cliff?

Sometimes. Startups and senior hires have the most room. You can ask for a shorter cliff, no cliff, credit toward the cliff for time you already worked, or a sign-on bonus to cover equity you give up. Get any change written into the offer or grant agreement.
What is cliff vesting in a 401(k)?

It means the employer’s contributions become 100% yours all at once after a set period of service. Federal law requires that period to be no longer than three years for a 401(k). Your own contributions from your paycheck are always fully vested from the start.

Pay equity.title: What Is Pay Equity? Equal Pay Laws and How to Check Your Pay
sections: What pay equity means

Pay equity means people doing the same or similar work, at the same level and with similar results, get paid the same. Differences in pay should come from job-related reasons such as skill, experience or performance, not from gender, race, age or other personal traits.

The idea also covers gaps that build up over time. A common example is pay compression, where new hires get more than long-serving staff in the same role because the market moved and existing salaries did not.
Pay equity is about the whole package. Base salary matters most, but bonuses, equity, raises and starting offers can all create unequal pay.
What US law says about equal pay

The federal Equal Pay Act of 1963 bans paying men and women differently for substantially equal work in the same workplace. Jobs are compared on skill, effort, responsibility and working conditions, not on job titles alone.

An employer can defend a pay gap if it comes from a seniority system, a merit system, a system based on quantity or quality of output, or another factor other than sex. Title VII of the Civil Rights Act also bans pay discrimination based on race, color, religion, sex or national origin, and other federal laws cover age and disability.

Many states go further. Some, such as California, New York and Massachusetts, compare “substantially similar” or “comparable” work, and several states and cities require pay ranges in job postings or ban questions about salary history. Rules differ by state, so check yours.
Why it matters and how employers check it
Unequal pay compounds over a career. A lower starting salary often means smaller raises, smaller retirement contributions and lower offers at the next job when pay is based on past pay.

Many employers run pay equity audits, often with a lawyer or outside analyst. They group employees by role and level, compare pay, and look for gaps that job-related factors do not explain, then fix them.
Clear salary bands, written rules for where a person sits in a band, and consistent raise rules make pay gaps less likely and easier to explain.
What a job seeker or employee can do

Before accepting an offer, ask for the pay range for the role and how the company decides where you land in it. Compare the offer with the posted range and with salary data for the same title and location.

Under the National Labor Relations Act, most private-sector employees have the right to discuss pay with coworkers, and many states protect this too. Comparing notes is often how people first find a gap.

If you think you are paid less for an unfair reason, keep records of your pay, duties and any comparisons. You can raise it with HR, contact the EEOC or your state labor or civil rights agency, or talk to an employment lawyer, since filing deadlines apply.
qa: What is the difference between pay equity and equal pay?

Equal pay usually means the legal rule that people doing the same or substantially equal work get the same pay. Pay equity is a wider idea. It also looks at similar or comparable work, gaps that build up over time and fairness across a whole organization.
Is it legal to pay two people different salaries for the same job?

Yes, if the difference comes from a legitimate, job-related reason such as seniority, merit, measurable output, education or experience. It is illegal when the difference is based on sex, race, color, religion, national origin, age, disability or another protected trait under federal or state law.
Can my employer stop me from talking about my salary?

Generally no. The National Labor Relations Act protects most private-sector employees who discuss pay with coworkers, and many states have their own pay transparency protections. Some groups, such as supervisors and certain government workers, fall under different rules, so check with your state labor department if unsure.
How do I know if I am being paid fairly?

Compare your pay with the posted range for your role, salary surveys for your title and location, and, where you can, what coworkers at your level earn. If you find a gap that skill, experience or performance does not explain, ask HR how your pay was set.
Where do I report pay discrimination?

You can file a charge with the US Equal Employment Opportunity Commission or your state’s civil rights or labor agency. Equal Pay Act claims can also go straight to court. Deadlines are short and differ by law and state, so act quickly and consider talking to an employment lawyer.

Passive candidate.title: What Is a Passive Candidate? Meaning and How Recruiters Find Them
sections: What a passive candidate is

A passive candidate is someone who already has a job and is not applying for new ones, but would consider a move if the right offer came along. The opposite is an active candidate, who is searching, applying and interviewing.
The line between the two is loose. Many people sit in between: they are not applying, but they read the odd posting and reply when a recruiter writes.
Some people would not move for any offer right now. When recruiters say passive candidate, they usually mean the larger group who are not looking but are willing to listen.
Why recruiters look for passive candidates
For many roles, the people with the right skills are already employed and busy doing the work. They never see a job ad, so recruiters go to them instead.
This is called sourcing. Recruiters search professional profiles, portfolios, code repositories, published work and conference talks, ask for referrals, and then send the first message themselves.

Hiring a passive candidate often takes longer and may need a stronger offer, because the person has no reason to leave unless the new job is clearly better. Agency recruiters and executive search firms, often called headhunters, do much of this work for senior and specialist roles.
What to do if you are a passive candidate
Keep your online profile and resume current, with your real job title, skills and results. A recruiter’s message can only be as accurate as what they found about you.

Many professional networking sites let you signal that you are open to offers, sometimes to recruiters only. A public setting can be seen by people at your own company, so check the privacy options before you turn it on.

When a message arrives, ask for the pay range, the team, the location or remote policy and why the role is open before you agree to a call. Since you already have a job, you are free to say no or to negotiate.
Keep any search discreet. Use a personal email and phone, do not use work devices, and book interviews outside work hours where you can.
How employers can approach passive candidates
Send a short, personal first message that says why you chose this person, what the role is and, if you can, the pay range. Generic messages sent to many people at once are easy to ignore.
Offer an informal conversation before asking for a formal application, and keep the process short. A passive candidate can drop out at any step, because staying in their current job is a safe choice.
Some states and cities require pay ranges in job postings and, in some places, on request during hiring. Check the rules where the job is based, or ask an employment lawyer if you are unsure.
qa: What is the difference between an active and a passive candidate?

An active candidate is looking for a job: applying, answering postings and interviewing. A passive candidate has a job and is not applying anywhere, but would talk about a good offer. The first usually finds the employer; with the second, the employer or recruiter makes the first contact.
How do recruiters find passive candidates?

They search professional networking profiles, online portfolios, code repositories, published articles and conference speaker lists. They also ask current employees and contacts for referrals. Once they find a likely match, they send a direct message or email about a specific role.
Should I reply to a recruiter if I am not looking for a job?

A short, polite reply is usually worth it. You can say you are not interested now, or ask for the pay range and details before deciding. Being courteous keeps the door open for a better role later, and you lose nothing by listening.
How can I show recruiters I am open to offers without my employer knowing?

Many networking sites have an open-to-work setting that can be shown to recruiters only, though no setting can fully guarantee privacy. Keep your profile current, use a personal email address, and tell trusted contacts in your field quietly rather than posting publicly.
Are passive candidates better hires than active ones?

Not by default. Some recruiters assume employed people are stronger, but many skilled people look for work because of layoffs, moves or career changes. A hire’s quality depends on skills and fit, not on whether they applied or were found by a recruiter.

Transferable skills.title: What Are Transferable Skills? Examples and How to Show Them
sections: What transferable skills are

Transferable skills are abilities you can carry from one job, field or setting to another. Writing clearly, planning a project, working with numbers, solving problems and dealing with people are useful almost anywhere.

They differ from job-specific skills, such as running a certain machine or coding in one language, which matter mostly in one kind of work. Many transferable skills are soft skills, but some are technical, such as spreadsheets or data analysis.
You build them in paid jobs, and also in school, volunteering, caregiving, the military, sports and side projects.
Why transferable skills matter

They matter most when you change careers, return to work after a break, leave the military or apply for your first job. In each case your past titles may not match the new posting, but your skills can.
Employers want proof that you can do the work, not just a matching job title. Showing how a skill worked in one setting helps a hiring manager picture you doing the same thing in theirs.
They also help you stay employable as jobs change, because tools and industries shift faster than core abilities like communication and problem solving.
Common examples of transferable skills
Communication: writing reports and emails, presenting, explaining complex ideas simply and listening well.
Organization and planning: managing time, setting priorities, running projects, meeting deadlines and keeping records.
Working with people: teamwork, customer service, training others, leading a group, negotiating and handling conflict.
Analysis and numbers: budgeting, reading data, spotting problems, finding causes and using spreadsheets or other common software.
How to show transferable skills on a resume and in interviews
Read several postings in your target field and note the words they use for skills. Then describe your own experience in those words, as long as they are true for you.
Back each skill with a result. Instead of “strong organizer”, write something like “planned weekly schedules for a team of 12 and cut overtime”, using real details from your work.
Put a short summary at the top of your resume that links your background to the new role. In interviews, tell brief stories that explain the situation, what you did and what happened.
qa: What are the top transferable skills employers look for?

Communication, problem solving, teamwork, organization, adaptability and basic computer skills come up in postings across most fields. Leadership, customer service and working with data are also widely valued. The exact list depends on the job, so check the postings you are targeting.
How do I list transferable skills on a resume?

Add a skills section using the words from the posting, and show the same skills in your experience bullets with a concrete result. A short summary at the top can explain how your past work connects to the new role, which helps when your job titles do not match.
Are transferable skills the same as soft skills?

Not exactly. Many transferable skills are soft skills, such as communication and teamwork. But some technical skills transfer too, like spreadsheets, writing, project management or data analysis. A skill is transferable when it is useful in more than one kind of job.
How do I find my transferable skills?

List the tasks you did in past jobs, school, volunteering or home life, then ask which abilities each task needed. Compare that list with postings in your target field. Feedback from coworkers and past performance reviews can point to strengths you overlook.
Do transferable skills help when changing careers?

Yes. They are often the main link between your old work and a new field. Show them with results and in the new field’s language, and fill any real gaps with a course, certificate or project if the posting requires specific knowledge.

Shift differential.title: What Is a Shift Differential? How Extra Pay for Shifts Works
sections: What a shift differential is
A shift differential is extra pay on top of your base hourly rate for working less popular hours. These are usually evening, overnight, weekend or holiday shifts.
Employers use it to fill shifts that fewer people want to work. It is common in hospitals and nursing homes, warehouses, factories, call centers, security, hotels and retail.
The extra pay applies only to the hours worked in the qualifying shift. If you work a mix of day and night hours, only the night hours usually earn the differential.
How shift differentials are paid
Most employers pay it in one of two ways. One is a flat amount added per hour, such as an extra two dollars. The other is a percentage of your base rate, such as ten percent more.
Each employer sets its own rules: which hours count as evening or night, whether weekends earn a separate rate, and whether differentials stack when a shift is both overnight and on a weekend.
Shift differential pay is taxed like the rest of your wages. It shows up on your pay stub, often as its own line, and on your W-2 as part of your total pay.
What the law says
The federal Fair Labor Standards Act does not require private employers to pay a shift differential. It is a choice the employer makes, or a term set in a union contract or an employment agreement.

If you are paid overtime, a night or evening shift differential generally counts as part of your regular rate under federal rules. That means your overtime rate should be figured on base pay plus the differential, not base pay alone.

Federal government employees get night pay set by federal law, and some state or local public jobs have their own rules. If you think your pay is calculated wrongly, ask your state labor department or the US Department of Labor’s Wage and Hour Division.
What job seekers should check

When you compare shift jobs, add the base rate and the differential together for the hours you would actually work. A lower base rate with a large night differential can pay more than a higher base rate with none.
Ask whether the differential is guaranteed in writing, which hours qualify, and whether it continues if you move to a different shift later.
Think about the cost of the schedule too. Overnight and weekend work can affect sleep, childcare and family time, so weigh the extra pay against what the hours ask of you.
qa: How much is a typical shift differential?

There is no standard amount. Employers set their own rates, often as a flat extra amount per hour or a percentage of the base rate. Night and weekend rates are often higher than evening rates. Check the job posting or ask the recruiter for the exact figure.
Is shift differential required by law?

Not for most private-sector jobs in the US. Federal law does not require it, so it depends on the employer’s policy, a union contract or your employment agreement. Federal government workers receive night pay under federal law, and some public employers have their own rules.
Does shift differential count toward overtime pay?

Generally yes. Under federal overtime rules, a differential paid for night or evening hours is included in your regular rate. Your overtime rate should be at least one and a half times that combined rate, not just your base rate. Holiday or weekend premiums paid at time and a half or more can be treated differently.
Is shift differential the same as holiday pay?

Not exactly. A shift differential is extra pay for working certain hours, such as nights. Holiday pay can mean pay for a day off on a holiday or premium pay for working on one. Private employers are not required by federal law to offer either.
Is shift differential taxed differently?
No. It is ordinary wages and is subject to the same federal, state and payroll taxes as your base pay. It is included in your total wages on your W-2.

Tech stack.title: What Is a Tech Stack? Meaning in Job Postings Explained
sections: What a tech stack means

A tech stack is the set of technologies a team uses to build and run its product. It usually includes programming languages, frameworks, databases, cloud services and the tools used to test and ship code.

It is called a stack because the pieces sit in layers. The front end is what users see in a browser or app, the back end is the server code and logic, and below that are the database and the infrastructure that hosts everything.
Some stacks have short names. LAMP stands for Linux, Apache, MySQL and PHP, and MERN stands for MongoDB, Express, React and Node.js. Most companies mix and match instead of following a named stack.
How the tech stack shows up in a job posting

Many tech job postings have a section called “Our stack” or “Tech we use”. It lists the tools you would work with every day, such as Python, React, PostgreSQL, Docker and a cloud provider like AWS, Google Cloud or Azure.
Postings often split the list into required skills and nice-to-have skills. The required ones are what the team expects you to use from day one, while the rest can usually be learned on the job.

The stack also tells you about the work. An older stack may mean maintaining existing systems, while a newer one may mean building fresh features, and a long list can mean a small team where each person covers many areas.
What to do as a job seeker
Compare the stack with what you already know. You rarely need every item, but you should be solid in the main language and framework the role names as required.

On your resume, list the technologies you have really used, and put the ones that match the posting first. Show them in context in your experience, for example “built an API in Python and PostgreSQL”, not only in a skills list.

In interviews, ask why the team chose its stack, what it plans to change and how much older code you would maintain. Do not claim tools you cannot discuss, because technical interviews often test them directly.
What employers should include

List the main languages, frameworks and services the role uses, and mark clearly which are required and which are a bonus. A clear, honest list helps the right people apply and saves time screening those who do not fit.
Keep the list current. A stack section that names tools the team has dropped confuses candidates and can lead to interviews that go nowhere.
qa: What is an example of a tech stack?

A common web stack is React for the front end, Node.js or Python for the back end, PostgreSQL as the database and a cloud provider such as AWS to host it. Named stacks include LAMP (Linux, Apache, MySQL, PHP) and MERN (MongoDB, Express, React, Node.js).
Do I need to know every tool in a company’s tech stack?

Usually not. Employers expect you to know the core language and framework marked as required, and they often teach the rest on the job. If you know a similar tool, such as one database instead of another, say so in your application and interview.
What is a full stack developer?

A full stack developer works on both the front end, which users see, and the back end, which runs on servers and handles data. They do not need to be experts in every layer, but they can build and change features across the whole stack.
How do I list my tech stack on a resume?

Add a short skills section grouped by type, such as languages, frameworks, databases and tools, with the ones the posting asks for first. Then mention the same technologies in your job bullet points, so readers and applicant tracking systems see where you used them.
Is a tech stack only for software developers?

No. Data analysts, designers, IT staff, marketers and other roles also have stacks, meaning the software they use daily, such as SQL, BI tools, design software or a CRM. Job postings for these roles often list them the same way.

Right to disconnect.title: What Is the Right to Disconnect? Laws, Policies and Your Options
sections: What the right to disconnect means

The right to disconnect is the idea that an employee does not have to read or answer work emails, messages or calls outside working hours. It also usually means the employee cannot be punished for staying offline.

It grew out of phones and remote work, which made it easy for work to reach people at night, on weekends and on vacation. Where it exists, it can be a law, a rule in a union contract or simply a company policy.
Where it is law and where it is not

France was an early adopter, requiring larger employers to set rules on off-hours contact from 2017. Portugal, Spain, Belgium and Australia have their own versions, and Ontario in Canada requires larger employers to have a written policy. The details differ a lot from country to country.

In the US there is no federal right to disconnect, and no state has passed a general one. Bills have been proposed, including in California and New York City, but none has become law as of this writing.

Australia’s law, which began in 2024, lets employees refuse to monitor or respond to off-hours contact unless the refusal is unreasonable. That shows a common pattern: the right is often limited, not absolute.
What US workers can rely on instead

Under the federal Fair Labor Standards Act, nonexempt workers must be paid for work the employer knows or should know about. Answering work emails or calls after hours generally counts as work time, and it can add up to overtime.
Exempt salaried workers do not earn overtime, so after-hours work is not paid separately. For them, limits on off-hours contact come only from company policy, a contract or the manager’s habits.

On-call rules are separate. Whether on-call time must be paid depends on how much it restricts you, and some states add their own rules. For a specific dispute, ask your state labor department or an employment lawyer.
What job seekers and employers should do
In interviews, ask how quickly people are expected to reply in the evening and on weekends, and whether there is an on-call rotation. Ask how time zones are handled on distributed teams.
Once hired, if you are nonexempt, record all time spent on work messages outside your shift. Turning off notifications and setting status hours can help, but check what your manager expects first.
Employers can write a clear policy on off-hours contact, use scheduled sending and define what counts as urgent. Paying nonexempt staff for after-hours work is required, not optional.
qa: Is there a right to disconnect in the US?

No. There is no federal right to disconnect, and no US state has passed a general right-to-disconnect law. Some bills have been proposed, including in California and New York City. Protection in the US comes mainly from wage law, which requires nonexempt workers to be paid for after-hours work, and from company policies.
Do I get paid for answering work emails after hours?

If you are a nonexempt employee in the US, time spent answering work emails or calls is generally work time that must be paid, including overtime when you go over 40 hours in a week. If you are exempt, your salary covers it. If you are unsure of your status, check with your state labor department.
Can I be fired for not answering work calls after hours?

In most US jobs, which are at-will, an employer can generally discipline or fire someone for not meeting its expectations about availability, unless a contract, union agreement or other law protects them. In countries with a right-to-disconnect law, such punishment may be restricted. Ask an employment lawyer about a specific case.
Which countries have a right to disconnect law?

France, Portugal, Spain, Belgium and Australia are among the countries with right-to-disconnect laws, and Ontario in Canada requires larger employers to have a written policy. Each law works differently, with different rules on which employers are covered and what counts as an exception.
How do I ask about after-hours expectations in an interview?

Keep it practical: ask how quickly people usually reply to messages in the evening or on weekends, whether the team has on-call duty, and how urgent issues are handled. Asking what a typical week looks like often gives an honest answer without sounding like you want to avoid work.

Relocation.title: What Is Relocation Assistance? How Relocation Packages Work
sections: What relocation means in a job offer
Relocation, or relocation assistance, is help from an employer to cover the cost of moving for a new job. It can apply to a move to another city, another state or another country.

The help is often called a relocation package. It may cover packing and moving your belongings, travel for you and your family, temporary housing, house-hunting trips and sometimes costs of selling or leaving a home.

In job postings you may also see “relocation offered” or “relocation not available”. A posting that asks if you are “open to relocation” is asking whether you are willing to move, not promising to pay for it.
Common types of relocation help
A lump sum is a fixed amount paid to you, usually through payroll. You decide how to spend it, and you keep anything left over, but you pay any costs above it yourself.
Reimbursement means you pay costs first and send receipts, and the employer pays you back up to a limit. Direct billing means the employer pays the moving company or a relocation firm itself.

For moves to another country, help may also cover visa and immigration costs, shipping, language or cultural training and support finding schools or housing. What is covered depends entirely on the employer and the role.
Taxes and repayment agreements

Under current federal law, employer-paid moving costs are generally taxable income for most employees, whether paid as a lump sum or as reimbursement. Active-duty military members moving under orders are a main exception.
Some employers pay extra to cover the tax, called a gross-up, so the move costs you less. State tax rules can differ from federal rules, so ask an accountant how your package will be taxed.
Many employers ask you to sign a repayment agreement. If you quit or are fired for cause within a set time, often one or two years, you may have to pay back all or part of the money.
What to ask before you accept
Ask whether the help is a lump sum, reimbursement or direct billing, what the limit is, and which costs count. Ask whether the employer grosses up for taxes.
Read the repayment terms closely. Check how long they last, whether the amount owed shrinks over time and whether you must repay if you are laid off.
Relocation help is often negotiable, especially for hard-to-fill roles. If the offer has none, you can ask for it, or ask for a signing bonus or a later start date instead.
qa: What does relocation mean in a job posting?

It means the employer may help pay for you to move to where the job is. “Relocation offered” or “relocation assistance available” signals help with moving costs, while “no relocation” means you must pay for any move yourself. The details are usually discussed during the offer stage.
Is relocation assistance taxable?

Yes, for most US employees employer-paid moving costs are treated as taxable wages under current federal law, with an exception for certain active-duty military moves. State rules can differ. Some employers add a tax gross-up to cover the extra tax. Ask an accountant about your own situation.
Do I have to pay back relocation if I quit?

Only if you signed an agreement that says so. Many relocation agreements require repayment if you leave within a set period, often one or two years, sometimes reduced month by month. Read the agreement before signing, and ask a lawyer if the terms are unclear.
Can I negotiate a relocation package?

Often yes. You can ask for a higher lump sum, a longer stay in temporary housing, a tax gross-up, a shorter repayment period or a signing bonus to cover moving costs. Give the employer a realistic estimate of your moving costs to support the request.
What is a relocation lump sum?

It is a fixed amount the employer pays you to cover your move, usually through payroll and taxed as wages. You choose how to spend it and keep what is left, but you pay any costs above the amount yourself.

Backfill.title: What Is a Backfill Position? Meaning in Hiring and What to Ask
sections: What a backfill means in hiring
A backfill is a job opening that exists because someone left a role and the employer is hiring a replacement. The job, its budget and its place on the team already exist. Only the person is new.
The opposite is a new or net-new role, sometimes called a growth hire or new headcount. The company adds it because the team is growing or taking on new work.
A role may need backfilling after a resignation, retirement, firing, promotion or internal transfer. Recruiters and hiring managers use the word often, but job postings rarely say it.
Temporary backfills for leave
Sometimes the person has not left for good. A temporary backfill covers someone on parental, medical or other extended leave, often through a staffing agency or a fixed-term contract.

Under the federal Family and Medical Leave Act, an eligible employee who returns from protected leave is generally entitled to the same or an equivalent job. So a temporary backfill usually ends when that employee comes back. Some states have their own leave laws with added protections.
If an opening covers someone’s leave, ask how long it is expected to last and whether a permanent position might follow.
Why a backfill matters to a job seeker

A backfill often moves faster than a new role because the budget is already approved and the team knows what the job involves. During a hiring freeze, some companies still allow backfills while pausing new roles. Others freeze both.
A backfill comes with a history. You can learn what the last person did well, where they struggled and how the job has changed since they were hired.
Several backfills for the same job in a short time can point to problems such as an unrealistic workload, a difficult manager or low pay. One departure on its own usually means little.
What to ask, and what employers should do

In the interview, ask why the position is open, how long the previous person was in the role and where they went. A promotion or an internal move is a good sign. Repeated quick exits deserve follow-up questions.
Ask whether the job is the same as before or has changed, and what the team expects in your first few months. If the previous person is still there, ask whether there will be a handover.

For employers, a departure is a chance to review the role before posting it. Update the job description to match the work as it is now, rather than copying the old one, and be ready to explain honestly why the job is open.
qa: What does backfill mean in a job?

It means the job is open because the person who held it left, moved to another role or went on leave, and the employer is hiring someone to fill the same position. It is a replacement hire, not a new role created for growth.
Is a backfill position a good thing?

It can be. The role is already budgeted and defined, so hiring is often quicker and expectations are clearer. Whether it is good for you depends on why the last person left. A promotion is reassuring, while several people leaving the same job quickly is worth asking about.
What is the difference between a backfill and new headcount?

A backfill replaces someone in a role that already exists and is already in the budget. New headcount is an extra position the company adds, usually for growth or a new project, and it often needs separate budget approval before hiring can start.
Is it OK to ask why a position is open?

Yes. It is a common and reasonable interview question. You can ask whether the role is new or a replacement, how long the last person stayed and how the job has changed. The answer tells you a lot about the team and the role.
Can an employer decide not to backfill a role?

Yes. An employer may leave a role empty, split the work among the team or remove the position, for example to cut costs or reorganize. Backfills are often reviewed before approval, and some are cancelled even after the job is posted.

Resume keywords.title: What Are Resume Keywords? How to Find and Use Them
sections: What resume keywords are
Resume keywords are the words and phrases that describe what a job needs. They include hard skills, software and tools, job titles, certifications, licenses and industry terms.

Recruiters type these words into an applicant tracking system (ATS), the software that stores applications, to search the applicant pool. Hiring managers also scan for them when they read a resume by hand.

Most keywords come straight from the job posting. A posting for an accountant might name “accounts payable,” “month-end close,” “GAAP” and “Excel,” and those are the words a recruiter is likely to search.
Soft skills such as “team player” or “hard worker” are rarely searched, because anyone can claim them. They count more when your results show them.
How keywords are used in hiring

In many ATS products, recruiters search or filter applicants by keyword, much like a search engine. If your resume says “client relations” and the recruiter searches “customer service,” you may not show up, even with the same experience.
Some systems also rank or score applicants by how closely their profile matches the posting. How this works differs by product and by employer, and many recruiters still read resumes themselves.
Keywords help you get found and read, but a person makes the hiring decision. A resume packed with keywords and no proof of what you achieved rarely leads to an interview.
How to find and use the right keywords

Read the posting and mark the skills, tools, certifications and titles it names, especially ones that appear more than once or sit under “requirements.” Compare a few postings for the same role to see which terms keep coming up.

Use the posting’s exact wording where it is true for you. List the main ones in a skills section and repeat them in your experience bullet points, where you show how and with what result you used them.
Spell out each acronym once, for example “certified public accountant (CPA).” Do not change past job titles; if your title was unusual, you can add the common equivalent in parentheses.
Never list skills you do not have or hide keywords in white or tiny text. Recruiters notice, some systems flag it, and it falls apart in the interview.
qa: What are examples of resume keywords?

Examples include hard skills such as “budgeting” or “patient care,” tools such as “Salesforce” or “Python,” certifications such as “PMP” or “CDL Class A,” and job titles such as “project manager.” The right keywords depend on the job, so take them from the posting you are applying to.
How many keywords should a resume have?

There is no set number. Aim to include the main skills, tools and qualifications the posting asks for that you really have, each used naturally once or twice. Repeating a word many times does not help and makes the resume harder to read.
Where should keywords go on a resume?

Put them in your summary, a skills section and your experience bullet points. The skills section makes them easy to find, while the bullet points prove you used them. Keep them in the main body of the document, not in headers, footers, tables or images that software may not read.
Will an ATS reject my resume if it is missing keywords?

Most systems do not reject people on their own for missing keywords. Rejections usually come from knock-out screening questions the employer set or from a recruiter who searched and did not find you. Missing keywords mainly make you harder to find and less convincing.
Should I change my resume keywords for each job?

Yes, adjust them for each application. Postings for the same role often use different words for the same skill, so swap in the posting’s terms where they are accurate. Keep a master resume and edit a copy for each job.

No degree required.title: What Does No Degree Required Mean in a Job Posting?
sections: What no degree required means
When a job posting says “no degree required,” the employer is stating that a college or university degree is not needed to apply or to be hired. That covers associate, bachelor’s and higher degrees.
It does not always mean no education at all. Many of these postings still ask for a high school diploma or GED, and some ask for a license, a certificate or a set number of years of experience.
The phrase is different from “degree preferred,” where a degree helps but is not a must. It is also different from “degree or equivalent experience,” where experience can stand in for the degree.
Why employers drop degree requirements

Many employers have moved toward skills-based hiring, which means judging candidates by what they can do rather than by their diplomas. Removing a degree requirement widens the pool of people who can apply.

Several state governments, starting with Maryland in 2022, have removed degree requirements from many state jobs. Some private employers have done the same for roles such as IT support, sales, customer service and skilled trades.
In practice, some hiring managers still favor degree holders even when the posting says it is not required. Strong evidence of your skills is what closes that gap.
How to apply for a job with no degree required

Read the requirements closely. Look for what the employer does ask for, such as a diploma, a driver’s license, a trade license, a security clearance or specific software skills, and make sure you meet those.
On your resume, lead with skills and results instead of education. Use numbers where you can, such as tickets closed per week, sales made or projects finished on time.

Add proof that a recruiter can check, such as certificates, a portfolio, links to past work, completed apprenticeships or military training. List any coursework you finished, even if you did not earn a degree.
In the interview, be ready to show the skill directly through a test, a work sample or examples from past jobs. Do not apologize for not having a degree.
qa: Does no degree required mean no experience needed?

No. The phrase only means a college degree is not needed. The employer may still ask for years of experience, specific skills, a license or a high school diploma. Look for words such as “entry level” or “no experience required” if you are just starting out.
Do I need a high school diploma if no degree is required?

Often yes. Many postings that drop the college degree still ask for a high school diploma or GED. If the posting does not mention it, check the full requirements list or ask the recruiter before you apply.
Should I put education on my resume if I have no degree?

You can include a high school diploma, GED, trade school, certificates or college courses you completed. Place the section near the bottom and put your skills and experience first, since those are what the employer is judging.
What kinds of jobs often say no degree required?

Common examples include skilled trades, customer service, sales, IT support, warehouse and logistics roles, some administrative jobs and many state government positions. Some tech roles also hire on skills and portfolios rather than degrees.
Can a job that says no degree required pay well?

Yes, some do, especially skilled trades, sales roles with commission and technical jobs that need certifications. Pay depends on the role, the employer and the location, so compare the posted pay range with similar jobs in your area.

Headcount.title: What Is Headcount? Approved Headcount and Hiring Explained
sections: What headcount means

Headcount is the number of people a team, department or company employs, or is allowed to employ. In hiring talk it usually means the second: the positions a budget pays for, whether or not someone fills them yet.

When a manager says “we have headcount”, they mean they have approval and money to hire. “One headcount” is one position. An open headcount, often called an open req, is an approved position waiting to be filled.

Headcount counts people, not hours. A part-time worker counts as one head, while full-time equivalent (FTE) adds up hours, so two half-time workers make one FTE. Contractors and agency temps are often tracked separately from employee headcount.
How headcount gets approved

Many companies plan headcount once a year along with the budget. Each department asks for roles, finance and leadership decide which ones to fund, and approved roles become job requisitions in the hiring system.

A backfill replaces someone who left, using headcount that already existed. New headcount is an extra role that grows the team. Backfills are often approved faster because the cost is already in the budget.

A headcount freeze, or hiring freeze, stops new approvals and sometimes pauses open roles too. Approved headcount can also be taken back if plans or revenue change, which is one reason a posted job sometimes closes without anyone being hired.
What headcount means for job seekers

A role with approved headcount has money behind it and a reason to be filled soon. Some postings are speculative, such as evergreen or pipeline postings that collect candidates for roles the company may open later.
In a first call it is fine to ask, “Is this a new role or a backfill?” and “Is the position approved and budgeted?” The answers tell you how urgent the hire is and why the job exists.
If a recruiter says a role is on hold pending headcount, keep applying elsewhere. Stay in touch, but do not turn down other offers while you wait for an approval that may never come.
qa: What does headcount mean in a job?

It means a position the company has approved and budgeted for. When a hiring manager says they have headcount, they have permission and money to hire someone. Without headcount, a manager may want to hire but cannot make an offer.
What is the difference between headcount and FTE?

Headcount counts people, so every employee counts as one no matter how many hours they work. FTE, or full-time equivalent, counts hours, so two people working half time add up to one FTE. Companies often use both numbers when planning budgets.
What is a headcount freeze?

A headcount freeze is a decision to stop adding positions for a period, usually to control costs. Some freezes also stop backfills and pause roles already posted. Candidates in the middle of interviews may see the process put on hold or cancelled.
What is a headcount reduction?

A headcount reduction is a cut in the number of employees. It can happen through layoffs, by not replacing people who leave, or by ending contracts. Under the federal WARN Act, covered employers must generally give 60 days’ notice of plant closings and mass layoffs, and some states have their own rules.
Is a backfill role more likely to be filled?

Often yes, because the position and its cost already exist in the budget, and the team usually feels the gap right away. It is still worth asking why the last person left, since the answer can tell you about the job and the manager.

Learning budget.title: What Is a Learning Budget? How It Works and What to Ask
sections: What a learning budget is

A learning budget is a set amount of money an employer lets each employee spend on their own professional development. It usually resets every year and covers things like online courses, books, workshops, certifications and conference tickets.

Job postings may call it a learning stipend, education allowance, training budget or professional development budget. It is a benefit, not part of your salary, and the amount and rules vary widely from one employer to the next.
It differs from tuition assistance, which usually pays toward a college degree, often with stricter rules. Some employers offer both, and some offer neither.
How a learning budget usually works
Most employers set a yearly amount per person. Unspent money often does not roll over to the next year, so it works on a use-it-or-lose-it basis unless the policy says otherwise.

You may pay first and claim the cost back with a receipt, or the company may pay the provider directly. Many policies require manager approval and limit spending to learning related to your current job or a role you could grow into.
Some employers add paid time for learning, such as a few days a year for conferences or study. Others expect you to learn outside work hours, so it is worth asking.
Taxes and repayment rules

In the US, job-related training an employer pays for is often tax-free to you as a working condition fringe benefit. Other education can be tax-free up to a yearly limit set by tax law if the employer has a written educational assistance program.
A flat cash stipend you can spend freely is usually treated as taxable wages. How your employer handles it depends on its policy, so ask HR or an accountant if you are unsure.

Some employers ask you to repay costly courses or certifications if you leave within a set time. Several states now limit these repayment agreements, so read the terms and contact your state labor department or a lawyer if a demand seems unfair.
What a job seeker should do
When a posting mentions a learning budget, ask how much it is, what it covers, who approves spending and whether you choose the courses or your manager does.
Also ask whether unused money rolls over, whether paid time for learning is included and whether any repayment agreement applies. These details show how much the benefit is really worth.
Once hired, plan your spending early in the year. Pick courses or events tied to skills your team needs, since that makes approval easier and helps your career at the same time.
qa: What is a typical learning budget?

There is no standard amount. It ranges from a small yearly sum for books and online courses to enough for a conference trip or a certification.
