Startups and tech companies often list one in postings, while others handle training case by case. Ask the recruiter for the exact figure and what it covers.
Is a learning stipend taxable?

It depends on how it is set up. In the US, employer-paid training tied to your job is often tax-free, and a written educational assistance program can cover other education tax-free up to a yearly limit. A cash stipend with no conditions is usually taxed as wages. Check your pay stub or ask HR.
Can I use my learning budget for anything?

Usually not. Most policies require the learning to relate to your current role or career path at the company, and many need manager approval first. Common approved items are courses, books, certifications and conferences. Read your company’s policy before you buy something.
Do I have to pay back my learning budget if I quit?

Normally not for small purchases like books or online courses. Some employers require repayment of larger costs, such as certifications or degrees, if you leave within a set period, but only if you signed an agreement. Some states restrict these agreements, so check the terms and your state’s rules.
Should I negotiate a learning budget in a job offer?

You can. If the salary is fixed, a learning budget, conference time or paid certification can be easier for an employer to add. Ask for it in writing in the offer letter so the amount and rules are clear.

Graduate program.title: What Is a Graduate Program? How Entry-Level Programs Work
sections: What a graduate program is

A graduate program is a structured first job for people who have just finished a degree. You join as a full-time, paid employee, often with a group of other new hires who start together, called a cohort.

Many programs rotate you through several teams or locations over one or two years. Others keep you in one function but add formal training, a mentor and regular reviews. At the end, you usually move into a permanent role.

The name varies by country. In the UK and Australia, “graduate scheme” or “graduate program” is the common term. In the US, the same idea is often called a rotational program, leadership development program, analyst program or new grad program.
A note on the other meaning
In the US, “graduate program” also means a master’s or doctoral degree program at a university. If you search for it, you may see both meanings mixed together.

In a job posting, the phrase almost always means an entry-level employment program. A university listing means further study. Check whether the page talks about salary and a start date or about tuition and admission.
How hiring for graduate programs works

Many large employers recruit months before the start date. In the US, it is common to apply in the fall of your final year for a job that starts the following summer. UK schemes often open in the autumn and close over the winter, though timing differs by employer and industry.
Some programs review applications as they arrive and close early once they are full, so a later deadline does not always mean you can wait. Others fill many places from their own internship programs.

The process often includes an online application, aptitude or skills tests, a recorded video interview and a final round, sometimes called an assessment center, with group tasks and interviews. Offers are usually conditional on finishing your degree.
What a job seeker should do
Make a list of employers you want in your field and check their careers pages early in your final year. Note each opening date and deadline in a calendar, and apply as soon as you are ready.

Read the eligibility rules closely. Programs may require a degree in certain subjects, graduation within a set number of years, a minimum grade or the right to work in the country without sponsorship.

Ask what happens at the end: whether a permanent role is expected, how rotations are chosen, whether you may need to relocate and whether the salary changes after the program. If a program is not open, standard entry-level roles are a good alternative.
qa: Is a graduate program a paid job?

Yes. A graduate program in the employment sense is a full-time job with a salary and usually the same benefits as other employees. It is different from an unpaid internship or from a university graduate program, where you pay tuition to study.
When should I apply for graduate programs?

Usually early in your final year of study, and often close to a year before the start date. Many close before their stated deadline once they have enough applicants, so check employer careers pages at the start of the season and apply early.
Can I join a graduate program if I graduated a few years ago?

Often yes, but it depends on the employer. Some programs accept anyone who graduated within a set number of years, while others want only final-year students or very recent graduates. The eligibility section of each posting says what that program accepts.
What is the difference between a graduate program and an entry-level job?

Both are for people early in their careers. A graduate program adds structure, such as a cohort start date, formal training, mentoring and often rotations through several teams. A regular entry-level job puts you straight into one role and usually hires all year round.
What is a rotational program?

A rotational program is a common US name for a graduate program in which you spend set periods, often several months each, in different teams or functions. At the end, you usually choose or are placed in one permanent role.

Job shadowing.title: What Is Job Shadowing? How It Works and How to Set One Up
sections: What job shadowing means
Job shadowing is spending time beside someone while they do their job, so you can see what the work is really like. You watch, listen and ask questions, but you do not do the work yourself.

A shadow can last a few hours, a full day or several days spread over weeks. It is usually unpaid and informal, arranged directly with the person you shadow or through a school, college or employer program.

Students use it to explore careers, career changers use it before they retrain, and new or moving employees use it to learn a role inside their own company. In the UK and some other countries the same idea is often called work shadowing.
How job shadowing differs from an internship
In an internship you do real work for the employer, often for pay and for weeks or months. In job shadowing you only observe, which is why it is short and usually unpaid.

An informational interview is a conversation about someone’s job, usually 20 to 30 minutes. A shadow lets you see the job itself: the meetings, the tools, the pace and the parts nobody mentions in a conversation.
An externship sits in between. It is usually a short, school-arranged placement, often unpaid, mostly observing with perhaps a few small tasks. The exact meaning varies by school and field.
How to set up a job shadow

Start with people you already know: friends, family, former coworkers, alumni of your school or contacts on professional networks. Ask a specific question, such as whether you could shadow them for half a day in the next month.
Explain why you want to shadow, keep the request short and offer to fit their schedule. Many people say yes when the ask is small and clear.

Expect some paperwork in certain settings. Hospitals, labs and schools often require a confidentiality agreement, a liability waiver, proof of vaccinations or a background check before you can shadow.
How to get the most from the day
Dress like the people who work there, arrive early and bring a notebook. Stay quiet in meetings with clients or patients unless you are invited to speak.
Ask about the hard parts as well as the good ones: the worst part of the week, what a bad day looks like, how people get into the field and what they wish they had known.
Send a thank-you note within a day or two. Keep in touch, because the person you shadowed may later be a reference or tell you about openings.
qa: Do you get paid for job shadowing?

Usually not. Job shadowing is meant for watching and learning, not doing productive work, so it is normally unpaid. If you are asked to do real work for the business, the arrangement may start to look like employment, and you can ask the state labor department or a lawyer whether pay is required.
How long does job shadowing last?

Most job shadows last from a few hours to a full day. Some run over several days or are spread across weeks, especially in healthcare, where students often need a set number of shadowing hours for school applications.
Does job shadowing count as experience on a resume?

It can go on a resume, but list it honestly as job shadowing, not as work experience. Put it under a section such as Career exploration or Relevant activities, with the field, the setting and what you observed.
Why is shadowing important for pre-med students?

Many medical schools expect applicants to show they understand what a doctor’s work involves, and shadowing physicians is a common way to show that. Requirements differ by school, so check each program’s admissions page for what it expects.
How do I ask someone if I can shadow them?

Send a short, polite message saying who you are, why you are interested in their field and what you are asking for, such as half a day in the next few weeks. Offer to work around their schedule and thank them whatever they answer.

Remote-first.title: What Is Remote-First? How It Differs From Remote-Friendly and Hybrid
sections: What remote-first means

A remote-first company builds its way of working around people who are not in an office. Meetings, documents, decisions and promotions are set up so that someone working from home has the same access as anyone else.
The company may still have offices or coworking spaces, but going there is optional. Some remote-first companies bring teams together in person a few times a year for planning or social events.
The term describes how the company works, not where every employee may live. Many remote-first employers still limit hiring to certain countries, states or time zones.
Remote-first compared with fully remote, remote-friendly and hybrid
Fully remote, also called remote-only or all-remote, means the company has no office at all. Remote-first means remote work is the default, even if an office exists.
Remote-friendly usually means the company is office-based but lets some people work from home. Those remote workers can miss informal talk and decisions made in the room.
Hybrid means employees split their time between home and the office, often on set days. A hybrid role with required office days is not remote-first, even if the posting uses the word remote.
Why it matters for a job seeker

In a remote-first company, work tends to be written down. Decisions live in shared documents, updates go in chat, and meetings are often recorded or summarized. This suits people who write clearly and manage their own time.

Location still matters. An employer generally has to follow the payroll tax, wage and leave rules of the state where you work, so some hire only in states where they are set up. Some also adjust pay by location.
Many remote-first roles expect you to overlap with your team’s working hours. Check any time zone requirement before you apply, especially if you live far from the rest of the team.
How to check whether a company is really remote-first

Read the posting’s location fields and look for words such as hybrid, in office or on-site. In interviews, ask how many people, including leaders, work remotely and how decisions are shared with people outside the office.
Ask about equipment, any home-office allowance, how often in-person meetups happen and whether travel for them is paid. Ask whether you may move to another state or country and keep the job.
Try to get the remote arrangement written into your offer letter. Policies can change, and a written record helps if the company later asks people to return to an office.
qa: What is the difference between remote-first and remote-friendly?

A remote-first company treats working from home as the normal setup and designs meetings and decisions around remote staff. A remote-friendly company is office-based and allows some remote work, so remote employees may be left out of informal conversations and decisions made in person.
Does remote-first mean I never have to go to an office?

Usually the office is optional for daily work, but many remote-first companies hold in-person meetups, team retreats or onboarding sessions a few times a year. Ask how often these happen, whether attendance is expected and whether the company pays for travel.
Can a remote-first company hire me from any state?

Not always. An employer generally has to register for payroll taxes and follow the employment laws of the state where you work, so some hire only in certain states. Working from another country raises tax, immigration and legal questions, so ask the employer before you move.
Do remote-first jobs pay less?

Not necessarily. Some companies pay the same rate wherever you live, while others adjust pay based on your location. Ask how the company sets pay and whether your salary would change if you moved to a different area.
Do I pay taxes in my state or the employer’s state if I work remotely?

It depends on the states involved. You generally owe state income tax where you live and work, but some states have special rules for remote workers employed by companies based there. If you live in one state and your employer is in another, ask an accountant or your state tax agency.

Exploding offer.title: What Is an Exploding Offer? How to Handle a Short Deadline
sections: What an exploding offer is
An exploding offer is a job offer with a very short deadline to accept, often 24 to 72 hours. If you do not say yes in time, the offer is withdrawn, or “explodes.”
The term is common in campus and internship recruiting, at startups and in sales, consulting and finance. It can also appear in any hiring process when an employer wants a fast answer.
A normal offer usually gives you several days to a week or more to decide. What makes an offer “exploding” is a deadline so tight that you cannot fairly compare it with other options.
Why employers use them and why it matters

Employers set short deadlines to fill roles quickly, to keep you from collecting competing offers, or to move to their second choice if you decline. Some simply have a hard start date or a small hiring budget.

For you, the risk is accepting a job before you know what else is available or before you have checked the pay, benefits and terms. In the US, setting a short deadline is generally legal, and an employer can usually withdraw an offer before you accept it.

Many university career centers ask employers who recruit on campus to give students a reasonable time to decide. If you are a student, your career office can tell you its policy and may speak to the employer for you.
What to do if you get one
Thank the employer, say you are interested and ask politely for more time. Give a specific date and a short reason, such as finishing other interviews or reviewing benefits with your family.
If you have other interviews in progress, tell those employers you have an offer with a deadline. Many will speed up their process if they want you.
Use the time you do have well. Get the full offer in writing, check the salary, start date, benefits, location and any non-compete or repayment clauses, and decide what you would need to say yes.
If the employer refuses any extension without a clear reason, take that as a sign of how it may treat you later. Decide based on the offer itself, not on pressure.
qa: Is an exploding offer legal?

Generally yes in the US. An employer can set any deadline it likes for accepting an offer, and it can usually withdraw an offer that has not been accepted. Campus recruiting guidelines from schools are policies, not laws, though employers who ignore them may lose access to campus recruiting.
How do you respond to an exploding offer?

Reply quickly and politely, thank them, confirm your interest and ask for a specific extension, such as one more week. Explain briefly why you need it. Meanwhile, tell other employers you are talking to that you have a deadline, and read the written offer carefully.
Will an employer rescind the offer if I ask for more time?

It is uncommon for a polite, reasonable request to cost you the offer. The usual outcome is a yes, a partial extension or a no with the original deadline still standing. An employer that withdraws an offer just because you asked for time is showing how it handles normal requests.
Can I accept an exploding offer and keep interviewing?

You can, but going back on an accepted offer can damage your reputation, especially in small industries or campus recruiting, where schools may have rules against it. Unless you signed something that says otherwise, US at-will employment usually means no legal penalty, but check any agreement you signed first.

Negotiation.title: What Is Salary Negotiation? How to Negotiate a Job Offer
sections: What negotiation means in a job search

In a job search, negotiation is the conversation after an employer makes you an offer, when you ask for better terms before you accept. The most common request is higher base pay, but you can also ask about equity, a sign-on bonus, a later start date, more paid time off or remote work.

Negotiation is a normal part of hiring in the US. Many employers expect it and leave some room in the first offer, though some have fixed pay bands or set salaries, such as many government and union jobs.
The goal is an agreement both sides are happy with. You are not trying to win at the employer’s expense, since you will likely work with the same people after you sign.
What you can negotiate
Base salary matters most because raises, bonuses and some retirement contributions are often calculated from it. If the employer cannot move on base pay, ask about other parts of the package.

Other items people negotiate include a sign-on bonus, equity such as stock options or RSUs, the job title, the start date, paid time off, a remote or hybrid schedule, relocation help and a review of pay after six months.
Some things rarely change for one person, such as the health plan, the retirement plan and company-wide holidays. Asking about them is fine, but expect a fixed answer.
How to negotiate an offer
First, get the full offer in writing and thank the employer. Ask for a few days to review it if you need them; a reasonable request for time is usually granted.

Research the market rate for the role, level and location using salary sites, the posted pay range and people you know in the field. A growing number of states and cities require employers to show a pay range in job postings, which gives you a starting point.

Ask once, with a specific number and a short reason, such as your experience, a competing offer or market data. Put the request in writing, or follow a phone call with an email, so the details are clear.

When the employer answers, decide whether to accept, make one final counter or decline. Do not accept verbally and then keep negotiating, and get the final terms in an updated written offer before you resign from your current job.
Common mistakes to avoid
Do not invent a competing offer or inflate your current pay. If the employer checks, it can cost you the job and your reputation.
Avoid giving a range when asked what you want, because the employer will often pick the bottom of it. Name one number, or a narrow range whose low end you would gladly accept.
Do not go back and forth many times on small amounts. One clear request, and perhaps one follow-up, keeps the process professional and short.
qa: Can a job offer be taken back if I negotiate?

It is possible, since most US jobs are at-will and an employer can generally withdraw an offer for any reason that is not illegal. It is uncommon when the request is polite and reasonable. The risk grows if you make demands, give ultimatums or negotiate for weeks.
How much more should I ask for when negotiating salary?

There is no fixed rule. Base your number on market data for the role and location, the posted pay range and your experience. Ask for a specific figure you can explain, and be ready to say what you would accept if the employer cannot meet it in full.
Should I negotiate salary by email or phone?

Either works. Some people find email easier because they can plan their words and keep a record. Others prefer a call because tone is easier to read. If you talk by phone, send a short email afterward summarizing what you asked for and what was agreed.
Is it OK to negotiate an entry-level job offer?

Yes. The room may be smaller, and some entry-level programs pay every new hire the same, but asking politely is rarely held against you. If base pay is fixed, ask about the start date, a sign-on bonus or relocation help instead.
Do I have to tell an employer my current salary?

No. Many states and cities ban employers from asking about pay history, and the rules differ by place, so check your state labor department. Where asking is allowed, you can still decline politely and talk about the pay you expect for the new role instead.

Offer deadline.title: What Is an Offer Deadline? How Long You Have and How to Extend It
sections: What an offer deadline means

An offer deadline is the date and time by which an employer wants you to accept or decline a job offer. It is usually stated in the offer email or letter, or said by the recruiter when the offer is made by phone.
Common deadlines range from a day or two to about a week for most jobs. Campus and internship offers sometimes allow several weeks, while some offers expire within a day.
No US law sets how long an offer must stay open. The employer chooses the deadline, and it can usually be changed if both sides agree.
Why employers set deadlines
Employers often have backup candidates waiting. If you say no or stay silent too long, they may lose their second choice to another company, so a deadline helps them plan.
A very short deadline meant to pressure you is called an exploding offer. It is legal, but it can be a sign of how the company treats people, so it is worth noticing.
Many university career centers ask employers who recruit on campus to give students a reasonable amount of time to decide. Check your school’s policy if you are a student and feel rushed.
How to ask for more time
Asking for a few extra days is normal and rarely costs you the offer. Thank the employer, say you are excited about the role, and give a specific date when you will answer.
Give a short, honest reason, such as wanting to review the benefits, talk it over with family, or finish another interview process you are already in. You do not have to name other companies.
Ask early, ideally when the offer arrives, not on the day it expires. Then keep to the new date, because missing a deadline you asked for damages trust quickly.
Handling more than one offer
If you have an offer from one company and are still interviewing elsewhere, tell the other company you have an offer with a deadline. Many will speed up their process if they are interested.

Use the time to compare pay, benefits, schedule, commute or remote work, and growth, and to ask any open questions in writing. Accept only when you are ready to stop your search, and decline the others politely.
qa: How long do you usually have to accept a job offer?

Most employers give somewhere between a couple of days and a week. Internship and new graduate offers may allow longer, and senior roles may involve more back and forth. If no deadline is stated, ask the recruiter when they need your answer so you both work from the same date.
Is it OK to ask for more time to consider a job offer?

Yes. Asking for a few more days is common and professional. Thank the employer, explain briefly why you need the time, and propose a specific date. Most employers agree to a short extension, though some cannot wait if they have other candidates lined up.
What happens if I miss an offer deadline?

The employer may withdraw the offer and move to another candidate, or it may still accept your answer if the role is open. Do not count on it. If you need more time, ask before the deadline passes rather than going silent.
What is an exploding offer?

An exploding offer is a job offer with a very short deadline, sometimes 24 to 48 hours, designed to make you decide before you can compare other options. It is legal in the US. You can still ask for more time, and how the employer responds can tell you something about the workplace.
Can an employer take back a job offer after I accept?

In most US jobs, which are at-will, an employer can withdraw an offer, even after acceptance, though some situations may give you legal claims and rules vary by state. If you gave up another job or moved because of the offer and it was pulled, talk to an employment lawyer or your state labor department.

Rejection email.title: What Is a Rejection Email? What It Means and How to Reply
sections: What a rejection email is

A rejection email is a message from an employer or its recruiter saying it will not move forward with your application. It can come after you apply, after a phone screen, after interviews or even after a final round.

Many are form letters sent automatically by the employer’s applicant tracking system (ATS), the software that collects applications. Others are written by a recruiter or hiring manager, especially after you have interviewed.
Common phrases include “we have decided to move forward with other candidates,” “the position has been filled” and “we will keep your resume on file.” They all mean this application is closed.
When and why rejection emails arrive
Timing varies a lot. A rejection can arrive within minutes if you failed a knock-out question, such as work authorization or location, or weeks later when the employer finally closes the opening.
Some employers never send one. In the US no general law requires an employer to tell applicants they were not chosen, so silence is common, often called ghosting.
A rejection does not always mean you were a weak fit. The role may have been filled by an internal candidate, put on hold, cancelled for budget reasons or given to someone who applied earlier.
What a rejection email can and cannot tell you
Most rejection emails give no reason. US employers are generally not required to explain why they turned you down, and many avoid details because of legal caution.

There is one federal exception worth knowing. If an employer rejects you based in whole or in part on a background check from a screening company, the Fair Credit Reporting Act requires it to send a notice first with a copy of the report and a summary of your rights, then a final notice.

Some states and cities add their own rules, for example about criminal history checks. If you believe you were rejected because of race, sex, age, disability or another protected trait, you can contact the EEOC, your state agency or a lawyer.
How to respond to a rejection email

You do not have to reply. If you want to be considered for future openings, a short note of thanks that says you remain interested is enough. Keep it polite and brief, and do not argue with the decision.
After an interview, you can ask once for feedback. Some recruiters will share a point or two, while many will not because of company policy, so take a non-answer in stride.
Save the recruiter’s name and email, note the date and stage you reached, and watch the company’s careers page. Employers often reach back out to earlier candidates when a similar role opens.
qa: Should I reply to a rejection email?

Reply only if you want to keep the door open. A two or three sentence note thanking them for their time and saying you would welcome hearing about future roles is enough. If the email came from a no-reply address after an online application, a reply is not needed.
Can I ask why I was rejected?

Yes, you can ask politely, especially after an interview. Many employers will not give a detailed reason because of company policy or legal caution, and in most cases US law does not require them to. If they do share feedback, thank them and do not debate it.
Why did I get a rejection email so fast?

A very fast rejection usually comes from an applicant tracking system. It often means your answer to a screening question, such as work authorization, location or a required license, did not match what the employer set. It can also mean the role was already filled or closed.
Can I apply to the same company again after a rejection?

Yes. A rejection usually applies only to that one opening. You can apply for other roles right away, and for the same type of role later, ideally after gaining a new skill or experience. Some employers ask you to wait a set time before reapplying to the same position.
What does “we will keep your resume on file” mean?

It means your application stays in the employer’s database and a recruiter may search it for future openings. It is not a promise of contact. If you want a real chance, apply again directly when a role that fits you is posted.

Talent pool.title: What Is a Talent Pool? How It Works and Whether to Join
sections: What a talent pool is

A talent pool is a group of people an employer keeps on file for future jobs. Instead of applying to one specific opening, you send your resume and details so recruiters can contact you when something suitable comes up.

Employers invite people in through pages called “Join our talent community,” “General application” or “Submit your resume.” Some job boards also carry these as postings that look like regular jobs but have no single role behind them.

The word is also used inside companies. Recruiters may call everyone who applied before, past interns, former employees and people they found online their talent pool, even if those people never joined on purpose.
Why employers keep talent pools
A talent pool lets a company fill jobs faster. When a role opens, a recruiter can search people already on file before posting anything, which saves time and advertising costs.

Employers that hire often for the same roles, such as nurses, drivers, retail staff or seasonal workers, use pools most. A pool also helps when a company expects to hire later but does not have approved openings yet.

Recruiters usually search a pool by keyword, job title, location or skills. They often use the same applicant tracking system or a recruiting CRM, software that stores candidate profiles and sends emails, to manage it.
What joining one means for you
Joining a talent pool is not the same as applying for a job. Nobody may read your profile until a matching role opens, and that could be months away or never.
Your details can also go stale. If you change skills, location or contact information, an old profile may not match a recruiter’s search, so update it or rejoin when things change.

How long an employer may keep your data depends on where you are. In the EU and UK, data protection law limits how long it can be kept and usually requires a clear purpose or consent, and some US states, such as California, give applicants rights over their personal information.
How to use talent pools well
Apply to real, current openings first, because those are being reviewed now. Treat a talent pool as an extra step for employers you especially want to work for.
When you join, fill in every field, choose the job types and locations you want, and upload a resume written for the kind of role you hope to get. Keyword searches are how recruiters will find you.
Sign up for the employer’s job alerts as well, and apply directly when a matching job appears. Do not assume a recruiter will spot you in the pool and reach out first.
qa: Is being in a talent pool good?

It does no harm and can help, but it is not a job application. It means an employer may contact you about a future role. Many people in a pool never hear back, so keep applying to real openings at the same time.
What does it mean when a company says you are in their talent pool?

Usually it means you were not chosen for the role you applied to, but the company wants to keep your details for future openings. It is a polite rejection with a door left open. Keep watching their careers page and apply again when a fitting job appears.
What is the difference between a talent pool and a talent pipeline?

A talent pool is the broad group of people an employer has on file. A talent pipeline usually means a smaller set of candidates the company is actively preparing for specific roles it expects to fill soon, often with regular contact from recruiters.
How long do companies keep you in a talent pool?

It depends on the company and the law where it operates. Many keep profiles for a year or more, and some ask you to confirm your interest from time to time. In the EU and UK, data protection rules limit how long they can keep your data.
Should I join a company’s talent community if there are no openings?

Yes, if you really want to work there and have nothing better to apply for at that company. Complete your profile, set alerts for the roles you want, and still apply directly when a matching job is posted.

Work-life balance.title: What Is Work-Life Balance? What It Means and How to Judge a Job
sections: What work-life balance means

Work-life balance is how well your job leaves time and energy for the rest of your life: sleep, family, friends, health, chores and interests. It is not an exact 50-50 split. What feels balanced differs from person to person and changes with your stage of life.

It depends on how many hours you work, how predictable your schedule is, how much say you have over when and where you work, how long your commute is, and whether calls and messages reach you after hours.
Two jobs with the same 40 hours can feel very different. One may end cleanly at the close of the day. The other may bring late emails, weekend on-call shifts and last-minute schedule changes.
What US law does and does not cover

Federal law does not cap how many hours most adults can work. The Fair Labor Standards Act requires overtime pay of at least one and a half times the regular rate for nonexempt employees who work more than 40 hours in a workweek. Exempt employees can work longer without extra pay.

No federal law requires paid vacation or paid holidays. Some states and cities require paid sick leave. The Family and Medical Leave Act gives eligible employees of covered employers up to 12 weeks of unpaid, job-protected leave a year for certain family and medical reasons.

Some states and cities have scheduling laws for certain industries, such as retail and food service, that require advance notice of shifts. Some countries, such as France and Australia, give workers a right to disconnect after hours, but the US has no such national rule. Rules differ by state, so check with your state labor department.
How to judge work-life balance before you accept a job
Many postings promise good work-life balance, so look for specifics. Ask what a normal week looks like, when the day usually ends and how often people work evenings or weekends.

Ask whether anyone is expected to answer messages after hours, how on-call duty works and whether it is paid or traded for time off. Ask how many days of paid time off people actually take, not only how many they get.
Ask how many people have left the team in the last year and why. Reviews from current and former employees and a short talk with a future teammate can show whether the answers match daily life.
How to protect it in the job you have
Set clear working hours, tell your team what they are, and turn off notifications outside them where your role allows. Use your paid time off instead of letting it pile up or expire.

If your workload keeps growing, raise it with your manager using concrete examples, and ask what can be dropped, delayed or shared. Ask about flexible hours, remote days or a compressed workweek if they would help.
If you think you are owed overtime pay or are being denied leave the law gives you, contact the US Department of Labor’s Wage and Hour Division, your state labor department or an employment lawyer.
qa: Why is work-life balance important?

Long hours and constant availability leave less time for sleep, health, family and rest, and can lead to burnout. People with a workable balance are more likely to stay in a job, do steady work and keep up the parts of life that matter to them outside it.
What is an example of good work-life balance?

A job with predictable hours, a manager who does not expect replies to evening messages, enough paid time off that people actually use, and some flexibility for appointments or family needs. Overtime and busy seasons happen, but they are the exception rather than the normal week.
How do I ask about work-life balance in an interview?

Ask neutral, factual questions rather than saying you want less work. For example: “What does a typical week look like?”, “How does the team handle urgent requests after hours?” and “How do people here plan time off?” These show you are judging fit, not avoiding effort.
Can my employer make me answer emails after work?

In the US, generally yes, because there is no national right-to-disconnect law and most jobs are at-will. However, nonexempt employees must be paid for time spent working after hours, including reading and answering emails. State rules vary, so check with your state labor department if unsure.
What is the difference between work-life balance and work-life integration?

Work-life balance usually means keeping clear limits between work time and personal time. Work-life integration means mixing the two more freely, such as stepping away midday and working later. Integration suits some people, but it can blur limits if work keeps spreading into personal time.

Screening call.title: What Is a Screening Call? What Recruiters Ask and How to Prepare
sections: What a screening call is

A screening call is a short first conversation between a job applicant and someone at the hiring company, most often a recruiter or HR coordinator. It usually lasts 15 to 30 minutes, takes place by phone or video, and comes before the formal interviews.
Its purpose is to check that you meet the basic needs of the role before the hiring manager spends time on you. People also call it a phone screen, recruiter screen or screening interview.
Staffing agency recruiters, who fill roles for client companies, also hold screening calls before they put you forward. In that case you are talking to the agency, not yet to the employer itself.
What recruiters ask on a screening call

Expect questions about why you applied, what you do in your current or last job, why you want to move, and a quick walk through your resume. The recruiter wants a clear, short story that fits the job.

Most calls also cover pay expectations, work authorization, location or willingness to relocate, remote or in-office preferences, your notice period and when you could start. A mismatch on these basics often ends the process at this stage.

Some states and cities bar employers from asking about your salary history, and some require them to share a pay range for the job. Rules differ by place, so check with your state labor department if you are unsure what an employer may ask.
How to prepare and what to ask
Read the posting again, keep your resume in front of you and prepare a one or two minute summary of your experience. Take the call somewhere quiet with a good signal, and answer on time.

Have a pay range ready, based on research for similar roles in the same location. Know your notice period and earliest start date, and answer work authorization questions truthfully, because they are often checked later.
Ask about the team, the main goals of the role, the interview steps and the hiring timeline. Before the call ends, confirm the next steps and who will contact you.
Write down the recruiter’s name and the main points discussed right after the call. A short thank-you email the same day is optional but can help you stay in mind.
qa: How long does a screening call usually last?

Most screening calls last 15 to 30 minutes. Some run shorter if the recruiter only needs to confirm a few basics, and some run longer for senior roles. The invitation usually says how much time to set aside, and you can ask if it does not.
Is a screening call an interview?

Yes, even though it feels informal. The recruiter is judging whether to move you forward, so treat it like a short interview: be prepared, be on time, speak clearly about your experience and give honest answers about pay, location and work authorization.
What should I say when asked about salary expectations on a screening call?

Give a researched range for the role and location rather than a single number, and say you are open to discussing the full package. If the posting lists a range, you can ask where the role sits within it. You do not have to share past pay, and some places forbid employers from asking.
What happens after a screening call?

If you are a good fit, the recruiter usually sets up the next step, such as an interview with the hiring manager, a skills test or an assignment. If not, you may get a rejection email or no reply. Ask about the timeline on the call so you know when to follow up.
How do I know if a screening call went well?

Good signs include the recruiter explaining the next steps in detail, asking about your availability for interviews or sharing more about the team and pay. Still, recruiters are often friendly with everyone, so the only sure sign is an invitation to the next stage.

Exit interview.title: What Is an Exit Interview? What to Expect and What to Say
sections: What an exit interview is

An exit interview is a conversation or survey an employer holds with an employee who is leaving. It usually happens in the last week or on the last day, after you have resigned or your departure has been set.
It is most often run by someone in HR rather than your direct manager. Some employers use an online questionnaire instead, and some hire an outside firm so people feel freer to speak.
The main goal is to learn why people leave and what the company could improve. It may also cover practical steps such as returning equipment, final pay and benefits.
Why employers hold them and what they ask

Employers use exit interviews to spot patterns, such as pay that lags the market, a difficult manager, poor training or few chances to move up. Answers are often combined across many departing employees before anyone acts on them.

Common questions include why you are leaving, what your new job offers that this one did not, how you got on with your manager, whether you had the tools and training you needed, and what would have made you stay.
Exit interviews are not always confidential. Notes may be kept in your file or shared with managers, so assume anything you say could be repeated.
How to handle your exit interview
Prepare one or two clear, factual reasons for leaving, such as a better salary, a promotion or a shorter commute. Calm, specific feedback is more useful and less risky than a list of complaints.
Stay professional and avoid personal attacks. Former colleagues and managers may later be asked for references or turn up at your next employer.

If you have a serious concern, such as harassment, discrimination, unpaid wages or a safety problem, put it in writing and keep a copy. For possible legal claims, talk to an employment lawyer or your state labor department rather than relying on the exit interview alone.

Use the meeting to confirm practical details: your last day, when you will get your final paycheck, any payout of unused paid time off under company policy or state law, and how your health coverage ends or continues.
qa: Do I have to do an exit interview?

In most US jobs an exit interview is voluntary, and you can politely decline or keep it short. Your employer still owes you wages you have already earned whether or not you take part. Rules on when the final paycheck must be paid vary by state.
What should I not say in an exit interview?

Avoid insults, gossip, personal attacks on coworkers and vague anger. Do not share confidential details about your new employer. Stick to a few honest, specific points stated calmly, since your words may be written down and shared with managers.
Is an exit interview confidential?

Not necessarily. Some employers report answers only in combined form, but notes may still go into your file or reach your manager. Ask how the information will be used, and assume anything you say could be repeated.
Should I be honest in an exit interview?

Yes, but measured. Honest, factual feedback about pay, workload, management or growth can help the company and the people you leave behind. Choose your one or two most important points and leave out anything you would not want quoted back to you.
What happens if I am offered a severance agreement at my exit interview?
You do not have to sign it on the spot. Read it carefully, especially any release of legal claims, and ask how long you have to decide. Consider having an employment lawyer review it before you sign.

Green card.title: What Is a Green Card? US Permanent Residence and Your Job Search
sections: What a green card is
A green card is the common name for the Permanent Resident Card (Form I-551). It proves that the holder is a lawful permanent resident of the United States, sometimes shortened to LPR.

A permanent resident can live in the US indefinitely and work for any employer, in almost any job, without a work visa or employer sponsorship. They can change jobs, work part-time, freelance or start a business.
A green card is not citizenship. Holders cannot vote in federal elections, and many must wait a set number of years before they can apply to become US citizens through naturalization.
How people get a green card

The main routes are family sponsorship by a US citizen or permanent resident relative, employment sponsorship by a US employer, the Diversity Visa lottery, and protection as a refugee or asylee. Other special categories also exist.

Most employment-based green cards take several steps. The employer usually completes a labor certification called PERM, then files an immigrant petition (Form I-140), and finally the worker applies to adjust status inside the US or goes through a US consulate abroad.
Waiting times depend on the category and the worker’s country of birth, because yearly limits create backlogs. The State Department’s monthly Visa Bulletin shows which applications can move forward.
Validity, renewal and keeping your status

Most green cards are valid for 10 years and are renewed with Form I-90. Permanent resident status itself does not expire when the card does, but you need a valid card to prove your status, so renew before it runs out.

Some people receive a conditional green card valid for two years, for example through a recent marriage or an investor visa. They must file to remove the conditions before it expires, or their status can end.

Long trips abroad can put permanent residence at risk. A stay of more than a year without a reentry permit can lead officials to treat the status as abandoned. Ask an immigration lawyer before any long absence.
Using a green card in your job search

On applications, answer “yes” to whether you are authorized to work in the US and “no” to whether you need sponsorship now or in the future. Saying this clearly in your resume summary or cover letter can help when a posting says it cannot sponsor visas.

When you are hired, you complete Form I-9. A valid green card is a List A document, which proves both identity and work authorization. You may choose which acceptable documents to show; the employer cannot demand a specific one.

Federal law generally bars employers from treating permanent residents worse than citizens in hiring, except where a law, regulation or government contract requires citizenship. If you think you were rejected unfairly, you can contact the Justice Department’s Immigrant and Employee Rights Section.
qa: Can a green card holder work any job in the US?

Almost any. A permanent resident can work for any private employer without sponsorship. Some jobs are limited to US citizens, such as most federal government positions and roles that need a security clearance, and some state and local rules or contracts add their own citizenship requirements.
Do green card holders need visa sponsorship?

No. A green card already gives permanent work authorization, so a holder should answer that no sponsorship is needed now or in the future. This removes a major cost and delay for employers, which is why it is worth stating clearly.
What happens if my green card expires?

You remain a permanent resident, but you lose easy proof of your status for jobs and travel. File Form I-90 to renew it, ideally within six months before the expiry date. A conditional two-year card is different: you must file to remove the conditions or your status can end.
What is the difference between a green card and a work visa?

A work visa such as an H-1B is temporary and usually ties you to a sponsoring employer and a specific job. A green card is permanent residence, lets you work for any employer and does not depend on one job. Many workers move from a work visa to a green card through employer sponsorship.
How long does an employer-sponsored green card take?

It varies widely. The process can take a year or two in some categories and many years in others, depending on the category, government processing times and backlogs for people born in high-demand countries. Check the Visa Bulletin and ask the employer’s immigration lawyer for your case.

Hiring freeze.title: What Is a Hiring Freeze? What It Means for Job Seekers
sections: What a hiring freeze is
A hiring freeze is a decision by an employer to stop or sharply limit filling jobs for a period of time. The people already on staff keep their jobs. The company simply stops adding new ones.

Employers usually freeze hiring to control costs. Common reasons include falling sales, an uncertain economy, a budget shortfall, a merger or a change in leadership that wants to review spending first.
A freeze is different from a layoff. In a layoff, current employees lose their jobs. In a freeze, nobody is let go, but open roles stay empty and new roles are not created.
How hiring freezes work in practice

A full freeze stops all hiring. A partial or soft freeze still allows some hires, such as replacing someone who quit, filling roles that bring in revenue, or hiring for jobs the business cannot run without.
Most freezes have no fixed end date. The company says it will review the decision later, often at the next budget cycle or quarter. Some end in weeks, while others last many months.

Government employers also use freezes. US presidents have at times ordered freezes on federal civilian hiring, usually with exceptions for roles such as the military and public safety. State and city governments may freeze hiring when their budgets are tight.
During a freeze, existing staff often take on extra work. Some employers allow internal transfers, contractors or temporary workers to cover gaps, while others freeze those too.
What a hiring freeze means for job seekers
If you applied before a freeze, your application may sit with no answer, interviews may be canceled, or the posting may disappear. This is usually about the budget, not about you.

In rare cases an employer withdraws a job offer it already made. In most US jobs, which are at-will, an employer can usually do this, though rules and possible claims vary by state. If you quit a job or moved because of the offer, ask an employment lawyer.
A freeze at one company does not mean the whole industry has stopped hiring. Competitors, smaller firms and companies in other sectors may still be actively looking for people.
What to do if an employer freezes hiring
Send the recruiter or hiring manager a short, polite note. Say you are still interested and ask to be contacted when hiring resumes. Recruiters often return to candidates they already know.
Keep applying elsewhere and do not put your search on hold for one employer. Treat any role at a frozen company as uncertain until you have a written offer and a start date.

If you have an offer in hand, confirm it in writing and ask whether the role is approved and funded. If you are already employed somewhere that froze hiring, use the time to build skills and keep records of the extra work you take on.
qa: How long does a hiring freeze usually last?

There is no standard length. Some freezes last a few weeks until a budget is approved, while others last many months or until business conditions improve. Most employers do not set an end date in advance and review the decision at regular points, such as each quarter.
Is a hiring freeze a sign of layoffs?

Not always. Many companies freeze hiring to avoid layoffs by saving money through open roles that stay empty. But a freeze can also be an early step when finances are poor, so it is worth watching other signs, such as budget cuts or canceled projects.
Can a company hire during a hiring freeze?

Yes, often. Many freezes are partial and allow exceptions for critical roles, replacements for people who left, or jobs that bring in revenue. Some employers also keep using contractors or temporary staff. A posting that stays open during a freeze may be one of those exceptions.
Should I still apply to a company with a hiring freeze?

You can, especially if the role is still posted, since it may be an approved exception. Just do not count on it. Keep applying to other employers, and stay in touch with the company’s recruiter so you hear when hiring starts again.
Can a job offer be withdrawn because of a hiring freeze?

It can happen. In most US at-will jobs, employers can generally withdraw an offer before you start, though state laws and the facts of your case matter. If you resigned from another job or relocated because of the offer, talk to an employment lawyer about your options.

Offboarding.title: What Is Offboarding? What Happens When You Leave a Job
sections: What offboarding means

Offboarding is the set of steps a company follows when an employee leaves. It covers handing over work, returning equipment, closing system access, settling the final paycheck and explaining what happens to benefits.
It applies however the job ends: resigning, being laid off, being fired, retiring or finishing a contract. Some steps change with the reason for leaving, but most happen every time.
It is the opposite of onboarding, the process of bringing a new hire into the company. HR, your manager and the IT team usually share the work.
What usually happens during offboarding
Once your last day is set, you document your tasks, pass open projects to colleagues and tell clients or partners who will take over. Your manager may ask for a written handover note.
Near the end, you return the laptop, phone, badge, keys and any company card. IT closes your email and system accounts, often on your last day or right after a layoff meeting.

Many companies hold an exit interview, a conversation or survey about why you are leaving and what could improve. HR may also ask you to sign documents, such as a reminder of confidentiality duties or, after a layoff, a separation agreement.
Pay, benefits and records to check

Final paycheck timing is set by state law, not federal law. Some states require payment on the last day when an employer ends the job, while others allow until the next regular payday. Your state labor department can tell you the rule.

Payout of unused vacation also depends on the state and the employer’s written policy. Some states require it, many leave it to the policy. Ask HR in writing what you will receive for leave, commissions and any bonus.

Group health coverage often ends on your last day or at the end of that month. Employers with 20 or more employees must usually offer COBRA, which lets you keep the same plan by paying the full cost, and many states have similar rules for smaller employers.

Your vested 401(k) balance stays yours. You can usually leave it in the plan, roll it into a new plan or an IRA, or cash it out, which may bring taxes and penalties. Update your mailing address so your W-2 reaches you.
How to prepare for your own offboarding

Before your access ends, save copies of your pay stubs, benefits details, offer letter, performance reviews and any equity or bonus documents. Do not take company files or customer data, since that can break your agreements.
Remove personal files and passwords from work devices, and move personal contacts to your own phone. Note the names and emails of colleagues you want to keep in touch with.
If you are given a separation agreement, read it before signing, because it often includes a release of legal claims. If the terms are unclear or a lot of money is involved, ask an employment lawyer.
qa: What is the difference between onboarding and offboarding?

Onboarding brings a new employee into the company: paperwork, equipment, accounts and training. Offboarding is the reverse when someone leaves: handing over work, returning equipment, closing accounts and settling final pay and benefits. Both are usually run by HR with help from the manager and IT.
How long does offboarding take?

It usually runs through your notice period, often about two weeks in the US, and finishes on your last day or shortly after. After a layoff or firing it can happen in a single day, with access cut at once and pay and benefits details sent later in writing.
When will I get my final paycheck after leaving a job?

It depends on your state. Some states require final pay on the last day when the employer ends the job, while others allow until the next regular payday. The rule can also differ for quitting versus being let go. Check with your state labor department if your pay is late.
Do I get paid for unused vacation when I leave?

It depends on your state law and your employer’s written policy. Some states require employers to pay out earned, unused vacation, while others allow a policy that says it is lost. Sick leave is often not paid out. Ask HR for the amount in writing before your last day.
Do I have to do an exit interview?

Usually no law requires it, and you can decline or keep answers brief. If you take part, stay factual and polite, since notes may be kept on file. Raise serious issues such as harassment or unpaid wages in writing to HR, separately from the interview.

Onboarding.title: What Is Onboarding? What Happens When You Start a New Job
sections: What onboarding means

Onboarding is the process a company uses to bring a new employee in, from accepting the offer through the first weeks or months. It covers paperwork, accounts and equipment, training, first tasks and meeting the people you will work with.

It is broader than orientation. Orientation is usually a single day or session about company policies, culture and benefits, while onboarding also includes learning the actual job and settling into the team. Many companies plan onboarding around the first 90 days, and some stretch it over a year.

Part of it often happens before your first day, which some employers call preboarding. You may sign forms online, receive a laptop by mail and get an email saying where to go, when to arrive and whom to ask for.
Paperwork you usually complete in the US

Every new hire in the US fills in Form I-9, which confirms identity and the right to work. You complete Section 1 no later than your first day, and the employer must review your original documents within three business days of your start date.

Form W-4 tells the employer how much federal income tax to withhold from your pay. Many states have their own withholding form, and some states have no income tax, so this part depends on where you work.

Expect forms for direct deposit, emergency contacts and policy acknowledgments, such as confirming you received the employee handbook. Some jobs add a confidentiality agreement, a background check or a drug test if the offer said so.

Benefits enrollment usually has a deadline after your start date, often about 30 days. If you miss it, you may have to wait for the next open enrollment period unless you have a qualifying life event, so note the date your employer gives you.
What good onboarding looks like
On day one your computer, email and system access work, someone expects you and you know who your manager is. Many teams also assign a buddy, a coworker you can ask everyday questions.
You get clear first tasks and a plan for what to learn and deliver in the first 30, 60 and 90 days. Your manager meets you regularly to check progress and answer questions.
Weak onboarding shows up as missing equipment, no one to ask and no idea what success means. It does not always mean a bad job, but it is worth raising early rather than waiting for a review.
What to do as a new employee

Before you start, ask what to bring, where and when to report, what the first week looks like and what to wear. Have your I-9 documents ready, such as a passport, or a driver’s license plus a Social Security card.

In the first weeks, take notes, ask questions and set up short meetings with the people you will work with most. Agree with your manager on what a good first 90 days looks like, so you both measure the same thing.

Be careful if a so-called employer asks you to buy equipment with your own money and wait for reimbursement, or wants bank details before any real interview. That pattern is common in job scams, so verify the company first.
qa: How long does onboarding usually take?

It varies by employer and role. The paperwork and orientation part usually fits into the first day or week, while learning the job and becoming fully productive is often planned over about 90 days. Complex or senior roles can take longer, and some companies run structured onboarding programs for up to a year.
What is the difference between onboarding and orientation?

Orientation is usually a one-time session that explains company policies, benefits, safety rules and culture. Onboarding is the whole process of bringing you in, including orientation, setting up accounts, training, first assignments, meeting your team and check-ins with your manager over your first weeks or months.
Do you get paid during onboarding?

Yes. Onboarding is part of your job, so required training, meetings and paperwork done as an employee are generally paid work time. If you are told to complete unpaid training before or after your start date, ask HR to explain, and contact your state labor department if you think you are not being paid correctly.
What documents do I need for onboarding in the US?

For Form I-9 you need one document from List A, such as a US passport or permanent resident card, or one from List B, such as a driver’s license, plus one from List C, such as a Social Security card or birth certificate. You will also need bank details for direct deposit and information for your W-4.
What does onboarding mean as a job application status?

In many applicant tracking systems, an onboarding status means you have accepted an offer and the employer has moved you into its new-hire process. You will usually receive emails or a portal link with forms to complete, start-date details and any background check steps before your first day.

Career fair.title: What Is a Career Fair? How It Works and How to Prepare
sections: What a career fair is

A career fair, also called a job fair or career expo, is an event where many employers gather in one place to meet job seekers. Each employer has a table or booth staffed by recruiters or team members who answer questions, collect resumes and hold short conversations.

Colleges and universities run many of them through their career centers, often for students and sometimes for alumni. Others are organized by industry groups, professional associations, cities, local workforce agencies such as American Job Centers, and private event companies.

Some fairs are general and open to anyone. Others focus on one field, such as tech, health care or skilled trades, or on one group, such as veterans, students in a certain major or people seeking diversity-focused employers.
How a career fair works
At an in-person fair you usually register, get a map or list of employers, and walk from booth to booth. Conversations are short, often a few minutes, because recruiters want to meet many people.

A virtual career fair runs on an online platform. You create a profile, upload a resume and join employer booths through text chat, video calls or group sessions, often booked in time slots ahead of the event.

The fair itself rarely ends in a job offer. Its purpose is to get your name in front of a person, learn what roles are open and earn a next step, such as an interview invitation. Some events labeled hiring events do hold interviews on the spot, especially for hourly or seasonal roles.
How to prepare and follow up

Check the list of attending employers a few days before and choose the ones you care about most. Read their open jobs, note the job titles that fit you and prepare one specific question for each employer.

Practice a short introduction of about 30 seconds: who you are, what you do or study, and what kind of role you want. Bring printed copies of your resume, a pen and a simple folder, and dress one step more formal than the jobs you are seeking.

Ask each recruiter for their name and the best way to follow up, and write a quick note after each conversation so you remember who said what. Within a day or two, send a short thank-you email or message that mentions what you discussed and apply online if they asked you to.
qa: What should I bring to a career fair?

Bring several printed copies of your resume, a pen, a small notebook or phone for notes, and a folder to keep papers neat. If you have a portfolio or work samples, have a link ready to share. For a virtual fair, upload your resume to the platform beforehand and test your camera and microphone.
What should I say to a recruiter at a career fair?

Start with a short introduction: your name, your background or field of study, and the kind of role you want. Then ask a specific question about one of their open jobs or teams. End by asking how to follow up, and thank them for their time.
What is the difference between a career fair and a job fair?

In everyday use they mean the same thing. Some people use career fair for events at colleges or for professional roles and job fair for events aimed at immediate hiring, often for hourly jobs, but there is no fixed rule.
What should I wear to a career fair?

Wear clean, neat clothes that are a little more formal than what people wear in the jobs you want. Business casual works for most fairs, and a suit suits finance, law or corporate roles. Choose comfortable shoes, since you may stand and walk for hours.
Are career fairs worth going to?

They can be, especially when you are a student, changing fields or looking for local employers. You meet recruiters in person, learn about roles that may not be widely posted and can earn an interview. They work best when you prepare, target a few employers and follow up afterward.

Equity refresh.title: What Is an Equity Refresh? How Refresher Stock Grants Work
sections: What an equity refresh is

An equity refresh, also called a refresher grant, is a new grant of company stock or stock options given to someone who already works at the company. It comes on top of the new-hire grant promised in the original offer letter.

Public companies usually give refreshers as restricted stock units (RSUs), which are promises of shares delivered as they vest. Startups and other private companies more often give stock options, though some later-stage private companies also grant RSUs.
Refreshers are not a legal right. Each company decides whether to give them, how large they are and who gets them, usually through its equity plan and internal pay policies.
How refresh grants work

Many companies give refreshers once a year as part of the performance review cycle. Others give them at a promotion, as a retention grant to keep someone likely to leave, or when much of the first grant is close to fully vesting.

Each refresher has its own vesting schedule, often spread over several years from its own grant date. Some companies skip the one-year cliff for refreshers because the employee has already been there a while, while others keep it.

Because grants overlap, a long-serving employee may vest shares from several grants at the same time. Stock options in a refresher usually get a strike price equal to the stock’s fair market value on the new grant date, which can be higher than in the first grant.
The size of a refresher often depends on your performance rating, your level and the stock price. At many companies a yearly refresher is smaller than the new-hire grant.
Why refreshes matter for your pay

If your first grant vests over four years and no refreshers follow, your stock pay drops sharply once that grant is fully vested. Refreshers are how companies keep total pay steady or growing for people who stay.
When comparing offers, look past the first grant. An offer with a large new-hire grant and no refreshers can pay less over time than one with a smaller grant and regular refreshers.
Refreshers are taxed like other equity. RSUs are generally taxed as ordinary income when they vest, and option taxes depend on the type of option, so ask an accountant about your own situation.
What to ask and what to do

Before you accept an offer, ask whether the company gives refreshers, how often, how the amount is decided and when you first become eligible. Ask whether most employees at your level receive one or only top performers.
When you get a refresher, read the grant agreement. Check the grant date, vesting start date, any cliff, how often it vests and what happens to unvested shares if you leave.
Keep a simple list of all your grants and their vesting dates. When you discuss a promotion or a raise, you can ask about a refresher as part of the package, not only base salary.
qa: What is a refresher grant?

A refresher grant is extra equity, such as RSUs or stock options, that a company gives to a current employee after hiring. It is separate from the new-hire grant, has its own vesting schedule and is often given yearly, at promotion or to keep a valued employee.
How often do companies give equity refreshes?

Many companies give them once a year, often tied to performance reviews. Others give them only at promotions, as one-off retention grants or when the first grant is nearly vested. Some companies give none, so ask during the offer stage.
Do equity refreshers have a cliff?

It depends on the company. Some refreshers start vesting monthly or quarterly right away because the employee has already passed a cliff on the first grant. Others keep a one-year cliff. Your grant agreement states the exact schedule.
Are equity refreshes guaranteed?

Usually not. Most companies treat refreshers as discretionary, meaning they decide each time based on performance, budget and stock price. Unless your offer letter or a written agreement promises a specific refresher, plan as if it may not come.
How big is an equity refresh compared with the first grant?

There is no standard size. Many companies make yearly refreshers smaller than the new-hire grant, while promotion or retention grants can be larger. Ask the recruiter or your manager what a typical refresher looks like for your level.

On-call.title: What Is On-Call Work? How It Works, Pay Rules and What to Ask
sections: What being on call means

Being on call means you are off your normal shift but must be reachable and ready to work if something urgent comes up. You might be called to fix a server outage, see a patient, repair a broken water main or cover a missing coworker.

On-call duty is common in hospitals, IT and software, utilities, maintenance, social work, security and some retail and restaurant jobs. Many teams share it through a rotation, so each person is on call for a set week or set nights.
How on-call time is paid under US law

Under the federal Fair Labor Standards Act, the key question for hourly workers is how free you are while waiting. If you must stay at the workplace, or so close and with so many limits that you cannot really use the time for yourself, the waiting time usually counts as hours worked and must be paid.

If you only need to carry a phone, answer within a reasonable time and can otherwise go about your life, the waiting time usually is not paid work. The time you actually spend handling a call, including remote work from home, does count as hours worked.

Salaried exempt employees, common in software and management roles, are not owed overtime for on-call time under federal law. Some employers still pay them a weekly stipend or give time off after a busy night.

Some states and cities add rules, such as reporting-time pay, call-in pay or predictable scheduling laws that limit last-minute on-call shifts in retail and food service. Check with your state labor department, or a lawyer if you think you were not paid correctly.
Common ways employers handle on-call pay

Employers may pay a flat on-call stipend per shift or week, a lower hourly rate for standby time, or a minimum number of paid hours whenever you are called in. Others pay nothing for waiting and pay only for time spent working.
Good on-call setups also limit how often you are on duty, give a backup person, and offer time off or a late start after a night spent fixing problems.
What to ask before you accept a job with on-call duty
Ask how often you will be on call, how long each shift lasts and how many people share the rotation. A small team usually means more frequent duty.
Ask how many calls a typical shift brings, how fast you must respond and whether you must stay within a set distance of the workplace. These limits affect your evenings, weekends and travel.
Ask exactly how on-call time and call-outs are paid, and whether you get time off afterward. Get the answers in writing, such as in the offer letter or a written on-call policy.
qa: Do you get paid for being on call?

It depends on how restricted you are and on your job type. Hourly workers in the US must be paid for on-call time if they cannot use it freely for themselves, and always for time spent actually working calls. Many employers also pay a stipend for being available, but federal law does not require it when you are free to do your own things.
Can I refuse to be on call?

In most US jobs, which are at-will, an employer can make on-call duty part of the job, and refusing may cost you the job. A union contract, an employment contract or a local scheduling law may set limits. Ask about on-call duty before accepting an offer, since it is harder to change later.
Does on-call time count toward overtime?

For non-exempt hourly workers, any on-call time that counts as hours worked, including time spent handling calls, is added to your weekly total. Hours over 40 in a workweek must then be paid at overtime rates under federal law, and some states have extra daily overtime rules.
What does on call mean in a hospital?

Hospital staff on call, such as doctors, nurses or technicians, must be ready to come in or give advice if a patient needs them. Some stay in the hospital during the shift, while others wait at home and must arrive within a set time. Pay and rules vary by employer and union contract.
How often is a normal on-call rotation?

There is no standard. Many tech teams rotate weekly, so each person is on call one week every few weeks, while hospitals often schedule on-call nights or weekends each month. The smaller the team, the more often each person is on duty, so ask about team size.

Job alert.title: What Is a Job Alert? How Job Alerts Work and How to Set Them Up
sections: What a job alert is

A job alert is an automatic message that tells you when a new job matching your saved search is posted. It usually arrives by email, but many job boards and apps also send push notifications or text messages.
You create one by running a search with the keywords, location and filters you want, then saving it as an alert. From then on, the site checks for new postings that match and sends them to you.
Job boards, company careers pages, professional networking sites and recruiting agencies all offer job alerts. Most are free, and you can usually have several running at once.
How job alerts work and why they matter

Each alert is tied to a set of search rules, such as job title, keywords, city or radius, remote options, salary range, job type and experience level. When a new posting fits those rules, it is added to your next alert.

Many sites let you choose how often alerts arrive, such as right away, once a day or once a week. Instant alerts suit popular roles where applications pile up fast, while a weekly digest suits a slower, more selective search.

Alerts matter because early applicants are often read first. Some employers review applications as they come in and may close a posting once they have enough strong candidates, so seeing a job on its first day can help.
Alerts also save time. Instead of running the same searches every day, you let the site do the checking and spend your time on applications.
How to set up job alerts that stay useful
Keep each alert narrow. A specific title and location usually gives fewer, better matches than a broad keyword, and you are more likely to keep opening alerts that are worth reading.
Set up separate alerts for different targets, such as one for your main job title and one for a related title or a second city. That is easier to manage than one wide search that mixes everything.
Review your alerts every few weeks. If most results are a poor fit, tighten the keywords or filters; if you get almost nothing, widen the location, add a similar title or remove a filter.
Use an email folder or filter for alerts so they do not bury other messages, and turn off alerts you no longer need once you accept a job.
Watching out for fake job alerts

Scammers sometimes send emails that look like job alerts to collect personal details or money. Be careful with any message you did not sign up for, especially one offering a high-paying job with no interview.

Before applying, open the job board or the employer’s careers page yourself rather than clicking a link in an unexpected message. A real employer will not ask you to pay fees or share bank details before a formal offer.
qa: How do I set up a job alert?

Search for jobs on the job board or careers site with the title, keywords, location and filters you want. Then look for a button such as “Create alert” or “Save search” and choose how often you want messages. You usually need an account or an email address to receive them.
How often do job alerts come?

It depends on the setting you choose and on how many new jobs match. Most sites offer instant, daily or weekly alerts. If no new postings match your search, you may get no alert at all for that period.
Do employers see my job alerts?

No. A job alert is a private saved search between you and the site that sends it. Employers do not see what alerts you have set up, though some sites use your searches to suggest jobs or show you to recruiters if you choose to share your profile.
How do I stop getting job alerts?
