Click the unsubscribe link at the bottom of an alert email, or sign in to the site and delete or pause the alert in your account settings. If you deleted the account but still get messages, use the unsubscribe link or contact the site’s support.
Why am I getting job alerts that do not match what I want?

Your search is probably too broad, or a keyword appears in many unrelated postings. Add a more specific job title, set a tighter location or radius, and use filters such as job type or salary. Some sites also add suggested jobs, which you can often turn off.

Salary band.title: What Is a Salary Band? How Pay Bands Work and How to Use Them
sections: What a salary band means

A salary band is the pay range a company sets for one level of one job, such as a mid-level software engineer or a senior accountant. It has a minimum, a midpoint and a maximum, and everyone at that level is meant to be paid somewhere inside it.
Companies usually group jobs into levels or grades, often with names like Level 3 or Band B. Each level gets its own band, and the bands for higher levels start and end at higher pay.

Bands are also called pay bands, pay grades or salary ranges. Many companies set them using market pay surveys for similar jobs in similar locations, and some set different bands for different cities or regions.
How salary bands work inside a company

Your place in the band usually reflects your experience and performance. New hires with less experience often start below the midpoint, while people who fully meet the role’s needs tend to sit near the midpoint.
Raises move you up within the band. Once you reach the maximum, your base pay usually stops growing much until you are promoted to the next level, which has its own higher band.
Bands often overlap, so the top of one level can pay more than the bottom of the next. Senior levels tend to have wider bands than entry levels, because experience in those roles varies more.
Salary bands and pay transparency laws

There is no federal law requiring employers to share salary bands. Several states and cities, including California, Colorado, New York and Washington, require many employers to include a pay range in job postings or to share it on request.

The rules differ by place, by employer size and by what must be disclosed, such as whether benefits must be listed too. Check your state labor department’s website for the rules where you live or where the job is based.
Separately, many states and cities ban employers from asking about your salary history. These laws push employers to set pay from the band and the role rather than from what you earned before.
What a job seeker should do
Ask the recruiter for the band for the role, not just the offer. Knowing the minimum and maximum shows where your offer sits and how much room you have to grow without a promotion.

If an offer is near the bottom of the band and you have strong experience, you can ask to start closer to the midpoint. Asking for more than the maximum rarely works unless the company agrees to place you at a higher level.
Ask how the level was chosen and what it takes to move up. A higher level often matters more for long-term pay than a small raise inside a lower band.
qa: What is the difference between a salary band and a salary range?

The terms are often used the same way. Strictly, a salary band is the internal pay range for one level of one job, while a salary range in a job posting may cover several levels or only part of the band. Ask the recruiter which one you are looking at.
What happens when you reach the top of your salary band?

Your base pay usually stops rising much, or rises only slowly with small adjustments. To earn more, you typically need a promotion to the next level, a change of role, or a company update to the bands when market pay rises.
Can you negotiate a salary outside the band?

It is hard, because companies use bands to keep pay fair between people at the same level. If you deserve more than the maximum, a better path is to ask whether the role can be leveled higher, or to negotiate a signing bonus, equity or other terms.
Is it okay to ask an employer for the salary band?

Yes. Asking for the band is a normal and professional question during hiring. In some states and cities, employers must include a pay range in postings or share it if you ask, but rules vary, so check your state labor department’s website.
Where should I be in my salary band?

Many companies place people who fully meet the role’s expectations near the midpoint. New or less experienced people often start lower, and long-serving top performers sit higher. Ask your manager or HR where you sit and why.

Bootcamp.title: What Is a Bootcamp? How Career Bootcamps Work and If They Pay Off
sections: What a bootcamp is
A bootcamp is a short, intensive training program that teaches the skills for one type of job. Most last from a few weeks to several months, compared with years for a college degree.

Common subjects are software development, data analytics, UX and UI design, cybersecurity, IT support, digital marketing and tech sales. Some run full time on weekdays, others part time in evenings and on weekends, and many are fully online.
Bootcamps focus on practical work. Students build projects, often for a portfolio, and many programs add career help such as resume reviews, mock interviews and introductions to employers.
How bootcamps differ from degrees and certificates

Most bootcamps are not accredited colleges, so they do not award degrees or college credit. Some are run by or with a university, often under the school’s name, but the program may still be operated by a private company.

Because most bootcamps are not accredited, federal student aid such as Pell Grants and federal student loans usually does not apply. Students pay upfront, use private loans, use installment plans or sign deferred tuition agreements.

An income share agreement, or ISA, means you pay a share of your future income for a set time instead of tuition upfront. Federal regulators treat these as private student loans, so read the cap, the income floor and the term closely before signing.

Rules for private training schools differ by state. Many states require them to be licensed or registered, and some have tuition refund rules, so check with your state’s education or postsecondary oversight agency.
Do bootcamps lead to jobs

Results vary widely between programs, subjects and job markets. A bootcamp can help someone switch careers, but employers still judge you on your skills, projects and interviews, and entry-level roles in some fields are very competitive.

Job placement numbers published by schools are not always comparable. Some count any job, part-time work, contract work or jobs outside the field, and some leave out students who did not finish or stopped answering surveys.
A bootcamp tends to work best for people who have tested the subject first with free material, can commit the time, and are ready to keep job searching for months after finishing.
How to choose a bootcamp

Ask for a written outcomes report that shows how many students started, how many finished, how many found a job in the field within a stated time, and the median starting pay. Ask how each number was counted.

Talk to recent graduates you find yourself, for example on professional networking sites, rather than only the ones the school suggests. Read the refund policy and the full loan or ISA contract before you pay anything.

Look for free or low-cost options too. Local American Job Centers can tell you whether you qualify for training funds under federal workforce programs, and veterans can check which programs are approved for GI Bill benefits through the VA’s comparison tool.
qa: Are bootcamps worth it?

They can be for people who want a fast, focused path into a specific skill and are ready to work hard during and after the program. They are less likely to pay off if you have not tested the subject first, if the school cannot show verified job results, or if the cost would leave you with debt you cannot handle.
Can I use financial aid for a bootcamp?

Usually not federal student aid, because most bootcamps are not accredited colleges. Some programs run through accredited schools do qualify. Other options include private loans, payment plans, employer tuition help, workforce training funds through American Job Centers and GI Bill benefits for approved programs.
Do employers hire bootcamp graduates?

Many do, especially for roles where a portfolio shows what you can do, such as web development or design. Some employers still prefer or require a degree. Your projects, skills tests and interviews usually matter more than the bootcamp’s name.
How long does a bootcamp take?

Most full-time bootcamps take about two to four months. Part-time programs often take six months to a year. The schedule and expected weekly hours should be stated before you enroll, and full-time programs can leave little room for a job.
Is a bootcamp the same as a certification?

No. A bootcamp is a course you take, and it usually gives a certificate of completion from the school. A certification is a credential you earn by passing an exam set by an industry body or vendor. Some bootcamps prepare students for certification exams.

Sabbatical.title: What Is a Sabbatical? How Sabbatical Leave Works and Who Gets It
sections: What a sabbatical is

A sabbatical is an extended break from work that your employer approves in advance, after which you come back to the same employer. It usually lasts from a few weeks to a year and can be paid, partly paid or unpaid.

People use sabbaticals to rest, travel, study, volunteer, care for family or work on a personal project. The main difference from quitting is that you keep your employment relationship and plan to return.
The word comes from the idea of a sabbath, a rest after a set period of work. Universities used it first, and many private employers now offer some form of it.
How sabbatical programs usually work

No US federal law requires employers to offer sabbaticals, and no state requires private employers to offer them as far as general rules go. Whether you can take one depends on your employer’s written policy or an agreement you make with your manager.
Most policies require a minimum length of service, often several years. They also set how long the break can be, how often you can take one and whether pay continues in full, in part or not at all.

Some employers attach conditions, such as agreeing to return for a set time afterward or repaying sabbatical pay if you leave soon after. Some also limit what you may do during the break, for example working for a competitor.

Benefits can change during the break. Retirement contributions usually stop if your pay stops, and health coverage depends on your plan’s rules; if it ends, you may be able to continue it through COBRA or a state continuation law.
Sabbaticals in universities and schools

In academia, sabbaticals are a long-standing benefit for tenured and tenure-track faculty. A common pattern is eligibility after about six years of service, with a choice such as one semester at full pay or a full year at reduced pay.

Academic sabbaticals are usually meant for research, writing or professional growth, and faculty often must submit a plan before and a report after. Rules for public schools and state universities can also be set by state law or union contracts, so they differ by state and institution.
How to plan and ask for a sabbatical

Start by reading the employee handbook or asking HR whether a sabbatical policy exists, who qualifies and how far ahead you must apply. If there is no policy, you can still propose an unpaid leave to your manager.
Make your request in writing. Explain the dates, the purpose, how your work will be covered while you are away and how you will hand it back when you return.

Get the final terms in writing, including pay, benefits, your return date and whether you return to the same or an equal job. If the terms are unclear or a dispute comes up, ask HR, a lawyer or your state labor department.
qa: Is a sabbatical paid?

It depends on the employer. Some pay full salary, some pay part of it and many sabbaticals are unpaid. Academic sabbaticals are often paid in full for a shorter break or at reduced pay for a longer one. Check the written policy or your leave agreement before you plan.
How many years do you have to work to get a sabbatical?

There is no legal standard in the US. Each employer sets its own rule, and it is often several years of continuous service. In universities, faculty commonly become eligible after about six years. Your handbook or HR team can tell you the exact requirement.
Is my job protected during a sabbatical?

Only as far as your employer’s policy or written agreement says. No federal law guarantees your job during a sabbatical, and the Family and Medical Leave Act covers medical and family reasons, not personal breaks. Get a written promise of your return date and role before you leave.
What is the difference between a sabbatical and a career break?

A sabbatical is an agreed break after which you return to the same employer. A career break often means leaving a job entirely and looking for a new one later. In the UK, “career break” is also used for employer schemes of long unpaid leave with a right to return.
How do I explain a sabbatical on my resume?

If you stayed with the same employer, you usually do not need to list it, since your employment was continuous. If asked, describe it briefly and positively, such as study, travel or caregiving, and mention any skills or projects that relate to the job you want.

Staffing agency.title: What Is a Staffing Agency? How Temp and Direct-Hire Work
sections: What a staffing agency is

A staffing agency is a company that fills jobs for other businesses, called its clients. It recruits and screens candidates, then either places them in permanent jobs with the client or employs them itself and assigns them to work at the client’s site.

People also call them temp agencies, employment agencies or recruiting firms. Some cover many fields. Others focus on one area, such as warehouse and light industrial work, office support, nursing, IT or accounting.
In most cases the client company pays the agency, not you. Many US states restrict or ban fees charged to job seekers, and you should never pay to be placed in a job.
The main types of placement

In a temporary or contract assignment, the agency is your employer on paper, often called the employer of record. It pays your wages, withholds taxes, gives you a W-2 and handles workers’ compensation, while the client directs your daily work.

In temp-to-hire, you start as the agency’s employee and the client can hire you directly after a trial period. The client usually pays the agency a conversion fee, so the timing and terms are set in their contract, not by you.
In direct hire, the agency finds a candidate and the client hires that person from day one. The agency earns a one-time fee from the client and has no role in your pay after you start.
How pay and benefits work
The agency bills the client an hourly rate that is higher than what it pays you. The difference, called the markup, covers payroll taxes, insurance, overhead and the agency’s profit.

Benefits differ by agency and by how much you work. Some offer health insurance, paid sick time or retirement plans to eligible workers, and some state and local laws require paid sick leave for temps too.

Unemployment rules for agency workers differ by state. In some states you may be expected to ask the agency for a new assignment when one ends before you claim benefits, so check with your state labor department.
What a job seeker should do
Before you accept, ask who pays you, how often, what the hourly rate is, how long the assignment should last and what happens when it ends. Ask whether the role could become permanent and when.
Read anything you sign. Some agency agreements limit when you can join the client directly without the agency, so ask about that before you start talking to the client about a permanent job.
Working with more than one agency at once is common and usually fine. Keep track of which agency sent your resume to which company, so two agencies do not submit you for the same job.
qa: Do staffing agencies charge you to find a job?

Legitimate staffing agencies are paid by the client company, not by the worker. Many states restrict or ban fees charged to job seekers. If an agency asks you to pay for placement, training or a background check before you are hired, treat it as a warning sign and check with your state labor department.
Is the staffing agency or the company my employer?

For temporary and contract assignments, the agency is usually your legal employer. It pays you, withholds taxes and issues your W-2. The client directs your work day to day. In some legal matters, such as workplace safety or discrimination, both can share responsibility. For direct-hire placements, the client is your only employer.
How much does a staffing agency take from your pay?

The agency does not take money out of your paycheck. It bills the client a higher rate than it pays you and keeps the difference to cover taxes, insurance, overhead and profit. The size of that markup varies by industry and contract, and agencies rarely share it.
Can I collect unemployment when a temp assignment ends?

Often yes, if you meet your state’s rules, but they differ by state. Some states expect temp workers to contact the agency for a new assignment first, and turning down suitable work can affect your claim. Check with your state unemployment office.
Is working through a staffing agency a good way to get hired?

It can be. Temp and temp-to-hire roles let you gain experience and show your work to an employer who may hire you directly. They can also mean fewer benefits and less job security, so weigh the specific offer against your needs.

Cost per hire.title: What Is Cost per Hire? Formula, What to Count and Why It Matters
sections: What cost per hire means

Cost per hire is the average amount a company spends to bring one new employee on board. It adds up all recruiting costs over a period, such as a quarter or a year, and divides them by the number of people hired in that period.
It is one of the most common recruiting metrics. HR teams use it to plan budgets, compare hiring channels and see whether hiring is getting more or less expensive over time.

The basic formula is simple: total recruiting costs divided by total hires. A widely used version, published as an ANSI and SHRM standard, splits costs into external costs and internal costs before adding them together.
What costs go into the number
External costs are money paid to outside parties. Examples include job board ads, recruitment agency fees, background checks, assessment tests, career fairs, candidate travel and relocation help.

Internal costs are what the company spends in-house. They include the pay of recruiters and HR staff for the time they spend hiring, the hours hiring managers and interviewers spend on interviews, referral bonuses, and the share of software such as an applicant tracking system.
Staff time is the cost most often left out, because no invoice arrives for it. Leaving it out makes hiring look cheaper than it really is, especially for roles with many interview rounds.

Agency fees can make one hire far more expensive than others, since many agencies charge a percentage of the new employee’s first-year salary. This is why companies often track cost per hire separately by channel, department or job level.
How employers can use and lower it

Track costs the same way every period, so changes in the number reflect real changes and not a new way of counting. Compare similar roles, since hiring a senior engineer and hiring a seasonal worker will never cost the same.
Look at which channels bring hires at the lowest cost and with the best results. Referral programs, a clear careers page and well-written job posts often reduce reliance on paid agencies.

Do not chase the lowest number on its own. A cheap hire who leaves after a few months costs more than a well-chosen one, so read cost per hire next to quality of hire, time to hire and early turnover.
Why it matters to job seekers
Cost per hire explains some employer habits. Companies often favor referred candidates because referrals tend to be cheaper and faster than paid ads or agencies.

It also explains why some employers hesitate over candidates sent by an agency, since that hire carries an extra fee. Applying directly or through an employee referral can sometimes make you a simpler choice for the employer.
qa: How do you calculate cost per hire?

Add all external recruiting costs, such as ads, agency fees and background checks, to all internal costs, such as recruiter pay, interviewer time and software. Then divide the total by the number of hires made in the same period. For example, if a company spent a set amount in a year and made 20 hires, it divides that amount by 20.
What is a good cost per hire?

There is no single good figure. It depends on the industry, the job level, the location and how hard the role is to fill. The most useful comparison is with your own past numbers for similar roles, read alongside quality of hire and early turnover, rather than a general average.
What is the difference between cost per hire and cost of vacancy?

Cost per hire measures what a company spends to fill a job. Cost of vacancy estimates what the company loses while the job sits empty, such as lost output, delayed projects or overtime paid to other staff. A slow, cheap hiring process can still be costly once the vacancy cost is counted.
Does cost per hire include salary?

No. The new employee’s salary and benefits are not part of cost per hire, because they are the cost of employing the person, not of finding them. Some companies track onboarding and training costs separately. Sign-on bonuses and relocation help are often counted as hiring costs, but practices vary.
Why is cost per hire important?

It shows how much a company spends on recruiting and where the money goes. It helps HR teams set budgets, choose between job boards, agencies and referrals, and spot when the hiring process is becoming slow or wasteful. It works best alongside other measures, such as time to hire and quality of hire.

Seasonal work.title: What Is Seasonal Work? Types, Timing and How to Get Hired
sections: What seasonal work means

Seasonal work is a job that exists only for part of the year, when an employer gets busier than usual. It starts and ends with the season, so you know from the start that it will last weeks or months rather than years.
Common examples are holiday retail and warehouse jobs, summer camps, lifeguarding, resorts and national parks, ski areas in winter, farm harvests, landscaping, and tax preparation in the spring.
A seasonal job can be full-time or part-time. You may be hired directly by the employer or through a staffing agency, and you can be a regular employee or, less often, an independent contractor.
How seasonal jobs work and what rules apply

Most seasonal workers are employees, so the employer withholds income tax, Social Security and Medicare from each paycheck. If you work only part of the year, too much tax may be withheld, and you may get some back when you file your return.

Federal minimum wage and overtime rules cover most seasonal employees. Some seasonal amusement and recreational businesses, such as certain camps and parks, can be exempt under federal law, and state law may still protect you, so check with your state labor department.

Whether you can collect unemployment benefits after the season ends depends on your state. Some states limit benefits for workers whose jobs are seasonal by nature, so ask your state unemployment agency.
Teens often take summer jobs. Federal child labor rules limit the hours of 14- and 15-year-olds, with somewhat later hours allowed in summer, and many states add their own rules.
How to find and get a seasonal job
Apply early. Many employers start hiring two or three months before the season, and some summer camps and resorts recruit in winter.

Be clear about your availability, including your start date, the last day you can work and whether you can cover weekends and holidays. Employers often care most about people who can stay until the busy period ends.
Ask how many hours a week you can expect, whether housing or meals are included for remote jobs, and whether the job can turn into a year-round position.
Do the job well even though it is short. A good record can bring an invitation to return next season, a permanent offer or a strong reference.
qa: How long does seasonal work last?

It depends on the season and the employer. Holiday retail jobs often run from about October or November to early January, summer jobs usually cover June to August, and harvest or ski jobs follow the weather. The posting or the offer should state the expected start and end dates.
Can a seasonal job become permanent?

Yes, sometimes. Some employers use seasonal hiring to find people they want to keep, especially in retail, logistics and hospitality. Ask during the interview whether seasonal workers are ever kept on, and tell your manager during the season that you are interested.
Do seasonal workers get benefits?

Usually fewer than year-round staff. Seasonal employees often do not qualify for health insurance, paid vacation or retirement plans, though some employers offer employee discounts or bonuses for staying through the season. Paid sick leave may be required by your state or city, so check local rules.
Can I collect unemployment after a seasonal job ends?

It depends on your state. Some states pay benefits if you meet the usual earnings and work requirements, while others restrict benefits for workers in jobs that are seasonal by nature. Contact your state unemployment agency to find out whether you qualify.
Is seasonal work the same as temporary work?
They overlap but are not the same. Seasonal work is tied to a busy time of year and often repeats every year. Temporary work can happen at any time, for example to cover a leave or a short project.

Lateral move.title: What Is a Lateral Move? Meaning, Pros and Cons, and When to Make One
sections: What a lateral move means
A lateral move is a change to a job at about the same level as your current one. The title, seniority and pay stay roughly the same, but the team, the work or the employer changes.

It can happen inside your company, such as moving from sales operations to marketing operations, or between companies, such as taking a similar role at a competitor. It is different from a promotion, which moves you up, and a demotion, which moves you down.
Pay in a lateral move is usually close to what you earn now. Between companies it is sometimes a little higher, because a new employer often has to offer something to get you to switch.
Why people make a lateral move
Common reasons are learning a new skill, getting out from under a bad manager, joining a team with more room to grow, or moving closer to a field you want to work in later.

A lateral move can also lead to a promotion later. Experience in a second function, product or region can make you a stronger candidate for a role that needs broad knowledge, such as a team lead or manager.
Other reasons are practical: a shorter commute, remote or hybrid work, better hours, better benefits or a more stable employer, even when the title does not change.
Risks and how to judge a lateral move
The main risk is spending time without gaining anything. If the new job uses the same skills on similar work, you may simply reset the clock on your next promotion.

Moving to a new company also means starting over on trust and reputation. Check how benefits and timing will change, such as when health coverage starts, whether unvested equity or employer retirement contributions will be lost, and whether you lose accrued paid time off under your employer’s policy and your state’s law.
Before you accept, ask what you will own in the first year, which skill you will gain and what the path to the next level looks like. Vague answers are a warning sign.
How to explain a lateral move
On a resume, list the new role like any other job and show what you did and learned there. A lateral move does not look bad when the reason is clear.
In an interview, describe it as a choice with a goal, such as building data skills or learning a new product line. Avoid speaking badly of a former manager, even if that was part of the reason.
If you want an internal lateral move, talk to your manager or HR early. Many companies have an internal transfer process, and some require a minimum time in your current role first.
qa: Is a lateral move a good idea?

It can be, when it gives you a new skill, a better manager, broader experience or a clearer path to promotion. It is a poor choice when the work, skills and prospects are about the same as what you have now. Judge it by what you will learn and own, not by the title.
Does a lateral move come with a pay raise?

Not always. Inside the same company, pay often stays the same because the level does not change. When moving to another company, you can usually negotiate, and new employers sometimes offer a modest increase to attract you. Compare the full package, including benefits, bonus and equity, not just base salary.
Does a lateral move look bad on a resume?

Usually not. Recruiters see lateral moves often and care more about what you did in each role. It helps to show new skills, results or responsibilities in the new job. Many short lateral moves in a row, with no clear reason, can raise questions, so be ready to explain your goals.
What is the difference between a lateral move and a promotion?

A promotion moves you to a higher level, usually with a bigger title, more responsibility and more pay. A lateral move keeps you at about the same level and pay but changes your team, duties or employer. A lateral move can set you up for a later promotion.
How do I ask for a lateral move at work?

Learn your company’s internal transfer policy first, then talk to your manager about your goals and the role you want. Explain what you will bring to the new team and what you want to learn. Some employers ask you to apply through the internal job board or to stay in your current role for a set time first.

Clawback.title: What Is a Clawback? How Bonus Repayment Clauses Work
sections: What a clawback means

A clawback is a clause that lets an employer take back money it already paid you. In a job offer, it usually covers a sign-on bonus, a relocation package or tuition help, and it applies if you leave before a set date.
For example, an offer may say you must repay the full sign-on bonus if you resign within 12 months. Some clauses cover a longer period or several payments, such as moving costs plus a bonus.

The word also has a second meaning for executives. Companies listed on US stock exchanges must have policies to recover incentive pay that was too high because of an accounting error later corrected, under rules from the Securities and Exchange Commission.
How a clawback works in practice

The contract or a separate repayment agreement sets the period, the amount and what triggers repayment. Common triggers are resigning or being fired for cause. Many clauses do not apply if you are laid off or let go without cause, but only if the text says so.
Some clauses are prorated, meaning the amount you owe shrinks each month you stay. Others are all or nothing, so leaving one day early means repaying everything.

You may be asked to repay the gross amount, before taxes, even though you received less after withholding. Repaying in the same year is simpler for taxes than repaying in a later year, so ask an accountant if this applies to you.
What the law says

Clawback clauses are generally allowed in the US, but states set limits. Many states restrict deducting money from a paycheck, including a final one, without your written consent, and federal law limits deductions that cut a non-exempt worker’s pay below minimum wage.

Some states have started to restrict so-called stay-or-pay terms, where a worker must pay money back for leaving early. Rules differ by state and change, so check with your state labor department or an employment lawyer if an employer demands repayment.
What to do before you sign
Read the offer for words like repayment, clawback or reimbursement. Note how long the period is, how much you would owe and whether it is prorated.
Ask for changes that make the clause fairer. Common requests are prorated repayment, a shorter period and no repayment if you are laid off or let go without cause.
When you compare offers, treat a bonus with a clawback as money you only fully keep after the period ends. Keep it in savings until then if you are unsure you will stay.
qa: Do I have to pay back my sign-on bonus if I quit?

Only if your contract or bonus agreement says so. Most sign-on bonuses come with a clawback that requires repayment if you resign within a set period, often one year. Read the exact terms to see the period, whether repayment is prorated and what events trigger it.
Can my employer take the clawback out of my final paycheck?

It depends on your state. Many states limit paycheck deductions or require your written consent first, and federal law limits deductions that push a non-exempt worker’s pay below minimum wage. If money was taken without your agreement, contact your state labor department.
Does a clawback apply if I am laid off?

Often not, but only if the clause says so. Many agreements trigger repayment only when you resign or are fired for cause. If the text is silent or unclear, ask the employer to add a written exception for layoffs before you sign.
Do I repay the bonus before or after taxes?

Many agreements ask for the gross amount, before taxes were withheld. Some employers ask only for the net amount you received. The tax treatment depends on whether you repay in the same year or a later one, so check the agreement and ask a tax professional.
What is a prorated clawback?

A prorated clawback reduces what you owe the longer you stay. For example, with a 12-month period, leaving after six months might mean repaying about half. It is fairer than an all-or-nothing clause and is a common thing to ask for.

Retention bonus.title: What Is a Retention Bonus? How It Works, Taxes and What to Check
sections: What a retention bonus is
A retention bonus is extra money an employer promises to pay if you stay in your job until a set date or until a project ends. It is also called a stay bonus.
Employers offer them when losing certain people would be costly. Common times are a sale or merger of the company, a restructuring, a system launch, a plant closing or a busy season.
It is different from a signing bonus, which rewards you for joining, and from a performance bonus, which depends on results. A retention bonus mainly depends on you still being there.
How a retention bonus works
The terms are usually set out in a retention agreement or letter. It names the amount, the date or event you must stay until, and how the money is paid, such as one lump sum or several installments.
Some bonuses are paid at the end of the retention period. Others are paid up front with a clawback, meaning you must pay some or all of it back if you leave before the date.
The agreement should say what happens if the company ends your job before the date. Many pay the bonus in full if you are let go without cause, but some do not, so read that part closely.
How retention bonuses are taxed
In the US, a retention bonus is taxable wages. Social Security and Medicare taxes apply, along with federal income tax and any state or local income tax where you work.

Employers usually treat it as supplemental wages and often withhold federal income tax at a flat supplemental rate set by the IRS. That withholding may be more or less than what you finally owe when you file your return.
Whether the bonus counts toward your 401(k) contributions or employer match depends on your plan’s rules. For questions about your own taxes, ask an accountant or tax preparer.
What to do if you are offered one
Get the full terms in writing and signed before you rely on the money. Check the amount, the exact date or event, how and when it is paid, and any conditions such as staying in good standing.
Ask what happens if you are laid off, if your role changes, if the company is sold again or if you resign for a good reason. Also ask whether any part must be repaid and how.

You can often negotiate the amount or the terms, especially if the employer clearly needs you. If a large sum or a repayment dispute is involved, ask an employment lawyer or your state labor department.
qa: Do I have to pay back a retention bonus if I quit?

It depends on your agreement. If the bonus was paid at the end of the retention period, quitting early usually means you never receive it. If it was paid up front with a clawback clause, you may have to repay some or all of it. State laws limit how employers can collect repayment from wages, so ask your state labor department if there is a dispute.
Do I get my retention bonus if I am laid off?

Only if the agreement says so. Many retention agreements pay the full bonus if the employer ends your job without cause before the date, but some pay nothing or only part. Read the termination section carefully and ask HR to confirm in writing before you sign.
How much is a typical retention bonus?

There is no standard amount. Employers set it based on how important the role is, how long they need you to stay and what it would cost to replace you. It may be a flat sum or a share of your base salary, and it is often negotiable.
Is a retention bonus taxed differently from salary?

It is taxed as ordinary wages, so the total tax owed is figured the same way as on salary. The difference is in withholding: employers often withhold federal income tax at a flat supplemental rate set by the IRS, so the amount withheld may not match what you owe when you file.
What is the difference between a retention bonus and a signing bonus?

A signing bonus is paid to get you to accept a new job and is often paid near your start date. A retention bonus is paid to keep you in a job you already have until a set date or event. Both can come with repayment terms if you leave early.

401(k) match.title: What Is a 401(k) Match? How Employer Matching Works
sections: What a 401(k) match is

A 401(k) match is money your employer adds to your 401(k) retirement account because you put in money yourself. The match is tied to your own contributions, so if you contribute nothing, you usually get no match.

A 401(k) is a US workplace retirement plan. You choose a share of each paycheck to save, and it goes into investments you pick from the plan’s menu. Nonprofits and public schools often offer a similar plan called a 403(b), which can also have a match.
Employers are not required by law to offer a match. Many do because it helps them hire and keep staff, and the amount is part of your total pay even though it does not show up in your salary.
How match formulas work
The plan document sets a formula. A common one is 50 cents for every dollar you put in, up to 6% of your pay. Another is a dollar-for-dollar match up to 3% or 4% of your pay.
For example, if you earn $60,000 and the match is 50% up to 6%, you contribute 6%, or $3,600, and your employer adds $1,800. If you contribute only 3%, the employer adds just $900.

Some plans match each paycheck. If you reach the IRS yearly contribution limit early in the year, you may miss match on later paychecks unless the plan does a year-end “true-up” to make up the difference.

Some employers instead make a contribution for all eligible workers whether or not they save, called a nonelective or profit-sharing contribution. That is not a match, though job ads sometimes describe it loosely as one.
Vesting, taxes and the rules around the match
Money you put in yourself is always 100% yours. The employer’s match may vest over time, meaning you keep it only after a set period of service.

Federal law caps how slow vesting can be. With a cliff schedule, the match must be fully yours after no more than three years. With a graded schedule, it must vest gradually and be fully yours after no more than six years. Some plans vest the match immediately.

A traditional match goes in before tax, grows without yearly tax and is taxed as income when you withdraw it. Since the SECURE 2.0 Act, a plan may let you take the match as Roth money instead, which is taxed in the year it goes in.
What a job seeker should do

When comparing offers, ask what the match formula is, when you become eligible, how vesting works and whether there is a true-up. Two jobs with the same salary can differ by thousands of dollars a year in match.
Once you join, contribute at least enough to get the full match. Check your first pay stubs and account statements to confirm both your contribution and the employer’s are showing up.
If you plan to leave soon, check how much of the match is vested first. For questions about withdrawals, rollovers or taxes in your own situation, ask the plan administrator or a tax professional.
qa: What is a good 401(k) match?

There is no official standard. Common formulas are 50% of what you contribute up to 6% of pay, or 100% up to 3% to 6% of pay. To compare plans, work out the most the employer will add as a percent of your salary, then check how fast it vests.
Does the employer match count toward my 401(k) contribution limit?

It does not count toward the yearly limit on what you can contribute from your own pay. It does count toward a separate, higher limit on total contributions from you and your employer combined. The IRS sets both limits and updates them each year.
What happens to my 401(k) match if I quit?

You keep the vested part of the match and everything you contributed yourself. Any unvested match is forfeited and goes back to the plan. You can usually leave the money in the old plan, roll it into an IRA or roll it into a new employer’s plan if that plan accepts rollovers.
Is the 401(k) match taxed?

A traditional match is not taxed when it goes into your account. You pay income tax when you withdraw it, usually in retirement. If your plan lets you choose a Roth match and you do, it counts as taxable income in the year it is contributed.
Is a 401(k) match free money?

In a sense, yes. It is extra pay you get only by saving in the plan, so skipping it means turning down part of your compensation. The catches are vesting rules, which can take some of it back if you leave early, and penalties that often apply to withdrawals before age 59½.

Constructive dismissal.title: What Is Constructive Dismissal? Meaning, Examples and Your Rights
sections: What constructive dismissal means

Constructive dismissal happens when your employer does not fire you but changes or treats your job so badly that you feel you have no real choice but to quit. The law in some countries then treats your resignation as if the employer had dismissed you.

Common examples include a large pay cut imposed without your agreement, a demotion, a major change to your duties, hours or work location, unpaid wages, or harassment and bullying that the employer allows to continue.

The term is used mainly in the UK, Canada, Ireland, Australia and other common law countries. In the US the usual term is constructive discharge, and it works differently because most US jobs are at-will.
How it works in the UK and other countries

In the UK, constructive dismissal is a form of dismissal under the Employment Rights Act 1996. You must show that the employer seriously breached your contract, that you resigned because of that breach, and that you did not wait so long that you seemed to accept the change.

To claim unfair dismissal in the UK you usually need two years of service, though some reasons, such as whistleblowing or certain discrimination claims, do not need a qualifying period. You must normally contact Acas for early conciliation before going to an employment tribunal, and strict time limits apply.
Canada, Ireland and Australia have their own rules, tests and deadlines. If you work outside the US, check with the official employment advice service or a lawyer where you work.
Constructive discharge in the US
Because most US jobs are at-will, an employer can usually change pay, duties or hours going forward without breaking the law. Quitting over a bad change is not, by itself, a legal claim.

Constructive discharge matters when the reason behind the treatment is illegal, such as discrimination, harassment based on a protected trait, or retaliation for reporting a problem. Courts ask whether working conditions were so intolerable that a reasonable person would have felt forced to resign.

If that test is met, the resignation can be treated like a firing in a discrimination or retaliation claim. Some states also recognize claims based on a written contract. Deadlines for filing a charge with the EEOC or a state agency are short, so act quickly.
What to do if you think it is happening
Keep a written record of each change or incident with dates, names and what was said. Save emails, pay slips, schedules and any messages that show the change.
Raise the problem in writing with your manager or HR, or use the formal grievance process if there is one. This shows you objected and gives the employer a chance to fix it.

Get advice before you resign. In the US, talk to an employment lawyer or your state labor department; in the UK, contact Acas or a solicitor. Resigning too early, too late or without a clear reason can weaken a claim.
qa: What counts as constructive dismissal?

It is usually a serious change or breach by the employer that leaves you no reasonable choice but to quit. Examples include a large unagreed pay cut, a demotion, unpaid wages, a major change in duties or location, or harassment the employer will not stop. Minor changes or ordinary disagreements usually do not count.
Is constructive dismissal illegal in the US?

Not on its own. Most US jobs are at-will, so a bad change is usually legal. Constructive discharge becomes part of a legal claim when the employer forced you out for an illegal reason, such as discrimination or retaliation, or in breach of a contract. An employment lawyer can say whether your situation fits.
Can I get unemployment benefits if I quit because of constructive dismissal?

Possibly. In the US, people who quit usually do not qualify, but many states pay benefits when you quit for good cause, such as a large pay cut or unsafe conditions. The rules differ by state, so file a claim and explain the reasons with your records.
How hard is it to prove constructive dismissal?

It is often harder than proving an ordinary unfair firing, because you must show the employer’s conduct was serious enough to force a reasonable person to leave. Written records, complaints you raised and evidence from coworkers make a claim much stronger.
Should I resign before making a constructive dismissal claim?

In the UK and similar systems, resigning is usually part of the claim, but timing and wording matter, so get advice first. In the US, staying while you file a complaint may be possible. Either way, talk to a lawyer or advice service before you quit.

Tuition reimbursement.title: What Is Tuition Reimbursement? How It Works and What to Check
sections: What tuition reimbursement means

Tuition reimbursement is an employee benefit where your employer pays back some or all of what you spend on courses, certificates or a degree. It is usually part of a written education policy that sets the rules.

In the classic version you pay the school first, finish the course and then send proof of payment and your grade to get the money back. Some employers pay the school directly or up front, which is often called tuition assistance.
Plans differ a lot. Some cover only courses related to your current job, some cover any degree the company sees as useful, and some include books, fees or exam costs.
Common rules and the repayment agreement
Most plans set a yearly cap, ask you to get approval before you enroll and require a minimum grade, such as a C or a B. Many also make you wait a set time after you are hired before you qualify.

Many employers ask you to sign a repayment agreement. It says you must stay for a set time after each course, often one or two years, or pay back part or all of the money if you quit or are fired for cause.

Some agreements reduce the amount owed the longer you stay, and some do not ask for repayment if you are laid off. Some states have begun limiting these stay-or-pay agreements, so the rules depend on where you work.
How tuition reimbursement is taxed

Under Section 127 of the federal tax code, an employer with a qualifying educational assistance plan can pay up to a yearly limit set by federal law without it counting as your taxable income. The course does not have to be job-related to qualify.

Payments above that limit are usually added to your taxable wages. They can stay tax-free if the education counts as a working condition fringe benefit, which generally means it maintains or improves skills for your current job and does not qualify you for a new line of work.
Federal law also lets employers use these plans to help pay off student loans. Your state’s tax treatment may differ, so ask an accountant if your situation is unclear.
What a job seeker or employee should do
When comparing offers, ask for the written policy. Check the yearly cap, which programs and schools count, whether you pay up front, the grade rule and how long you must stay after each course.
Get every course approved in writing before you enroll, and keep receipts, grade reports and the signed agreement. Before you resign, work out what you would owe and when.
If an employer asks for repayment you think is not allowed, or wants to take it from your final paycheck, contact your state labor department or an employment lawyer.
qa: Do I have to pay back tuition reimbursement if I quit?

Only if you signed an agreement that says so. Many employers require you to stay for a set time after each course, often one or two years, and to repay some or all of the money if you leave sooner. Read your signed agreement, since terms and state rules differ.
Is tuition reimbursement taxable income?

Usually not, up to a yearly limit set by federal tax law for qualifying educational assistance plans. Amounts above the limit are generally taxable unless the education is job-related and counts as a working condition fringe benefit. State rules can differ, so check your pay stub and W-2 or ask an accountant.
What is the difference between tuition reimbursement and tuition assistance?

With tuition reimbursement you usually pay the school first and the employer pays you back after you pass the course. With tuition assistance the employer often pays up front or directly to the school. Many people use the two terms for the same benefit.
Do I have to repay tuition reimbursement if I am laid off?

Many agreements do not require repayment when the employer ends your job without cause, such as in a layoff, but some do. The answer depends on the wording you signed and on your state’s law, so read the agreement and ask your state labor department if unsure.
Can I use tuition reimbursement for any degree?

It depends on the employer’s policy. Some plans cover only courses related to your current or likely future job, while others cover a wider range of degrees. Most require approval before you enroll, so confirm in writing that your program qualifies.

Working interview.title: What Is a Working Interview? Pay, Rules and What to Expect
sections: What a working interview is

A working interview is a hiring step where you do the actual job for a set time, usually a few hours to a few days, before the employer decides whether to make an offer. You work alongside the team, often with real customers, patients or tasks.
It is common in dental and medical offices, restaurants, salons, trades, retail and small businesses. Some tech and creative employers use a paid trial project instead of a take-home assignment.
The goal on both sides is a real preview. The employer sees how you work and fit with the team, and you see the workplace, the pace and the people before you commit.
Should a working interview be paid

Under the federal Fair Labor Standards Act, a person who does productive work that benefits the employer is generally treated as an employee and must be paid at least minimum wage for that time. Calling it an interview does not change that.

Simply watching, shadowing or answering questions is different from working. The line between the two depends on the facts, such as whether you served customers, produced work the business used or replaced a paid worker.

Many states have their own wage rules, often stricter than federal law. If you did real work and were not paid, contact your state labor department or the US Department of Labor’s Wage and Hour Division, or ask an employment lawyer.
How employers usually set one up

Careful employers put the candidate on payroll for the trial, often as a short temporary hire, so wages are recorded and taxes are withheld. Some pay as a contractor, though worker classification rules still apply.
Being on payroll also matters for safety. If you are hurt during the trial, workers’ compensation coverage generally depends on your status as an employee, which varies by state.
Employers should explain the length, duties, pay and next steps in writing beforehand, and give a decision within a stated time after the trial ends.
What a job seeker should do
Before you agree, ask whether it is paid and at what rate, how long it lasts, what you will work on, who will supervise you and when you will hear back. Get the answers in an email.
Treat the day like a first day on the job. Arrive early, bring any required licenses or tools, ask questions, follow the workplace’s procedures and notice how staff treat each other.

Be cautious if the employer wants many unpaid days, asks you to do billable work for clients, or keeps a pool of trial workers with no offers. Unpaid work that a company then uses is a reason to walk away.
qa: Are working interviews legal?

Yes, a working interview itself is legal. The issue is pay: if you do productive work that benefits the employer, federal law generally requires at least minimum wage for those hours. State rules can add more protections. Your state labor department can tell you what applies where you live.
How long does a working interview last?

Most last a few hours to one full shift. Some run two to five days, and paid project trials in office jobs can last a week or more. Ask for the exact length in advance so you can plan around your current job.
What should I wear to a working interview?

Wear what the staff wear on a normal working day, adjusted to look neat. For clinical, kitchen or trade roles, ask whether you need scrubs, non-slip shoes or safety gear, and whether the employer provides them.
Do I get paid if I am not hired after a working interview?

If you did real work for the business, you are generally owed pay for those hours whether or not you get the job. Being hired or not does not change wage rules. If pay never arrives, contact the employer in writing first, then your state labor department.
What is the difference between a working interview and a probation period?

A working interview happens before any offer and decides whether you are hired. A probation period starts after you are hired and is an early stretch of the job when the employer reviews your performance more closely.

Skip-level meeting.title: What Is a Skip-Level Meeting? Purpose, Questions and Tips
sections: What a skip-level meeting is
A skip-level meeting is a conversation between an employee and their manager’s manager. It skips the level in between, which is where the name comes from.

Most are one-on-one talks, but some leaders hold them as small group sessions with several people from the teams below their direct reports. How often they happen depends on the company; some hold them every quarter, others once or twice a year.
In hiring, the term also describes an interview with the hiring manager’s boss. It is often one of the last steps before an offer.
Why companies hold them

Senior leaders use skip-level meetings to hear directly how a team really works. They want to know what slows people down, what is going well and how people feel, without everything passing through the middle manager first.
The meeting is not meant to judge your manager or let you go over their head. Still, honest feedback about problems can come up, and a good leader will listen and handle it with care.
For employees, a skip-level meeting gives visibility with someone more senior. It is also a chance to learn about company plans and ask about career paths beyond your own team.
How to prepare as an employee
Bring three or four questions. Good topics are where the company is heading, how team goals are set, what the leader sees as the biggest challenges and what growth looks like in your area.
If you share a problem, describe the situation and its effect on the work, and suggest a fix if you have one. Focus on processes and results, not personal complaints about coworkers.

Serious issues such as harassment, discrimination or safety concerns usually belong with HR as well, because HR has formal steps to follow. You can mention them in the meeting, but do not rely on it alone.
Let your manager know about the meeting if they do not already. Most companies expect it, and it avoids any sense that you are working around them.
How to handle a skip-level interview

When you meet the hiring manager’s boss during an interview process, expect broader questions. They often look at your judgment, how you communicate and whether you fit the wider organization, rather than testing detailed skills.
Prepare questions about how the team supports company strategy, how success is measured and how goals are set across teams. These show you think about the whole organization, not only your own tasks.
Treat it as a full interview, even if it feels relaxed. This person may have the final say on whether you get an offer.
qa: What should I ask in a skip-level meeting?

Ask about the company’s direction, the team’s top priorities, how goals are set and what success looks like this year. You can also ask what skills matter for growth in your area and whether there is anything the leader wants to hear more about from your team.
What should you not say in a skip-level meeting?

Avoid personal attacks on your manager or coworkers, gossip and complaints with no context. If you raise a problem, explain its effect on the work and suggest a fix. Do not share anything you would not be comfortable having repeated to your manager.
Is a skip-level meeting a good sign?

It is usually neutral. Many companies hold them as a routine for everyone. Being invited to one does not mean you are in trouble or about to be promoted, though it does give you a chance to be noticed by a senior leader.
Is a skip-level interview a good sign?
Often it means you have passed earlier rounds and the hiring manager wants their boss to approve the choice. It is not a guarantee of an offer, so prepare for it as seriously as any other interview.
Should I tell my manager about a skip-level meeting?
Yes, in most cases. Many companies tell the direct manager anyway, and mentioning it yourself keeps trust. You do not need to share every detail of what you discussed unless you choose to.

Apply on company site.title: What Does Apply on Company Site Mean? How It Works and What to Check
sections: What “apply on company site” means
“Apply on company site” is a button on a job listing that sends you away from the job board to the employer’s own careers page. You fill in and submit the application there, not on the board.

Many job boards show this button when the employer collects applications through its own website or hiring software. It differs from a quick or one-click apply, where the board sends your saved profile or resume to the employer for you.
On this site every job uses this kind of link. The site lists jobs and points you to the employer, but it never collects or stores your application.
What happens after you click

The link usually opens the job on the employer’s careers page or in its applicant tracking system (ATS), the software that collects and sorts applications. Addresses with names like greenhouse.io, lever.co, ashbyhq.com or myworkdayjobs.com belong to these hiring systems.
You may be asked to create an account, upload a resume, retype your work history and answer screening questions. Some systems let you apply as a guest without an account.

Because you applied with the employer directly, the job board cannot see your application or its status. Confirmation emails, interview invitations and rejections come from the employer or its hiring system.
How to apply safely
Before you type anything, look at the address bar. The domain should be the employer’s own website or a known hiring system, and the company name on the page should match the listing.

Real employers do not charge application fees or ask you to buy equipment, pay for training or send money. Be wary of any page that asks for your bank account details or a copy of your ID before you have a job offer.
If a page looks wrong, close it and find the careers page by searching for the company yourself. You can report job scams to the Federal Trade Commission at ReportFraud.ftc.gov.
Tips for a smoother application
Save a copy of the job posting or its key points before you apply. Postings are often taken down once the job closes, and you will want the details when an interviewer calls.
Keep a simple list of where you applied, the date and the login you used. Many people forget which hiring system accounts they created and miss status updates sent there.
Tailor your resume to the posting before you upload it, and answer screening questions carefully. A wrong answer to a required question can end the application before a person reads it.
qa: What does apply on company site mean on a job board?

It means the job board does not take applications for that job. Clicking the button opens the employer’s careers page or hiring system, where you submit your resume and answer its questions. The employer, not the board, receives and handles your application.
Is it better to apply on the company website or use easy apply?

Neither guarantees a better result. Applying on the company site takes longer but lets you answer every question the employer asks and confirms your application reached its system. Quick apply is faster, but check the employer’s requirements so your profile does not leave out anything important.
Why does the company site say the job is no longer available?

The employer may have filled the job or stopped taking applications, and the listing on the job board has not updated yet. Check the employer’s careers page for similar openings, and consider setting a job alert for that company.
Do I need to create an account to apply on a company site?

Often yes, because many employers use hiring software that stores your application under an account. Some systems allow guest applications. Use an email address you check often, since updates and interview invitations are usually sent there.
How do I know a company application page is real?

Check that the web address is the employer’s own domain or a known hiring system, and that the company name and job match the listing. Be cautious if the page asks for fees, bank details or ID documents before any offer. When in doubt, go to the company’s website directly.

Culture fit.title: What Is Culture Fit? Meaning, Bias and How to Show It
sections: What culture fit means

Culture fit is how well a person matches the way a team or company works. That includes its values, how people communicate, how decisions get made, the pace of work and how much structure or freedom people have.

Employers mention it in job postings, interview feedback and rejection notes. A hiring manager might say a candidate “wasn’t a culture fit” when the skills matched but something about working style or values seemed off.
Fit also matters to you. A job that clashes with how you like to work, such as constant meetings when you need focus time, can wear you down even when the pay and title are right.
Why culture fit is controversial

The term is vague, so it can turn into a stand-in for “people like us.” Interviewers may favor candidates who share their background, hobbies, school or sense of humor, which shuts out good people and makes teams less varied.

Federal law bars employers from rejecting candidates because of race, color, religion, sex (including pregnancy, sexual orientation and gender identity), national origin, age 40 or over, disability or genetic information. Calling a rejection “fit” does not make it legal if the real reason is one of these, and many states add more protected traits.

Because of this, many employers now talk about values fit or culture add. Culture add asks what new skills, views or experience a person brings, rather than how closely they match the people already there.
How employers can assess fit fairly

Write down the few values that really matter for the job, such as owning mistakes, sharing information or meeting deadlines. Then ask every candidate the same questions about them and score answers against the same guide.
Behavioral questions work well, such as “Tell me about a time you disagreed with a teammate.” Avoid judging by small talk, shared interests or whether you would enjoy a drink with the person.
Ask interviewers to give a specific reason when they flag a fit concern. If they cannot point to a work behavior, the concern is likely about likeness, not values.
How to show culture fit as a job seeker
Before the interview, read the company’s values page, recent posts and employee reviews, and note how they describe the way they work. Pick the values that are true for you too.
Prepare short stories that show those values in action: how you work with others, a disagreement you resolved, a mistake you owned and something you learned. Use real details and the result.
Ask your own questions, such as how decisions are made, how feedback is given and what a typical week looks like. The answers help you judge whether the team fits you, not only whether you fit it.
qa: What does it mean when an employer says you are not a culture fit?

It means the interviewers felt your working style or values did not match the team’s. Sometimes that is a real difference, such as wanting more structure than the team offers. Sometimes it is vague or reflects bias. You can politely ask for specific feedback, though many employers do not give it.
Is it legal to reject someone for culture fit?

Rejecting a candidate over genuine job-related fit, such as how they handle feedback, is generally legal. Using fit as cover for rejecting someone because of a protected trait like race, sex, age, religion or disability is illegal. If you think that happened, you can contact the EEOC, your state’s fair employment agency or an employment lawyer.
What is the difference between culture fit and culture add?

Culture fit asks whether a person matches how the team already works. Culture add asks what a person would bring that the team lacks, such as new skills, experience or ways of thinking. Many employers now look for shared core values plus culture add.
How do you answer culture fit interview questions?

Use short, true stories that show how you work: a time you helped a teammate, solved a disagreement or adapted to a change. Link them to values the company states, and be honest about how you like to work so both sides can judge the match.
Why is culture fit important?

People who share a team’s core values and working style tend to settle in faster and work well with others. Fit matters to job seekers too, because a poor match can make a job stressful. It is most useful when based on clear work values, not on personal likeness.

Competitive salary.title: What Does Competitive Salary Mean in a Job Posting?
sections: What “competitive salary” means
“Competitive salary” is a phrase employers put in job postings instead of a pay figure. It suggests the pay is in line with what other employers offer for similar work, but it does not say how much.

The employer decides what “competitive” means. It may be compared with large national employers, local companies or just the employer’s own past hires. The phrase can describe pay that is well above the market, right at it or below it.
You will also see close cousins such as “competitive pay”, “competitive compensation” and “salary commensurate with experience”. None of them give you a number you can compare with other offers.
Why employers use it and when the law limits it
Employers leave out a figure for several reasons. They may want room to negotiate, may not want current staff or competitors to see the range, or may not have set a budget yet.

A growing number of US states and some cities now have pay transparency laws. In places such as Colorado, California, Washington and New York, many employers must include a good-faith pay range in postings, so “competitive salary” alone is not enough there.

The rules differ by state and city: who counts as a covered employer, whether remote jobs are included, and whether the range must be in the posting or only given on request. Your state labor department’s website explains the local rules.
How to find out the real pay
Ask for the range early, ideally in the first call with the recruiter. A simple question such as “What is the budgeted range for this role?” is normal and does not hurt your chances.

Before you name your own number, look at what similar jobs in your area state as their pay. Postings that list ranges, government wage data and pay surveys from professional groups give you a realistic picture.

When you are asked for your expectations, give a range based on that research rather than your current pay. Many states and cities ban employers from asking about your salary history, so you may not have to share it.
Compare the full offer, not just the base salary. Bonus, overtime eligibility, health insurance costs, retirement matching and paid time off can change what a job is really worth.
qa: Is a competitive salary good?

Not necessarily. The phrase only means the employer thinks its pay is in line with the market. It could be above, at or below what similar jobs pay. You only know once you see a number and compare it with other postings for the same kind of work in your area.
Why do employers say competitive salary instead of a number?

Common reasons are wanting room to negotiate, keeping pay private from staff and competitors, or not having fixed a budget yet. Some employers also want to see a candidate before deciding where in a range to place them.
Is it legal to post a job without a salary?

It depends on where the job is. Several states and cities, including Colorado, California, Washington and New York, require many employers to include a pay range in postings. Elsewhere, leaving pay out is usually legal. Check your state labor department for the rules that apply to you.
How do I ask about salary when the posting says competitive?

Ask the recruiter directly in the first conversation, for example: “Could you share the salary range budgeted for this role?” It is a common, professional question. Asking early saves both sides time if the pay does not fit your needs.
What should I say if they ask my salary expectations first?

Give a range based on what similar jobs in your area pay, not your current salary. You can also say you would like to hear their range first. In many states and cities employers are not allowed to ask about your past pay.

Cost of living.title: What Is Cost of Living? How It Affects Your Pay and Job Offers
sections: What cost of living means
Cost of living is the amount of money you need to cover everyday needs in a particular place. It usually includes housing, food, transportation, health care, child care, utilities and taxes.

The same salary can feel very different from one area to another. Rent in a large coastal city can take a far bigger share of your paycheck than rent in a small town, even when the job and the pay are the same.
Cost of living is often shown as an index. A place is compared with a national average, so a score above the average means things cost more there, and a score below means they cost less.
How cost of living affects pay

Many employers set pay by location. A company may pay more for the same role in a high-cost city than in a lower-cost area. The federal government does something similar with locality pay for many of its workers.

A cost-of-living adjustment, or COLA, is a raise meant to keep pay in step with rising prices. Social Security benefits get a COLA each year based on a federal price index. Some union contracts and pensions include one, but most private employers are not required to give one.
If your raise is smaller than the rise in prices, your pay buys less than it did before. This is why people talk about real wages, which means pay after adjusting for inflation.
How to compare job offers in different places

Start with take-home pay, not the salary figure. Taxes differ by state and sometimes by city. Some states, such as Texas and Florida, have no state income tax on wages, while some cities add their own income tax.

Then list your main monthly costs in each place: rent or a mortgage, utilities, commuting, groceries, child care and insurance. Use real listings for rent in the neighborhoods you would consider, not just averages.
Subtract those costs from your take-home pay. The offer that leaves you more each month is often the better deal, even if its headline salary is lower.
Free cost-of-living calculators can give a quick estimate, but each uses its own data and method. Treat the result as a starting point and check the biggest costs yourself.
qa: What is a cost-of-living adjustment?

A cost-of-living adjustment, or COLA, is an increase in pay or benefits meant to match rising prices. Social Security applies one each year based on a federal price index. Some employers, union contracts and pensions also include one, but most private employers in the US do not have to offer it.
Is cost of living the same as inflation?

No. Cost of living is how much it costs to live in a place at a given time. Inflation is how fast prices rise over time. Inflation raises the cost of living, but two cities can have very different costs of living even when prices rise at the same rate in both.
Can I negotiate a higher salary because of cost of living?

Yes, especially if you are relocating to a more expensive area. Show the employer real numbers, such as typical rent for the area, and the market pay for the role there. Many employers already use location-based pay ranges, so ask which range applies to your location.
Do remote jobs pay based on cost of living?

Some do and some do not. Some companies adjust remote pay to where you live, so moving to a cheaper area can lower your pay. Others pay one rate for everyone. Ask how the company sets remote pay, and whether moving later would change it, before you accept.
How do I compare the cost of living between two cities?

Estimate take-home pay in each city after federal, state and local taxes. Then add up your main monthly costs, starting with housing, transport, child care and insurance. Online calculators help for a quick view, but check actual rent listings and commuting costs for the most accurate picture.

Closed job.title: What Is a Closed Job? What It Means and What to Do Next
sections: What a closed job means
A closed job is an opening the employer has stopped taking applications for. The posting may say “closed”, “no longer accepting applications”, “position filled” or “this job has expired”.
On this site, a closed job keeps its page so old links and bookmarks still work. The page is marked as closed and points you to open jobs of the same kind.
A closed posting tells you the employer is not reviewing new applicants for that opening. It does not always mean someone was hired.
Why employers close a job
The most common reason is that the role was filled or the employer chose finalists. Many employers also close a posting once they have enough applicants to review, even before anyone is interviewed.

A job can close because a deadline passed, the budget was cut, the team changed plans or the role was put on hold. Some postings close automatically after a set time in the employer’s system or on a job board.
Sometimes a job closes and comes back later as a new posting. This can happen when the first round of candidates did not work out or the job description changed.
When your application shows “closed”

Many applicant tracking systems, the software employers use to manage applications, show a status such as “position closed” or “no longer under consideration”. If you applied and see this, the employer is usually no longer considering you for that opening.
It can mean someone else was chosen, the role was canceled or the posting was simply taken down. The status alone rarely tells you which, and many employers do not send a separate message.
What to do when a job is closed
Do not try to apply through another route just to get around the closed posting. Instead, look for open jobs of the same kind, at the same employer or elsewhere.

If you really want to work for that employer, follow its careers page or set up a job alert for similar titles. A polite note to a recruiter you already talked to, asking to be kept in mind, is reasonable.
If you were interviewed and the job closed, you can ask for brief feedback. Keep it short and do not expect a detailed answer.
qa: Does “job closed” mean I was rejected?

Often, but not always. It means the employer is no longer taking or reviewing applications for that opening. The role may have been filled by someone else, canceled or put on hold. If you were not contacted for an interview, it is safest to treat it as a no and keep applying elsewhere.
Can I still apply to a closed job?

Usually no. The application link is turned off, and emailed applications are often ignored or sent back to the careers page. Your time is better spent on open jobs of the same kind. You can follow the employer for new openings.
Why did a job close so quickly after it was posted?

Some employers close a posting once they have enough applicants to review, sometimes within days. Others had an internal or referred candidate in mind, or the plans for the role changed. Applying soon after a job is posted gives you the best chance of being seen.
Can a closed job be reopened?

Yes. If the chosen candidate turns down the offer, leaves early or the first round of applicants does not work out, an employer may reopen the role or post it again. If you applied before, it is fine to apply again to the new posting.
How long do job postings usually stay open?

There is no fixed rule. Some stay open for a few days, others for weeks or until the role is filled. Government and some public sector jobs often list a closing date. Private employers usually do not, so apply while the posting is open.
