Hard skills.title: What Are Hard Skills? Examples and How to Show Them
sections: What hard skills are

Hard skills are specific abilities you learn through study, training or practice, and that someone can test or check directly. Examples are speaking Spanish, writing Python, using Excel, reading blueprints, running payroll or driving a forklift.

They differ from soft skills, such as communication, teamwork or problem solving, which describe how you work with people and handle situations. Soft skills matter just as much, but they are harder to prove with a test or a certificate.
Many hard skills come with proof, such as a license, a certification, a degree, a test score or a portfolio of work. Others you show through what you have built, fixed or delivered in past jobs.
Why hard skills matter in a job search

Job postings usually list hard skills as requirements, because they are the easiest way to tell whether someone can do the work from day one. A nursing job may require an RN license, and a data job may require SQL.

Recruiters and applicant tracking systems often search resumes for these exact skill names. If the posting says “Microsoft Excel” and your resume only says “spreadsheets,” a keyword search may miss you.

Employers often check hard skills directly during hiring, through skills tests, coding exercises, typing tests, work samples or license lookups. Claiming a skill you do not have usually comes out at this stage.
How to show your hard skills
Read the posting and note every tool, method, language and license it names. List the ones that are true for you, using the posting’s own words and spelling.

Add a short Skills section to your resume, then back each key skill up in your Experience section. Say where you used it and what came of it, such as “Built monthly sales reports in Excel using pivot tables.”

Include licenses and certifications with their full name, issuing body and, where relevant, the license number or expiry date. If a skill is rusty or basic, say so honestly, for example “conversational Spanish.”

If you lack a required hard skill, consider a course, a certification or a small project that lets you show it. Some postings separate required skills from preferred ones, and you can often apply without every preferred skill.
qa: What are examples of hard skills?

Common examples are foreign languages, programming languages such as Python or Java, software such as Excel or QuickBooks, bookkeeping, data analysis, graphic design, welding, phlebotomy, CNC machining, commercial driving with a CDL and medical coding. Each can be taught and checked with a test, a license or a work sample.
What is the difference between hard skills and soft skills?

Hard skills are specific, teachable abilities you can test directly, such as coding or accounting. Soft skills are personal and social abilities, such as communication, teamwork and time management, that shape how you work. Most jobs need both, and employers judge soft skills mainly through interviews and references.
How many hard skills should I put on my resume?

There is no fixed number. List the hard skills that the job asks for and that you can actually use, usually a short focused list rather than everything you have ever touched. Drop skills that have nothing to do with the role, and show the most important ones in your work history too.
Is Microsoft Office a hard skill?

Yes. Using Word, Excel, PowerPoint or Outlook is a hard skill because it can be taught and tested. It helps to name the specific program and level, such as “Excel: pivot tables, VLOOKUP, charts,” rather than just writing “Microsoft Office.”
Is communication a hard skill?

General communication is a soft skill. Some specific forms of it count as hard skills, such as technical writing, sign language, a foreign language or court reporting, because they follow learnable methods and can be tested.

Hiring committee.title: What Is a Hiring Committee? How It Decides on Job Offers
sections: What a hiring committee is

A hiring committee is a small group of people who review a candidate’s interview results and decide whether the company should make an offer. The decision rests with the group instead of one hiring manager.

Members are often senior employees, managers or recruiters. At some companies they did not interview the candidate themselves. They judge the case from written feedback, scores, the resume and any work samples.
Some large employers use them for most roles. In universities, public agencies and nonprofits, a similar group is often called a search committee and may also run the interviews.
How a hiring committee makes its decision
After your interviews, each interviewer writes notes and usually gives a rating. A recruiter or the hiring manager collects this into a packet, sometimes with a summary and a recommendation.
The committee meets or reviews the packet on its own schedule. Members look for consistent evidence across interviews, check whether the bar for the level was met and question weak or mixed feedback.

The outcome is usually an approval, a rejection, a request for one more interview, or a decision to consider you for a different level or team. Pay and offer details are often settled afterward by the recruiter or another approval step.
Employers use committees to reduce one person’s bias, keep the hiring standard the same across teams and spread the responsibility for each hire.
What a hiring committee means for job seekers
Every interviewer’s notes reach the committee, so a single weak interview can hurt even if the others went well. Treat each conversation as if it decides the outcome.

Give concrete examples with clear results, because the committee reads what interviewers wrote down, not how warm the room felt. Specific numbers, actions and outcomes are easier to record and repeat.
Expect the process to take longer than a single manager’s decision. It is reasonable to ask the recruiter when the committee meets and when you will hear back.
What employers should keep in mind
A committee works best when interviewers use the same questions and rating scale for each role and write feedback soon after the interview. Vague notes make fair decisions harder.
Keep the timeline short and tell candidates what to expect. Long waits can cost you good applicants who accept other offers first.
Base decisions on job-related evidence. Federal and state anti-discrimination laws apply to committee decisions just as they do to one manager’s choice.
qa: What does it mean when my application goes to the hiring committee?

It means your interviews are finished and your feedback has been gathered for a final review. The committee will decide whether to approve an offer, reject, or ask for more information. It is a normal step, not a sign of trouble.
How long does a hiring committee take to decide?

It varies by employer. Some committees meet weekly, so a decision may come within days, while others take a few weeks, especially when more interviews are requested. Ask your recruiter when the committee meets and when you should expect news.
Can a hiring committee reject you after good interviews?

Yes. If one interviewer raised a concern, or the feedback was positive but thin on specific evidence, the committee may decide the bar was not met. It may also suggest a different level or team instead of a clear rejection.
Is a hiring committee the same as an interview panel?
Not always. An interview panel is the group that interviews you, often at the same time. A hiring committee reviews the results and makes the decision, and its members may never have met you.
Does the hiring manager still have a say?

Usually yes. The hiring manager often gives a recommendation or sits on the committee, and in many companies can argue for or against a candidate. But the final approval belongs to the group, not the manager alone.

Employer brand.title: What Is Employer Brand? Meaning and How Job Seekers Can Read It
sections: What employer brand means
Employer brand is the reputation a company has as a place to work. It is what job seekers, current staff and former staff believe about its pay, culture, managers, workload and growth chances.
It is different from the consumer brand. A company can sell a well-liked product and still be known as a hard place to work, or be little known to shoppers and well regarded by its own staff.

A company shapes its employer brand on purpose through its career page, job ads, social media posts and recruiting events. It also gets shaped without its control by employee reviews, word of mouth and news stories.
Why employer brand matters
For employers, a strong employer brand can make hiring easier. More people apply, more candidates accept offers, and staff may stay longer when the job matches what they were told.

For job seekers, the employer brand is a first picture of what working there might be like. It is only a picture, though, because the polished parts are written by the company and the reviews are written by a small, self-selected group.

Some companies use the term employer value proposition, or EVP, for the main reasons they give people to join, such as pay, flexibility, mission or training. The EVP is the message; the employer brand is how people actually see the company.
How to read an employer brand as a job seeker
Compare several sources: the career page, job postings, review sites, posts by current employees and any recent news. Look for what they agree on and where they disagree.
Pay attention to patterns, not single comments. One angry review means little, but the same complaint about pay, managers or turnover repeated over many months means more.
Check that the details are recent. A review from years ago may describe different leaders or policies, while a run of new reviews may show a change for better or worse.
In interviews, ask questions that test the brand, such as why the role is open, how long people usually stay on the team and how work hours look in a busy week.
What employers can do to build it
Describe jobs honestly, including the hard parts, so new hires are not surprised. A brand built on promises the job does not keep tends to show up later in reviews.
Treat candidates well during hiring by replying to applicants, keeping them updated and giving clear decisions. Many people share how a hiring process felt, whether or not they were hired.
Respond to public reviews calmly and fix the problems they point to. Staff who are treated fairly are usually the most believable voice for a company.
qa: What is an example of employer brand?

A company known for flexible hours and good training has an employer brand built on those points. People hear about it through staff posts, reviews and the career page. Another company may be known for long hours and high turnover, which is also an employer brand, just a negative one.
What is the difference between employer brand and EVP?

The employer value proposition, or EVP, is what a company says it offers workers, such as pay, benefits, flexibility and growth. The employer brand is the reputation people actually hold about working there. A good EVP helps build a good employer brand only if the job really delivers it.
Can I trust company reviews when judging an employer brand?

Treat them as one source among several. People with strong feelings are more likely to post, so reviews can lean very positive or very negative. Look for repeated themes, recent dates and details about the specific team or location you are applying to.
Who is responsible for employer brand in a company?

It often sits with human resources, talent acquisition or marketing, sometimes with a dedicated employer brand role. In practice, managers and employees shape it every day through how people are treated, which is why it cannot be fully controlled by one team.
Why should job seekers care about employer brand?

It gives early clues about pay, culture, workload and how managers treat staff before you commit to a job. A mismatch between what the company says and what employees report is worth asking about during interviews.

Employee stock purchase plan (ESPP).title: What Is an ESPP (Employee Stock Purchase Plan)? How It Works
sections: What an employee stock purchase plan is

An employee stock purchase plan, or ESPP, lets you buy your employer’s shares with money taken from your paycheck. The shares are usually sold to you at a discount to the market price, often up to 15%.

ESPPs are offered mostly by companies whose shares trade on a stock exchange, because there has to be a market price to discount from. Joining is voluntary, and you choose how much of each paycheck to set aside, up to a cap the plan sets.

Most US plans are “qualified” plans under Section 423 of the tax code. They follow federal rules on who can join, how big the discount can be and how much stock you can buy, and they get better tax treatment than non-qualified plans.
How an ESPP works step by step

The plan runs in offering periods, often six months, though some last longer and contain several purchase periods. During each period your deductions build up in an account, and on the purchase date the money buys shares at the discounted price.

Many plans have a lookback. The discount then applies to the lower of the share price at the start of the offering period or on the purchase date. If the price rose during the period, your real gain can be much larger than 15%.
Qualified plans cap purchases at $25,000 worth of stock per calendar year, measured at the price on the first day of the offering. Your plan may set a lower limit, such as a percentage of pay.

You can usually stop or withdraw from an offering before the purchase date and get your saved deductions back in cash. Check your plan’s rules, because some do not let you rejoin until the next offering.
How ESPP shares are taxed
In a qualified plan you owe no tax when the shares are bought. Tax comes when you sell, and the amount depends on how long you held them.

A sale is a qualifying disposition if you hold the shares more than two years from the start of the offering and more than one year from the purchase date. Part of the gain, tied to the discount, is taxed as ordinary income and the rest as a long-term capital gain.

If you sell sooner, it is a disqualifying disposition. The difference between the market price on the purchase date and what you paid is taxed as ordinary income, usually shown on your W-2, and any further gain or loss is a capital gain or loss.

Your employer sends Form 3922 for shares bought in a qualified plan. Brokers’ cost basis figures on Form 1099-B often leave out the discount already taxed as income, so check them or ask an accountant to avoid paying tax twice.
What to consider before you join
Look at the discount, whether there is a lookback, how long each offering lasts and whether you may sell shares as soon as they are bought. Some plans require a holding period.
Selling right away locks in the discount as extra income, minus taxes and any fees. Holding on can lower your tax but exposes you to the share price falling.
Keep in mind that your paycheck already depends on your employer. Putting a large share of your savings in the same company’s stock means one bad year could hit both your job and your investments.
Only set aside money you will not need before the purchase date. For questions about your own tax situation, talk to an accountant or tax adviser.
qa: Is an ESPP worth it?

Often yes, if the plan has a real discount and you can afford the deductions. Buying at 15% off and selling right away gives a return of more than 15% on the money you put in, before taxes. The risk grows if you hold the shares a long time, because the stock price can fall.
Should I sell my ESPP shares immediately?

Selling right away turns the discount into near-certain extra pay and avoids holding too much of your employer’s stock. Holding for a qualifying disposition can lower your tax but means taking the risk that the price drops. Which is better depends on your finances, so ask a tax adviser if the amounts are large.
What is the ESPP lookback?

A lookback means the purchase price is based on the lower of the share price at the start of the offering period or on the purchase date, then discounted. If the stock rose during the period, you buy at a discount to the older, lower price, which can make the gain much bigger.
What happens to my ESPP if I leave the company?

Under most plans, leaving ends your participation, and deductions not yet used to buy shares are refunded to you in cash. Shares you already bought stay yours, and you can keep or sell them. The holding periods for tax purposes still apply after you leave.
How much can I put into an ESPP?

Each plan sets a cap, usually a percentage of your pay. Qualified plans also limit purchases to $25,000 worth of stock per calendar year, valued at the share price on the first day of the offering. Your plan documents give the exact limits.

Elevator pitch.title: What Is an Elevator Pitch? How to Write and Say Yours
sections: What an elevator pitch is
An elevator pitch is a short spoken summary of who you are, what you do well and what you are looking for. It is meant to fit in the time of a short elevator ride, usually 30 to 60 seconds.

In a job search you use it when someone asks “So, what do you do?” or “Tell me about yourself.” That can happen at a career fair, a networking event, a recruiter phone screen or the start of an interview.
A written version of the same idea often appears as the summary at the top of a resume or a LinkedIn profile, or as the opening lines of a networking email.
Why it matters in a job search
People you meet briefly remember little. A clear pitch tells them what kind of job you want, so they can think of an opening, a contact or a referral for you.
Recruiters often start a screen by asking you to introduce yourself. A prepared answer sounds confident, keeps you from rambling and points the conversation toward your strongest experience.
Having one also helps you. Writing it forces you to decide what job you are aiming for and which result best proves you can do it.
How to write your elevator pitch
Start with your current or most recent role in plain words, such as “I’m a payroll specialist at a 300-person manufacturer.” Avoid internal job titles that outsiders will not understand.
Add one specific result, with a number if you can, such as cutting processing time, handling a set number of accounts or training a team. Only use figures that are true and that you can explain.
End with what you want next and, where it fits, a question or request, such as asking whether they know anyone hiring for that kind of role.
Keep it to about four or five sentences. Write it down, cut every word that does not add meaning, then rewrite it in the way you actually speak.
How to deliver it well
Practice it out loud until it feels natural, but do not memorize it word for word, or it will sound like a script. Time yourself so you stay within a minute.
Adjust it to the listener. A recruiter for a specific role needs the parts that match that job, while a new contact at an event may need a simpler version with less detail.
Stop after the pitch and let the other person respond. A good pitch starts a conversation rather than replacing one.
qa: How long should an elevator pitch be?

Usually 30 to 60 seconds when spoken, which is roughly four to six short sentences. At a busy career fair, shorter is often better. In an interview, when asked to tell them about yourself, you can expand it to about one or two minutes.
What are the parts of a good elevator pitch?

Most strong pitches have three parts: who you are and what you do now, one concrete result or strength that proves your value, and what you are looking for next. Many end with a simple question or request, such as asking for advice or a referral.
Is an elevator pitch the same as “tell me about yourself”?

They are closely related. Your elevator pitch is a good base for answering “tell me about yourself” in an interview. In the interview version, you can add a little more detail about your background and explain why you are interested in that specific job and company.
Can I use an elevator pitch if I am changing careers or a student?

Yes. Lead with relevant skills, training or projects instead of a job title, mention one result from school, volunteering or past work, and say clearly which field or role you are moving toward. Being clear about your goal matters more than having years of experience.
Should I memorize my elevator pitch?

Know the key points and your main result by heart, but not every word. Practicing out loud several times helps you sound natural. Reciting a fixed script tends to sound stiff and makes it harder to adjust to the person you are talking to.

Equal opportunity employer.title: What Is an Equal Opportunity Employer (EOE)? What It Means for You
sections: What equal opportunity employer means

An equal opportunity employer, often shortened to EOE, is an employer that says it does not make job decisions based on protected traits. These include race, color, religion, sex, national origin, age, disability and genetic information.

The promise covers more than hiring. It also applies to pay, promotions, job assignments, training, discipline, layoffs and firing, and it includes a ban on harassment and on punishing people who complain about discrimination.
You often see it as a line at the bottom of a job posting, sometimes in a longer form such as “EOE/M/F/D/V”, which stands for minorities, female, disabled and veterans.
The laws behind the statement

In the US, federal laws set the rules whether or not an employer prints the line. Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964 bans discrimination based on race, color, religion, sex and national origin. Since a 2020 Supreme Court decision, sex includes sexual orientation and gender identity.

The Americans with Disabilities Act protects people with disabilities, and the Age Discrimination in Employment Act protects workers aged 40 and older. The Equal Pay Act requires equal pay for men and women doing substantially equal work, and the Pregnancy Discrimination Act covers pregnancy.

Most of these federal laws apply to employers with 15 or more employees; the age law applies at 20 or more, and the Equal Pay Act covers almost all employers. Many states and cities cover smaller employers and protect extra traits, so the rules differ by location.

Federal contractors have extra duties, for example toward protected veterans and people with disabilities. Some contractor rules changed in 2025, so employers should check current guidance from the Department of Labor.
What a job seeker should do
Treat the EOE line as the legal minimum, not proof of a fair or friendly workplace. Clear duties, a posted pay range, real benefits and how the company treats you during interviews tell you more.

You may be asked to fill in a voluntary self-identification form about race, gender, veteran status or disability. It is optional, should be kept apart from your application and is used for government reporting, so declining should not affect your chances.

If you believe you were treated unfairly because of a protected trait, write down dates, names and what was said. You can file a charge with the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission (EEOC) or your state agency, and a lawyer can advise on your specific case.
What an employer should do

Printing the statement is easy; following the law takes work. Use the same job-related criteria and interview questions for every candidate, and avoid asking about age, family plans, religion or health.

Provide reasonable accommodations for disability and religion unless they cause undue hardship, and train managers on harassment and retaliation. For questions about your obligations, ask an employment lawyer or your state labor department.
qa: What does EOE mean on a job posting?

EOE stands for equal opportunity employer. It means the employer states that it does not hire, pay, promote or fire people based on protected traits such as race, sex, religion, national origin, age or disability. In the US, most employers must follow these rules even if they do not print the line.
Are all employers required to be equal opportunity employers?

Most are. Federal anti-discrimination laws generally apply to employers with 15 or more employees, or 20 or more for age discrimination, and the Equal Pay Act covers almost all employers. Many state and local laws reach smaller employers too, so very few US employers are fully exempt.
Do I have to answer the voluntary self-identification questions?

No. Questions about race, ethnicity, gender, veteran status or disability on these forms are voluntary. Employers use the answers for government reports and should keep them separate from hiring decisions. Choosing not to answer should not hurt your application.
How long do I have to file a discrimination complaint?

For most private-sector and state or local government jobs, you must file a charge with the EEOC within 180 days of the event. This extends to 300 days if a state or local agency enforces a similar law. Federal employees follow a different, shorter process, so check the exact deadline quickly.
What is the difference between EOE and affirmative action?

EOE means not discriminating against anyone based on protected traits. Affirmative action refers to active steps to recruit and advance groups that were underrepresented, which some federal contractors have been required to take. The rules for contractors have changed over time, so details depend on current federal policy.

Performance improvement plan (PIP).title: What Is a PIP (Performance Improvement Plan)? What to Do on One
sections: What a performance improvement plan is

A performance improvement plan, or PIP, is a formal written document from a manager, often prepared with HR. It says where your work falls short, what must change, how progress will be measured and by when.

Common lengths are 30, 60 or 90 days. A typical plan lists specific goals, a schedule of check-in meetings, any training or support offered, and what happens if the goals are not met, which is often further discipline or the end of the job.
A PIP is different from a regular performance review. A review looks back over a whole period, while a PIP is a short, targeted plan that starts because of a specific problem.
Why employers use PIPs and where they lead

Some managers use a PIP to give a struggling worker a clear and fair chance to improve. Others use it to document reasons for a dismissal they have mostly decided on already. Both happen, and the document alone rarely tells you which one you face.

No federal law requires a PIP. Most US jobs are at-will, so an employer can usually end a job without one, as long as the reason is not illegal, such as discrimination or retaliation. Montana is an exception: after a probation period, its law generally requires good cause to fire someone.

Union contracts and some company policies require steps of progressive discipline, such as a verbal warning, a written warning and then a PIP. Employers also like the written record because it helps show that a dismissal was about performance if it is challenged later.
A PIP can end with the worker meeting the goals, the plan being extended, or the job ending. Some employers offer a choice at the start: try the plan or leave with a severance agreement.
What to do if you are put on a PIP

Read the plan closely and ask what exactly will be measured, who decides whether you passed and what success looks like. If a goal is vague, ask for a number, a deadline or an example, then confirm the answers in a short follow-up email.

Your signature usually confirms that you received the plan, not that you agree with it. You can often add a written response with your side of the story. Keep it factual and calm, because it may go into your personnel file.
Do the work and keep your own record: dates, finished tasks, feedback received and emails sent. Ask for the check-in meetings the plan promises, and write down what was said in each one.

At the same time, update your resume and start looking quietly, especially if the goals seem unreachable. If you believe the PIP is discrimination or retaliation, for example after a complaint or medical leave, talk to an employment lawyer, the EEOC or your state’s fair employment agency.
How employers should write a fair PIP

Name the specific problems with examples, set goals that can be measured, and give a realistic time frame. A goal like “improve communication” is hard to judge; “reply to client emails within one business day” is clear.

Offer real support, such as training or regular feedback, hold the check-ins you schedule, and apply the same standards you use for other workers in the same role. Ask HR or an employment lawyer to review the plan if a dismissal may follow.
qa: Does a PIP mean I will be fired?

Not always. Some workers meet the goals and keep their jobs, but many PIPs end in dismissal or a resignation. Clear, reachable goals and a manager who gives real feedback are better signs than vague goals and missed check-ins.
Should I sign a PIP?

In most cases your signature only confirms you received the plan, not that you agree with it. Ask what the signature means if the form is unclear. Refusing to sign usually does not stop the plan and can look uncooperative, so many people sign and add a written comment.
Can I quit while on a PIP?

Yes. In an at-will job you can resign at any time. Quitting may affect unemployment benefits, because people who leave voluntarily usually do not qualify unless they had good cause under state rules. Some workers instead ask HR about a severance agreement before deciding.
Can I get unemployment if I am fired after a PIP?

Often yes. In many states, losing a job for not meeting performance standards despite trying is not treated as misconduct, so it does not by itself disqualify you. Rules and decisions differ by state, so file a claim and check with your state unemployment office.
Do I have to tell a new employer I was on a PIP?

You usually do not need to bring it up, but do not lie if asked directly. Many employers only confirm dates and job title in reference checks, though policies vary. If asked why you left, give a short, honest answer focused on what you learned.

Day rate.title: What Is a Day Rate? How to Set and Negotiate Yours
sections: What a day rate means

A day rate is a fixed price for one day of work. Contractors, freelancers and consultants often quote one instead of an hourly rate or a yearly salary, so the client pays the same amount for each day you work.

Day rates are common in consulting, IT and software contracting, film and TV crews, events, photography and some oil, gas and construction jobs. In the UK, day-rate contracting is a standard way to work in tech and finance.

The contract should say how many hours count as a day, often seven and a half or eight. It should also say what happens if you work longer, such as a half-day rate, an extra day charge or nothing extra.
How to work out your day rate

Start with what you want to earn in a year. Then add the costs an employer would usually cover, such as health insurance, retirement savings, equipment, software, business insurance and accounting fees.

As a 1099 contractor in the US, you also pay both the employee and employer shares of Social Security and Medicare through self-employment tax. You get no paid holidays, vacation or sick days, so build those into your price.
Divide the total by the days you will really bill, not every weekday. Leave out holidays, time off, sick days, gaps between contracts and unpaid time spent finding work and doing admin.

For example, if you want $100,000, expect $25,000 in costs and think you will bill 200 days, your day rate is $125,000 divided by 200, or $625. Then check it against what others in your field and city charge.
Day rates for employees in the US
Some employers pay employees, not contractors, a day rate. Under the federal Fair Labor Standards Act, a day rate alone does not make a worker exempt from overtime.

A non-exempt employee paid by the day is still owed overtime for hours over 40 in a workweek, usually at half the regular rate on top of the day pay already earned. The regular rate is found by dividing the week’s total pay by total hours worked.

In 2023 the Supreme Court ruled that a highly paid worker paid only by the day was not on a salary basis and so was not exempt. Some states add their own overtime rules, such as daily overtime. If you think you are owed overtime, ask your state labor department or an employment lawyer.
What to check before you agree
Confirm the hours in a day, the overtime or extra-day terms, whether travel days are paid, who pays expenses and how many days the contract is expected to last.

Check payment terms, such as invoicing weekly or monthly and how many days the client has to pay. Ask whether you are a 1099 contractor, a W-2 employee of a staffing agency or paid through your own company, because taxes and benefits differ.
qa: How do I convert a day rate to a salary?

Multiply the day rate by the days you expect to bill in a year, then subtract your own costs and the extra taxes a self-employed person pays. A day rate times 260 weekdays overstates what you earn, because contractors are not paid for holidays, time off or gaps between contracts.
Is a day rate better than an hourly rate?

It depends on the work. A day rate is simpler to invoice and rewards you when you finish quickly, but it can leave you unpaid for long days unless the contract defines hours. An hourly rate pays for every hour but needs careful time tracking.
Do day-rate workers get overtime?

Independent contractors do not get overtime under federal law; they set their own price. Employees paid a day rate usually do: if they are non-exempt, the Fair Labor Standards Act requires overtime pay for hours over 40 in a workweek. Some states also have daily overtime rules.
Should my day rate include expenses?

It can, but many contractors bill travel, lodging and other job costs separately so the rate stays the same across clients. Whatever you choose, write it in the contract so the client knows what is covered.
How many hours is a day rate?
There is no legal standard. Most contracts define a day as seven and a half or eight hours, and some set a half-day rate for shorter work. Agree on the hours in writing before you start.

WARN notice.title: What Is a WARN Notice? Layoff Warnings Under the WARN Act
sections: What a WARN notice is

A WARN notice is a written warning that a US employer gives before a large layoff or the closing of a site. It comes from the federal Worker Adjustment and Retraining Notification Act of 1988, usually called the WARN Act.
The law’s purpose is to give workers time to look for new jobs, find training and plan their money before their pay stops. The standard notice period is 60 calendar days before the first job losses.

The employer must send notice to each affected worker or their union, to the state’s dislocated worker unit, often called the rapid response team, and to the local government’s chief elected official.
When the WARN Act applies

The federal law covers most employers with 100 or more full-time employees. It also covers employers with 100 or more workers, part-time staff included, who together work at least 4,000 hours a week, not counting overtime.

Notice is required for a plant closing that causes 50 or more full-time workers at one site to lose their jobs within 30 days. It is also required for a mass layoff at one site of 500 or more workers, or of 50 to 499 workers if they make up at least a third of the site’s full-time workforce.

A job loss under the law includes being let go for reasons other than misconduct, a layoff longer than six months, or hours cut by more than half in each month of a six-month period. Quitting, retiring and being fired for cause do not count.

Shorter notice is allowed in limited cases, such as a business circumstance that could not be foreseen, a natural disaster, or a struggling company seeking money that would have prevented the closing. The employer must still give as much notice as it can and explain why it is short.
State mini-WARN laws
Many states have their own laws, often called mini-WARN laws, that go further than the federal one. They may cover smaller employers, smaller layoffs or require longer notice.

For example, New York and New Jersey require 90 days of notice, and New Jersey also requires severance pay in covered layoffs. California and Illinois cover employers with 75 or more workers. Rules change, so check your state labor department’s website for the current details.
Most states publish the WARN notices they receive online. Job seekers can search these lists to see whether a company they are considering has had recent layoffs.
What to do if you get a WARN notice

Read the notice for your expected last day, whether the job loss is permanent or temporary, and the name of a contact who can answer questions. Ask in writing what pay, health coverage and other benefits continue until then, and whether severance is offered.

Use the notice period to update your resume, contact your network and start applying while you still have a paycheck. Your state’s rapid response team or local American Job Center can help with job search services, training and unemployment insurance information.

If you believe your employer did not give the notice the law requires, you can talk to an employment lawyer. The federal WARN Act is enforced through lawsuits in federal court, not by the US Department of Labor.
qa: Do you get paid during a WARN notice period?

Yes. The notice period is time you are still employed, so you keep your normal pay and benefits until your last day. Some employers let workers stop working but keep paying wages and benefits for the full 60 days, which is often called pay in lieu of notice.
What happens if an employer does not give a WARN notice?

Under the federal law, an employer that fails to give required notice can owe each affected worker back pay and benefits for each day of missing notice, up to 60 days. It may also owe a civil penalty to the local government. Workers usually recover this through a lawsuit, so talk to an employment lawyer about a specific case.
Can I be fired after getting a WARN notice?

Yes, in most cases. A WARN notice does not protect you from being fired for misconduct before your scheduled last day. Most US jobs are at-will, but an employer cannot use a firing to avoid the WARN Act’s notice and pay rules.
Can I collect unemployment after a WARN notice?

Usually you apply once your job actually ends, not when you receive the notice. Pay received in lieu of notice or severance may delay or reduce benefits in some states. Rules differ by state, so check with your state unemployment office.
Where can I find WARN notices for a company?

Most states post the WARN notices they receive on their labor or workforce agency website, often searchable by company, city and date. These lists show the employer, location, number of affected workers and planned layoff date.

Four-day week.title: What Is a Four-Day Week? Types, Pay and What to Ask
sections: What a four-day week means

A four-day week is a work schedule where you work four days and have three days off, instead of the usual five days on and two off. The phrase covers two quite different setups, so the label alone does not tell you much.

In the first type, you work fewer total hours, often around 32, for the same pay as a full-time job. This is sometimes called the 100-80-100 model: 100% of pay for 80% of the time, in return for keeping 100% of the output.

In the second type, called a compressed workweek, you work the same total hours in fewer days. The most common pattern is four ten-hour days, often written as 4/10. Your pay and workload stay the same; only the shape of the week changes.
A third version is simply part-time work: four days at reduced pay. Some employers call this a four-day week too, so always check the salary attached.
How pay, overtime and benefits work
Under the federal Fair Labor Standards Act, overtime for non-exempt workers is based on hours over 40 in a workweek, not hours in a day. So four ten-hour days usually do not trigger federal overtime.

A few states, including California, also count overtime by the day. In California, a four-ten schedule without daily overtime is allowed only through a formal alternative workweek process, which includes a secret-ballot vote by the affected employees. Rules differ by state, so check with your state labor department.

Paid time off often changes on a compressed schedule. If PTO and holidays are counted in hours, one day off may use ten hours, and a holiday that falls on your regular day off may or may not be replaced. Ask how the employer handles both.

If a four-day week cuts your hours, check whether you still meet the hours needed for health insurance, retirement plan contributions and other benefits. Eligibility rules depend on the employer’s plans and, for some benefits, on federal law.
Why employers offer it and what can go wrong
Employers use a four-day week to attract and keep staff, reduce burnout and cut costs such as office space or commuting days. Workers value the extra day for rest, family, appointments or study.
Not every job fits. Roles with customers, patients or shift coverage may need the team split across different days off, so your day off might be a Wednesday rather than a Friday.
Some programs start as a trial and can end. Long ten-hour days can also be tiring, make childcare harder or eat into evenings, so the extra day off is not free.
What a job seeker should ask
Ask which type it is: fewer hours at the same pay, the same hours in longer days, or reduced hours at reduced pay. Then ask for the exact daily hours and the total weekly hours.
Ask whether the schedule is written into your offer letter or contract, or whether it is a pilot the company can end. Find out if your day off is fixed, rotating or chosen by your manager.
Ask how PTO, holidays, overtime and benefits work on the schedule. Get the answers in writing before you accept, and compare the real hourly rate with other offers.
qa: Is a four-day week the same as part-time?

Not always. A four-day week can mean fewer hours at full-time pay, the same 40 hours in four longer days, or reduced hours at reduced pay. Only the last one is really part-time work. Check the pay, the weekly hours and your benefits to know which you are being offered.
Do you get overtime working four ten-hour days?

Usually not under federal law, because overtime is based on hours over 40 in a workweek. Some states, such as California, have daily overtime rules, and California allows four-ten schedules without daily overtime only under a formal alternative workweek arrangement. Check your state labor department’s rules.
How many hours is a four-day work week?

It depends on the type. A reduced-hours four-day week is often around 32 hours, while a compressed schedule is usually 40 hours worked as four ten-hour days. Some employers set other totals, so ask for the exact weekly hours.
Do four-day weeks get paid the same?

In a compressed workweek and in the 100-80-100 model, pay usually stays the same as a full-time five-day job. If the employer treats it as reduced hours, pay is usually cut in proportion. The offer letter should state your salary or hourly rate and expected hours.
How does PTO work on a four-day week?

Many employers count PTO in hours, so a day off on a four-ten schedule uses ten hours instead of eight. Holidays that fall on your scheduled day off may or may not be replaced with another day. Ask the employer for its written policy before you start.

Career change.title: What Is a Career Change? How to Switch Careers Step by Step
sections: What a career change means

A career change is a move into a different kind of work, not just a new employer or a promotion in the same line of work. Examples include a teacher becoming an instructional designer, a nurse moving into health IT, or a retail manager moving into human resources.

Some changes are small steps, such as keeping your industry but switching to a new function, or keeping your function in a new industry. Others are full switches that need new training, a degree or a license.
People change careers for many reasons: burnout, a layoff, better pay, a field that is shrinking, health, family needs, or a wish for work that fits their interests better.
Why transferable skills matter

Transferable skills are abilities that work in many jobs, such as managing people, serving customers, writing, budgeting, analyzing data and running projects. They are the bridge between your old work and the new one, because employers want evidence you can do the job.

The easiest changes reuse much of what you already know. If you keep either your industry or your function, you can often start above entry level. If you change both at once, expect to start lower and build up.

Some fields need a license or certification that each state sets, such as nursing, teaching, real estate, cosmetology or electrical work. Rules differ by state, so check the state licensing board before you spend money on training.
How to make a career change
Start with research. Read many job postings for your target role, list the skills and tools that keep coming up, and talk to people who do the work through short informational interviews.

Close the gaps with proof you can show: an online course with a finished project, a community college certificate, volunteer work, freelance jobs or a small portfolio. Your local American Job Center may help pay for training through the Workforce Innovation and Opportunity Act if you qualify.

Rewrite your resume for the new role. Name the target job in your summary, put relevant skills near the top, and describe past work by results the new field cares about. A combination resume, which mixes a skills section with your work history, often suits career changers.
Plan your money before you jump. A move may mean a lower starting salary for a while, so test the field with a side project or part-time work while you still have your current job, if you can.
qa: Is 40 too old for a career change?

No. People change careers in their 40s, 50s and later, and their experience with people, deadlines and problems often helps. The federal Age Discrimination in Employment Act protects workers 40 and older from age discrimination by employers with 20 or more employees, and some states protect more workers.
How do I explain a career change in an interview?

Keep it short and forward-looking. Say why the new field draws you, which skills from your past work carry over, and what you have done to prepare, such as a course, a project or volunteer work. Avoid long complaints about your old job.
Will I have to take a pay cut to change careers?

Not always. If the new role reuses many of your skills, you may keep or raise your pay. If you start over in a field where you have no experience, a lower starting salary is common for a while. Compare pay data for the new role before deciding.
How long does a career change take?

It depends on the gap between your old and new work. A move that reuses most of your skills can take a few months of job searching. A change that needs a new degree, license or apprenticeship can take a year or several years.
What is the best way to start a career change with no experience?

Build experience in small ways first. Take on related tasks in your current job, volunteer, do freelance or project work, or finish a course with a real project you can show. Then apply for entry-level or bridge roles that use what you already know.

Reasonable accommodation.title: What Is a Reasonable Accommodation? How to Ask and What Counts
sections: What a reasonable accommodation is

A reasonable accommodation is a change to a job, the workplace or the hiring process that lets a qualified person with a disability apply, do the essential parts of the job or enjoy the same benefits as other employees.

In the US the main law is the Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA). Its employment rules apply to private employers with 15 or more employees, plus state and local governments. Federal agencies are covered by the Rehabilitation Act.

Many state and city laws cover smaller employers or define disability more broadly, so your rights can depend on where you work. Your state’s civil rights agency or labor department can tell you what applies.

Other US laws use the same idea. The Pregnant Workers Fairness Act requires accommodations for limits tied to pregnancy or childbirth, and Title VII of the Civil Rights Act requires them for religious beliefs and practices.
Common examples and what is not required

Typical accommodations include a changed schedule, extra or longer breaks, remote work, a quieter workspace, screen-reading software, an ergonomic chair, a sign language interpreter, written instructions, or leave for treatment.
Accessible hiring counts too: an interview room without stairs, extra time on a test, or application materials in another format.
Reassignment to a vacant job you are qualified for is also a possible accommodation when nothing else works in your current role.

An employer does not have to remove an essential function of the job, lower its production standards, create a new job, or provide personal items such as glasses or hearing aids. It can refuse an accommodation that would cause undue hardship, meaning significant difficulty or expense for that employer.
How to ask for an accommodation

You can ask at any stage: when applying, before an interview, after an offer or years into the job. No special words or forms are required. Saying you need a change at work because of a medical condition is enough to start.
Putting the request in writing, such as an email to HR or your manager, gives you a record of what you asked and when.

The employer and you then talk through what you need and what would work, often called the interactive process. If your disability or need is not obvious, the employer may ask for reasonable medical documentation, usually from your doctor.
The employer can pick among effective options, so it may offer something different from what you asked for. The free Job Accommodation Network (askjan.org) lists ideas for many conditions.
If your request is refused
Ask for the reason in writing and whether another option would work. A refusal should be based on undue hardship or on the change not being needed, not on assumptions about your condition.

Retaliating against you for asking is illegal. If you think your rights were violated, you can file a charge with the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission (EEOC), generally within 180 days, or 300 days where a state or local agency enforces a similar law.
For advice on your own situation, talk to an employment lawyer, a disability rights organization or your state’s civil rights agency.
qa: What are examples of reasonable accommodations?

Common ones are a flexible or part-time schedule, remote work, extra breaks, a quieter or step-free workspace, assistive software, an interpreter, written instructions, extra time on hiring tests, unpaid leave for treatment and reassignment to a vacant job. What is reasonable depends on the job and the employer.
Do I have to tell my employer my diagnosis to get an accommodation?

Not always. You need to explain that a medical condition limits something and what change would help. If the need is not obvious, a US employer may ask for reasonable documentation of the disability and the need, but not your full medical history. That information must be kept confidential.
Can an employer deny a reasonable accommodation?

Yes, if it would cause undue hardship, meaning significant difficulty or expense for that employer, or if it would remove an essential job function. The employer can also offer a different accommodation that works instead of the one you asked for. It cannot refuse simply because it prefers not to.
Can I ask for an accommodation during a job interview?

Yes. Under the ADA you can ask for changes to the hiring process, such as an accessible location, an interpreter or extra test time. Before a job offer, employers generally may not ask about your disability, though they may ask what accommodation you need for the hiring process.
Does the ADA apply to small businesses?

The ADA’s employment rules cover employers with 15 or more employees. Many state and local laws cover smaller employers, some with only a few workers, so check with your state’s civil rights agency or labor department if your employer is small.

Skills-based hiring.title: What Is Skills-Based Hiring? How It Works and How to Prepare
sections: What skills-based hiring means

Skills-based hiring is a way of choosing candidates by what they can do, not by the degree they hold or the companies they worked for. The employer decides which skills the job needs, then looks for proof of those skills.

Proof can come from a work sample, a practical test, a portfolio, a certification or a past project with clear results. A degree may still count, but it is one possible sign of skill rather than a strict requirement.

It is also called skills-first hiring. Several US states and the federal government have dropped four-year degree requirements for many public jobs, and many private employers have made similar changes.
How it works in practice

A skills-based posting usually lists specific abilities, such as building a budget in a spreadsheet or writing SQL queries, instead of “bachelor’s degree required.” Some postings say “or equivalent experience” to show a degree is optional.
The hiring process often adds a skills check. This may be a short online assessment, a paid or unpaid take-home task, a live exercise during the interview or a review of work you already did.
Interviews tend to ask how you solved real problems. Interviewers may score every candidate against the same list of skills, which is meant to make comparisons fairer.
Rules employers should know

Under federal law, if a hiring test screens out people of a protected group, such as a race or sex, at a higher rate, the employer must be able to show the test is job-related and consistent with business necessity.

The Americans with Disabilities Act also requires reasonable accommodations in testing, such as extra time, for qualified candidates with disabilities. Some states and cities add their own rules, so employers should check with an employment lawyer before adding new assessments.
What job seekers should do
Put proof of your skills near the top of your resume. A short projects or key results section works well, especially if you lack a degree or are changing careers.
Describe results with specifics you can back up, such as what you built, fixed or improved. Link to a portfolio, code repository or writing samples when they fit the job.

Prepare for assessments by reading the posting closely and practicing the main tasks it names. If a take-home task looks like it would take many hours, it is reasonable to ask how long it should take and how it will be used.
qa: What is an example of skills-based hiring?

A company hiring a data analyst drops its degree requirement and instead asks every applicant to clean a small data set and explain the findings. Candidates who do the task well move on to interviews, whether they learned the skill in college, a bootcamp or on the job.
Do I still need a degree for skills-based jobs?

Often not, but it depends on the job. Some roles still require a degree or license by law, such as nursing, teaching or law. For many others, employers using skills-based hiring accept experience, certifications or a strong work sample in place of a degree.
How is skills-based hiring different from traditional hiring?

Traditional hiring often screens on credentials first, such as a degree, years of experience or well-known past employers. Skills-based hiring starts with the abilities the job needs and checks for them directly through tests, samples or structured interviews.
How do I show my skills on a resume?

Add a projects or achievements section near the top and describe what you did and the result, with numbers where they are true. List tools and skills using the words the posting uses, and include links to work people can see.
Are skills tests in hiring legal?

Generally yes. Under federal law, an employer must show a test is job-related and consistent with business necessity if it screens out a protected group at a higher rate, and it must offer reasonable accommodations to people with disabilities. State and local rules can add more.

Gig work.title: What Is Gig Work? How It Works, Pay, Taxes and Your Rights
sections: What gig work means

Gig work is paid work done one task, ride, delivery or project at a time, usually found through an app or online platform. Common examples are ride-hailing, food and grocery delivery, errands, pet care, and freelance projects such as writing, design or coding.

In the US most gig workers are treated as independent contractors, not employees. That means no employment contract, no set schedule and no guaranteed hours. You choose when to log in and which tasks to accept, and the platform takes a fee or sets the pay for each task.
The word “gig” comes from music, where a gig is a single paid performance. The wider group of platforms and workers is often called the gig economy.
How gig pay really works
Pay is usually per task, sometimes with tips, bonuses or higher rates at busy times. The amount shown in the app is not what you keep, because you usually cover your own costs.

Those costs can include fuel, car maintenance, insurance, phone data, equipment and platform fees. Time spent waiting for orders or driving to a pickup is often unpaid, so your real hourly earnings can be much lower than the rate per task suggests.

To compare gig work with a job, track your hours from login to logout, add up your costs and divide what is left by the total hours. A few cities and states have set minimum pay rules for some app-based drivers or delivery workers, so check the rules where you work.
Taxes, benefits and worker status

As a contractor, no tax is usually withheld from your pay. All gig income is taxable, whether or not the platform sends you a Form 1099. If your net self-employment earnings for the year are $400 or more, you also owe self-employment tax, which funds Social Security and Medicare.

Many gig workers make quarterly estimated tax payments to avoid IRS penalties, and they can deduct business costs such as mileage. Keep records of income and expenses, and ask an accountant or tax preparer about your own situation.

Contractors generally do not get minimum wage, overtime, employer health insurance, workers’ compensation or unemployment insurance. Whether a worker is truly a contractor depends on which law applies: the federal FLSA weighs several factors, the IRS uses its own test, and states such as California, Massachusetts and New Jersey use a stricter ABC test for some laws.

California voters passed Proposition 22 in 2020, which keeps app-based ride and delivery drivers as contractors while giving them some earnings guarantees and benefits. If you think you are misclassified, contact your state labor department or an employment lawyer.
What to do before you start
Read the platform’s terms on pay, fees, deactivation and how disputes are handled. Check whether your personal car insurance covers work driving, because many personal policies do not.
Set aside part of every payment for taxes, keep a mileage log and save receipts from day one. Treat gig work as a small business, even if it is only a side income.
If you list gig work on a resume, describe it like any job: the platform or type of work, dates, and results such as ratings, number of tasks completed or client feedback.
qa: Is gig work considered self-employment?

Usually yes. Most US platforms treat gig workers as independent contractors, so the IRS treats their earnings as self-employment income. You report it on your tax return and owe self-employment tax if your net earnings for the year are $400 or more. A worker’s legal status can still be challenged under federal or state law.
Do gig workers have to pay taxes?

Yes. All gig income is taxable, even if you do not receive a Form 1099. Because platforms usually do not withhold tax, many gig workers make quarterly estimated payments. You can deduct ordinary business costs such as mileage. An accountant or tax preparer can help with your own case.
Can gig workers get unemployment benefits?

Generally not, because unemployment insurance is funded by employers for their employees, and contractors are not covered. If a state decides you were misclassified and were really an employee, you may qualify. Rules and decisions differ by state, so ask your state unemployment office.
What is the difference between gig work and freelancing?

The terms overlap. Gig work often means short, app-assigned tasks like rides or deliveries with pay set by the platform. Freelancing usually means project work for clients, where you set your own rates and terms. Both are normally done as an independent contractor.
Is gig work a good way to make money?

It depends on your costs, location and hours. It offers flexibility and quick start-up, but pay can vary from week to week and there are no employer benefits. Work out your real hourly earnings after fees, expenses and unpaid waiting time before relying on it.

Full-time and part-time.title: What Is Full-Time vs Part-Time Work? Hours, Benefits and Rights
sections: What full-time and part-time mean
No single US law defines full-time or part-time work. Each employer sets its own line, often somewhere between 35 and 40 hours a week for full-time, and anything below that counts as part-time.

Some rules use their own definitions. Under the Affordable Care Act’s employer rules, a full-time employee averages at least 30 hours a week or 130 hours a month. In its labor statistics, the Bureau of Labor Statistics counts people who usually work fewer than 35 hours a week as part-time.
Because definitions differ, the same 32-hour job can be full-time at one company and part-time at another. Always check how the employer classifies the role, not just the hours listed.
How the difference affects pay and benefits

Minimum wage and overtime rules apply the same way to both. Under the Fair Labor Standards Act, a non-exempt worker earns at least 1.5 times the regular rate for hours over 40 in a workweek. Some states, such as California, also require overtime after a set number of hours in a day.

Employers with 50 or more full-time employees, counting full-time equivalents, must offer affordable health coverage to nearly all employees working 30 or more hours a week, or they may owe a federal penalty. Federal law does not require coverage below 30 hours, but Hawaii’s Prepaid Health Care Act requires coverage for most employees working 20 or more hours a week.

Federal law does not require paid vacation or holidays, and many employers give them only to full-time staff. Many state and city paid sick leave laws do cover part-time workers, with leave building up by hours worked. Federal rules also require many 401(k) plans to let long-term part-time workers contribute once they meet set hour and service requirements.

Unpaid, job-protected leave under the Family and Medical Leave Act has several conditions. You must have worked for the employer at least 12 months, worked at least 1,250 hours in the 12 months before the leave, and work at a site where the employer has 50 or more employees within 75 miles.
What to ask before you accept a job

Ask how many hours a week are guaranteed, whether the hours are fixed or change week to week, and how far ahead schedules are posted. Oregon and cities such as New York City, Seattle, Chicago and San Francisco have fair workweek laws that require certain large employers in retail and food service to give schedules in advance.

Ask which benefits you get at your expected hours and what hour threshold unlocks each one, such as health insurance, paid time off or retirement matching. Get the answer in writing, ideally in the offer letter.

If your hours are later cut, you may qualify for partial unemployment benefits, but the rules differ by state. Contact your state’s unemployment office or labor department to find out what applies to you.
qa: How many hours is full-time in the US?

There is no single legal number. Most employers treat 35 to 40 hours a week as full-time. For the Affordable Care Act’s employer health coverage rules, an average of 30 hours a week or 130 hours a month counts as full-time.
Is 32 hours a week full-time?

It depends on the employer. Some companies call 32 hours full-time and some call it part-time. Under the Affordable Care Act’s employer rules, 32 hours counts as full-time because it is at least 30 hours a week, which matters for health coverage at large employers.
Do part-time employees get benefits?

Some do. Employers often limit paid vacation and health insurance to full-time staff, but many offer them to part-time workers too. Many state and city paid sick leave laws cover part-time workers, and Hawaii requires health coverage for most employees working 20 or more hours a week. Ask the employer what applies at your hours.
Can part-time workers get overtime pay?

Yes, if they are non-exempt. Federal law requires overtime at 1.5 times the regular rate for hours over 40 in a workweek, whatever the job is called. Some states, such as California, also require overtime after a set number of hours in one day.
Can my employer change me from full-time to part-time?

In most US jobs, which are at-will, an employer can generally reduce future hours unless a contract or union agreement says otherwise. You may lose benefits tied to full-time status. Depending on your state, you may qualify for partial unemployment benefits, so check with your state’s unemployment office.

Annual leave.title: What Is Annual Leave? Meaning, Entitlement and the US Equivalent
sections: What annual leave means

Annual leave is the paid time off you earn each year to rest, travel or deal with personal matters. You are paid your normal wage on those days, and you choose when to take them, usually with your employer’s approval.

The term is standard in the UK, Ireland, Australia, New Zealand and many other countries. In the US, most private employers call it vacation or PTO (paid time off), though the federal civil service officially uses the term annual leave.
Annual leave is separate from sick leave, parental leave and unpaid leave. Some employers combine vacation and sick days into one PTO bank, which is common in the US.
How much annual leave you get depends on the country

In the US, no federal law requires private employers to give paid vacation. It is a benefit set by company policy or a contract. A few states, such as Maine, Nevada and Illinois, require some employers to give paid leave that can be used for any reason, and many states and cities require paid sick leave.

In the UK, most workers have a legal right to 5.6 weeks of paid holiday a year, which is 28 days for someone working five days a week. Employers may count bank holidays inside those 28 days, so check your contract.

European Union law sets a minimum of four weeks of paid annual leave, and many EU countries give more. Australia gives most full-time employees four weeks. In Canada, minimums are set by each province and territory, and by the Canada Labour Code for federally regulated employers.
Carry-over, accrual and payout
Many employers let you earn, or accrue, leave gradually through the year, such as a set number of hours each pay period. New starters may have only part of the yearly amount available at first.

Whether unused days roll into the next year depends on your employer’s policy and local law. Some US employers use a use-it-or-lose-it rule, but California does not allow employers to take away vacation you have already earned, though it allows a cap on how much you can build up.

In the UK, carry-over rules are detailed and depend on the situation, so check your contract and the guidance from Acas or GOV.UK. If your leave is refused or not paid, contact your state labor department in the US or Acas in the UK.
What to check before accepting a job
Ask how many days of annual leave or PTO you get, whether public holidays are included in that number, and whether the amount grows with years of service.
Ask how leave accrues, how much notice you must give to book it, how much can carry over and whether unused leave is paid out when you leave.
If a US employer offers unlimited PTO, ask how many days people on the team actually take, since there is no set balance to carry over or be paid out.
qa: What is the difference between annual leave and PTO?

Annual leave usually means paid holiday time only. PTO, the common US term, often combines vacation, sick days and personal days into one bank of paid hours. Some US employers keep vacation and sick leave separate, so read the policy to see what your days cover.
How much annual leave are you entitled to in the US?

Federal law does not require private employers in the US to give any paid vacation. The amount comes from your employer’s policy or contract. Some states and cities require paid sick leave or general paid leave, so check your state labor department’s website for local rules.
Do bank holidays count as annual leave in the UK?

They can. UK employers may include the eight usual bank holidays in England and Wales inside the 5.6-week legal minimum, or give them on top. Your contract should say which applies, so read it before comparing job offers.
Do you get paid for unused annual leave when you leave a job?

In the UK, you are paid for statutory leave you earned but did not take by your last day. In the US it depends on the state and your employer’s policy; some states, such as California, treat earned vacation as wages that must be paid out, while others leave it to the policy.
Is annual leave paid?
Yes. Annual leave is paid time off, so you receive your normal pay on those days. Time off without pay is called unpaid leave and is a separate arrangement agreed with your employer or set by law.

Open enrollment.title: What Is Open Enrollment? How It Works and What Happens If You Miss It
sections: What open enrollment means

Open enrollment is a set window each year when you can sign up for health insurance, switch plans, add or drop family members, or cancel coverage. Outside that window, most changes are locked until the next one.

The term is used in three main places in the US: employer benefit plans, the health insurance Marketplace for people who buy their own coverage, and Medicare. Each has its own window and its own rules.

At work, open enrollment often covers more than health insurance. It can include dental, vision, life and disability insurance, flexible spending accounts (FSAs) and other benefits your employer offers.
How open enrollment works at work and on the Marketplace

Employers set their own open enrollment period, usually a few weeks once a year before the plan year starts. Many plan years start on January 1, so fall enrollment is common, but your employer’s dates may differ.

A new hire does not wait for open enrollment. You usually get a first-time enrollment window that starts when you are hired or become eligible, often 30 or 31 days. Check the exact deadline with HR in your first week.

For people who buy their own coverage, the Marketplace on HealthCare.gov has a yearly open enrollment period in the fall. Federal rules set the dates, they have changed in recent years, and state-run marketplaces can set their own, so check your state’s site each year.

Medicare has its own fall open enrollment period for changing Medicare Advantage or drug plans. Medicaid and the Children’s Health Insurance Program (CHIP) are different: you can apply at any time of year.
Changing coverage outside open enrollment

Outside open enrollment, you can usually change coverage only after a qualifying life event. For employer plans, common events include marriage, divorce, the birth or adoption of a child, and losing other health coverage.
Employer plans usually give you a short window after the event, often 30 days, to ask for the change. Losing Medicaid or CHIP coverage generally gives you 60 days.

On the Marketplace, a special enrollment period usually lasts 60 days and the rules are narrower. Losing coverage, getting married, having or adopting a child and some moves can qualify, but divorce counts only if it makes you lose your coverage.
What to do during open enrollment
Read what is changing for next year, such as premiums, deductibles, doctor networks and drug coverage. A plan that suited you last year may cost more or cover less now.

Compare the total yearly cost, not just the paycheck deduction. Add premiums to what you expect to pay in deductibles, copays and coinsurance, and check that your doctors and prescriptions are covered.
Find out what happens if you do nothing. Some employers roll your choices over, but FSA elections often have to be made again each year. Save a confirmation of what you chose.
qa: What happens if I miss open enrollment?

You usually have to wait for the next open enrollment period unless you have a qualifying life event, such as losing other coverage or having a baby. Medicaid and CHIP accept applications all year, so check whether you qualify for them in the meantime.
When is open enrollment?

It depends on the plan. Employers set their own dates, often in the fall for a January start. The Marketplace and Medicare each have a yearly fall window set by federal rules, and state-run marketplaces may use their own dates. Check your HR portal, your state marketplace or Medicare.gov for this year’s deadlines.
Do I have to wait for open enrollment if I start a new job?

No. New employees usually get their own enrollment window that starts when they are hired or become eligible, often 30 or 31 days. If you miss it, you may have to wait until the employer’s next open enrollment unless you have a qualifying life event.
Can I change my health plan after open enrollment ends?

Usually only after a qualifying life event, and you must ask within a set window, often 30 days for employer plans and 60 days on the Marketplace. Which events count differs between employer plans and the Marketplace, so check with HR or your marketplace.
Do my benefits renew automatically if I do nothing?

Many employer plans roll over your current choices, and the Marketplace may re-enroll you in the same or a similar plan. But flexible spending account elections often do not carry over, and prices and coverage can change, so review your options each year.

Knockout question.title: What Is a Knockout Question? How It Screens Out Job Applications
sections: What a knockout question is

A knockout question is a yes or no question on a job application that decides at once whether the application goes forward. If you give the answer the employer marked as disqualifying, the application is rejected or set aside before a recruiter reads your resume.

Employers set these questions for requirements they cannot bend, such as the legal right to work in the US, a required license or a minimum amount of experience. They save the recruiter from reading applications from people who cannot be hired for that role.
Common knockout questions

Typical questions ask whether you are legally authorized to work in the United States, whether you will now or in the future need visa sponsorship, and whether you have a set number of years of experience in a field.

Others ask whether you hold a specific license or certification, such as a commercial driver’s license or a nursing license, whether you can work certain shifts, whether you can travel or relocate, or whether you are at least 18 years old.

Some topics are limited by law in certain places. Many states and cities have ban-the-box rules that stop many employers from asking about criminal records on the application, and several states bar questions about past pay. The rules differ by state and city.
How knockout questions work in an ATS
Knockout questions are a feature of most applicant tracking systems, the software behind company careers pages. The employer writes each question and marks which answer disqualifies the applicant.

When you submit, the system checks your answers. Depending on how the employer set it up, a wrong answer may send an automatic rejection email, move you to a rejected stage, or simply hide your application from the main list the recruiter works through.
This is why an application can be turned down within minutes. The software did not read your resume and decide; it applied a rule the employer chose.
How to answer knockout questions

Read the screening questions before you fill in the rest of the form when the system lets you see them. If you cannot honestly give the required answer, you can move on to another job and save your time.

Answer truthfully. A false answer may get you past the software, but it often comes out in the interview, a background check or the work authorization check every US employer must do, and it can cost you the offer or the job later.

Read each question closely, since some are worded in reverse, such as asking whether you will need sponsorship. If you are close to an experience requirement or unsure how to count your years, answer honestly and explain in your cover letter or a note to the recruiter.
qa: What happens if I answer a knockout question wrong?

Usually the application is rejected right away or moved to a rejected list without anyone reading your resume. Some systems send a rejection email within minutes. If you made a genuine mistake, contact the recruiter or reapply if the system allows it, since many systems keep the first answer on file.
Should I lie on a knockout question to get past the ATS?

No. Answers about work authorization, licenses and experience are checked later through documents, background checks and interviews. A false answer can lead to a withdrawn offer or being fired after you start, and it can harm your standing with that employer for future openings.
Can I change my answer to a knockout question after submitting?

Most application systems do not let you edit answers once submitted. You can email the recruiter or hiring manager, explain the error and ask them to review your application by hand. Some employers allow a new application for the same job, but others block repeat applications for a set period.
Are employers allowed to ask knockout questions?

Yes, as long as the questions are lawful and tied to the job. Asking whether you are authorized to work in the US or need sponsorship is allowed. Some topics, such as criminal history or past pay, are restricted on applications in many states and cities. For a specific concern, ask your state labor department or a lawyer.
What if I have slightly less experience than the knockout question asks for?

Answer honestly. If you say no, the system will likely reject the application, so consider whether related work, internships or education truly count toward the requirement. If they do, you can answer yes and explain how in your resume. If not, reaching the recruiter directly may be a better route.
