Median.title: What Is the Median? Median Salary vs Average Pay Explained
sections: What the median means
The median is the middle value in a set of numbers sorted from lowest to highest. Half of the values sit at or below it and half sit at or above it.

With an odd number of values, the median is the one exactly in the middle. With an even number, it is the average of the two middle values. Salaries of $40,000, $50,000, $55,000 and $60,000 give a median of $52,500.
In a job search you meet the median in salary reports, government wage data and pay surveys. It is also called the 50th percentile, because 50 percent of the values fall below it.
Median vs average pay
The average, or mean, adds up all the values and divides by how many there are. A few very high salaries pull the average up, so it can describe pay that few people actually get.
Say five people earn $45,000, $50,000, $52,000, $55,000 and $300,000. The average is $100,400, but the median is $52,000, which is much closer to what most of the group earns.
Pay data often has a small number of very high earners, so the average is often higher than the median. That is why the median is usually the better guide to typical pay.
The median does not show how spread out pay is. For that, look at percentiles: a quarter of workers earn less than the 25th percentile, and a quarter earn more than the 75th percentile.
How to use the median when judging an offer

Find the median for the same job title, level and location as the offer. In the US, the Bureau of Labor Statistics publishes median wages by occupation, state and metro area, and many salary sites and job postings show pay figures too.

Check what each figure includes. Sources differ: BLS wage estimates, for example, include commissions, production bonuses and tips but not overtime premium pay or the value of benefits, while other surveys report base pay only or total cash pay.
Also check whether the figure is hourly or yearly, how old the data is, and how many people it is based on. A median from a handful of self-reported salaries can be far off.
Use the median as a starting point, not a rule. Someone new to a role may reasonably start below it, while someone with strong experience or rare skills has a case for asking above it.
qa: What is the difference between median and average salary?

The median salary is the middle one when all salaries are lined up from lowest to highest. The average adds all salaries and divides by the number of people. A few very high salaries raise the average a lot but barely move the median, so the median usually shows typical pay better.
How do you calculate the median?

Sort the numbers from lowest to highest. If there is an odd number of values, take the one in the middle. If there is an even number, add the two middle values and divide by two. For example, the median of 3, 5, 8 and 10 is 6.5.
Is median salary before or after taxes?

Salary figures in wage surveys and government data are normally gross pay, meaning before income taxes and other deductions are taken out. Your take-home pay will be lower. Check the notes of each source to see exactly what its figures include.
Is it good to earn above the median salary?

It means you earn more than at least half of the group the median describes. Whether that is good depends on the group. Being above the median for all workers in your area is different from being above the median for people with your job title and experience.
Is the median the same as the 50th percentile?

Yes. The median and the 50th percentile are the same value: half of the numbers fall below it and half above it. Salary reports often list it next to the 25th and 75th percentiles to show the range of pay.

New grad.title: What Is a New Grad Role? Who Qualifies and When to Apply
sections: What new grad means in a job posting

A new grad role is a job written for people who have just finished a degree or will finish one soon. It is usually a first full-time job after college, and the employer expects to train you rather than hire someone with years of experience.

Employers set their own eligibility window. Many accept people who graduated within the past year or who will graduate within the coming months. Some allow up to two years after graduation, and some ask for a specific range of graduation dates.
You will also see names such as university grad, campus hire, early career, graduate program or analyst program. They point to the same idea: a role or program built around recent graduates.
Where new grad hiring is common

Software engineering, consulting, banking, accounting and large corporate rotational programs often hire new grads in groups, called classes or cohorts, that start on the same date and train together.

In nursing, new grad RN jobs and nurse residency programs are for recent nursing-school graduates. Many hire graduate nurses before they pass the NCLEX licensing exam, then require them to pass and get licensed by a deadline. Check each program’s rules and your state board of nursing.

Many new grad hires come from the employer’s own interns, who receive a return offer at the end of a summer internship. Other new grad openings are filled through campus career fairs, school job portals and online applications.
How the hiring timeline works
Large employers often open new grad applications in the late summer or autumn before your final year ends, and some fill most places by winter. Start dates are often the following summer or autumn.
Smaller companies, nonprofits and many local employers hire closer to graduation or all year, because they fill one opening at a time when it appears.
An offer made before graduation usually depends on finishing your degree. Some employers also run background checks or ask for a final transcript before your start date.
What to do as a new grad job seeker
Read the eligibility line in each posting first. If it lists a graduation window, make sure your date fits, and put your expected graduation month and year clearly on your resume.

Use your school’s career center, internships, class projects, part-time jobs and campus activities as your experience. Employers know new grads have short work histories and look for skills and results instead.

If you are an international student, ask your school’s international student office how Optional Practical Training (OPT) applies to you, and check whether each employer can sponsor a work visa later.
qa: How long are you considered a new grad?

It depends on the employer. Many count you as a new grad for about a year after you finish your degree, some allow up to two years, and some list an exact range of graduation dates. Always check the eligibility line in the posting.
Can I apply for new grad jobs before I graduate?
Yes. Most new grad roles expect you to apply during your final year, often months before graduation. Offers made then usually depend on you finishing your degree before the start date.
What is the difference between new grad and entry level?

New grad is about when you graduated, while entry level is about how much experience a job needs. An entry-level job is open to anyone without much experience, including career changers, while a new grad role is usually limited to recent or soon-to-be graduates.
Do new grad nurses need to pass the NCLEX before applying?

Often not. Many new grad RN and nurse residency programs accept graduate nurses who have not yet passed the NCLEX, but they require you to pass and hold a license by a set deadline. Rules differ by employer and state, so check the posting and your state board of nursing.
When should I start applying for new grad jobs?

For large employers with structured programs, start in the late summer or autumn of your final year, since many fill places by winter. Smaller employers often hire closer to graduation or year-round, so keep looking after the main season ends.

Talent acquisition.title: What Is Talent Acquisition? Meaning, Team Roles and Tips
sections: What talent acquisition means

Talent acquisition, often shortened to TA, is the work of finding, attracting and hiring people for an employer. It also names the team that does that work, as in “the talent acquisition team will be in touch.”

Many companies now use the name where they once said “recruiting” or “staffing.” The team usually sits within or beside human resources, which also handles pay, benefits, policies and employee relations after someone is hired.

Some people use talent acquisition for the long-term side of hiring, such as workforce planning and employer branding, and recruiting for filling one opening. In practice, many employers use the two words for the same work.
Who is on a talent acquisition team

Recruiters, sometimes called talent acquisition partners or specialists, manage openings from posting to offer. They screen applicants, run the process and talk with candidates about pay and start dates.

Sourcers search for people who have not applied, often on professional networking sites, and contact them about a role. Recruiting coordinators schedule interviews, send calendar invites and handle travel or video links.

The hiring manager is usually not part of the TA team. That is the person you would report to, who defines the job and makes or approves the final choice. Some employers also hand part of their hiring to outside recruiting agencies.
How talent acquisition works in a hiring process

A typical process starts when a hiring manager asks to fill a role. TA writes or posts the job, collects applications, often in an applicant tracking system, and screens candidates against the requirements.

The recruiter usually holds a first phone or video screen, then passes promising candidates to interviews with the hiring manager and team. After interviews, TA gathers feedback, may run reference or background checks and prepares the offer.
In small companies one person may do all of this, or the founder and an HR generalist share it. In large companies TA may be split into teams by region, department or level of role.
How job seekers should work with talent acquisition

Send questions about the process, timeline, scheduling, pay range or benefits to the recruiter or TA contact named in the posting or emails. Keep questions about the actual work, team and goals for the hiring manager.

Treat the recruiter screen as a real interview. Recruiters often decide who moves forward, so be ready to explain why you fit the role and to give clear answers about location, work authorization and availability.
Reply promptly and politely, and keep your messages short. If you have not heard back by the date you were given, one follow-up email to your TA contact is reasonable.
qa: What is the difference between talent acquisition and recruiting?

Recruiting usually means filling specific open jobs. Talent acquisition can be broader, including planning future hiring needs, building a pool of possible candidates and shaping how the employer looks to job seekers. Many companies, though, use the two terms interchangeably for the same team and work.
Is talent acquisition the same as HR?

Not exactly. Talent acquisition focuses on bringing people into the company. Human resources usually covers the wider employee relationship, such as pay, benefits, policies and workplace issues. The TA team typically sits within or beside HR, depending on how the employer is organized.
What does a talent acquisition specialist do?

A talent acquisition specialist manages hiring for open roles. The work usually includes posting jobs, reviewing applications, screening candidates by phone or video, coordinating interviews with hiring managers, gathering feedback and helping prepare offers. Titles vary, and the same job may be called recruiter or talent acquisition partner.
What does it mean when talent acquisition contacts me?

It usually means a recruiter wants to talk about a role, either because you applied or because a sourcer found your profile. Often the first step is a short screening call to check your interest, experience, location and pay expectations before any interview with the hiring manager.
Should I contact talent acquisition after applying?

You can, if a TA contact is named or you already have a recruiter’s email. Keep it brief and ask a clear question about the process or timeline. If no contact is given, waiting a week or two before a polite follow-up is usually reasonable.

Job title.title: What Is a Job Title? Meaning, Levels and How to Search by Title
sections: What a job title means
A job title is the official name of a position, such as “Senior Data Analyst” or “Warehouse Associate”. It tells others, in a few words, what kind of work you do and roughly how senior you are.

Employers choose their own titles, so there is no single national rule for what a title must mean. The same work can be called “Customer Success Manager” at one company and “Account Manager” at another.
A title usually has two parts: a function, such as analyst, engineer or nurse, and often a level or specialty, such as junior, senior, lead or pediatric.
How seniority words in titles work

Many companies use level words to show experience. Common ones run from intern, junior or associate, through mid-level with no prefix, to senior, lead, staff, principal, manager, director and vice president.

These words do not mean the same thing everywhere. A “senior” title at a small startup may match a mid-level role at a large employer, and some companies give bigger titles instead of higher pay, which is often called title inflation.
Because of this, read the duties, the reporting line and the pay range in a posting, not just the title, to judge whether a role fits your level.
Why the title matters in a job search
Job boards and employer search tools match postings mainly by title and keywords. If you search only one title, you can miss openings for the same work listed under other names.
Recruiters also search resumes by title. Using the common, recognizable name for your work helps them find you and helps an applicant tracking system file your experience correctly.
Your title also shapes how future employers see your career path, and it is one of the details that employment verification and background checks often confirm.
What job seekers should do

Search under several titles for the work you want, including older and newer names, and note which titles employers in your field use most. Government resources such as O*NET list many reported titles for each occupation.

On your resume, keep your official title accurate. If it was unusual, you can add a short common equivalent in parentheses, such as “Client Happiness Lead (Customer Success Manager)”, so readers understand it without misstating what you held.
When you get an offer, check that the title matches the level and duties discussed. A title is often easier to negotiate than salary, and it can matter for your next move.
qa: What is the difference between a job title and a job position?

People often use the words the same way. Strictly, the job title is the name of the role, while a position is a specific seat in the organization. A company can have ten positions that all carry the same title, such as “Sales Representative”.
Can I change my job title on my resume?

You should not claim a title you did not hold, because employers may confirm titles during background or reference checks. You can keep the official title and add a common equivalent in parentheses, or describe your real duties clearly in the bullet points below it.
Does my job title decide whether I get overtime?

No. Under the federal Fair Labor Standards Act, a title alone does not make you exempt from overtime. What counts is mainly your actual duties and, for many exemptions, how and how much you are paid. Some states have stricter rules. Ask your state labor department or a lawyer if you are unsure.
What is title inflation?

Title inflation is when a company gives a grander title than the work or level would usually earn elsewhere, such as “Director” for a role with no team. It can look good on paper, but it may make it harder to land a similar title at a larger employer.
Should I negotiate my job title?

It can be worth asking if the title in the offer does not match the duties or seniority discussed. Explain why the title fits the role, using common titles in your field as examples. Some employers have fixed title structures, so they may not be able to change it.

Termination for cause.title: What Is Termination for Cause? What It Means and What You Lose
sections: What termination for cause means

Termination for cause means an employer ends your job for a reason it says is your fault, such as theft, violence, serious dishonesty, repeated policy violations or refusing reasonable instructions. It is the opposite of termination without cause, such as a layoff or a cut role, where the reason is the business, not your conduct.

What counts as cause is usually defined in an employment contract, union agreement, severance plan or equity plan. Typical lists include gross misconduct, fraud, a crime, breaking company policy after a warning and serious neglect of duties. If no document defines it, the label mostly reflects the employer’s own view.
In the UK and some other countries, a firing for gross misconduct is often called summary dismissal, and the employer may end the job without notice. Rules on fair process differ by country.
Why the label matters in the US

Most US jobs are at-will, which means the employer can end them for any reason that is not illegal, or for no stated reason, without proving cause. Montana is the main exception: after a probationary period, its law requires good cause for a firing.

So cause matters most when a document gives you rights that depend on it. A contract may promise notice or severance only for terminations without cause, a union agreement may require just cause, and some equity plans shorten the time to exercise options after a for-cause firing.
It can also affect unemployment benefits. States can deny benefits for misconduct connected with work, but each state defines misconduct itself, and the state agency decides, not the employer.

Federal COBRA covers group health plans of employers with 20 or more employees, and under it a firing for gross misconduct is not a qualifying event, so it can end your right to continue coverage. Smaller employers fall under state continuation laws, which vary and do not exist in every state.
What you are still owed
Being fired for cause does not cancel pay you already earned. Your final paycheck must include wages for all hours worked, and state law sets how fast it must arrive, in some states on your last day.

Payout of unused vacation depends on your state and your employer’s written policy. Some states, such as California, treat earned vacation as wages that must be paid out; others let the policy decide. Vested money in a 401(k) stays yours.

Severance is not required by federal law. Whether you get any after a for-cause firing depends on your contract, the company’s severance plan or what you negotiate, and some agreements exclude for-cause terminations entirely.
What to do if you are fired for cause

Ask for the reason in writing and keep copies of your contract, handbook, warnings, performance reviews and any messages about the firing. Some states require employers to give a written reason or service letter when you ask for one.

Apply for unemployment anyway if you think your conduct was not serious misconduct; the state will look at the facts. If you believe the real reason was discrimination, retaliation or another illegal reason, talk to an employment lawyer or your state labor department soon, because filing deadlines apply.
In interviews, give a short, honest account of what happened and what you learned. Many employers only confirm dates and job title, but do not assume a former employer will say nothing.

Employers who fire for cause should follow their written policy, document warnings and facts, and apply rules the same way to everyone, since inconsistent treatment can support a discrimination claim.
qa: Can you get unemployment if you are terminated for cause?

Sometimes. States can deny benefits when the firing was for misconduct connected with work, but each state defines misconduct, and poor performance or an honest mistake often does not count. The state agency decides after hearing both sides, not the employer, so it is usually worth applying.
Do you get severance if you are fired for cause?

It depends. No federal law requires severance, so it comes only from a contract, a company severance plan or a negotiation. Some agreements that promise severance exclude for-cause terminations, while others leave room to negotiate. Read your documents and ask an employment lawyer if the amount is significant.
What is the difference between termination for cause and without cause?

Termination for cause is based on something the employer says you did wrong, such as misconduct or breaking a clear rule. Termination without cause is for business reasons, such as a layoff or restructuring. The difference matters mainly for severance, notice pay, equity and unemployment benefits.
Does being fired for cause go on your record?

There is no central public record of firings. A former employer may tell a future employer why you left, though many only confirm dates and job title. Background checks usually verify employment, and applications sometimes ask whether you were ever fired, which you should answer honestly.
Do I still get my final paycheck if I am fired for cause?

Yes. Wages you already earned must be paid no matter why the job ended, and state law sets the deadline for the final paycheck. Whether unused vacation is paid out depends on your state and your employer’s written policy.

Zero-hours contract.title: What Is a Zero-Hours Contract? Rights, Pay and How It Works
sections: What a zero-hours contract is

A zero-hours contract is a work agreement, mostly used in the UK, where the employer does not promise any minimum hours. You are offered shifts when there is work, and in principle you can say no to any shift offered.
You are paid only for the hours you actually work. One week might bring forty hours, the next none, so your income can change a lot from week to week.

They are common in retail, hospitality, care work, delivery, events and seasonal jobs, where demand goes up and down. Some people like the flexibility, for example students or people with other jobs or caring duties.
Your rights on a zero-hours contract in the UK

Most people on zero-hours contracts count as workers under UK law, and some count as employees. Either way, you are not self-employed: you are paid through PAYE and are entitled to at least the National Minimum Wage or National Living Wage for the time you work.

You are entitled to paid holiday, rest breaks and protection from discrimination. Because hours are irregular, holiday is worked out from the hours you actually do, and Great Britain has special rules for irregular-hours workers in leave years starting from April 2024. Northern Ireland has its own rules.

In Great Britain, clauses that stop zero-hours workers from working for other employers have been unenforceable since 2015, and this protection was later extended to other low-paid workers. Northern Ireland has separate employment law, so check nidirect if you work there.

The Employment Rights Act 2025 is changing rules for zero-hours and low-hours workers in Great Britain, including rights around guaranteed hours, shift notice and Statutory Sick Pay, in stages from 2026. Check GOV.UK or Acas for which parts are in force.
Is there a zero-hours contract in the US

The term is not used in US law. Similar US jobs are called on-call, as-needed, per diem or PRN work. Federal law does not require employers to guarantee any minimum hours or give advance notice of schedules.

Some states and cities add protections. California, New York and Massachusetts, among others, have reporting-time or call-in pay rules for workers sent home early, and Oregon and several cities, such as New York City, San Francisco, Seattle and Chicago, have predictive scheduling laws for certain industries.
These rules differ in who they cover and how much they pay. Your state labor department can tell you what applies where you work.
What to check before you accept

Ask how many hours people in the same role worked over the last few months, and how much notice they usually get for shifts and cancellations. That tells you more about your likely earnings than the hourly rate.
Ask whether turning down shifts affects how many you are offered later. On paper you can refuse, but in practice some managers offer fewer shifts to people who say no often.
Keep a record of hours worked, shifts offered and pay received. It helps you check your pay and holiday, and it is useful if you later claim benefits or ask for more regular hours.
qa: Can I turn down shifts on a zero-hours contract?

Yes, in principle. A true zero-hours contract does not oblige you to accept work, just as the employer does not have to offer it. In practice, refusing often may lead to fewer offers, so ask the employer how it handles this before you sign.
Do you get holiday pay on a zero-hours contract?

Yes, in the UK. Zero-hours workers are entitled to paid holiday based on the hours they actually work. Great Britain has special calculation rules for irregular-hours workers for leave years starting from April 2024, and Northern Ireland has its own rules.
Can I work for another employer on a zero-hours contract?

In Great Britain, yes. Since 2015 a clause banning zero-hours workers from working elsewhere cannot be enforced. Northern Ireland has separate employment law, so check nidirect or a local advice service if you work there.
Is a zero-hours contract the same as being self-employed?

No. Most zero-hours staff are workers, and some are employees. Tax and National Insurance are taken through PAYE, and you are entitled to the minimum wage, paid holiday and rest breaks, which self-employed people do not get.
Are zero-hours contracts legal in the US?

The term is not used in US law, but on-call and as-needed jobs with no guaranteed hours are legal. Some states and cities require reporting-time pay or advance schedule notice for certain jobs, so check your state labor department.

Sick leave.title: What Is Sick Leave? Paid Sick Days, State Laws and Your Rights
sections: What sick leave means

Sick leave is time off work when you are ill, injured or need medical care. It can be paid, meaning you get your normal wages for the hours you miss, or unpaid, meaning you earn nothing for that time.

Many employers and many state laws also let you use sick leave to care for a sick family member or to attend doctor’s appointments. Some state and local laws add safe leave for victims of domestic violence or sexual assault.
Some employers keep sick days separate from vacation days. Others combine them into one bank of paid time off (PTO) that you can use for any reason.
Sick leave laws in the US

No federal law requires most private employers to offer paid sick leave. Whether you get it depends on your state, your city or county, and your employer’s own policy. Certain federal contractors must provide paid sick leave under a separate federal rule.

A growing number of states and cities require paid sick leave, including California, New York, New Jersey, Washington, Oregon, Colorado, Arizona and Massachusetts. Rules differ on which employers are covered, how many hours you earn and how much you can use each year.

Under these laws you usually earn sick time as you work, for example one hour for every 30 or 40 hours worked, depending on the state. Some laws let employers give a full amount at the start of the year instead.

The federal Family and Medical Leave Act (FMLA) gives eligible employees up to 12 weeks of unpaid, job-protected leave a year for a serious health condition. You qualify only if your employer has 50 or more employees within 75 miles and you have worked there 12 months and at least 1,250 hours.
When unpaid sick time is risky

Unpaid time off is protected only when a law covers you, such as the FMLA, a state or local sick leave law, or a disability law that requires leave as an accommodation. Without that, an at-will employer may be able to discipline or fire you for missing work.

A few states, such as California, New Jersey, New York, Rhode Island and Hawaii, have state disability insurance or paid family and medical leave programs. These can replace part of your wages during a longer illness, but they do not always protect your job on their own.
If you are unsure whether an absence is protected, check with your state labor department or an employment lawyer before you rely on it.
What to do as a job seeker or employee
Before you accept an offer, read the leave section or ask HR how many sick days you get, how they are earned, whether they carry over and whether they are separate from vacation.
Learn your employer’s call-in rules, such as how early you must report an absence and to whom. Keep a short written record, like an email or text, each time you call in sick.

Some state and local laws limit when an employer can ask for a doctor’s note, often only after several days in a row. Your employee handbook and your state labor department website will show the rules that apply to you.
qa: Is sick leave required by law in the US?

Not under federal law for most private employers. Many states and some cities require employers to give paid sick leave, and the FMLA gives eligible employees unpaid, job-protected leave for serious health conditions. Check your state and city rules, since coverage differs from place to place.
Do I get paid for unused sick days when I quit?

Usually not. Most state sick leave laws do not require a payout of unused sick time at the end of a job. If your employer uses a combined PTO bank, some states treat it like vacation pay, which may have to be paid out. Your state labor department can confirm the rule.
Can my employer ask for a doctor’s note?

Often yes, but some state and local paid sick leave laws limit it, for example allowing a request only after you miss several days in a row. Where no such law applies, employers can usually set their own documentation rules in their policy.
Can I be fired for calling in sick?

It depends. If a law such as the FMLA or a state or local sick leave law covers the absence, your employer generally cannot punish you for using that leave. Without legal protection, an at-will employer may be able to discipline or fire you. Ask a lawyer or your state labor department about your situation.
What is the difference between sick leave and PTO?

Sick leave is time off meant for illness and medical care. PTO, or paid time off, is a single bank of days you can use for sickness, vacation or personal reasons. Some employers offer both, and some offer only PTO.

Direct hire.title: What Is a Direct Hire Job? Meaning vs Contract and Temp
sections: What direct hire means
A direct hire job is one where the company that needs the work puts you on its own staff from your first day. You are its employee, not a worker loaned out by a staffing agency.

The term is used most often by recruiters and staffing agencies. When an agency fills a direct hire role, it finds and screens candidates, but the client company makes the offer and employs the person it chooses. The industry also calls this permanent placement or direct placement.
Direct hire is the opposite of temporary or contract work through an agency. In those setups the agency stays your employer and bills the client company for your hours.
Direct hire vs contract-to-hire and temp
In a temp or contract role, the agency pays you and is usually your employer. The assignment can end at any time or at a set date, and benefits come from the agency, if it offers any.
In contract-to-hire, you start on the agency’s payroll for a trial period. If both sides are happy, the company then hires you directly. If not, the contract simply ends.

With direct hire, there is no trial period on someone else’s payroll. You are usually eligible for the company’s own benefits on its normal schedule, such as health insurance and a retirement plan, subject to any waiting period the company sets.
Who pays and who sends your paperwork

In most direct hire searches, the employer pays the agency a placement fee after you start. Some states allow licensed employment agencies to charge job seekers fees that the state regulates, so read any agreement before you sign and ask your state labor department if you are unsure.

Once hired, you are usually a W-2 employee on the company’s payroll. Some companies use a professional employer organization, or PEO, that runs payroll and benefits under shared employment. In that case your W-2 and onboarding forms may carry the PEO’s name, which is normal and not a sign of a problem.
What a job seeker should check

Make sure the offer letter names the company you will actually work for, along with the job title, pay, start date and benefits. If a PEO or payroll provider is involved, ask the company to confirm that arrangement in writing.

Ask the recruiter whether the role is direct hire, contract or contract-to-hire before you interview, because pay, benefits and job security differ. Ask whether you will owe any fee, and get the answer in writing.

Expect the full process to run through the company: its interviews, its background check and its offer. The recruiter may stay in touch during the early months, since many agencies only keep their fee if the new hire stays for an agreed period.
qa: What does direct hire mean on a job posting?

It means the company will employ you on its own payroll from your first day. Even if a recruiter or staffing agency found you, you will not work for the agency on a temporary or contract basis first. You are a regular employee of the company.
Is direct hire better than contract-to-hire?

It depends on your situation. Direct hire usually gives you the company’s benefits and more stability from the start. Contract-to-hire lets both sides try the fit first, but you may have fewer benefits and no promise of a permanent job. Compare pay, benefits and the chance of conversion before choosing.
Do I have to pay a recruiter for a direct hire job?

Usually not, because the employer typically pays the placement fee. However, some states, such as New York and California, let licensed employment agencies charge job seekers fees within limits the state sets. Ask about any fee before you sign anything, and check with your state labor department if something seems wrong.
Is a direct hire job permanent?

It is meant to be ongoing rather than tied to an end date, which is why it is also called permanent placement. In most US states, though, jobs are at-will, so either you or the employer can usually end the job at any time, unless a contract or law says otherwise.
What is direct hire authority in federal jobs?

It is a different use of the term. Direct hire authority lets US federal agencies fill certain jobs faster when there is a severe shortage of candidates or a critical hiring need. It allows them to skip some of the usual competitive steps, such as ranking candidates against each other.

Thank-you email.title: What Is a Thank-You Email After an Interview? What to Write and When
sections: What a thank-you email is

A thank-you email is a short message you send to each person who interviewed you, on the same day as the interview. It thanks them for their time, repeats that you want the job and reminds them of one or two reasons you fit.
It is not required, and leaving it out rarely costs anyone an offer on its own. But many interviewers notice it, and it gives you one more chance to make your case after the conversation is over.
It applies to phone screens, video calls and in-person interviews alike. If you met several people, each one should get a separate email.
Why it matters to the hiring process

Interviewers often meet several candidates in a few days and write their notes or score sheets soon after. A note that arrives the same day keeps your name and your strongest points fresh while they decide.
It also shows skills the employer may be judging anyway: clear writing, follow-through and attention to detail. A note full of typos or sent to the wrong name can hurt more than no note at all.
It can fix a small gap. If you forgot to mention a relevant project or gave a weak answer, one sentence in the email can add what was missing.
What to write in a thank-you email
Keep it to a short greeting, three to five sentences and a sign-off. Use a clear subject line, such as “Thank you for today’s interview” with the job title.
Thank the person by name, mention one specific thing you talked about, link it to what you would bring to the role and say you look forward to the next step.
For a panel, change the specific detail in each email so the notes are not copies of each other. Interviewers sometimes compare them.
Check names, titles and spelling before you send it. If you do not have someone’s email address, ask the recruiter or the person who scheduled the interview to pass on your thanks.
When to send it and what comes next
Send it the same day as the interview, ideally within a few hours while the details are fresh for both of you. Write it soon after you leave, then reread it once before sending.
After that, wait for the timeline the employer gave you. If that date passes with no word, a short, polite follow-up email asking about the status is reasonable.
qa: Should I send a thank-you email after every interview?
Yes, it is a good habit after every round, including a short phone screen. It takes a few minutes, it is expected by many interviewers and it gives you a last chance to repeat why you fit the role.
How long should a thank-you email be?

Short. A greeting, three to five sentences and a sign-off is enough. Thank the person, mention one specific point from the conversation, connect it to the job and say you look forward to hearing about next steps.
Should I send one thank-you email to the whole panel or separate ones?

Separate ones are better. Send each interviewer a personal email and change the specific detail you mention in each, so the notes do not read like copies. If you only have the recruiter’s address, ask them to pass on your thanks.
Is a handwritten thank-you note better than an email?

Email is the standard in most US hiring today because it arrives the same day, before decisions are made. A handwritten card can be a nice extra in some fields, but send the email first so it is not too slow to count.
Can a thank-you email change the hiring decision?
It rarely changes a clear decision, but it can help when candidates are close. It keeps you in mind, shows good follow-through and lets you add a point you missed in the interview.

Panel interview.title: What Is a Panel Interview? How It Works and How to Prepare
sections: What a panel interview is

A panel interview is a job interview where two or more people interview you at the same time. The panel often includes the hiring manager, a future teammate, someone from human resources and sometimes a person from another department you would work with.

Each panelist usually covers a different area. One may ask about your technical skills, another about teamwork, and another about pay, schedule or policies. Some panels take turns asking from a shared list of questions.
It is different from a group interview, where several candidates are interviewed together. In a panel interview you are the only candidate in the room or on the call.
Why employers use panel interviews
A panel lets several people meet you once instead of scheduling separate interviews. It saves time for both sides and lets the interviewers compare their impressions of the same answers.

Many panels use structured questions and a scoring sheet, so every candidate gets the same questions and is rated the same way. This can make the decision fairer and easier to explain. Government agencies, schools, universities and hospitals often hire this way.
Panels also show the employer how you handle several people, follow-up questions and a bit of pressure, which matters in jobs where you report to or work with many people.
How to prepare and answer
Ask the recruiter who will be on the panel and look up their roles. Think about what each person is likely to care about, and prepare examples that speak to each area.
At the start, learn each panelist’s name and role, and write the names down if that helps. Answer the person who asked the question, but turn to the others too, so everyone feels included.
Use specific examples with a clear situation, action and result. If one panelist asks a follow-up that seems to challenge you, stay calm and answer it directly.
Prepare at least one question for the panel, and if time allows, ask a question aimed at a panelist’s own area. At the end, thank the whole panel.
In person versus on video
Panel interviews can take place in a room or on a video call, and some of the advice differs. Clear examples, learning names and including every panelist matter in both formats.
In person, bring enough printed copies of your resume for each panelist plus one extra, greet each person, and shift your eye contact between them as you speak.

On video, you cannot look at each person, so look at the camera when you speak and glance at the screen to read reactions. Check your sound and connection beforehand, and wait a moment before answering, since people may talk over each other.
qa: How many people are usually on a panel interview?

Most panels have two to five interviewers, though it varies by employer and role. Public sector, academic and senior roles sometimes have larger panels. If you want to know, ask the recruiter or hiring contact before the interview who will attend and what their roles are.
Who should you look at in a panel interview?

Start your answer looking at the person who asked the question, then shift your attention to the other panelists as you go, and finish with the person who asked. On a video call, look at the camera while you speak rather than at any one face on the screen.
Is a panel interview a good sign?

It usually means you have moved past early screening, since several people are giving their time to meet you. It is not a promise of an offer, though. Some employers use panels for every candidate at a certain stage, so treat it as a normal step rather than a signal.
Should I send a thank-you note to each person on the panel?

It is a good idea when you have their contact details. Send a short, separate note to each panelist within a day, and mention something specific from their questions. If you only have the recruiter’s email, send one note and ask them to share your thanks with the panel.
What is the difference between a panel interview and a group interview?

In a panel interview, several interviewers meet one candidate. In a group interview, one or more interviewers meet several candidates at once, often to see how they interact. Employers sometimes use the terms loosely, so check the invitation or ask which format to expect.

Return offer.title: What Is a Return Offer? How Interns Get Full-Time Job Offers
sections: What a return offer is
A return offer is a job offer an employer makes to an intern near or after the end of the internship. It invites the intern to come back as a permanent, usually full-time, employee.

For students, the job normally starts after graduation, which can be several months or a full year after the offer. For graduates or career changers in an internship, the start date can be much sooner.

The offer usually comes as a formal letter with the job title, team or program, base salary, start date and any signing bonus or relocation help. It works like any other job offer: you can accept it, decline it or ask questions first.
How employers decide on return offers

Many employers treat a summer internship as a long interview. Managers and mentors watch the quality of your work, how you take feedback, how you work with the team and whether you would fit the full-time role.
Some programs end with a final presentation or project review, followed by a meeting where managers compare notes on each intern. Others leave the decision to the intern’s own manager.

Business needs matter too. Even strong interns may not get an offer if the company has a hiring freeze, cuts its graduate hiring or has no open headcount on the team. A missing offer does not always mean poor performance.
What to do during the internship
Early in the internship, ask your manager or recruiter how return offers are decided, who makes the call and when you will hear. Knowing the process helps you focus on what counts.
Ask for feedback at the midpoint, not only at the end, so you have time to fix problems. Finish your projects, document your work and meet people outside your own team.
Near the end, it is fine to tell your manager you would like to return and ask what you could do to strengthen your case.
What to do once you have an offer

Read the offer letter closely and note the deadline to respond. Deadlines vary a lot by employer and industry, and some are short. If you need more time, ask politely and give a reason, such as finishing other interviews.
You can try to negotiate salary, start date or signing bonus, but many large intern programs pay set rates to every new graduate hire, so room to move may be small.
Think hard before accepting. Backing out of an accepted offer later can damage your relationship with the employer, and some university career offices have rules against it.
qa: Is a return offer guaranteed after an internship?

No. Employers decide based on your performance and their hiring needs, and some interns do not get one even after good work. Some companies hire most of their interns and others hire only a few. Ask the recruiter early how many interns usually receive offers.
When do interns find out about return offers?

Many employers tell interns in the last week of the internship or within a few weeks after it ends. Others wait until early fall. Ask your recruiter or manager about the timeline so you can plan other job applications.
Can you negotiate a return offer?

You can ask, but results vary. Large internship programs often pay the same starting salary to every graduate hire, so salary may be fixed. You may have more luck asking for a later deadline, a different start date, a team preference or relocation help.
Is it bad to decline a return offer?

Declining is normal and acceptable if you do it politely and before the deadline. Thank the people you worked with and keep in touch. Declining after you have already accepted is much more harmful to the relationship than declining at the start.
What should I do if I don’t get a return offer?

Ask your manager for honest feedback and whether the reason was performance or budget. Then apply to other employers using the skills and projects from the internship. Recruiters, especially in finance, consulting and tech, often ask whether you got a return offer, so prepare a short, truthful answer.

Pay stub.title: What Is a Pay Stub? What It Shows and How to Read It
sections: What a pay stub is
A pay stub is the statement you get with each paycheck or direct deposit. It shows how much you earned in the pay period, what was taken out and how much was actually paid to you.

It may come on paper attached to a check or as a page in your employer’s payroll portal. In the UK and some other countries the same document is called a payslip, and UK employers must give one by law.
Pay stubs are for employees. Independent contractors usually get paid by invoice and receive a Form 1099 for tax purposes instead of a stub with each payment.
What a pay stub shows
Most stubs list your employer’s name, the pay period, the pay date, your hours and pay rate if you are paid by the hour, and your gross pay. Gross pay is what you earned before anything is taken out.

Next come deductions. Taxes usually include federal income tax, Social Security and Medicare, plus state or local income tax where your state or city has one. Other deductions can include health insurance premiums, retirement contributions, union dues or a wage garnishment ordered by a court or agency.
Net pay, often called take-home pay, is what remains after all deductions. Many stubs also show year-to-date (YTD) totals, which add up each figure from January 1 through the current pay date.
Whether employers must give you one
No federal law requires a private employer to hand out pay stubs. Federal law requires employers to keep payroll records, but the rules on giving workers a wage statement come from the states.

Most states require some kind of pay statement, and the required details differ. California and New York, for example, set out in law what a wage statement must include. A few states have no such requirement.

Many states allow electronic pay stubs, often on the condition that the employee agrees or can ask for a paper copy instead. Your state labor department can tell you the rules that apply where you work.
How to check and keep your pay stubs
Check each stub against what you expect: your hours, your rate, any overtime, and every deduction you signed up for. Mistakes are easier to fix soon after they happen than months later.

If something looks wrong, ask your payroll or HR team first and keep a written record of the request. If it is not fixed, contact your state labor department or the US Department of Labor’s Wage and Hour Division.
Keep your stubs, at least until you have compared them with your Form W-2. Lenders, landlords and some government offices often ask for recent stubs as proof of income.
qa: Are employers required to give pay stubs?

Not under federal law. Most US states require employers to give some form of pay statement, and each state sets what it must show and whether it can be electronic. A few states have no requirement. Your state labor department can confirm the rule where you work.
What does YTD mean on a pay stub?

YTD means year to date. It is the running total of each line, such as gross pay, taxes and deductions, from the first pay date of the calendar year up to the current stub. It helps you track earnings and check your Form W-2 at year end.
Why doesn’t my W-2 match the YTD gross pay on my last pay stub?

Box 1 of the W-2 shows taxable wages, not total gross pay. Some pre-tax deductions, such as traditional 401(k) contributions and certain health insurance premiums, are left out of Box 1, so it is often lower than YTD gross pay. If the gap still seems wrong, ask your payroll team.
How can I get a copy of an old pay stub?

Look in your employer’s payroll portal first, since many keep past stubs online. If you cannot find it, ask HR or payroll, including at a former employer. Some states require employers to provide copies of pay records on request.
Can I get a pay stub if I am paid in cash?

Being paid in cash does not change the rules. If your state requires a pay statement, the employer must give one whether you are paid by check, direct deposit or cash. A stub is also useful proof of income and of the taxes withheld.

Job board.title: What Is a Job Board? How Job Sites Work and How to Use Them
sections: What a job board is

A job board is a website that lists job openings from many employers in one place. You can search by job title, keyword, location, pay or work type, read the posting and then apply or follow a link to apply.

It differs from a company careers page, which lists only that one employer’s jobs. A job board gathers openings from hundreds or thousands of employers, so you can compare many options without visiting each company’s site.
Most job boards are free for job seekers. They usually earn money from employers, who pay to post jobs, to promote them higher in results or for each click or application they receive.
Types of job boards
General job boards cover every industry and level. Niche job boards focus on one field, such as nursing, tech, remote work, education or nonprofits, and often have fewer but more targeted listings.

Aggregators collect postings automatically from careers pages and other sites, then send you to the original source to apply. Some boards mix both: jobs posted directly by employers and jobs pulled in from elsewhere.
Government sites also act as job boards. USAJOBS lists federal government jobs, and most states run a free job bank through their workforce or labor agency, often linked to local career centers.
Why some listings are stale or not real

A posting can stay online after the job is filled, paused or canceled, especially when it was copied from another site and never rechecked. Some employers also keep evergreen postings open to collect resumes for future openings.

Scammers sometimes post fake jobs to collect personal data or money. Warning signs include requests to pay for training or equipment, offers made without an interview, vague company details and contact only through chat apps or personal email addresses.
Boards that show the source of each job and the date it was posted or last checked make it easier to judge whether an opening is likely still active.
How to use a job board well
Search with several versions of your job title and set up email alerts, so new postings reach you early. Openings often get the most attention in the first days after they appear.

Before applying, look for the employer’s name, the date and where the posting came from. A matching posting on the company’s own careers page is a good sign the job is real and active, though it is not proof that it is still open.

Never pay to apply, and do not share your Social Security number or bank details until you have verified the employer and received a real offer. You can report job scams to the Federal Trade Commission at ReportFraud.ftc.gov.
qa: What is the difference between a job board and a job aggregator?

A job board hosts postings, often placed there directly by employers who pay for them. A job aggregator collects postings automatically from careers pages and other sites, then sends you to the source to apply. Many sites today do a mix of both.
Are job boards free for job seekers?

Most are free to search and apply. Employers usually pay to post or promote jobs. Some sites sell optional paid extras to job seekers, such as resume reviews or profile boosts, but you should never have to pay simply to apply for a job.
Is it better to apply on the job board or the company website?

Either can work. Applying on the company’s own careers page often puts your application straight into its hiring system and lets you check the posting is real. If the board links to the employer’s site anyway, applying there avoids duplicate or lost applications.
How can I tell if a job board posting is fake?

Be careful if the posting has no clear company name, promises high pay for little work, asks you to pay for anything, or moves you to a chat app quickly. Look up the employer independently and check whether the job also appears on its official site.
What is a niche job board?

A niche job board lists jobs in one field, industry, location or type of work, such as healthcare, tech, remote jobs or nonprofits. It usually has fewer listings than a general board, but they are more closely matched to that area.

Internship.title: What Is an Internship? Pay, Timing and How to Get One
sections: What an internship is

An internship is a short, structured period of work at an employer, meant to give a student or recent graduate real experience in a field. The intern does actual tasks, learns from staff and usually has a set start and end date.
Most internships in the US run over the summer for about 10 to 12 weeks. Others take place during the school term, often part time, or last a semester or longer.

Internships exist in almost every field, from software and finance to journalism, government, nonprofits and health care. Some are run as formal programs with a group of interns, while others are a single role at a small company.
Paid and unpaid internships

Many internships are paid by the hour or with a fixed stipend. Paid interns are usually employees, so federal and state minimum wage rules apply, taxes are withheld and they get a W-2 form at year end.

At a for-profit company, an unpaid internship is legal under the federal Fair Labor Standards Act only if the intern, not the employer, is the primary beneficiary. The Department of Labor looks at factors such as training tied to education, academic credit and whether the intern replaces paid staff.

Some states have their own rules on unpaid internships, and rules for government agencies and nonprofits differ. If you are unsure whether an unpaid role is lawful, ask your state labor department or the federal Department of Labor’s Wage and Hour Division.
When and how to apply

Large employers often open summer internship applications in the late summer or fall of the year before, and some fill most spots by winter. Smaller employers and nonprofits often hire later, into the spring.

Use your school’s career center, career fairs, job boards and company careers pages. A one-page resume listing coursework, projects, campus jobs and activities is normal, since most applicants have little work experience.

International students on an F-1 visa need work authorization first. Curricular Practical Training (CPT) is authorized by the school’s designated school official, while Optional Practical Training (OPT) also requires applying to USCIS and receiving an approved Employment Authorization Document before starting work.
How to get the most from an internship
Ask early what a good result looks like for your project, and check in with your manager regularly. Keep notes on what you built, fixed or learned, so you can describe it on your resume later.
Meet people outside your own team and ask for short conversations about their work. These contacts can lead to references or job leads after the internship ends.
Many employers use internships to find future hires and may make a return offer for another internship or a full-time job. Ask near the end whether that is possible and what the timeline is.
qa: Are internships paid?

Many are, especially at larger companies and in fields such as tech, engineering and finance. Some are unpaid, more often at nonprofits, in government or in creative fields. At for-profit companies, unpaid internships are legal under federal law only when the intern is the primary beneficiary, and some states add their own rules.
What is the difference between an internship and a co-op?

A co-op, short for cooperative education, is usually run with a college and is often full time for a whole semester or longer, sometimes repeated with the same employer. An internship is usually shorter, often one summer, and may or may not be arranged through a school.
Can you do an internship if you are not a student?

Yes, some employers take recent graduates or people changing careers, and some programs, often called returnships, are for people coming back after a career break. Many internships, though, require you to be enrolled in school, so check the eligibility rules in the posting.
How long does an internship last?

Summer internships in the US usually last about 10 to 12 weeks. Term-time internships often run for a semester, part time, and some last six months or more. The posting or offer letter should give the exact dates.
Do internships turn into full-time jobs?

Sometimes. Many employers use internships to find people to hire and make return offers to interns who did well, but there is no guarantee. Even without an offer, an internship gives you experience, references and contacts for your job search.

Work from anywhere.title: What Is a Work From Anywhere Job? What “Anywhere” Really Means
sections: What work from anywhere means
A work from anywhere job is a remote job whose posting names no country, state or region. In theory, you can do the work from wherever you live, as long as you have a reliable internet connection.
It differs from a job that says only “remote.” Many remote postings are limited to one country, a list of states or a range of time zones. A work from anywhere posting sets no such limit in the text.
In practice, “anywhere” rarely means every country. Hiring rules, payroll, taxes, sanctions and time zones still shape who the company can actually hire and pay.
Why “anywhere” usually has limits

To pay an employee, a company generally needs a legal way to run payroll in the country where that person works. Many use an employer of record (EOR), a service that legally employs the worker on the company’s behalf, but it may not cover every country.

Some companies avoid this by hiring people abroad as independent contractors. Contractors are usually paid per invoice, get no employer benefits and handle their own taxes. The posting may not say which arrangement applies until later in the process.
Even inside the US, a remote job is sometimes open only in certain states, because each state where an employee works can bring its own payroll tax registration and employment law rules.
Time zones matter too. A team that meets daily may need you online during set hours, which can rule out people far away even when the posting says anywhere.
What to check before you apply or accept
Ask which countries or states the company can hire in, whether you would be an employee or a contractor, and how and in what currency you would be paid.
Ask about expected working hours, required overlap with a time zone, travel for team meetings and whether you can move to another country later.

Check whether you are allowed to work where you plan to live. Working while on a tourist visa is often not permitted, and some countries offer special visas for remote workers. The country’s immigration office is the place to confirm.
Taxes depend on where you live and work, your citizenship and how you are paid. For anything beyond the basics, ask an accountant who knows the countries involved.
qa: Does work from anywhere really mean anywhere in the world?

Rarely. The posting names no country, but the company can usually hire and pay only in places where it has a legal setup, an employer of record or a way to pay contractors. Sanctions and time zones also limit the list. Ask the recruiter which countries they can actually hire in.
What is the difference between remote and work from anywhere?

A remote job lets you work outside an office, but it is often limited to one country, certain states or a time zone. A work from anywhere job names no location at all in the posting, though practical limits may still apply once you ask.
Do I pay taxes when I work from anywhere?

Often, but it depends on where you live, your citizenship and how you are paid. Many countries tax people based on where they live and work. US citizens and green card holders must file a US return when their income meets the filing threshold, with worldwide income counted, wherever they live. Ask an accountant about your own situation.
Can I travel while working a work from anywhere job?

Sometimes, but check first. Some employers allow short trips, while others need you to stay in a country where they can pay you. Working in another country may also require a visa that permits work, and staying long enough can create tax obligations there.
Are work from anywhere jobs usually contractor roles?

Not always, but many are. Hiring someone as an employee in a new country takes a local entity or an employer of record, so some companies use contracts instead. Ask whether the role is employment or contracting, since it changes your benefits, taxes and job protections.

On-site.title: What Is an On-Site Job? On-Site vs Remote and Hybrid Work
sections: What on-site means in a job posting
An on-site job is one where you do your work at the employer’s office, store, plant or other workplace on your scheduled days. You are expected to be there in person rather than working from home.

Job boards and employers use on-site as one of three common work arrangements. The other two are remote, where you work from anywhere or from home, and hybrid, where you split your week between home and the workplace.

On-site does not always mean a company office. It can mean a hospital, a construction site, a warehouse, a school or a client’s premises, depending on the job. Some postings write it as onsite, in-office or in-person.
Why the work arrangement matters
Working on-site shapes your daily costs and time. You pay for the commute in gas, parking, transit fares or car wear, and you spend hours each week getting there and back.
It also affects where you can live. An on-site job ties you to a reasonable distance from the workplace, so a move or a long commute may be part of accepting the offer.

Many roles can only be done on-site, such as nursing, retail, manufacturing, lab work and skilled trades. For office jobs, some people prefer on-site work for face-to-face training, easier teamwork and a clear line between work and home.
What to check before you apply or accept
Read the posting for the exact location and schedule. Ask in the interview whether the role is fully on-site, whether that could change later, and whether any remote days are allowed.
Work out the real cost of the commute in time and money. Compare it with remote or hybrid offers, since a slightly higher salary can be eaten up by a long or expensive daily trip.

Ask about commuting help. Some employers offer free or paid parking, transit passes, shuttles or pre-tax transit and parking benefits, which let you pay these costs from pay before income tax up to a monthly limit set by the IRS.
qa: What does on-site mean in a job posting?

It means you are expected to work in person at the employer’s location, such as an office, store, warehouse or job site, rather than from home. The posting should name the city or address where you would report to work.
What is the difference between on-site, hybrid and remote?

On-site means you work at the employer’s location on all your scheduled days. Hybrid means you split your time between the workplace and home, often on set days. Remote means you work away from the workplace, usually from home, though some remote jobs still limit which states or countries you may live in.
Can an employer require me to work on-site?

In most US jobs, yes, unless your contract or a union agreement says otherwise. If you have a disability and the employer has 15 or more employees, you can ask for an accommodation under the ADA, but it can refuse remote work if in-person presence is an essential job function or would cause undue hardship. Some state and local laws go further.
Is commuting to an on-site job tax deductible?

Generally no for federal income tax. The IRS treats travel between home and your regular workplace as a personal expense. Some employers offer pre-tax transit and parking benefits up to a monthly limit set by the IRS. Ask an accountant about your own situation.
Do on-site jobs pay more than remote jobs?

There is no fixed rule. Pay depends on the role, the employer and the local job market. Some employers set pay by location, so an on-site job in a high-cost city may pay more than a remote version of the same role, while others pay the same either way.

Career ladder.title: What Is a Career Ladder? Levels, Pay Bands and Promotions Explained
sections: What a career ladder is

A career ladder is a company’s set of levels for one kind of work, such as software engineering, sales or nursing. Each level, or rung, describes what someone at that step is expected to do and how much responsibility they carry.

A typical ladder runs from entry level to senior and beyond. In engineering, for example, titles might go Engineer I, Engineer II, Senior Engineer, Staff Engineer and Principal Engineer. Other fields use labels such as associate, specialist, lead and director.
Many companies tie each level to a pay band, a salary range with a minimum and a maximum. Moving up a rung usually means moving into a higher band, not just getting a raise within the same one.
How career ladders work inside a company

Companies often write the ladder down in a leveling guide or competency matrix. It lists skills and behaviors for each level, such as scope of work, independence, influence on others and quality of results.

Promotion usually means showing you already work at the next level for a while. Many companies review promotions on a schedule, often once or twice a year, and a manager or committee decides using the written criteria.

Some companies run a dual ladder. One track is for individual contributors who stay hands-on, and the other is for people managers. The dual ladder lets strong specialists earn more without having to manage a team.
Ladders are not standard across employers. A Senior title at one company can match a mid-level role at another, which is why level matters more than the title alone.
What a job seeker should do
When you get an offer, ask which level it is for and where the salary sits in that level’s band. A salary near the top of a band can leave little room for raises until you are promoted.
Ask to see the leveling guide or a summary of what the next level requires. Also ask how often promotions happen and how long people usually spend at your level.
If you think the role is set too low for your experience, you can negotiate the level itself, not only the pay. A higher level often brings a higher band, more equity and a different scope.

Some US states and cities require employers to show pay ranges in job postings. Whether a posting must include one depends on the rules where the job is based and on the employer’s size, so a range may or may not be listed.
qa: What is an example of a career ladder?

A software engineering ladder might run Engineer I, Engineer II, Senior Engineer, Staff Engineer and Principal Engineer. Each step expects broader scope, more independence and more influence on others, and each usually has its own pay band.
What is the difference between a career ladder and a career path?

A career ladder is a company’s formal set of levels within one kind of work. A career path is the broader route a person takes over time, which can include moves across teams, fields or employers, not only steps up one ladder.
What is a dual career ladder?

It is a system with two tracks: one for individual contributors who keep doing hands-on work and one for people managers. Senior levels on both tracks can carry similar pay, so moving up does not require becoming a manager.
How do you move up a career ladder?

Learn the written expectations for the next level, then show over time that you already meet them. Ask your manager for regular feedback, keep a record of your results and find out when promotion reviews happen at your company.
What is a career lattice?

A career lattice is a model where growth can also go sideways, such as moving to another team or function, instead of only up one ladder. Some companies use it to keep employees who want new skills rather than a higher title.

Reskilling.title: What Is Reskilling? Meaning, Examples and How to Start
sections: What reskilling means
Reskilling means learning the skills for a different kind of work. The goal is usually a new role or a new career, not getting better at the job you already have.

A retail manager who learns bookkeeping to become an accounts assistant is reskilling. So is a warehouse worker who trains as an electrician’s apprentice, or a teacher who learns instructional design for corporate training jobs.
The word is also used by employers. A company may reskill staff whose jobs are changing or disappearing, training them for open roles elsewhere in the business instead of letting them go.
Reskilling vs upskilling
Upskilling means adding or deepening skills for the path you are already on, such as a nurse earning a specialty certification or an analyst learning a new data tool.
Reskilling means moving sideways into different work. The line between them is not always sharp, because many career changes reuse a large part of what you already know.
The difference matters when you plan. Upskilling often fits around your current job, while reskilling may take longer, cost more and require you to start at a more junior level in the new field.
Ways to reskill and how to pay for it

Common routes include community college certificates, apprenticeships, bootcamps, online courses, industry certifications and on-the-job training programs. Some fields, such as nursing, the skilled trades and commercial driving, also need a state license or a specific credential before you can work.

Public help exists. Under the federal Workforce Innovation and Opportunity Act, local American Job Centers can fund approved training for eligible people, including many laid-off workers. Rules and funding vary by state and local area.

Some employers offer tuition assistance, and federal tax law lets them pay part of an employee’s education costs tax-free up to a set limit. Federal student aid such as Pell Grants covers some programs at eligible schools, but not most short bootcamps.
How to plan a career change through reskilling

Start with a field that reuses what you already do well. Customer service skills carry into sales or customer success, and project coordination carries into operations, which shortens the time you need to train.
Check job postings in the new field before you pay for anything. Note which skills, tools and credentials come up again and again, and ask a few people who do the work what actually got them hired.

Build one piece of proof before you apply, such as a portfolio project, a certification or volunteer work. Then rewrite your resume around the new role, leading with transferable skills and the new training, not your old job titles.
qa: What is an example of reskilling?

A bank teller who takes a certificate in IT support and moves into a help desk job is reskilling. Other examples are a restaurant worker training as a medical assistant, or an administrative assistant learning payroll to work in HR.
What is the difference between reskilling and upskilling?

Reskilling trains you for a different kind of work, usually to change roles or careers. Upskilling builds new or deeper skills for the work you already do, so you can perform better or move up on the same path.
How long does reskilling take?

It depends on the field and how much of your experience carries over. Some changes need a few months of courses and a certification, while licensed fields or apprenticeships can take a year or several years. Check the training and licensing rules for the field in your state.
Can I get free training to change careers?

Often, yes. Your local American Job Center may fund approved training through the Workforce Innovation and Opportunity Act if you qualify, and some employers, unions and community colleges offer free or low-cost programs. Eligibility and funding differ by state and local area.
Is it worth reskilling later in your career?

It can be, especially when the new field reuses your experience, because you bring skills a younger career changer lacks. Weigh the cost, the time in training and any starting pay cut against the job openings and pay you can expect after you finish.

JobPosting markup.title: What Is JobPosting Markup? How Jobs Get Into Google Search
sections: What JobPosting markup is

JobPosting markup is structured data placed in the code of a single job page. It uses the JobPosting vocabulary from schema.org, a shared standard that search engines read. Visitors do not see it; it tells search engines the job’s title, employer, place, pay and dates in a fixed format.

Google uses it to show jobs in its job search experience, the expandable list of openings that appears when someone searches for jobs. People often call this Google for Jobs. Without the markup, a job page can still show as an ordinary search result, but not in that job list.

Google recommends writing the markup in JSON-LD, a short script inside the page’s HTML. Many applicant tracking systems, careers site tools and job boards add it automatically, so many employers never write it by hand.
Which fields Google needs

Google requires five fields: title, description, datePosted, hiringOrganization and jobLocation, which is the address where the person will work. If a required field is missing or invalid, Google may leave the job out of its job search.

For a fully remote job, set jobLocationType to TELECOMMUTE and use applicantLocationRequirements to list the countries, or states, where applicants may live. If the job also has an office people can use, include jobLocation as well.

Google recommends further fields, such as baseSalary, validThrough, employmentType, directApply and identifier. The baseSalary field takes a single amount or a range, a currency and a unit such as hour or year. These fields let Google show more details on the job listing.
Rules Google sets for job markup

Use the markup only on a page about one job, with the full description visible to readers. Do not add it to pages that list many jobs or to search results pages. The details in the markup must match what the page shows.

When a job closes, remove the page, remove the markup, or set validThrough to a date that has passed. Google suggests telling it about new and removed jobs through its Indexing API or an updated sitemap, so old jobs drop out sooner.
Markup that is misleading or breaks Google’s guidelines can lead to a manual action, where Google stops showing the site’s jobs in its job search until the problem is fixed.
What employers and job seekers should do

Employers should check whether their careers site or applicant tracking system already adds the markup. Test a live job page with Google’s Rich Results Test, and watch the job posting report in Google Search Console for errors and warnings.
Correct markup makes a job eligible, but it does not guarantee that Google will show it; Google decides what appears. Google’s job search is also not offered in every country.

Pay transparency is a separate matter. Several states and cities, such as Colorado, California, Washington and New York, require pay ranges in job ads, whatever the markup says. Employers unsure of the rules should ask the state labor department or a lawyer.
Job seekers who find openings in Google’s job list should check the date posted and, where possible, apply on the employer’s own site, since the same job often appears on several boards.
qa: What is Google for Jobs?

It is the common name for Google’s job search feature: a list of openings shown when someone searches for jobs, with filters and job details. Google builds the list from job pages that carry JobPosting markup on employer sites and job boards. It is free and there is no separate place to submit jobs.
How do I get my job posting on Google?

Publish each job on its own page with valid JobPosting markup, either on your careers site or through a job board or applicant tracking system that adds it. Make sure Google can crawl the page, then test it with the Rich Results Test. Google decides whether and when the job appears.
Is salary required in JobPosting markup?
