No. Google lists baseSalary as a recommended field, not a required one, though it lets Google show the pay on the listing. Separately, some states and cities require pay ranges in job ads under pay transparency laws, so check the rules where the job is based.
How do I test JobPosting structured data?

Paste the job page’s address or code into Google’s Rich Results Test, which shows whether the markup is valid and which fields are missing. After launch, the job posting report in Google Search Console lists errors and warnings across all of the site’s job pages.
What should I do with the markup when a job is filled?

Remove the job page, remove the markup from it, or set validThrough to a date in the past. Then tell Google, for example through its Indexing API or an updated sitemap, so the closed job stops appearing in its job search.

Furlough.title: What Is a Furlough? Pay, Benefits and How It Differs From a Layoff
sections: What a furlough is
A furlough is unpaid time off that an employer orders, usually to cut costs when money or work runs short. You stay an employee, but you do not work and are not paid for the furlough time.

A furlough can be full, where you stop working entirely for a set period, or partial, where your hours are cut, such as one unpaid day each week. Employers often set an expected return date, but they do not have to keep it.

The word once meant any leave of absence, such as military leave. In the UK it became widely known through the Coronavirus Job Retention Scheme, which ran from 2020 to 2021 and paid part of furloughed workers’ wages.
Furlough versus layoff
In a layoff, your job usually ends. In a furlough, the job continues on paper and the employer expects you to come back, though that is not guaranteed.

A furlough can turn into a layoff if business does not recover. Under the federal WARN Act, which covers employers with 100 or more employees, a layoff of more than six months, or hours cut by more than half in each month of a six-month period, can count as an employment loss that requires 60 days’ notice when enough workers are affected.
Some states have their own WARN laws with different rules. Ask your state labor department or a lawyer if you think notice rules were not followed.
Pay, benefits and unemployment during a furlough

Whether health insurance continues depends on your employer and the plan’s terms. Some employers keep coverage and may still take your share of premiums. If coverage ends because your hours are cut, you may be offered COBRA or a similar state continuation plan.

Under federal wage law, salaried exempt employees who do any work in a week generally must be paid their full salary for that week, with some exceptions. That is why many employers tell furloughed staff not to answer email or do any work at all.

Many states let furloughed workers claim unemployment benefits, including partial benefits when hours are reduced. Eligibility, amounts and rules about job searching vary by state, so check with your state unemployment agency as soon as the furlough starts.
Some employers let or require you to use paid time off during a furlough. Policies differ, and some state laws affect how paid time off can be used.
What to do if you are furloughed
Ask for the details in writing: the start date, the expected end date, whether it is full or partial, what happens to benefits and paid time off, and who to contact about returning.

Ask whether you may take other work during the furlough. Many employers allow it, but some policies or contracts limit outside jobs. If you claim unemployment, report any earnings as your state requires.
Keep your resume current and start looking quietly if the end date is vague. On a resume you can list the job as continuous, since you were still employed during the furlough.
qa: Do you get paid during a furlough?

No, a furlough is unpaid time off for the hours or days you are furloughed. In a partial furlough you are paid only for the hours you still work. Some employers let you use paid time off to cover part of the gap, and many states allow unemployment benefits.
Can you collect unemployment while furloughed?

In many states, yes. Furloughed workers and those with hours cut often qualify for full or partial unemployment benefits. Rules on eligibility, waiting weeks and job search requirements differ by state, so apply through your state unemployment agency and follow its instructions.
Is a furlough the same as being laid off?

No. A furlough keeps you employed while you take unpaid time off, with an expected return. A layoff usually ends the job. A furlough can become a layoff if the employer decides it cannot bring workers back.
Can I work another job while on furlough?

Often yes, but check your employer’s policy and any contract first, because some limit outside work or work for competitors. If you get unemployment benefits, you must report earnings from other work, and they may reduce your weekly benefit.
What happens to federal employees in a government shutdown?

Non-excepted employees of agencies that lack funding are furloughed and stop working. Excepted employees, whose work is needed for safety or other essential duties, must keep working without pay until funding returns. Employees of agencies that are still funded are not affected.

Employment contract.title: What Is an Employment Contract? What It Covers and What to Check
sections: What an employment contract is

An employment contract is a written agreement between you and an employer that sets the terms of your job. It usually covers pay, hours, duties, start date and benefits, and sometimes how much notice either side must give to end the job.

In the US, most workers do not get a formal contract. They get an offer letter that lists the job title, pay and start date and usually says the job is at-will, which means either side can end it at any time for any lawful reason.

Formal contracts are more common for executives, doctors, teachers, some sales roles and fixed-term jobs. Union members are covered by a collective bargaining agreement, a contract negotiated between the union and the employer.
Montana is the one state that limits at-will employment by law. After a probationary period, an employer there generally needs good cause to fire someone.
What a contract usually includes
Common terms are your job title and duties, pay and how it is calculated, bonus or commission rules, working hours, work location or remote work, benefits, paid time off and your start date.

Many contracts add clauses on confidentiality, ownership of work or inventions you create, non-solicitation of clients or staff, non-competes, and arbitration. Arbitration sends disputes to a private arbitrator instead of a court.

A fixed-term contract runs for a set period, such as one year, and may say what happens if either side ends it early. Some contracts say the job can end only for cause, meaning a defined reason such as serious misconduct.

A contract cannot take away rights the law gives you, such as minimum wage, overtime for nonexempt workers or protection from discrimination. A clause that tries to waive those rights is generally not enforceable.
Non-competes and other state rules
A non-compete clause says you will not work for a competitor or start a competing business for a time after you leave. Whether a court will enforce it depends heavily on state law.

California, Minnesota, North Dakota and Oklahoma ban most non-competes for employees. Many other states allow them only within limits, such as a minimum salary, a reasonable time and area, or advance notice to the worker, and these rules change often.
If a contract has a non-compete, non-solicitation or invention clause and you are unsure how it affects your next job, ask an employment lawyer in your state before you sign.
What to do before you sign
Read the whole document and compare it line by line with the offer you were given. Check that pay, title, start date, bonus, equity and remote work terms match what was promised.
If something promised in the interview is missing, ask in writing for it to be added. Spoken promises are hard to prove, and a signed document usually wins over what was said.
Look closely at clauses that cost you money if you leave, such as repaying a signing bonus, relocation money or training costs, and at any non-compete or arbitration clause.
Ask questions and propose changes before you sign, not after your first day. Keep a signed copy of everything, including later changes to your pay or role.
qa: Is an offer letter the same as an employment contract?

Not usually. An offer letter is a written record of key terms like pay and start date, but most US offer letters say the job is at-will and is not a promise of employment for any set period. How binding specific terms are depends on the wording and state law.
Can I be fired if I have an employment contract?

Yes, but the contract may limit how. A fixed-term or for-cause contract can restrict when the employer may end the job, and breaking those terms can lead to a claim for damages. If the contract says the job is at-will, you can be let go at any time for a lawful reason.
Do I have to sign an employment contract?

No one can force you to sign, but an employer can usually make signing a condition of the job and withdraw the offer if you refuse. You can ask questions and propose changes before signing, and many employers will discuss reasonable requests.
What happens if I break an employment contract?

It depends on the terms. Quitting an at-will job is not a breach. Leaving a fixed-term contract early can mean losing a bonus, repaying a signing bonus or relocation money, or, less often, a claim for damages. Courts do not force anyone to keep working. Ask an employment lawyer about your own situation.
Is the employee handbook part of my employment contract?

Usually not in the US. Most handbooks say plainly that they are not a contract and do not change at-will status, and employers can update them. Treat handbook policies as the current workplace rules, and rely on your signed agreement for the terms that matter most.

Bar raiser.title: What Is a Bar Raiser? The Interviewer Who Guards the Hiring Bar
sections: What a bar raiser is

A bar raiser is an interviewer who does not belong to the team that is hiring. Their job is to judge whether a candidate would raise the overall standard of the company, not just fill an open seat quickly.

The term started at Amazon, which runs a formal Bar Raiser program with trained interviewers. Some other companies have borrowed the term or the idea, and how much authority the role carries differs from one employer to the next.
The idea is simple. A hiring manager under pressure to fill a role may lower the bar, while someone with no stake in that team can focus on long-term fit and quality.
How the role works in an interview loop

The bar raiser is usually one interviewer in a series of interviews, often called a loop. They tend to ask broad behavioral questions about how you make decisions, handle conflict, take ownership and learn from mistakes.
After the interviews, the bar raiser often joins or leads the debrief, where interviewers compare notes. They may push the group to back up opinions with evidence from the interviews.

In the strictest versions, such as at Amazon, the bar raiser is widely described as able to block a hire even when the hiring manager wants to make an offer. At other companies the bar raiser’s view is one input among several.
How to prepare for a bar raiser interview
Prepare several detailed stories from your past work, using a structure such as situation, task, action and result. Pick stories that show judgment and impact, not only skill with one team’s tools.
Expect follow-up questions that dig into your own role. Say clearly what you did, what you decided, why, and what happened, including what you would do differently.

If the company publishes values or principles, read them and match your stories to them where that is honest. You may not be told which interviewer is the bar raiser, so treat every interview with the same care.
qa: What does a bar raiser do in an interview?

A bar raiser interviews you like the others but from outside the hiring team. They usually focus on behavior and judgment, such as how you solve problems, own results and work with others, and then help decide in the debrief whether you meet the company’s standard.
Can a bar raiser reject a candidate?

It depends on the company. At some large companies, Amazon being the best-known example, the bar raiser can block an offer. At other employers their opinion carries weight but the final decision rests with the hiring manager or the group.
How do I know which interviewer is the bar raiser?

Often you will not know. Some recruiters mention it, but many do not. The bar raiser may come from a different department and ask fewer questions about the job’s technical details, so prepare equally for every interview in the loop.
What questions does a bar raiser ask?

Mostly behavioral questions, such as “Tell me about a time you disagreed with your manager” or “Describe a decision you made with incomplete information.” Expect detailed follow-ups asking what you personally did, what data you used and what the outcome was.
Is the bar raiser interview harder than the others?

It can feel harder because the questions probe deeper and the interviewer has no reason to favor filling the role. It is not meant to trick you; clear, specific and honest examples are the best way to handle it.

Time to hire.title: What Is Time to Hire? How Long Hiring Takes and Why
sections: What time to hire means

As used here, time to hire is the number of days between a job being posted and a candidate accepting the offer. Employers track it to see how quickly they fill openings, and job seekers use it to judge how long a search may take.

Employers do not all measure it the same way. Some HR teams start the clock when a particular candidate applies or is first contacted, and some use the related term time to fill for a span that starts when the job is approved. When you compare numbers, check which start date was used.

In most definitions the clock stops when the offer is accepted, not on the first day of work. Steps after acceptance, such as a background check, new-hire paperwork and your notice period at your current job, affect your start date but usually fall outside this measure.
What makes hiring faster or slower

Several things affect the length of a hiring process. These include the number of interview rounds, how many people must agree on a candidate, how quickly interviews can be scheduled and whether the budget for the role has been signed off.

Many delays have nothing to do with you. A hiring manager may be on leave, the team may be reorganizing, an internal candidate may be under review, or reference checks before the offer may take days to complete.

Senior roles, government jobs and jobs that need a license or security clearance often take longer than entry-level or hourly roles. Some employers hiring for hourly work make offers within days of an application.
What job seekers should do
Ask about the timeline early, for example at the first interview: how many steps there are and when the team expects to decide. Write down what you are told so you know when a follow-up makes sense.

If a promised date passes, or you hear nothing for about a week after an interview, send a short, polite email to the recruiter asking about next steps. One follow-up, then another about a week later, is usually enough.

Keep applying and interviewing elsewhere until you have accepted an offer in writing. If another offer arrives while you wait, tell the slower employer honestly; it may speed up its decision or tell you where you stand.
qa: What is the difference between time to hire and time to fill?

Both measure how long hiring takes, but employers define them differently. Many HR teams use time to fill for the span from when a job is approved or posted until an offer is accepted, and time to hire for the span from when a specific candidate enters the process until that person accepts. Always check which definition a figure uses.
How do you calculate time to hire?

Count the days from the chosen start date, such as the posting date or the date the candidate applied, to the date the offer was accepted. To get an average, add up the days for each hire over a period and divide by the number of hires.
How long should I wait to hear back after an interview?

If the employer gave you a date, wait until it passes. If not, about a week of silence is a reasonable point to send a short, polite email asking about next steps. Keep it brief and keep looking at other jobs meanwhile.
Why is the hiring process taking so long?

Common reasons include several interview rounds, busy interviewers, approvals needed from several managers, budget questions, reference checks or other candidates still being interviewed. A slow process does not always mean you are out of the running, so a polite question to the recruiter is the best way to find out.
Does time to hire include the background check?

Usually not. Most employers stop the clock when the offer is accepted, and background checks often happen after a conditional offer is accepted. The check can still delay your start date, so ask how long it usually takes.

Upskilling.title: What Is Upskilling? Meaning, Examples and How to Start
sections: What upskilling means

Upskilling means learning new skills, or deepening the ones you have, so you can do your current kind of work better or take on more of it. You stay in the same field, but your skills keep up with how the work is changing.
Examples include a bookkeeper learning new accounting software, a nurse earning a specialty certification, a marketer learning data analysis or a warehouse worker getting certified on new equipment.
Upskilling is different from reskilling. Reskilling means learning skills for a different kind of job, such as a retail worker training to become a medical coder.
Why upskilling matters in a job search
Tools, software and methods change in most fields. Skills that were rare a few years ago can become basic requirements in job postings, and people who lack them may be passed over.

New skills can help you qualify for a promotion, move to a higher-paying role in your field or stay useful to your employer when work is reorganized. They also give you concrete things to add to your resume and talk about in interviews.
Employers upskill their staff because training current workers can be easier than finding new hires who already have the skills.
How to choose and fund the right skill
Read 10 to 20 current postings for the job you want next. Note the skills, tools and certifications they name often, and pick one you do not have yet.

Ask your employer first. Many offer in-house training, paid courses or tuition assistance, and some will let you learn during work hours. If your employer requires a course, it usually arranges and pays for it.

Other options include community college classes, online courses, professional associations and apprenticeships. Your local American Job Center may help pay for approved training through a federal program, though eligibility rules vary by state and situation.
Once you finish, show the skill. Add it to your resume, list any certificate, and describe a real task or project where you used it.
qa: What is the difference between upskilling and reskilling?

Upskilling builds new or better skills for the kind of work you already do, so you can advance in the same field. Reskilling teaches skills for a different job, often when someone changes careers or their old role is disappearing.
Will my employer pay for upskilling?

It depends on the training. Training the law requires for your job, such as OSHA-required safety training, must be provided at the employer’s expense, and time spent in training your employer requires is generally paid work time for hourly workers. Optional courses you choose for your own growth are up to the employer, though many offer tuition assistance or paid courses. Ask HR what is available.
What are examples of upskilling?

Common examples are learning a new software program used in your field, earning an industry certification, taking a course in data analysis or project management, learning new equipment or improving skills such as writing, public speaking or managing people.
How do I put upskilling on my resume?

List new certifications under a Certifications or Training section with the date. Add new tools to your Skills section, and in your job entries describe a result you achieved using the skill. A specific example is more convincing than a course title alone.
Is tuition assistance for upskilling taxable?

Federal law lets employers give workers educational assistance tax-free up to a yearly limit, under a qualifying plan. Amounts above the limit, or benefits outside such a plan, may be taxable. Ask your HR department or an accountant how it applies to you.

Work authorization.title: What Is Work Authorization? Meaning, Proof and Sponsorship
sections: What work authorization means

Work authorization is the legal permission to hold a job in a country. In the US, citizens and nationals have it automatically, lawful permanent residents (green card holders) have it as part of their status, and many other noncitizens have it through a visa or an Employment Authorization Document (EAD).

Some authorization is open, meaning you can work for almost any employer. Some is limited to one employer, one job or one field. An H-1B worker, for example, may work only for the employer that filed the petition, under the terms that were approved.

Every country sets its own rules. In the UK, for instance, employers must carry out a right to work check before someone starts. Being authorized to work in one country does not let you work in another.
How US employers check it

Federal law requires every US employer to verify the identity and work authorization of each new hire on Form I-9. You complete Section 1 no later than your first day of work, and the employer must review your documents within three business days of your start date.

You choose which acceptable documents to show: one from List A, such as a US passport or a green card, or one from List B for identity plus one from List C for work authorization, such as a driver’s license and an unrestricted Social Security card.

Some employers also use E-Verify, an online system that checks I-9 information against government records. Certain federal contractors must use it, some states require it for some or all employers, and other employers use it by choice.
Sponsorship and the questions on applications

Applications often ask two questions: whether you are legally authorized to work in the US, and whether you will now or in the future need visa sponsorship. Sponsorship means the employer files paperwork with the government, such as an H-1B petition, so you can work for it.

Employers may lawfully ask both questions, and many do not sponsor. If your current permission ends on a set date, as with OPT, the honest answer to the future sponsorship question may be yes, so read it carefully.

Answer truthfully. A false answer usually comes out at the I-9 stage and can cost you the offer. If you are unsure how your status applies, ask an immigration lawyer or, if you are a student, your school’s international student office.
Protections in the hiring process

US citizens, nationals and certain protected individuals, such as refugees, asylees and some permanent residents, are protected from citizenship status discrimination in hiring by employers with four or more employees, with exceptions such as jobs that require citizenship by law. Temporary visa holders are not covered by that rule.

During the I-9 process, employers may not demand specific documents, ask for more documents than the form requires, or reject documents that reasonably appear genuine because of a worker’s citizenship or national origin. Complaints can go to the Justice Department’s Immigrant and Employee Rights Section.
qa: Do green card holders need visa sponsorship?

No. A lawful permanent resident is authorized to work for any employer, and that status does not end when the date printed on the card passes. Employers may not reverify a permanent resident card. Conditional residents with two-year cards have a separate process for removing conditions and should check their own case.
What is an EAD card?

An Employment Authorization Document is a card issued by USCIS that proves certain noncitizens may work, such as some asylum applicants, people applying for a green card and students on OPT. What work it allows depends on the category; OPT work must relate to the field of study, for example. Some EADs are automatically extended past the printed date while a renewal is pending.
What does “authorized to work in the US” mean on a job application?

It asks whether you can legally work in the US right now without the employer filing anything for you. Citizens, green card holders and people with a valid EAD or work visa that covers this job can usually answer yes. If your permission is tied to a different employer, the answer may be no.
Can an employer ask about my work authorization before hiring me?

Yes. Employers may ask whether you are authorized to work in the US and whether you will need sponsorship. Form I-9 documents are reviewed after you accept an offer, not at the application stage, and the employer may not tell you which acceptable documents to show.
Is a Social Security number proof of work authorization?

Not by itself. An unrestricted Social Security card counts as a List C document on Form I-9, but it must be paired with an identity document from List B. Cards marked as valid for work only with DHS authorization, or not valid for employment, do not prove work authorization.

Interview scorecard.title: What Is an Interview Scorecard? How Interviewers Rate Candidates
sections: What an interview scorecard is
An interview scorecard is a form that every interviewer fills in for every candidate. It lists the same skills, traits or job requirements for everyone, with a rating scale and space for notes.

The points on the card are agreed before the first interview, usually by the hiring manager and recruiter. That way each candidate is judged against the needs of the job, not against whoever was interviewed just before.

Many companies keep scorecards inside their applicant tracking system, so interviewers submit ratings online right after the conversation. Smaller employers often use a simple printed sheet or a shared document.
What goes on a scorecard
Most scorecards list three to eight competencies taken from the job description. Examples are technical skill, problem solving, communication, teamwork or a required license or certification.
Each competency gets a rating on a fixed scale, such as 1 to 4 or 1 to 5. Good scorecards describe what each level looks like, so a 3 means the same thing to every interviewer.
There is usually a notes field for evidence, such as what the candidate said or did, and an overall recommendation like strong yes, yes, no or strong no.
When several people interview, each one often covers different competencies. This avoids five interviewers asking the same questions while nobody checks a key skill.
Why employers use scorecards

Scorecards are part of a structured interview, where candidates get the same or similar questions and are rated against the same standard. This makes comparisons fairer and helps reduce snap judgments based on first impressions or personal liking.
Asking interviewers to submit scores before the group discussion, often called the debrief, keeps one strong voice from swaying everyone else. It also forces each person to back a rating with notes.

Written ratings tied to job requirements also create a record of why a decision was made. Federal rules require many employers to keep hiring records for a set time, and clear, job-related notes are easier to explain if a decision is questioned.

For employers, the main steps are simple. Agree on the criteria and what a good answer looks like before interviews start, train interviewers to use the scale, and score right after each interview while memory is fresh.
What scorecards mean for job seekers
You will rarely see the scorecard, but you can guess most of it from the job posting. The required skills and duties listed there are usually the points you will be rated on.
Prepare one or two specific stories for each main requirement. Interviewers look for evidence they can write down, so describe the situation, what you did and the result.
It is fine to ask, “What does success look like in this role?” or “What skills matter most for this team?” The answer often tells you what is on the card.

If you believe a hiring decision was discriminatory, you can contact the EEOC or your state’s fair employment or civil rights agency. Filing deadlines apply, so act promptly and consider asking an employment lawyer.
qa: What is an interview scorecard used for?

It is used to rate every candidate for a job on the same criteria. Interviewers score skills and traits tied to the role and add notes, then the hiring team compares the scorecards to decide who moves forward or gets an offer.
What should be included in an interview scorecard?

A short list of competencies from the job description, a rating scale with a description of each level, space for evidence and notes, and an overall hiring recommendation. Some also list the questions each interviewer should ask.
Can I ask to see my interview scorecard?

You can ask, but in the US employers are generally not required to share interview notes with candidates, and most do not. In the UK and the EU, data protection law generally lets you request a copy of your personal data, which can include interview notes.
What rating scale is best for an interview scorecard?

There is no single standard. Many teams use 1 to 4 or 1 to 5. A four-point scale has no middle score, which pushes interviewers to lean one way. Whatever the scale, write down what each number means so interviewers apply it the same way.
Should interviewers share scores before the debrief?

Common practice is no. Each interviewer submits their scorecard independently first, then the team discusses. This keeps early or senior opinions from influencing others and makes sure every rating reflects what that interviewer actually saw.

Moonlighting.title: What Is Moonlighting? Rules for Working a Second Job
sections: What moonlighting means
Moonlighting means doing a second paid job alongside your main one. The name comes from the idea of working at night, after the day job, but a moonlighting job can happen at any time.
It can be a part-time job with another employer, freelance or contract work, gig work such as delivery or rideshare driving, or running a small business of your own.
People moonlight to earn extra money, build new skills, test a career change or grow a business before leaving their main job.
Rules and limits that can apply

Many employers have a written policy on outside work. It may ban jobs with competitors, require you to tell your manager or get approval, or bar using company time, equipment or information for the second job.

Even without a written policy, US employees owe their employer a duty of loyalty while they work there. In general, that means not competing with the employer and not using its confidential information or trade secrets for another business.

Most US jobs are at-will, so in most states an employer can fire someone for moonlighting even without a written policy or a conflict of interest. A few states, such as Colorado, limit firing for lawful off-duty activity, with exceptions such as conflicts of interest. A contract or union agreement can also change the rules.

Some workers face extra limits. Many visa holders, such as H-1B or F-1 workers, cannot take extra work without authorization. Government employees, medical residents and some licensed or regulated jobs also have their own rules on outside work.
Pay, hours and taxes with two jobs
Under federal law, hours worked for two separate, unrelated employers are usually not added together for overtime. Each employer counts only the hours you work for it.
Each employer withholds tax as if its job were your only one, so too little may be withheld. The multiple jobs step on Form W-4 helps fix this.
If the second job is freelance or self-employed work, no one withholds tax for you. You may owe self-employment tax and need to make quarterly estimated payments. Ask an accountant if you are unsure.
What to do before you start a second job
Read your offer letter, contract, employee handbook and any confidentiality or non-compete agreement for rules on outside work and conflicts of interest.
If a policy requires it, tell your manager or HR in writing and keep a copy of any approval. Keep the second job off company time, laptops, phones and email.
Plan your hours so the second job does not hurt your performance at the first. If you are unsure whether a job is allowed, ask HR, a lawyer or your state labor department.
qa: Is moonlighting illegal?

For most US citizens and permanent residents, holding a second job is not against the law. It can still break your employer’s policy or contract and cost you your job. Many visa holders, such as H-1B or F-1 workers, need authorization before taking extra work, and some government and regulated jobs have their own limits.
Can my employer fire me for moonlighting?

In most states, yes. Most US jobs are at-will, so an employer can generally fire you for having a second job even without a written policy or a conflict of interest. A few states protect some lawful off-duty activity, and a contract or union agreement may give more protection. Ask your state labor department or a lawyer about your case.
Do I have to tell my employer about a second job?

No general US law requires it, but your contract or company policy may. Some employers ask you to disclose outside work or get approval first, and many government jobs require approval for certain outside activities. Check your handbook and agreements before you start.
Does a second job affect my taxes?

Your total income is taxed together, but each employer withholds as if it were your only one, so you may owe tax at filing time. Use the multiple jobs step on Form W-4. Freelance income usually means self-employment tax and quarterly estimated payments.
What is the difference between moonlighting and a side hustle?

Moonlighting covers any second paid job held alongside a main job, including a part-time job for another employer. A side hustle usually means work you run yourself, such as freelancing, gig work or a small business. Many side hustles are a form of moonlighting.

Performance review.title: What Is a Performance Review? How It Works and How to Prepare
sections: What a performance review is
A performance review is a formal look at how well you did your job over a set period. Your manager compares your work with your goals and duties, gives feedback and usually records a rating.
Many employers hold reviews once a year, often with a shorter check-in at mid-year. Some hold them every quarter or replace them with regular informal feedback.

It is also called a performance appraisal, performance evaluation or annual review. In the US, private employers are not required by law to hold reviews, so the format depends on each company’s own policy.
How a performance review usually works
Many companies start with a self-review, where you describe your results, strengths and areas to improve. Some also ask coworkers or people you manage for input, known as 360-degree feedback.

Your manager then writes the review and gives a rating, often on a scale such as “does not meet,” “meets” or “exceeds expectations.” At larger companies, managers may meet in calibration sessions to compare ratings across teams before they are final.
The rating often affects your raise, bonus and chances of promotion. A low rating can lead to a performance improvement plan (PIP), a written plan with goals and a deadline to improve.
How to prepare and what to do in the meeting
Keep a running list of your results through the year, with numbers where you can, such as sales closed, time saved or projects delivered. Memory fades, and specific evidence is hard to argue with.
Reread your goals and job description before the review. Write your self-review honestly, link your results to those goals, and name one or two areas where you want to grow.
In the meeting, listen first and ask for examples of any criticism. If you want a raise or promotion, say so clearly and ask what you would need to show to get it.
Afterward, ask for a copy of the written review and agree on goals for the next period, so you know how you will be judged next time.
If you disagree with your review
Stay calm and ask for specific examples behind the rating. Then reply in writing with facts, dates and results, and ask whether your response can be attached to the review.
Many companies have an appeal or HR review process for disputed ratings. Check your employee handbook for the steps and any deadline.

If you believe a review was unfair because of race, sex, age, disability or another protected trait, or as retaliation for a complaint, you can contact the EEOC or your state’s fair employment or civil rights agency. Strict filing deadlines apply, often 180 or 300 days, so consider speaking with an employment lawyer early.
qa: What should I say in a performance review?

Talk about your main results with numbers, how they helped your team or company, and what you learned. Name one or two areas you want to improve and the support you need. If you want a raise or promotion, ask directly and ask what you must achieve to earn it.
Do I have to sign my performance review?

Many employers ask you to sign to confirm you received and discussed the review, not that you agree with it. Read the wording first. If you disagree, you can usually sign and add a written comment or rebuttal, and ask HR how your disagreement will be recorded.
Are performance reviews required by law?

No. US law does not require private employers to hold performance reviews, so whether they happen and how they work depends on company policy or a union contract. Federal and some state and local government jobs have their own rules for employee appraisals.
Can I get a copy of my performance review?

Most employers will give you one if you ask. Some states also give employees a legal right to see or copy their personnel file, which often includes reviews, while others do not. Your state labor department can tell you the rule where you work.
What is a self-evaluation in a performance review?

A self-evaluation is a form you fill in before the review, rating and describing your own work against your goals. Your manager reads it before writing the review, so it is your chance to list results they may have missed. Be specific and honest rather than modest or inflated.

Commission.title: What Is Commission? How Sales Commission Pay Works
sections: What commission means
Commission is pay that depends on results, usually a percentage of each sale or deal you close. It is most common in sales, real estate, insurance, recruiting, retail and car dealerships.

In most sales jobs, commission comes on top of a base salary or hourly wage. A smaller number of jobs pay commission only, with little or no fixed pay, so always check which kind of job you are looking at.
Employers often quote OTE, or on-target earnings. That is the base pay plus the commission you would earn if you hit your full sales target, not a guaranteed amount.
How commission plans work
A commission plan sets the rate, what it is paid on and when it is paid. The rate may be a share of revenue, a share of profit, or a flat amount per sale.
Many plans use a quota, a sales target for a month, quarter or year. Some pay more per sale after you pass the quota, called accelerators or tiers, and some pay nothing until you reach a set level.
Some plans have a cap, a ceiling on how much commission you can earn in a period. Others include clawbacks, where commission is taken back if a customer cancels, returns the product or does not pay.
A draw is an advance paid against future commission. A recoverable draw must be paid back from later commission, while a non-recoverable draw does not have to be repaid.
Your rights and taxes in the US

Under the federal Fair Labor Standards Act, most employees paid mainly by commission must still earn at least the minimum wage for their hours. Outside sales employees, who mostly sell away from the employer’s place of business, are exempt from this rule.
Independent contractors paid by commission are not covered by minimum wage law. Some states, such as California, require commission agreements for employees to be in writing.
Commission paid to employees is taxable wages. Employers withhold federal income tax on it, often under the IRS rules for supplemental wages, along with Social Security and Medicare taxes.
Whether you get commission on deals that close after you leave depends on your plan and your state’s law. If pay is withheld, contact your state labor department or an employment lawyer.
What to ask before you accept
Ask for the written commission plan and read it before you sign. Check the rate, the quota, any cap, clawbacks and exactly when a commission counts as earned.
Ask what share of current salespeople hit their quota and what they actually earned last year. A high OTE means little if few people reach it.
Find out how often commission is paid, monthly or quarterly, and whether the plan can change during the year. Plans often allow the employer to change terms with notice.
qa: What does 10% commission mean?

It means you earn 10 percent of the amount the plan counts for each sale. If the plan pays on revenue and you sell a $5,000 contract, you earn $500 in commission. Check whether the percentage applies to revenue, profit or only the amount above a quota.
Is a commission-only job legal?

Yes, but rules apply. In the US, most employees paid only by commission must still receive at least the minimum wage for hours worked, unless an exemption such as outside sales applies. Independent contractors are not covered by minimum wage law, so check whether you would be an employee or a contractor.
Is commission taxed more than salary?

No. Commission is taxed as ordinary income, like salary. It can look heavier because employers may withhold federal tax on it using the IRS rules for supplemental wages. Your actual tax is settled when you file your yearly return, so you may get some back or owe more.
Do I get my commission if I quit?

It depends on your commission plan and your state’s law. Many plans pay commission that was fully earned before you left, but define earned in different ways, such as when the customer pays. If you think earned commission was withheld, ask your state labor department or an employment lawyer.
What is the difference between commission and a bonus?

Commission is usually tied directly to each sale you make and follows a set formula. A bonus is often a separate payment based on wider goals, such as company or team results, and may be discretionary, meaning the employer decides whether to pay it.

Fixed-term contract.title: What Is a Fixed-Term Contract? How It Works, Ends and Renews
sections: What a fixed-term contract means
A fixed-term contract is a job agreement that runs for a set period, such as six months, one year or the length of a project. The end date, or the event that ends it, is written into the contract.
You are usually an employee of the company during the term, paid through payroll with taxes withheld. That is different from an independent contractor, who runs their own business and sends invoices.

Common uses include covering parental leave, seasonal peaks, grant-funded research, school and university posts, sports coaching and executive roles. The label “contract role” on a job board can mean either a fixed-term employee or a contractor, so check which one the employer means.
How fixed-term contracts work in the US

Most US jobs are at-will, meaning either side can end the job at any time for any lawful reason. A written fixed-term contract can change that, because both sides have promised to continue until the end date unless the contract allows an earlier exit.

Many fixed-term contracts include an early termination clause. It may let either side end the contract with a set amount of notice, or only for cause, such as serious misconduct. If one side ends it early without a contractual reason, that can be a breach of contract.

What happens at the end date depends on the contract and state law. Some contracts renew automatically, some end unless both sides sign a new one, and in some states, such as California, continuing to work after the end date without a new agreement can be presumed to renew it on the same terms.
How fixed-term contracts work in the UK
In the UK, fixed-term employees have a legal right not to be treated less favorably than comparable permanent staff on pay and conditions, unless the employer can objectively justify the difference.

Under UK rules, if an employee has worked on successive fixed-term contracts for four years or more, the latest contract is usually treated as permanent unless the employer can justify keeping it fixed-term.
Not renewing a fixed-term contract counts as a dismissal under UK law. An employee with two years of service can have unfair dismissal rights and may be owed redundancy pay.
What to check before you sign

Read the start date, end date and whether the end is tied to a project or a person returning from leave. Ask whether the role is likely to be extended or turned into a permanent job, and how that decision is made.

Check the early termination clause, the notice each side must give and whether the notice period still applies near the end of the term. Confirm which benefits you get, such as health insurance, paid time off and retirement plan access.

If the contract is long, high-paying or limits what you can do afterward, ask an employment lawyer to review it. For questions about state rules on renewal or final pay, your state labor department can help.
qa: Is a fixed-term contract the same as being a contractor?

No. A fixed-term worker is usually an employee for a set period, paid through payroll with taxes withheld and covered by employment law. An independent contractor runs their own business, invoices the client and pays their own self-employment taxes. Some job postings use “contract” for both, so ask which one applies.
Can I quit a fixed-term contract early?

Check the contract first. Many include a clause letting you leave with a set amount of notice. Leaving early without a contractual right can be a breach of contract, which may hurt references or lead to a claim. In most US states, wages you have already earned must still be paid in full when you leave.
Can an employer end a fixed-term contract early?

Only as the contract allows, usually with notice or for cause such as serious misconduct. If an employer ends it early without a contractual reason, it may owe damages, sometimes the pay for the rest of the term, depending on the contract and state law. An employment lawyer can say what applies in a specific case.
Can I get unemployment when a fixed-term contract ends?

Often yes, because the job ending on schedule is usually not treated as a voluntary quit, but each state decides eligibility. A key exception: teachers and school staff with “reasonable assurance” of working again next term are generally barred from benefits between academic terms. Ask your state unemployment office.
Does a fixed-term contract renew automatically?

It depends on the contract and the state. Some contracts say they renew unless one side gives notice, and others simply end on the date. In some states, such as California, working on past the end date without a new agreement can be presumed to renew it on the same terms.

Minimum wage.title: What Is Minimum Wage? How It Works in the US and Who It Covers
sections: What minimum wage means

Minimum wage is the lowest hourly pay an employer may legally pay an employee for work. It is a floor set by law, not a suggested rate, and it applies to most jobs whether you are paid by the hour, by salary or by the piece.
In the US, the federal minimum wage comes from the Fair Labor Standards Act (FLSA). It has been $7.25 an hour since July 2009, and only Congress can change it.
Other countries set their own rates. In the UK, for example, the National Living Wage and National Minimum Wage rates depend on the worker’s age.
How federal, state and city rates fit together
Many states set a minimum wage above the federal one, and some cities and counties set a higher rate still. When more than one rate applies to your job, the employer must pay the highest.

Many states and cities raise their rate every year, often on January 1 and often tied to inflation. A few states have no minimum wage law or one below the federal rate; there, the federal rate applies to jobs the FLSA covers.
Because rates change often, check the current figure for the place where you actually work on your state labor department’s website or the US Department of Labor’s site.
Exceptions and special rules

Tipped workers can be paid a lower cash wage under federal law if tips bring them up to the full minimum; if not, the employer must make up the difference. Some states, such as California and Washington, do not allow this tip credit at all.
Federal law allows a youth minimum wage for workers under 20 during their first 90 calendar days with an employer. Many states do not allow a youth rate, so this exception does not apply everywhere.

Some salaried employees are exempt from minimum wage and overtime. Most exemptions require a salary at or above a federal level, and some states set a higher one, but some exempt jobs, such as outside sales, teachers, and licensed doctors and lawyers, have no salary test.

True independent contractors are generally not covered by the FLSA. Workers wrongly labeled as contractors are covered, and some places, such as New York City and Seattle, set minimum pay for certain app-based delivery or rideshare workers.
What to do as a job seeker
If a posting’s pay is close to the minimum, look up the rate for the city and state where the job is. If the offer is below the highest rate that applies, ask the employer about it before you accept.
Keep your own record of hours worked and pay received. Unpaid training, required meetings, or deductions for uniforms or tools can push your real hourly pay below the minimum.

If you think you were underpaid, contact your state labor department or the US Department of Labor’s Wage and Hour Division. Retaliating against you for complaining is illegal, and a lawyer can advise on your specific case.
qa: What is the federal minimum wage right now?

The federal minimum wage is $7.25 an hour and has not changed since July 2009. Many states and cities set higher rates, and when several apply, your employer must pay the highest one for the place where you work.
Does minimum wage apply to salaried employees?

Yes, unless the job is exempt. A non-exempt salaried employee’s pay for each workweek, divided by the hours worked, must reach the minimum wage. Most exempt jobs must also pay at least a salary level set by federal law, or a higher one in some states.
Can a tipped worker be paid less than minimum wage?

Under federal law, the employer can pay a lower cash wage if tips bring total pay up to the full minimum, and must make up any shortfall. Some states, such as California and Washington, require the full state minimum wage before tips.
Which minimum wage applies if I work remotely?

Generally the rules of the place where you physically do the work apply, not where the employer is based. Rules can be complicated across state lines, so check with your state labor department if you are unsure.
What can I do if my employer pays less than minimum wage?

Write down your hours and pay, then file a complaint with your state labor department or the US Department of Labor’s Wage and Hour Division. You may be owed back wages, and time limits apply, so act promptly or speak with an employment lawyer.

Pre-employment assessment.title: What Is a Pre-Employment Assessment? Types, Rules and How to Prepare
sections: What a pre-employment assessment is
A pre-employment assessment is a test an employer asks candidates to take during hiring. It can come right after you apply, between interview rounds or near the end, before an offer.
The goal is to check something a resume cannot show well, such as whether you can write clean code, handle a spreadsheet, type fast enough or deal with a tricky customer.
Most assessments are taken online through a link sent by email, often run by an outside testing platform. Some are done in person or on a video call with an interviewer watching.
Common types of assessments
Skills tests check job knowledge, such as accounting rules, a programming language, Excel formulas or grammar. Typing and data entry tests measure speed and accuracy.
Cognitive or aptitude tests ask timed questions on logic, numbers and reading. Situational judgment tests describe work scenarios and ask which response you would choose.

Personality questionnaires ask how much you agree with statements about how you work. Work samples or take-home tasks ask you to do a small piece of real-looking work, such as a short writing piece, a sales pitch or a coding exercise.
How employers use results and what rules apply
Employers usually combine the score with your resume and interviews. Some use a cutoff score to decide who moves forward, while others treat the result as one input among many.

Under federal law, an employer cannot use a test to discriminate against people because of race, color, religion, sex, national origin, disability or, for workers 40 and older, age. A test that screens out a disproportionate share of a protected group can be challenged, and the employer may need to show it relates to the job.

Under the Americans with Disabilities Act, an employer cannot require a medical exam before a conditional job offer, and it must provide reasonable accommodations for tests when asked. Most private employers also cannot use lie detector tests for hiring. State laws may add more rules, so ask your state labor department or a lawyer about a specific concern.
How to prepare and take one
Ask the recruiter what the assessment covers, how long it takes, whether it is timed and when it is due. Many online tests cannot be paused or retaken once started.
Set aside a quiet block of time, use a reliable computer and internet connection, and close other tabs. Read the instructions fully before you start the timer.

For skills tests, review the tools named in the posting and try free practice questions of the same type. For personality questionnaires, answer honestly and consistently rather than guessing what the employer wants.
If you have a disability, ask for an accommodation, such as extra time or a format that works with a screen reader, before you begin the test.
qa: Can you fail a pre-employment assessment?

Yes, if the employer uses a cutoff score and yours falls below it, you may not move to the next stage. Many employers, though, look at the score alongside interviews and experience. Personality questionnaires usually have no right or wrong answers, but some employers compare results with a profile they want for the role.
How long does a pre-employment assessment take?

Short typing or skills tests often take 10 to 30 minutes, and cognitive or personality tests often take under an hour. Take-home work samples can take several hours. Ask the recruiter for the expected time before you start, since the length varies by employer and role.
Are personality tests legal in hiring?

In general, yes, US employers can use personality tests. However, a test designed to diagnose a mental health condition may count as a medical exam under the Americans with Disabilities Act, which cannot be required before a conditional job offer. Some states add their own limits, so check with your state labor department if unsure.
Can I ask for an accommodation on a pre-employment test?

Yes. If you have a disability, you can ask for a reasonable accommodation, such as extra time, a quiet room or a screen reader-friendly format. Ask the recruiter or HR before taking the test. You do not usually need to share your full medical history, only enough to explain the need.
Should I do a long unpaid take-home assignment?

It is your choice. A short task is common, but if the work looks like something the employer could use for real, or takes many hours, ask how it will be used, whether it is paid, and whether a shorter version is possible. Your answer may also show you how the employer values your time.
